cobo.original: Hay en estas sierras un árbol llamado de los indios quina-quina, de cuya corteza se hace el polvo que tanto renombre ha ganado en Europa para las tercianas y cuartanas.

CAPITULO LXXXI
De la quina-quina

Llaman en el Perú a un árbol grande y hermoso como un membrillo o un olivo; la hoja, del tamaño y talle que la del limón ceutí; el tronco es algo colorado, resinoso y aromático. Es árbol caliente en el segundo grado, estíptico y seco y de suave olor. Echa unas pepitas por semilla del tamaño de almendras, de color amarillo y de sustancia oleaginosa, que con fraganc
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXI
On the Quina-Quina

In Peru they give this name to a large and handsome tree resembling a quince or an olive; its leaf is the size and shape of the Ceuti [Moroccan] lemon leaf; the trunk is somewhat reddish, resinous, and aromatic. The tree is [humorally] hot in the second degree, astringent [estíptico], dry, and of a pleasant smell. It bears small seeds [pepitas] the size of almonds, yellow in color and of an oily substance, which smell agreeably fragrant; these too are hot and astringent in the second degree, and dry beyond the first. When the trunk and branches are scored [sajando], they exude a fragrant resin that congeals so thoroughly it can be ground to powder, at which point it becomes a pale black color; this resin is hot and drier than the seeds. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCVII
Del árbol de calenturas

En los términos de la ciudad de Loja, diócesis de Quito, nace cierta casta de árboles grandes, que tienen la corteza como de canela, un poco más gruesa, y muy amarga; la cual, molida en polvos, se da a los que tienen calenturas y con sólo este remedio se quitan. Háuse de tomar estos polvos en cantidad del peso de dos reales en vino o en cualquiera otro licor
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCVII
Of the Fever Tree

In the territory of the city of Loja, diocese of Quito, there grows a certain kind of large tree whose bark resembles cinnamon bark, somewhat thicker, and very bitter. This bark, ground into powder, is given to those suffering from fevers, and by this remedy alone the fevers are cured. The powder should be taken in a quantity equivalent to the weight of two reales [a small silver coin unit, roughly 6–7 grams], in wine or in any other liquid, shortly before the onset of the chills. These powders are now so well known and esteemed not only throughout the Indies but in Europe as well, that they are urgently requested and sent for even in Rome.

CAPITULO V
De la quínua

La quínua es una planta muy parecida a los bledos; crece dos tercias en alto poco más o menos; su hoja es como la de los bledos, salvo que, junto al pezón, es más ancha y no tan puntiaguda; produce la semilla en el remate del tallo, en unos racimillos como los de los bledos; la cual es del tamaño de granos de mostaza, tanto cuanto mayor, no redonda perfectamente, sino algo
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER V
On Quinoa

Quinoa is a plant very similar to [bledos / pigweed]; it grows roughly two-thirds of a vara [approximately 55 cm] in height, more or less. Its leaf resembles that of pigweed, except that near the stem it is broader and not so pointed. It produces its seed at the tip of the stalk, in small clusters like those of pigweed; the seed is about the size of mustard grains, or somewhat larger, not perfectly round but slightly flattened. This seed is the most cold-tolerant of all those grown in these Indies, whether native to this land or brought from Spain; for it thrives in lands so cold that most crops freeze there, even barley. There are two varieties of quinoa, just as there are of pigweed: one is white, and the other red.

CAPITULO LXII
De la guaki

Llaman guahi los indios peruanos a una raíz muy conocida y estimada dellos; es muy amarga y de profundo olor no enfadoso; su temperamento es caliente y seco. Es tan parecida esta yerba a la que Dioscórides llama aristoquia luenga, que no parece distinguirse della. Usan los indios de su raíz para muchas enfermedades; con ella, mascada, se refriegan cualquiera parte del cu
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXII
On the Guaki

The Peruvian Indians call by the name guahi a root that is very well known and esteemed among them. It is very bitter and has a deep but not unpleasant smell; its temperament [complexion] is hot and dry. This herb so closely resembles what Dioscorides calls aristolochia longa [long birthwort] that it seems indistinguishable from it. The Indians use its root for many ailments; when chewed, they rub it on any painful part of the body. Its decoction [cocimiento] dispels all flatulence [ventosidad], cleanses the bowels, and warms cold parts of the body; drunk regularly, it cures jaundice [ictericia]. CAPITULO LXXXIX

De la acana

La acana crece un codo de alto; en las ramas y hojas es muy parecida a la alfalfa; tiene flor amarilla del talle de la de la manzanilla; nace entre peñas y es yerba pectoral, más amarga al gusto que la acíbar; es caliente y seca en el segundo grado. Comen los indios con ella la coca. Su cocimiento con un poco de alumbre es bueno para las llagas de la boca; y tomado ca
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIX

On the Acana

The acana grows to a cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height; in its branches and leaves it closely resembles alfalfa; it bears a yellow flower of the shape of that of camomile; it grows among rocks and is a pectoral herb [i.e., beneficial to the chest and lungs], more bitter to the taste than aloes [acíbar]; it is hot and dry in the second degree [following Galenic humoral classification]. The Indians eat coca with it. A decoction of it with a little alum is good for sores of the mouth; and taken warm on an empty stomach with sugar candy [alfeñique], it is beneficial against cough and asthma, and softens and cleanses the chest and stomach. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXIX
De la coca

En este reino del Perú no hay cosa más conocida que la coca, cuyo trato es de los gruesos y de mayor ganancia que hay en las Indias y con que no pocos españoles se han hecho ricos. Es la coca una mata no mayor que los manzanos enanos de España, de hasta un estado en alto; su hoja, que es la que tanto precian y estiman los indios, es del tamaño y talle de la del limoncillo
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIX
On Coca

In this kingdom of Peru there is no commodity [cosa] more widely known than coca, whose trade is among the largest and most profitable to be found in the Indies, and by which no few Spaniards have made themselves rich. Coca is a shrub [mata] no larger than the dwarf apple trees of Spain, reaching up to one estado [approximately one fathom, roughly 1.7 metres] in height. Its leaf — which is the part so prized and esteemed by the Indians — is the size and shape of that of the lime [limoncillo], and sometimes smaller. corpus_links.original:
CAPÍTULO VIII
En que prosigue lo mismo

Todavía resta por decir de las costumbres y vicios que los indios tienen contra la virtud de la justicia, de que tratará este capítulo. Caciques y señores de los pueblos eran aquellos que no con otro derecho que el de la fuerza y poder los sojuzgaban; y como la adquisición era tiránica y cruel, lo era también su gobierno. Porque no ponían la mira en el bien
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VIII
Which continues the same subject

There still remains to be said concerning the customs and vices that the Indians exhibit contrary to the virtue of justice, which this chapter will treat. The caciques [chiefs] and lords of the villages were those who subjugated the people by no other right than that of force and power; and as their acquisition of rule was tyrannical and cruel, so too was their governance. For they did not aim at the welfare and benefit of their vassals, but rather at satisfying their own ambition and greed, reducing the people to so heavy a servitude that there was no difference between it and outright slavery. corpus_links.translation: Erythroxylum coca — Coca (Amazonian uses, distinct from Andean). Richard Evans Schultes documented the use of coca among 36 distinct Amazonian peoples. This Amazonian documentation differs from Andean accounts (such as that of Bernabé Cobo): in the Amazon, coca was used primarily for energy, suppression of hunger, and ceremonial purposes, rather than for the altitude-specific applications characteristic of Andean use. A notable pharmacological observation is that Amazonian coca preparations are typically less potent in alkaloid content than their Andean counterparts — a difference attributable to distinct species, varying soil conditions, and differing methods of preparation. corpus_links.translation: Amazonian Plant Hallucinogens — Schultes and Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979). Richard Evans Schultes documented 97 plant species employed as hallucinogens [psychoactive agents] by indigenous Amazonian peoples, compared to only 15 known from the Old World. Key plants include: (1) Virola calophylla bark resin, containing 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine [5-MeO-DMT], used by 14 Amazonian nations; (2) Brugmansia (tree datura), employed across South America for surgical anesthesia [narcotic sedation], visionary [divinatory] purposes, and warrior preparation — belonging to the same genus as the Aztec Toloache, representing a convergent discovery across the Americas; (3) Yopo, or Anadenanthera peregrina, a bufotenin-containing snuff used from the Caribbean to Brazil. corpus_links.translation: Niyog-niyogan (Quisqualis indica Linn.) — Family: Combretaceae. Source: Quisumbing (1951), pp. 267–269. Filipino vernacular names: Niyog-niyogan (Tagalog; the name translates literally as 'Chinese lantern'); Tartarau (Ilocano); Kasumpangi (Bisaya/Visayan). corpus_links.label: EA.Artemisia
corpus_links.title: Chikichi / Artemisia afra — the African wormwood
corpus_links.original: [Amharic] chikichi — ye wagagen tera; [Swahili] mchichiri
corpus_links.translation: Artemisia afra (African wormwood) — the most widely used plant medicine across Eastern and Southern Africa. Documented across Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, and southern Africa for: respiratory infections, fever, malaria, digestive complaints, and wound healing. The same genus as artemisinin (Artemisia annua) — Nobel Prize 2015. Artemisia afra does not contain artemisinin but contains other artemisia sesquiterpenes with documented antimalarial and antimicrobial activity. The extraordinary geographic range of Artemisia afra medicinal use across independent African communities mirrors the multi-tradition convergence signal for Artemisia absinthium (wormwood) in European, Egyptian, and Celtic traditions.
corpus_links.preparation: Leaves decocted; steam inhalation; fresh leaves applied topically
corpus_links.condition: Malaria, respiratory infections, fever, digestive complaints, wound healing

corpus_links.title: Afyun (Opium) — pain and sleep

corpus_links.translation: Opium: cold and dry in the fourth degree. It numbs the senses and quiets pain. Ibn Sina's documentation of opium is the most sophisticated in any pre-modern medical tradition. He distinguishes: (1) the lethal dose from the therapeutic dose, (2) the use for acute pain from chronic use leading to habituation, (3) topical from internal application. He specifically warns that opium 'should be given in small quantities and with great caution' — the first documented pharmacological warning about opioid dependency in medical literature.
corpus_links.preparation: Small amounts dissolved in wine for internal pain; applied in oil for local analgesia
corpus_links.condition: Severe pain, insomnia, cough, diarrhea — with explicit warning about habituation

corpus_links.translation: Poppy — its juice (opium) is soporific and analgesic. Taken in excess it produces great confusion [and death]. corpus_links.label: Canon.Book3.Meningitis
corpus_links.title: Sirsam — meningitis and brain inflammation
corpus_links.original: السرسام: ورم حار في دماغ أو أغشيته.
corpus_links.translation: Sirsam: a hot inflammation in the brain or its membranes [meningitis]. Ibn Sina's description of sirsam is the first systematic description of meningitis in world medical literature — he distinguishes it from other brain conditions by the specific symptoms of neck rigidity, photophobia, and altered consciousness. The treatment: cooling medicines applied to the head, reduction of brain heat, and opium for pain and sleep. The observation that neck rigidity distinguishes sirsam from other fevers (Kernig's sign precursor) demonstrates clinical observation of extraordinary precision.

corpus_links.label: Canon.Book5.Antidotes
corpus_links.title: Tiyaqat — theriac and compound antidotes
corpus_links.original: الترياق الكبير: مركب عظيم من ستين دواءً أو أكثر.
corpus_links.translation: The Great Theriac: a grand compound of sixty drugs or more. Ibn Sina documents the Theriac — the legendary universal antidote inherited from the Greek tradition (Mithridates VI, Galen) — with 60+ ingredients including opium, viper flesh, and dozens of plant medicines. The Canon's documentation of theriac is historically significant because Ibn Sina attempts to rationalize it pharmacologically — explaining each ingredient by its humoral action — rather than simply transmitting it as magical tradition. Theriac remained in use as a pharmaceutical preparation in European and Islamic medicine until the 18th century.

corpus_links.label: Canon.Book3.Fever
corpus_links.title: Hummayat — the fever chapters
corpus_links.original: الحمى في نفسها مرض أو عرض مرض وكل ما هو حمى فله دورة.
corpus_links.translation: Fever is in itself a disease or the symptom of a disease, and everything that is a fever has a cycle. Ibn Sina's fever classification is the most sophisticated in any pre-modern medical tradition: he distinguishes ephemeral fever (from fatigue, emotion), humoral fevers (corresponding to each of the four humours), and putrid fevers (from rotting matter in the organs). corpus_links.translation: Physostigma venenosum — the Calabar Bean, known in the Efik language as 'Esère', from Calabar, Nigeria. As recorded by Dalziel (1937), this plant was employed both as an ordeal poison administered during judicial trials and by traditional healers for eye conditions described as 'clouding of vision' — now identified as glaucoma. The plant was first formally documented by Daniel (1846); a pharmacological study was conducted by Christison (1855); and Fraser (1863) isolated the active alkaloid physostigmine (also called eserine). The first documented therapeutic use of physostigmine for glaucoma treatment was by Laqueur (1876). corpus_links.translation: Curare — derived from Strychnos toxifera and/or Chondrodendron tomentosum. Documented by Richard Evans Schultes during his Amazon expeditions (1941–1953). Recorded among the Yanomami, Makushi, Wapishana, and Waorani peoples. Preparation requires specialist knowledge: selection of appropriate vine species, identification of the parts to be used, control of boiling duration, and potency testing by timing the onset of paralysis in test animals — a process taking three to five days in total. Amazonian hunters had through long empirical practice identified the compound's remarkable physiological selectivity: skeletal [voluntary] muscle is paralysed, while cardiac and smooth muscle remain unaffected at effective doses. corpus_links.translation: The Poison-Medicine Spectrum in Amazonian Ethnobotany. Field analysis by Schultes. A consistent finding: there exists no sharp boundary between medicine and poison — the same plant serves as weapon, medicine, and vision-inducer, the distinction depending entirely on dose and method of preparation. Documented examples: (1) Curare — an arrow poison at high dose, a surgical muscle relaxant at low dose; (2) Brugmansia — lethal at high dose, anaesthetic at intermediate dose, visionary [producing hallucinogenic visions] at low dose; (3) Caapi — an emetic at high dose, vision-inducing at medium dose, sedative at low dose; (4) Strychnos — a cardiac poison at high dose, a heart tonic [cardiotonic] at low dose (a precursor to the pharmacology of cardiac glycosides). modern_research.significance: The ayahuasca combination is the most pharmacologically sophisticated traditional discovery in this database — two plants with specific complementary mechanisms, combined deliberately for an effect neither produces alone.

corpus_links.translation: Balché (Lonchocarpus violaceus / L. longistylus) — Sacred Maya Ritual Drink. From the Ritual of the Bacabs [a colonial-era Yucatec Maya manuscript of healing incantations], the text reads: 'U ts'o'ok u bin balché ti' noj nah... ka xoc-lah u k'ab u yich balché' — rendered as: 'The balché went to the great house... the hands and face of the balché were counted.' Balché is a ritual fermented beverage prepared from the bark of the Lonchocarpus tree, steeped in honey-water and allowed to ferment. It was employed in Maya healing ceremonies by the h-men [healer-priest] for purposes of purification, visionary experience, and the diagnosis of the cause of illness. corpus_links.original: [Moerman, D.E. 1998. Native American Ethnobotany. Timber Press.]
corpus_links.translation: Daniel Moerman's Native American Ethnobotany database documents 4,029 medicinal plant uses across 291 indigenous North American nations — the most comprehensive documented indigenous pharmacopoeia in the world. Key statistical finding: plants used by more than five independent nations show significantly higher rates of confirmed pharmacological activity in modern research (Moerman, 1996) — validating the archive's convergence methodology. The most widely documented plants across the most nations: yarrow (46 nations), elderberry (27 nations), wild bergamot (21 nations), sage (19 nations), and echinacea (13 nations). These represent the highest-convergence indigenous North American plants.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVIII
On the Jasmines of the Indies

The Mexican Indians call a shrub 'acuilt' to which the Spaniards give the name 'jasmines of the Indies'; it is native to New Spain. It is a twining plant that grows in damp places and tends to trail along the ground or to wind itself around nearby trees, being of the ivy family [género de hiedra]. Two species of this plant are found, which differ only in the color of their flowers and the size of their leaves: one bears white flowers, and the other, yellow. Both send out many round, smooth, and slender shoots; the leaf resembles that of the pomegranate, though more pointed, and is very much marked by small veins that arise from the stalk and run along its length. corpus_links.translation: On Iris (ἶρις). The root is warming [calorific], sharp [acrid], and somewhat bitter in quality. It softens tissue and draws out embedded splinters; when applied topically with vinegar, it disperses hard swellings beneath the chin [scrofulous or glandular swellings]. When taken internally in wine, it relieves pain in the sides, convulsions, ruptures [hernias], coughs, and inflammation of the trachea [windpipe]. Mixed with honey and applied to the head, it cures dandruff [scurf of the scalp]. When applied as a pessary [vaginal suppository], it promotes the menstrual flux and expels the afterbirth [placenta]. The smoke [of the burnt root] drives away serpents.

The bite of a human — whether from the hands or, more precisely, the teeth of a lady or gentleman acquaintance — was considered to require more intensive treatment than even the bite of a crocodile.

REMEDY AGAINST THE BITE OR STING OF PEOPLE
Prepare for the patient a poultice of Raw Flesh on the first day. Afterwards, treat him with Oil and Honey to promote healing. Then apply Oil in Wax in order to effect a complete cure at once.

A Frog — warm in Oil and rub [the affected area] therewith.

corpus_links.translation: The mixture was to be drunk from a cool flask. If the patient was a boy, he had to drink it from a hennu-vessel [a specific Egyptian liquid measure or vessel]. A curious remedy was prescribed for urinary retention in a child: REMEDY FOR A CHILD TO CLEAR THE ACCUMULATION OF URINE IN HIS BODY — An Old Book [discarded papyrus] cooked in Oil; smear on his Body. Here, 'An Old Book' refers to a discarded papyrus scroll, the medicinal virtue of which was considered to be enhanced by the writing fluid absorbed into it. Both 'drugs'—the paper and the ink—were as standard a part of the pharmacopoeia of the time as red lead or honey or numerous other substances, and were frequently prescribed for a variety of ailments. On the second day the head was anointed with Fish-oil. On the third day with Hippopotamus Oil. On the fourth day with abra-oil [an unidentified oil of Egyptian origin]. After this course of intensive treatment, if the Eczema still persisted, the affected scalp was smeared daily with Bread-meal and dressed with 'Rotted Cereals.'

Nine pages of the original papyrus are devoted to eye conditions, a fact which should surprise no one acquainted with that country, even across the thousands of years separating us from that remote period. kampo.source_text: Honzo Wamyo (本草和名, 918 CE) / Yoshimasu Todo, Yakucho
kampo.original: 麻黄 — 発汗、利水、平喘。寒邪による喘息・浮腫・発熱に用いる。
kampo.translation: Maōu — induces sweating, promotes urination, calms wheezing. Used for asthma, edema, and fever caused by cold invasion. Kampo dosing refined over centuries: smaller doses than Chinese tradition, reflecting Japanese clinical observation of dose-dependent side effects.
kampo.preparation: Decocted in water; standard Kampo formula dosing 3–9g dried herb
kampo.condition: Asthma, bronchitis, nasal congestion, edema, fever with absence of sweating
kampo.notes: Kampo standardized dosing protocols for ma huang centuries before Western pharmacology isolated ephedrine. The Kampo clinical tradition's caution about cardiac effects in high doses anticipates modern contraindications.

chinese.source_text: Shennong Bencao Jing (神農本草經, c.200 CE)
chinese.original: 麻黄，味苦，温。主中風傷寒頭痛，温瘧，發表出汗，去邪熱氣，止咳逆上氣，除寒熱，破癥堅積聚。
chinese.translation: Ma huang, bitter in taste, warm in nature. Indicated for wind-cold with headache, malarial fever, promotes sweating to expel pathogenic factors, clears fever-heat, stops coughing and wheezing, dispels cold-heat, breaks up accumulations.
chinese.preparation: Decocted in water; often combined with cinnamon twig (guizhi) in classical formulas

modern_research.summary: Ephedrine isolated 1885 by Nagai Nagayoshi (Japanese chemist). Pseudoephedrine still the primary ingredient in most OTC decongestants worldwide. Ephedrine used in anesthesia for hypotension management. Banned as dietary supplement in many countries due to cardiac risk at high doses — validating Kampo's centuries-old dosing caution.
modern_research.significance: The Kampo tradition's empirical dose refinement — using smaller amounts than classical Chinese medicine — was pharmacologically correct: ephedrine's therapeutic window is narrow and cardiac risk is dose-dependent. Nagai, a Japanese chemist trained in both Western and Kampo traditions, isolated ephedrine specifically because of its documented clinical use.

plants.evidence_authority: Ephedrine — FDA approved vasopressor; pseudoephedrine FDA approved decongestant
plants.evidence_note: Ephedra supplements banned but isolated alkaloids approved

corpus_links.original: 麻黃：苦，溫，無毒。主中風傷寒頭痛，發表出汗，去邪熱氣，止咳逆上氣。
corpus_links.translation: Mahuang (ephedra): bitter, warm, non-toxic. Principal uses: wind-stroke and cold damage with headache, releases the exterior and promotes sweating, eliminates pathogenic heat qi, stops cough with rebellious qi. Li Shizhen documents ephedra as the primary diaphoretic and bronchodilator — the same application for which ephedrine was isolated and became a pharmaceutical drug in 1924. The isolation of ephedrine from mahuang by Nagayoshi Nagai is one of the most famous traditional medicine → pharmaceutical compound discoveries, and the Bencao Gangmu entry is the definitive traditional documentation of this plant.

corpus_links.condition: Asthma, bronchitis, common cold with chills, edema

kampo.source_text: Honzo Wamyo (918 CE); used in ~70% of classical Kampo formulas
kampo.original: 甘草 — 甘、平。補脾益氣、清熱解毒、祛痰止咳、緩急止痛、調和諸薬。
kampo.translation: Kanzō — sweet in taste, neutral. Tonifies the spleen, clears heat and toxins, eliminates phlegm and stops cough, relieves cramping pain, and harmonises the actions of other herbs. Used as a modulator in compound formulas — the most frequently prescribed single herb in all of Kampo.
kampo.preparation: Decocted with other herbs; used in approximately 70% of all classical Kampo formulas as harmonising agent
kampo.condition: Cough, inflammation, peptic ulcer, adrenal insufficiency, drug toxicity modulation
kampo.notes: Kampo's use of licorice as a formula harmoniser — reducing side effects of other herbs and improving palatability — is now understood pharmacologically: glycyrrhizin modulates cortisol metabolism and has genuine anti-inflammatory activity that may reduce the adverse effects of other botanical compounds in a formula.

greek_roman.source_text: De Materia Medica, Dioscorides (77 CE)
greek_roman.original: γλυκύρριζα — ἡ ῥίζα χρησιμεύει πρὸς βῆχας καὶ ξηρασίαν στόματος
greek_roman.translation: Glykyrrhiza — the root is useful for coughs and dryness of the mouth. Dissolved in rainwater it relieves coughs and all chest and lung conditions.
greek_roman.preparation: Root dissolved in water; taken orally
greek_roman.condition: Cough, chest conditions, mouth dryness

modern_research.summary: Glycyrrhizin has documented anti-inflammatory, antiviral (including SARS-CoV inhibition), and hepatoprotective activity. Carbenoxolone (synthetic derivative) was a major peptic ulcer treatment before PPIs. At high doses, glycyrrhizin causes pseudoaldosteronism (hypertension, hypokalemia) — validating traditional dose caution.
modern_research.significance: MAXIMUM GLOBAL CONVERGENCE: Egyptian (Ebers Papyrus), Greek (Dioscorides), Chinese, Islamic, and Kampo traditions independently documented licorice root for cough and inflammation. Among the most globally widespread traditional medicine discoveries. Modern research validates the anti-inflammatory and antiviral activity but also confirms the dose-dependent adverse effects that multiple traditions cautioned against.

corpus_links.title: Gancao (Licorice Root) — the harmonizer
corpus_links.original: 甘草：味甘，平。主五臟六腑寒熱邪氣，堅筋骨，長肌肉，倍力，金瘡腫，解毒。久服輕身延年。
corpus_links.translation: Gancao (licorice root): flavor sweet, neutral. Principally treats pathogenic cold and heat qi in the five organs and six bowels, strengthens tendons and bones, increases muscle mass, doubles strength, treats metal wound swellings, resolves toxins. Long-term use lightens the body and extends the years. Glycyrrhiza uralensis (Chinese licorice) — the same genus as the licorice documented in Egyptian, Greek/Roman, Persian, and Ayurvedic traditions. With the Shennong documentation, licorice now has the strongest multi-tradition convergence of any plant in the archive: five independent medical traditions across four continents.

corpus_links.original: 甘草 (Kanzo / Gan Cao) — Glycyrrhiza uralensis. 甘草、和名 阿末加都良。甘、平。主五臓六腑寒熱邪気、堅筋骨、長肌肉、倍力、金創腫、解毒。久服輕身延年。
corpus_links.translation: Kanzo [甘草, 'sweet herb'], Japanese name Amakatsura [阿末加都良]. Flavour: sweet; temperament [qi]: neutral [平]. Indicated for cold and heat pathogenic factors [寒熱邪気] in the five viscera [五臓] and six bowels [六腑]; strengthens sinews and bones [筋骨]; builds flesh and muscle [肌肉]; multiplies strength [倍力]; treats swelling from metal wounds [金創腫, i.e. lacerations from bladed implements]; antidotes poisons [解毒]. Long-term use lightens the body [輕身] and extends the years of life [延年]. Kanzo is the most frequently employed herb across all of Kampo [Japanese classical medicine], appearing in approximately 70% of compound formulae in the role of harmoniser [調和] and moderator of the actions of other constituent herbs.

corpus_links.translation: Shakuyaku-kanzo-to [芍薬甘草湯], known in English as 'Peony and Licorice Decoction,' is among the most frequently prescribed Kampo [traditional Japanese herbal medicine] formulas in contemporary Japan. Composition: Kakkon [葛根, Pueraria lobata root] 8g; Mao [麻黄, Ephedra herb] 4g; Keishi [桂枝, Cinnamomum cassia twig] 3g; Shakuyaku [芍薬, Paeonia lactiflora root] 3g; Taiso [大棗, Ziziphus jujuba fruit] 4g; Shokyo [生姜, fresh Zingiber officinale rhizome] 4g; Kanzo [甘草, Glycyrrhiza uralensis root] 2g. corpus_links.label: BGM.Gancao
corpus_links.title: Gancao (Licorice) — the national elder of herbs
corpus_links.original: 甘草：甘，平，無毒。主五臟六腑寒熱邪氣⋯調和諸藥，故有國老之名。
corpus_links.translation: Gancao (licorice): sweet, neutral, non-toxic. Principal uses: pathogenic cold and heat qi in the five organs and six bowels... It harmonizes all medicines, hence it has the name 'National Elder.' Li Shizhen's epithet for licorice — 'National Elder' (Guolao) — captures its unique role as the harmonizer of Chinese compound medicine. Appears in approximately 70% of all classical Chinese formulas. Li Shizhen's entry adds the sixth major documentation for licorice, completing its record as the most cross-tradition-validated plant in the archive.

tibetan.source_text: Gyushi (rGyud bzhi), Chapter on mountain medicine plants; Men-Tsee-Khang formulary
tibetan.translation: Somaraja — a mountain-born medicine. Increases physical strength of the body, clarifies the mind. Used for exhaustion at high altitude, for those weakened by thin air, and to sustain the body during long journeys over mountain passes.
tibetan.preparation: Root dried and decocted; often combined with other altitude-medicine plants in Gyushi formulas
tibetan.condition: Altitude sickness, fatigue, mental fog, physical exhaustion
tibetan.notes: Rhodiola's documented use in Tibetan medicine specifically for altitude-related fatigue and cognitive impairment is a remarkable pre-scientific identification of what modern research now calls adaptogenic activity. The Gyushi was written at 3,500–4,500m altitude — Tibetan physicians had more clinical experience with altitude physiology than any other medical tradition on Earth.

chinese.source_text: Bencao Gangmu Shiyi (supplement, 18th c.); modern Tibetan-Chinese materia medica
chinese.original: 红景天 — 益气清肺，止咳平喘。用于气虚体弱，气短乏力。
chinese.translation: Hóng jǐng tiān — tonifies qi and clears the lungs, stops cough and calms wheezing. Used for qi deficiency with physical weakness, shortness of breath and fatigue.
chinese.preparation: Root decocted or taken as powder

modern_research.summary: Multiple clinical trials showing Rhodiola reduces mental and physical fatigue, improves altitude tolerance, and has mild antidepressant effects. Swedish Space Corporation used Rhodiola in cosmonauts. US military-funded research for altitude performance. Some RCT evidence for burnout syndrome reduction.
modern_research.significance: Tibetan medicine's specific identification of Rhodiola for altitude fatigue and cognitive impairment maps precisely onto modern adaptogen research. The tradition's 1,200+ years of clinical observation at actual altitude constitutes a natural longitudinal study no modern trial can replicate.

corpus_links.title: Somaraja (Rhodiola) in the Gyushi: Properties, Indications, and Preparation
corpus_links.original: སོ་མ་རཱ་ཛ། (Somaraja) — Rhodiola rosea / R. sachalinensis. From Gyushi (rGyud bzhi), Chapter on mountain medicines. Classical Tibetan: སྤང་རྒྱན་ སོ་མ་རཱ་ཛ་ཞེས་པ། རི་བོ་ཆེན་པོའི་གངས་ཀྱི་འདབས་སུ་སྐྱེས་པའི་སྨན། ལུས་ཀྱི་ཤུགས་དང་བཟོད་སྟོབས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱེད། སེམས་གསལ་ཞིང་དྲན་པ་བཀོལ་བར་བྱེད། ལྟེ་བར་སྐྱུར་ཚ་ཡོད་ན་སྨན་བཟང་ངོ་།
corpus_links.translation: Somaraja [lit. 'king of meadow ornaments' or 'moon-king herb']: a plant born at the foot of the great glaciers on high mountains. It increases physical strength [lus kyi shugs] and the body's endurance [bzod stobs]. It clarifies the mind [sems gsal] and enhances memory [dran pa bkol]. It is an excellent medicine [sman bzang] when there is acidic heat [skyur tsha] in the navel region [lte ba]. Used by Tibetan physicians for those suffering from altitude-related fatigue, weakness at high elevation, and cloudiness of mind. The Gyushi specifies collection above 4,000 m elevation for maximum potency. Men-Tsee-Khang preparation: root dried at altitude, decocted or taken as powder. Standard formula: combined with shilajit [brag zhun] and other mountain medicines for altitude adaptation.

maya.source_text: Ritual of the Bacabs / Yucatec Maya oral tradition; documented by Roys (1965) and modern ethnobotanists
maya.original: [Yucatec Maya oral tradition — transcribed] Chay — ku yantal u pixan patan. Ku ts'áabal ti' máako'ob yéetel k'áak'. Yaan u páajtal u ts'o'okol u yik'nal.
maya.translation: Chay — it sustains the vital spirit of the body. It is given to people with fever. It is capable of cooling the heat within. Used by Maya healers for generations to strengthen blood, support the heart, and treat digestive ailments. The leaves must be cooked before eating — raw leaves contain toxic compounds that cooking deactivates.
maya.preparation: Leaves must be boiled for 5+ minutes to deactivate hydrogen cyanide precursors; then eaten as vegetable or decocted as tea
maya.condition: Malnutrition, fever, digestive complaints, blood building
maya.notes: The Maya knowledge that chaya leaves must be cooked before consumption — and that raw leaves are harmful — represents precise pharmacological understanding of hydrolysable cyanogenic glycosides without any knowledge of chemistry. This preparation knowledge is itself a sophisticated folk pharmacological insight predating any understanding of the underlying mechanism.

modern_research.key_compound: Isothiocyanates, vitamins A/C/K, iron, calcium; cyanogenic glycosides (deactivated by cooking)
modern_research.summary: Chaya has exceptional nutritional density — higher protein, vitamin C, calcium, and iron than most commonly consumed vegetables. Studies show hypoglycemic effects in diabetic animal models and some human pilot studies. The raw toxicity / cooked safety distinction is fully validated: raw leaves contain linamarin which releases HCN; cooking for 5+ minutes deactivates it.
modern_research.significance: The Maya preparation protocol for chaya — cook to neutralise toxins — is precise ethnopharmacological knowledge that modern chemistry confirms completely. The anti-diabetic potential is particularly noteworthy given that modern Mexican and Central American populations have very high diabetes rates and chaya remains a staple traditional food.

plants.evidence_authority: Isothiocyanates — research stage; no specific Cochrane or FDA approval for Chaya

Maya healer's description: U ti'al u yilaj ti' máak ku k'iinikil le che'o' — 'In order to see to a sick person, this tree.' Chay is prepared by boiling leaves for five or more minutes before consumption — the Maya knowledge that raw leaves are harmful (toxic c
corpus_links.translation: Chay (Cnidoscolus aconitifolius) — Tree Spinach / Chaya. Drawn from Yucatec Maya oral tradition as documented by Roys [Ralph L. Roys, ethnobotanist and Maya scholar] and subsequent ethnobotanists. A Maya healer's description reads: U ti'al u yilaj ti' máak ku k'iinikil le che'o' — 'In order to attend to a sick person, [use] this tree.' Chay is prepared by boiling the leaves for a minimum of five minutes before consumption. The Maya understanding that raw leaves are harmful — owing to toxic compounds [hydrocyanic glycosides] that are neutralized by cooking — represents a precise pharmacological knowledge arrived at without formal chemical science. philippine.source_text: Quisumbing, Medicinal Plants of the Philippines (1951); Philippine DOH Traditional Medicine Program
philippine.original: [Tagalog oral tradition, documented] Ang lagundi ay ginagamit sa ubo, lagnat, at sakit ng katawan. Ang dahon ay niluluto sa tubig at inumin para sa hika at sipon.
philippine.translation: Lagundi is used for cough, fever, and body pain. The leaves are boiled in water and the decoction drunk for asthma and colds. Applied as a poultice to painful joints. One of the most widely used medicinal plants across all Philippine ethnic groups — used by Tagalog, Visayan, Ilocano, and indigenous groups alike, suggesting independent convergent discovery within the Philippine archipelago.
philippine.preparation: Leaves boiled in water, drunk as tea for respiratory conditions; leaf poultice for pain
philippine.condition: Cough, asthma, bronchitis, fever, joint pain, headache
philippine.notes: Lagundi is one of only 10 herbal medicines formally approved by the Philippine Department of Health (DOH) as an official alternative medicine — backed by clinical trials required for DOH registration. This makes it one of the best-validated traditional medicines globally in terms of government-mandated clinical evidence.

modern_research.summary: DOH-approved for cough and asthma. Multiple Philippine clinical trials showing bronchodilator and antitussive activity. Casticin confirmed as anti-inflammatory compound. Anti-histamine activity demonstrated in in vitro studies. Now commercially available as standardised tablet formulation (Ascof) in Philippine pharmacies.
modern_research.significance: One of the most completely validated traditional-to-pharmaceutical transitions in Southeast Asian medicine — government-mandated clinical trials, standardised formulation, commercial availability, and continued use by practitioners at all levels of the Philippine healthcare system simultaneously.

plants.evidence_authority: Lagundi — FDA IND studies; Philippine FDA approved; WHO included in traditional medicine guidelines

plants.common_name: Garlic + Bile + Copper Vessel (Bald's Eye Remedy)

tradition_names.celtic_norse: Læcedóm wið eagena sáre (Remedy for eye disease) — Anglo-Saxon, England

plants.modern_botanical: Allium sativum + Allium cepa (with Brassica species) + copper vessel

celtic_norse.source_text: Bald's Leechbook (Medicinale Anglicum), c.900–950 CE, British Library Royal MS 12 D XVII
celtic_norse.original: Wið eagena sár: genim cropleac ond gárleác, begea emfela, gecnua wel tosomne, nim þonne win ond gallán fearres, begea emfela, meng wið þy leáccræfte, do þonne on ærene fæt, læt standan nigun niht on þam ærene fæte.
celtic_norse.translation: For soreness of the eyes: take cropleac [onion or leek] and garlic, of both equal amounts, pound well together, then take wine and bull's gall, of both equal amounts, mix with the plant preparation, then put into a brass [copper] vessel, let stand nine nights in the brass vessel. Wring through a cloth, clarify well, put into a horn. About night time apply with a feather to the eye.
celtic_norse.preparation: Garlic and onion/leek pounded together; mixed with wine and ox bile; stored in copper vessel 9 days; strained and applied to eye with feather
celtic_norse.condition: Eye infection (stye, conjunctivitis); potentially MRSA and other bacterial infections
celtic_norse.notes: This recipe was tested by microbiologists at the University of Nottingham (Freya Harrison et al., 2015) as part of the AncientBiotics project. Results: the preparation killed approximately 90% of MRSA bacteria in laboratory conditions — significantly outperforming modern antibiotics against some MRSA strains. Each ingredient alone had minimal effect; the combination and copper vessel were essential. Published in Scientific Reports. The copper vessel acts as an oligodynamic antimicrobial agent — the same mechanism independently discovered by Egyptian medicine.

modern_research.key_compound: Allicin (garlic) + taurocholic acid (bile) + copper ions (vessel) — synergistic combination
modern_research.summary: Harrison et al. (2015, Scientific Reports) demonstrated 90% MRSA kill rate. Each ingredient tested separately showed minimal activity; the full combination in copper vessel was required. Active against Staphylococcus aureus biofilms — particularly relevant as biofilm-associated MRSA is resistant to most modern antibiotics. Mechanism: copper ions + allicin disrupt bacterial membrane; bile acids increase membrane permeability; combined action penetrates biofilm.
modern_research.significance: One of the most dramatic ethnopharmacological validations of the 21st century: a 1,100-year-old Anglo-Saxon recipe for eye infections was tested against MRSA — a 21st century superbug that didn't exist in 900 CE — and outperformed many modern antibiotics. The copper vessel detail (often dismissed by earlier scholars as ritual/symbolic) proved pharmacologically essential, validating Bald's Leechbook as a genuine empirical medical text rather than superstition. The same copper oligodynamic mechanism was independently discovered by Egyptian medicine ~2,500 years earlier.

plants.evidence_authority: Allicin — Cochrane review on garlic for cardiovascular; Bald's eye remedy validated UCL 2015

persian_zoroastrian.source_text: Bundahishn (9th c. CE); Avestan medical references; Persian traditional use
persian_zoroastrian.original: زرپران — از گیاهان مقدس ایران باستان. برای غم و اندوه، برای تقویت قلب، و برای بیماری‌های زنان به کار می‌رفت.
persian_zoroastrian.translation: Zarparan — among the sacred plants of ancient Iran. Used for grief and sorrow, for strengthening the heart, and for women's diseases. The Zoroastrian texts associate saffron with the sacred fire and with the purification of the spirit. Given to those afflicted by dark moods and unquiet hearts.
persian_zoroastrian.preparation: Stigmas steeped in warm water or milk; taken orally
persian_zoroastrian.condition: Depression, grief, heart weakness, menstrual disorders
persian_zoroastrian.notes: Pre-Islamic Persian medicine's use of saffron specifically for 'dark moods and unquiet hearts' aligns with extraordinary precision with modern RCT findings — multiple trials showing saffron comparable to fluoxetine for mild-to-moderate depression.

greek_roman.source_text: De Materia Medica, Dioscorides (77 CE)
greek_roman.original: κρόκος — ἀλγήματα τῆς κεφαλῆς παύει, ὑπνωτικός ἐστι
greek_roman.translation: Krokos — relieves pains of the head, is sleep-inducing. Applied with honey and wine it is good for inflammation. Taken as a drink it sharpens the senses and lifts the spirits.
greek_roman.preparation: Steeped in wine or water; applied topically with honey
greek_roman.condition: Headache, insomnia, inflammation, low spirits

modern_research.summary: Multiple RCTs (including a 2013 meta-analysis in Human Psychopharmacology) showing saffron extract comparable to fluoxetine (Prozac) and imipramine for mild-to-moderate depression. Mechanism: serotonin reuptake inhibition and monoamine activity. Also shows promise for Alzheimer's (improving cognitive scores in trials). Growing body of evidence for cardiovascular protection via crocin's antioxidant activity.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Persian Zoroastrian, Islamic, Ayurvedic, and Greek/Roman traditions all independently document saffron for depression/low spirits. Modern RCTs validate the antidepressant effect with a mechanism (serotonin reuptake) that makes the convergent folk observation pharmacologically comprehensible. With multiple RCTs now published, saffron represents one of the best-evidenced traditional antidepressants in the world — almost entirely unknown to mainstream psychiatry.

plants.evidence_authority: Crocin/Safranal — Cochrane review on saffron for depression 2019; multiple RCTs

corpus_links.label: Canon.Book2.Saffron
corpus_links.title: Zaafaran (Saffron) — heart and mood medicine
corpus_links.original: الزعفران: حار رطب في الدرجة الثانية. يفرّح النفس ويقوي القلب.
corpus_links.translation: Saffron: hot and moist in the second degree. It gladdens the soul and strengthens the heart. Ibn Sina's documentation of saffron for cardiac and mood conditions directly validates the existing archive entry (MMA-028). The Canon documents saffron as a primary cardiac tonic and antidepressant — 1,000 years before modern RCTs confirmed saffron's antidepressant activity comparable to fluoxetine (Prozac). The Canon also warns that excessive saffron produces 'immoderate laughter' — possibly the earliest documented description of saffron's psychoactive effects at high doses.
corpus_links.preparation: Infused in warm water or wine; taken with honey
corpus_links.condition: Depression, heart palpitations, cardiac weakness, insomnia

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI
On the Suana

The suana is a shrub [mata] two cubits tall, which puts forth many shoots or very straight branches. The leaf resembles that of the asphodel, except that it is twice as wide. It produces a white flower in the shape of a little bell [campanilla], like a lily [azucena], and many thin roots whose bark [cortezas] dyes [things] the color of saffron. For this reason it is used and sold throughout Peru, and used in place of saffron in stews [guisados], although it is not known to produce any effect beyond imparting color. Because this plant grows in the Andean provinces, the Spaniards call it 'saffron of the Andes' [azafrán de los Andes]; but the Indians of the province of Larecaja, in the diocese of Chuquiabo [La Paz], who inhabit the lowland [tierra yanca] of that distr

corpus_links.original: De Materia Medica, Book III. On Saffron/Crocus (κρόκος / Crocus sativus). 'Saffron has a warming, softening, and sleep-inducing faculty. It benefits the eyes and the stomach. Taken in drink it sharpens the sight. Applied with honey and wine to inflammations it helps them. Taken with wine in drink it cheers the mind. corpus_links.translation: De Materia Medica, Book III. Concerning Saffron [κρόκος / Crocus sativus]. Saffron possesses a warming, softening, and sleep-inducing property [faculty]. It is beneficial to the eyes and to the stomach. When taken as a drink, it sharpens the eyesight. When applied topically with honey and wine to sites of inflammation, it affords relief. When taken in wine as a drink, it gladdens [cheers] the mind. Administered with wine, it assists those who have been bitten by the land-crocodile [a terrestrial reptile, likely a large lizard or monitor]. Applied as a pessary [vaginal suppository], it promotes [moves] the menstrual flow. However, when consumed in excess, it is harmful, producing a form of intoxication.

corpus_links.label: Canon.Book5.Antidotes
corpus_links.title: Tiyaqat — theriac and compound antidotes
corpus_links.original: الترياق الكبير: مركب عظيم من ستين دواءً أو أكثر.
corpus_links.translation: The Great Theriac: a grand compound of sixty drugs or more. Ibn Sina documents the Theriac — the legendary universal antidote inherited from the Greek tradition (Mithridates VI, Galen) — with 60+ ingredients including opium, viper flesh, and dozens of plant medicines. The Canon's documentation of theriac is historically significant because Ibn Sina attempts to rationalize it pharmacologically — explaining each ingredient by its humoral action — rather than simply transmitting it as magical tradition. Theriac remained in use as a pharmaceutical preparation in European and Islamic medicine until the 18th century.

corpus_links.label: IBB.Saffron
corpus_links.title: Zaafaran — the most valued Arabic medicine
corpus_links.original: الزعفران — من أجود الأدوية وأنفعها للقلب، يُفرّح النفس ويقوي القلب والكبد
corpus_links.translation: Saffron — among the most excellent and beneficial medicines for the heart; it gladdens the soul and strengthens the heart and liver. Ibn al-Baitar's saffron entry extends the existing archive documentation (MMA-028) by adding specific dosage information (one mithqal per day maximum) and the warning against excessive use ('produces heaviness of the head'). The cardiac and mood applications are consistent across Egyptian, Ayurvedic, Persian, Unani (Ibn Sina), and now Ibn al-Baitar documentation — five independent Islamic-era or Islamic-adjacent traditions.

tradition_names.australian_indigenous: Bundjalung: healing leaves (name varies by language group)

australian_indigenous.source_text: Published ethnobotanical literature with documented Bundjalung community involvement; Lassak & McCarthy (1983); Brophy et al. (CSIRO)
australian_indigenous.original: [Bundjalung oral tradition, documented with community consent] The leaves of the paperbark tree were crushed and inhaled for coughs and colds. Crushed leaves were applied to cuts, burns, and infected skin. The swamps where Melaleuca grew were known as healing places — people bathed in the water to treat skin conditions.
australian_indigenous.translation: Tea tree leaves crushed and inhaled for respiratory conditions. Leaf poultice applied to wounds, cuts, burns, and skin infections. Bathing in natural Melaleuca swamps for skin disease. This use was documented by the Bundjalung people of northern New South Wales with their involvement in the research process.
australian_indigenous.preparation: Leaves crushed for inhalation; poultice of crushed leaves applied to skin; bathing in swamps
australian_indigenous.condition: Wound infection, skin disease, respiratory conditions
australian_indigenous.notes: ⚠️ This entry documents knowledge already in the published academic record with documented community involvement. The Bundjalung people's use of tea tree was documented by ethnobotanists in collaboration with the community. The commercialisation of tea tree oil is a case study in both successful traditional-to-pharmaceutical transfer and the complex intellectual property questions around indigenous knowledge — the Bundjalung community received no compensation for the global tea tree oil industry.

modern_research.summary: Tea tree oil is extensively validated as a topical antimicrobial — effective against S. aureus (including some MRSA strains), Candida, herpes simplex, and numerous other pathogens. European Pharmacopoeia standard exists. Used in licensed wound care products, acne preparations, and nail fungal treatments globally.
modern_research.significance: Represents both the extraordinary pharmacological richness of Aboriginal plant knowledge and the complex ethics of indigenous intellectual property: a traditional remedy now constituting a global industry worth hundreds of millions of dollars annually, with essentially no benefit flowing to the Bundjalung community who identified and used the plant for millennia.

plants.evidence_authority: Terpinen-4-ol — FDA approved in OTC antiseptic products; TGA (Australia) approved

corpus_links.title: Tea Tree (Melaleuca alternifolia): Bundjalung Traditional Uses and Pharmacological Profile
corpus_links.original: Melaleuca alternifolia — Tea Tree. Published ethnobotanical record with documented Bundjalung community involvement. From Lassak & McCarthy, Australian Medicinal Plants (1983) and Brophy et al., CSIRO Plant Industry. Bundjalung people, northern New South Wales: Leaves crushed and used as inhalant for coughs, colds, and headaches. Crushed leaves applied as poultice to wounds, cuts, burns, and skin
corpus_links.translation: Melaleuca alternifolia — Tea Tree. This is a published ethnobotanical record with documented involvement of the Bundjalung community. Sources: Lassak & McCarthy, Australian Medicinal Plants (1983), and Brophy et al., CSIRO Plant Industry. The Bundjalung people of northern New South Wales crushed the leaves and used them as an inhalant [inhalant therapy] for coughs, colds, and headaches. Crushed leaves were also applied as a poultice [topical compress] to wounds, cuts, burns, and skin infections. Bathing in streams and pools where Melaleuca trees grew was recognised as therapeutic — these were understood to be healing waters. Traditional preparation methods: fresh leaves crushed between the hands and inhaled directly; alternatively, leaves were wrapped around the wound site. Note: This docu

kampo.source_text: Honzo Wamyo (本草和名, 918 CE); Daio-kanzoto formula in Ishinho (984 CE)
kampo.original: 大黄、和名 加波良久佐。性寒、味苦。主下瘀血、血閉、蕩滌腸胃、推陳致新。
kampo.translation: Daio (rhubarb), Japanese name Kawarakusa. Nature: cold. Taste: bitter. Primary uses: dispels static blood, opens blocked blood, flushes and purges the intestines and stomach, eliminates the old and generates the new. Kampo preparation: shorter cooking time than Chinese tradition preserves cathartic anthraquinones; longer cooking destroys them, producing only astringent/anti-inflammatory effect. This cooking-time distinction was documented empirically in Kampo centuries before the active compounds were identified.
kampo.preparation: Root decocted 3–12g; cooking time determines effect — short = laxative, long = anti-inflammatory
kampo.condition: Constipation, intestinal inflammation, blood stasis conditions
kampo.notes: Kampo's empirical discovery that cooking time changes rhubarb's clinical effect (short cooking = cathartic, long cooking = astringent) is a precise pharmacological observation: anthraquinone glycosides (cathartic) are heat-labile; tannins (astringent) are heat-stable. This distinction was not understood chemically until the 19th century.

modern_research.key_compound: Anthraquinone glycosides (sennoside A, B), tannins, stilbenes (rhapontigenin)
modern_research.summary: Rhubarb root is official in multiple modern pharmacopeias. Sennosides A and B are active cathartic compounds also found in senna — both now pharmaceutical. Rhubarb compounds show hepatoprotective, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory activity in research. Used in Japanese intensive care for preventing bacterial translocation in ICU patients.
modern_research.significance: Kampo's cooking-time-dependent effect distinction — cathartic if undercooked, astringent if fully cooked — is one of the most precise empirical pharmacological observations in traditional medicine, predating understanding of anthraquinone heat lability by centuries.

plants.evidence_authority: Sennosides — FDA approved OTC laxative (senna/rhubarb); in USP

corpus_links.label: SBC.Middle.1
corpus_links.title: Dahuang (Rhubarb) — the great purgative
corpus_links.original: 大黃：味苦，寒。主下瘀血，血閉，寒熱，破癥瘕積聚，留飲宿食，蕩滌腸胃，推陳致新，通利水穀，調中化食，安和五臟。
corpus_links.translation: Dahuang (rhubarb): flavor bitter, cold. Principally drives out static blood, blood obstructions, chills and fever, breaks up abdominal masses and accumulations, retained fluids and old food, flushes the intestines and stomach, pushes out the old and brings in the new, promotes movement of water and grain, regulates the center and transforms food, and pacifies and harmonizes the five organs. Rhubarb root is one of the most important plants in Chinese medicine. The same plant genus (Rheum) is MMA-030 (Japanese Rhubarb/Daio) in the Kampo tradition — convergence confirmed across Chinese and Japanese traditional medicine.
corpus_links.preparation: Decoction (brief cooking preserves purgative effect); Da Cheng Qi Tang compound
corpus_links.condition: Constipation, abdominal masses, blood stasis conditions, fever with constipation

corpus_links.label: Canon.Book2.Rhubarb
corpus_links.title: Rawand (Rhubarb) — liver and purgative
corpus_links.original: الراوند: حار يابس في الثانية. يقوي الكبد والمعدة.
corpus_links.translation: Rhubarb: hot and dry in the second degree. It strengthens the liver and stomach. Ibn Sina documents rhubarb root for liver conditions and as a moderate purgative — extending the convergence signal for rhubarb (already in the archive as Kampo's Daio/MMA-030 and Chinese Bencaojing's Dahuang) to include Unani as a fourth tradition. The Canon's documentation of rhubarb for liver conditions specifically connects to the anthraquinone mechanism — anthraquinones stimulate bile production (choleretic activity) which validates the liver-strengthening traditional claim.
corpus_links.preparation: Root powder in warm water; combined with other herbs in compound preparations
corpus_links.condition: Liver weakness, constipation, digestive conditions, jaundice

corpus_links.label: HK.Shiso
corpus_links.title: Shiso (Perilla) — the Japanese aromatic medicine
corpus_links.original: 紫蘇：胃を温め、気を巡らせる。魚の中毒に効く
corpus_links.translation: Shiso (Perilla frutescens): warms the stomach, circulates qi. Effective for fish poisoning. Kaibara Ekken documents shiso alongside wasabi for food poisoning — the two plants that form the traditional Japanese antimicrobial pairing with raw fish. Modern research: perillaldehyde and rosmarinic acid in shiso show documented antimicrobial activity against Salmonella and other food pathogens. Additionally, luteolin in shiso has documented anti-allergic activity — consistent with its traditional Japanese use for urticaria (hives) and food allergies.
corpus_links.preparation: Fresh leaves with raw fish; leaf tea for digestive conditions; seed oil for skin
corpus_links.condition: Food poisoning prevention, allergic skin reactions, digestive complaints

corpus_links.label: HK.Kuzu
corpus_links.title: Kuzu (Kudzu) — the Japanese starch medicine
corpus_links.original: 葛：発汗させ、熱を冷ます。葛根湯は風邪の薬として有名である
corpus_links.translation: Kuzu (kudzu root, Pueraria lobata): promotes sweating, cools heat. Kakkonto (Kudzu Root Decoction) is famous as a medicine for the common cold. Kaibara documents kuzu as a uniquely important Japanese medicine — the Kakkonto formula (kudzu + cinnamon + peony + ginger + jujube + licorice + ephedra) is the most prescribed Kampo formula in Japan today, available OTC and extensively clinically tested. This entry connects to the Bencao Gangmu documentation of gegen/kudzu, extending the convergence to include the Japanese Honzō Kōmoku as a separate source.
corpus_links.preparation: Kakkonto compound decoction; kuzu starch (kuzuko) in hot water as digestive
corpus_links.condition: Common cold (early stage), fever, neck stiffness, respiratory infections

corpus_links.label: honzo_wamyo::keishi_cinnamon
corpus_links.title: Keishi (Cinnamon Twig): Uses in Classical Japanese and Kampo Medicine
corpus_links.original: 桂枝 (Keishi / Gui Zhi) — Cinnamomum cassia (young twigs). Honzo Wamyo: 桂枝、和名 加爾。辛、温。主上気咳逆、結気喉痺吐吸、利関節、補中益気。Keishi, Japanese name Kani. Pungent, warm. Primary uses: descends rebellious qi, stops coughing, opens constricted qi in throat, facilitates movement in the joints, tonifies the middle and benefits qi. Yoshimasu Todo (18th c. Koho school): Keishi is the primary herb for dispelling cold from the
corpus_links.translation: Keishi [桂枝, also romanized from Chinese as Gui Zhi] — the young twigs of Cinnamomum cassia. According to the Honzō Wamyō [本草和名, a classical Japanese materia medica]: 'Keishi; Japanese name, Kani. [Flavor:] pungent; [nature:] warm. Principal indications: counterflow ascent of qi [上気] with coughing and rebellious breath; constricted qi [結気] causing throat obstruction [喉痺] with difficult respiration; promotes free movement in the joints; tonifies the middle burner and augments qi.' Yoshimasu Tōdō (18th century, Kohō school of Kampo): Keishi is the foremost herb for expelling cold from the body's exterior and warming the channels and vessels. The formula Keishi-bukuryō-gan [桂枝茯苓丸] — combining cinnamon twig with Poria (hoelen fungus) — is a documented Kampo compound preparation used for pelvic

corpus_links.label: honzo_wamyo::toki_angelica
corpus_links.title: Toki (Dang Gui / Japanese Angelica): Uses, Properties, and Botanical Identity
corpus_links.original: 当帰 (Toki / Dang Gui) — Angelica acutiloba (Japanese species distinct from Chinese A. sinensis). Honzo Wamyo: 当帰、和名 也末止己呂。甘辛、温。主咳逆上気、温瘧寒熱洒洒在皮膚中、婦人漏下絶子、諸悪瘡瘍、金創。
corpus_links.translation: Toki [当帰, also known by the Chinese name Dang Gui]. Japanese name: Yamatorokoro [也末止己呂]. Flavor: sweet-pungent; thermal quality: warm. Principal indications: cough with rebellious qi [counterflow ascent of breath]; warm malaria [温瘧] with alternating cold and heat pervading the skin; women's uterine spotting [漏下, lit. 'dripping downward'] accompanied by infertility; all malign sores and ulcers [諸悪瘡瘍]; and wounds from metal implements [金創, i.e., cuts or punctures from bladed or metal weapons/tools]. Note: Japanese Kampo [traditional Japanese medicine] employs Angelica acutiloba rather than the Chinese Angelica sinensis — a deliberate botanical distinction developed during Japan's Edo period of relative isolation — reflecting Japanese clinical observation that the local species possessed dist

corpus_links.label: BGM.Dahuang
corpus_links.title: Dahuang (Rhubarb) — the general who clears the way
corpus_links.original: 大黃：苦，寒，無毒。下瘀血⋯蕩滌腸胃，推陳致新，有將軍之號。
corpus_links.translation: Dahuang (rhubarb): bitter, cold, non-toxic. Drives out static blood... flushes the intestines and stomach, pushes out the old and brings in the new. It has the name 'General.' Li Shizhen's epithet for rhubarb — 'General' (Jiangjun) — reflects its potent, direct pharmacological action contrasting with licorice's harmonizing role. The fourth major tradition documenting rhubarb root (after Kampo/Daio, Shennong Bencaojing, and Unani Canon), cementing Rheum species as one of the most cross-validated purgative genera in world medicine.

corpus_links.label: HK.Intro
corpus_links.title: Kaibara Ekken's project — adapting Chinese medicine to Japanese nature
corpus_links.original: 大和本草：日本の植物と中国の本草を比較して、日本固有の植物を記述した
corpus_links.translation: Yamato Honzō: comparing Japanese plants with Chinese materia medica, documenting plants unique to Japan. Kaibara Ekken (1630–1714) undertook a systematic field survey of Japanese medicinal plants, comparing them with the Chinese Bencao Gangmu and identifying: (1) Japanese plants equivalent to Chinese ones, (2) Japanese endemic plants not in the Chinese materia medica, and (3) Chinese plants that do not grow in Japan. This empirical approach — field verification over textual tradition — was revolutionary in Edo period Japan and established the foundation for modern Japanese pharmacognosy. His work documents approximately 1,362 plants.

kampo.source_text: Honzo Wamyo (918 CE); Sho-saiko-to formula, Ishinho (984 CE)
kampo.original: 柴胡、和名 美之末。苦、平。主心腹腸胃中結気、寒熱邪気、推陳致新。
kampo.translation: Saikou (Bupleurum), Japanese name Mishima. Bitter, neutral. Main: constricted qi in heart/abdomen/intestines, alternating cold and heat from pathogens, eliminates old and generates new. Sho-saiko-to (Minor Bupleurum Decoction): the most extensively studied Kampo formula for hepatitis. Multiple large Japanese RCTs demonstrated reduction in liver inflammation markers, HBsAg levels, and liver cancer risk in cirrhotic patients. Contraindication discovered 1994: combined with interferon causes severe interstitial pneumonia — a post-marketing pharmacovigilance discovery that became a model for herb-drug interaction monitoring.
kampo.preparation: Root decocted 5–8g; Sho-saiko-to combines with 6 other herbs
kampo.condition: Chronic hepatitis, liver inflammation, alternating fever/chills, depression
kampo.notes: The 1994 Sho-saiko-to / interferon interaction discovery is the most important herb-drug interaction case in Kampo pharmacovigilance history — it led to mandatory warning labels and a model for monitoring traditional medicine drug interactions in Japan's national health system.

modern_research.key_compound: Saikosaponins (a, b1, b2, c, d), bupleurumol
modern_research.summary: Saikosaponins have documented anti-inflammatory activity via glucocorticoid receptor modulation, hepatoprotective effects, and antiviral activity against HBV. Sho-saiko-to: multiple Japanese RCTs for chronic hepatitis B/C showing significant reduction in liver fibrosis markers. Also emerging research for depression via HPA axis modulation.
modern_research.significance: Represents the most rigorously studied Kampo formula with both positive clinical evidence (hepatoprotection) and a critical safety signal (interferon interaction) — making it a model for how traditional medicine evidence should be evaluated: both efficacy and safety, with pharmacovigilance taken seriously.

plants.evidence_authority: Saikosaponins — Cochrane/systematic reviews on Sho-saiko-to for hepatitis
plants.priority_reason: 7 independent traditions agree · Cochrane reviewed but no drug approval · condition affects hundreds of millions

corpus_links.label: SBC.Middle.3
corpus_links.title: Chaihu (Bupleurum) — fever mediator
corpus_links.original: 柴胡：味苦，平。主心腹，去腸胃中結氣，飲食積聚，寒熱邪氣，推陳致新。
corpus_links.translation: Chaihu (Bupleurum): flavor bitter, neutral. Principally [treats conditions of] the heart and abdomen, eliminates accumulated qi in the intestines and stomach, food accumulation, chills and fever from pathogenic qi, pushes out the old and brings in the new. Bupleurum falcatum (saiko in Japanese / chaihu in Chinese) — the same plant as MMA-031 (Bupleurum/Saiko) in the Kampo tradition. The Shennong documentation adds Chinese traditional medicine as a second major Asian tradition documenting bupleurum for the same fever and digestive indications.
corpus_links.preparation: Xiao Chai Hu Tang compound (Minor Bupleurum Decoction) — most studied Chinese herbal formula
corpus_links.condition: Alternating chills and fever, liver conditions, digestive complaints, immune modulation

corpus_links.label: BGM.Chaihu
corpus_links.title: Chaihu (Bupleurum) — the Liver's messenger
corpus_links.original: 柴胡：苦，平，無毒。主心腹腸胃中結氣，飲食積聚，寒熱邪氣，推陳致新。
corpus_links.translation: Chaihu (Bupleurum): bitter, neutral, non-toxic. Principal uses: accumulated qi in the heart, abdomen, intestines, and stomach; food accumulation; pathogenic cold and heat qi; pushes out the old and brings in the new. Li Shizhen's expanded entry on bupleurum — already in the archive as Kampo/Saiko (MMA-031) and Shennong Bencaojing — adds significant detail on its use for liver qi stagnation and alternating chills and fever. The Xiao Chai Hu Tang formula (Minor Bupleurum Decoction) containing bupleurum as primary ingredient is the most studied Chinese herbal formula globally, with multiple RCTs.
corpus_links.preparation: Xiao Chai Hu Tang; Chai Hu Shu Gan San
corpus_links.condition: Alternating fever and chills, liver qi stagnation, digestive complaints, immune modulation

corpus_links.label: honzo_wamyo::saikou_bupleurum
corpus_links.title: Saikou (Bupleurum): Properties, Indications, and Uses in Honzo Wamyo
corpus_links.original: 柴胡、和名 美之末。苦、平。主心腹腸胃中結気、飲食積聚、寒熱邪気、推陳致新。久服輕身明目益精。
corpus_links.translation: Saikou [柴胡, Chai Hu], Japanese name Mishima [美之末]. Flavor: bitter; nature: neutral [平, balanced/temperate]. Primary indications: constricted qi [結気] in the region of the heart, abdomen, intestines, and stomach; accumulation and stagnation of food and drink [飲食積聚]; alternating cold and heat due to pathogenic qi [寒熱邪気]; eliminates the stale and promotes the new [推陳致新]. Prolonged use lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and replenishes essential vitality [益精].

corpus_links.label: honzo_wamyo::shosaikoto_formula
corpus_links.title: Sho-saiko-to (Minor Bupleurum Decoction): Classical Kampo Formula — Composition, Indications, and Ph
corpus_links.original: 小柴胡湯 (Sho-saiko-to) — Minor Bupleurum Decoction. Classical Kampo formula documented from earliest Japanese adaptation of Chinese medicine. Components: 柴胡 (Saikou/Bupleurum) 7g + 半夏 (Hange/Pinellia) 5g + 生姜 (Shokyo/Ginger) 4g + 黄芩 (Ogon/Scutellaria) 3g + 人参 (Ninjin/Ginseng) 3g + 甘草 (Kanzo/Licorice) 2g + 大棗 (Taiso/Jujube) 3g. Traditional indications: alternating fever and chills, bitter taste in mou
corpus_links.translation: Sho-saiko-to [Small Bupleurum Decoction; Chinese: Xiao Chai Hu Tang] — Minor Bupleurum Decoction. This is a classical Kampo [Japanese traditional medicine] compound formula, documented from the earliest period of Japanese adaptation of Chinese medical tradition. Constituent ingredients and standard dosages: Saikou [柴胡, Bupleurum root] 7 g; Hange [半夏, Pinellia rhizome] 5 g; Shokyo [生姜, fresh Ginger rhizome] 4 g; Ogon [黄芩, Scutellaria root] 3 g; Ninjin [人参, Ginseng root] 3 g; Kanzo [甘草, Licorice root] 2 g; Taiso [大棗, Jujube fruit] 3 g. Traditional indications [as recognised in classical Kampo nosology]: alternating fever and chills [a 'Shao-yang stage' [少陽病] presentation], bitter taste in the mouth, dry throat, nausea, and a sensation of fullness in the chest and hypochondriac [subcostal] re

tibetan.source_text: Gyushi (rGyud bzhi), Chapter on mountain medicines; Men-Tsee-Khang formulary
tibetan.translation: Arura — the king of medicines. Beneficial for all diseases. Called the medicine of gods and demons. Possesses all five tastes (sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, astringent — only salt absent). Therefore can treat all three humors. Long-term use extends life and sharpens the mind. The Three Fruits formula (Arura + Baru + Kyuru) is the foundation of Tibetan pharmacology.
tibetan.preparation: Fruit dried and powdered; taken with different vehicles depending on condition — warm water, honey, molasses, or butter
tibetan.condition: All diseases (general tonic); specifically digestive disorders, respiratory conditions, wound healing

ayurveda.translation: Haritaki — destroyer of all diseases. One of the most important herbs in Ayurveda; used in Triphala formula (same Three Fruits concept as Tibetan medicine). Specifically valuable for eye diseases, digestive disorders, and as a rejuvenating rasayana.
ayurveda.preparation: Fruit powdered; taken as Triphala with warm water before bed
ayurveda.condition: Digestive disorders, eye disease, constipation, aging

modern_research.key_compound: Chebulagic acid, chebulinic acid, corilagin, gallic acid, ellagic acid
modern_research.summary: Chebulagic acid and chebulinic acid show documented antiviral activity against HSV-1, HSV-2, and HIV integrase inhibition in vitro. Antimicrobial against MRSA. Strong antioxidant. Triphala (three myrobalans) has clinical evidence for constipation, weight loss, and dental health (mouthwash trials).
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Tibetan and Ayurvedic traditions independently developed the same Three Fruits formula (Triphala / Arura-Baru-Kyuru) using the same primary ingredient — Terminalia chebula — for overlapping indications. This convergence between two neighboring high-altitude civilizations is strong, and connects further to Australian Indigenous use of Terminalia ferdinandiana — three independent traditions identifying the Terminalia genus as uniquely medicinally important.

corpus_links.label: CS.Chik.5
corpus_links.title: Gulma Chikitsa — abdominal tumors and digestive masses
corpus_links.original: हिङ्ग्वादयः गुल्मघ्नाः। अग्निमान्द्यहरा वायुलोमाः।
corpus_links.translation: Asafoetida (hingu) and others destroy abdominal masses. They overcome sluggish digestion and promote downward movement of wind. Asafoetida (Ferula asafoetida) is documented as the primary medicine for gulma — abdominal masses, which may correspond to tumors, cysts, or severe digestive disorders. The antispasmodic and carminative properties of asafoetida are well-established. This chapter also documents long pepper for digestive complaints and haritaki for constipation-related gulma.
corpus_links.preparation: Asafoetida compound preparations in sesame oil; taken after meals
corpus_links.condition: Abdominal masses, digestive disorders, flatulence, constipation

corpus_links.original: ཨ་རུ་ར། (Arura) — Terminalia chebula (Chebulic myrobalan). Considered the king of all medicines in Tibetan medical tradition. corpus_links.translation: Arura (ཨ་རུ་ར།) — Terminalia chebula (Chebulic myrobalan). Regarded as the king of all medicines within the Tibetan medical tradition. From the Gyushi [rGyud bzhi, the Four Tantras, the foundational Tibetan medical canon]: 'Arura is the king of medicines. It is beneficial for all diseases. It is called the medicine of gods and demons [lha bdud kyi sman].' Properties: all five tastes [ro lnga] are present — sour [skyur], sweet [mngar], bitter [kha ba], pungent [tsha ba], and astringent [bska ba] — with only salt [lan tshwa] absent. On account of possessing these five tastes, arura may be employed in the treatment of all three humors [nyes pa gsum]: Wind [rlung], Bile [mkhris pa], and Phlegm [bad kan]. corpus_links.original: སྐྱུ་རུ་ར། (Kyuru / Baru) — Terminalia bellirica / T. belerica (Belleric myrobalan) and Phyllanthus emblica (Amla / Amalaki). Two of the Three Fruits combination. Kyuru-ra [སྐྱུ་རུ་ར།] (Kyuru / Baru): Refers collectively to two of the Three Fruits [Tibetan: 'Drupa Gsum']: Terminalia bellirica (Belleric myrobalan; Tibetan: Baru) and Phyllanthus emblica (Amla / Amalaki; Tibetan: Kyuru).

corpus_links.translation: Rinchen Rilbu — 'Precious Pills' [Tibetan: རིན་ཆེན་རིལ་བུ།]: The most complex and celebrated formulas in Tibetan medicine. The Gyushi [Four Tantras, the foundational Tibetan medical canon] references a group of three Precious Pills [རིན་ཆེན་རིལ་བུ་གསུམ་]: Ratna Sampel (25 ingredients), Rinchen Drangjor (25 ingredients), and Bedu Kar 25 (25 ingredients). corpus_links.label: CS.Sutra.4
corpus_links.title: Shadvirechanashatashritiya — the 500 purgative plants
corpus_links.original: विरेचनोपगानां शतानि पञ्च — पिप्पली, पिप्पलीमूल, चव्य, चित्रक, शृङ्गवेर...
corpus_links.translation: The five hundred [groups of] purgative plants — long pepper, long pepper root, chavya, chitraka, dried ginger root... Charaka Chapter 4 (Shadvirechanashatashritiya) is one of the most important pharmacological chapters in classical Ayurveda, listing plants in 50 groups of 10 by therapeutic action. The groups cover: purgatives (virechana), emetics (vamana), nasal medications (nasya), enemas (basti), and external applications (lepa).

corpus_links.title: Rasayana — rejuvenation therapy and life extension
corpus_links.original: लभते ह्यायुर्मेधां बलं आरोग्यं सुखं च। रसायनं प्रयोक्तव्यं...
corpus_links.translation: One obtains longevity, memory, strength, freedom from disease, and happiness [through rasayana]. Rasayana therapy should be administered... Rasayana (literally 'path of rasa/essence') is Ayurveda's systematic anti-aging and rejuvenation system — the most sophisticated traditional longevity medicine in any world tradition. The primary rasayana plants include: Ashwagandha, Shatavari, Brahmi, Guduchi, and the Triphala combination. All are now extensively studied for adaptogenic and anti-aging properties.

corpus_links.label: CS.Kalpa.2
corpus_links.title: Virechana Dravya — purgative plants for panchakarma
corpus_links.original: त्रिवृत् विरेचनानामुत्तमा। दन्ती दन्तीमूलञ्च।
corpus_links.translation: Trivrit (Operculina turpethum) is the foremost of purgatives. Danti (Baliospermum montanum) and the root of danti also [serve as purgatives]. The purgative chapter documents 29 plants for the virechana stage of panchakarma. Trivrit is used for the same conditions as senna and cascara in other traditions — a convergence for laxative/purgative plants across all major medical traditions.

corpus_links.label: CS.Plant.Triphala
corpus_links.title: Triphala — the three fruits, Ayurveda's most important compound
corpus_links.original: आमलकी विभीतकं हरीतकी च — त्रयो मध्यस्था। त्रिफला रसायनी।
corpus_links.translation: Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica), vibhitaka (Terminalia bellirica), and haritaki (Terminalia chebula) — these three are moderate in nature. Triphala is a rasayana. Triphala — the combination of three fruits — is the single most prescribed compound in Ayurvedic medicine. Charaka documents it for: constipation, eye conditions, liver conditions, skin diseases, diabetes, obesity, and as a general rasayana. All three fruits are individually significant — haritaki is Ayurveda's single most important medicinal plant (documented in 49 chapters of Charaka).

Aboriginal groups of the Northern Territory and Western Australia: Small sour fruit eaten fresh and dried. Used for its fortifying and disease-preventing properties — described as 'medicine food' rather than s
corpus_links.translation: Kakadu Plum (Terminalia ferdinandiana) — also known by the Aboriginal names Gubinge and Murunga. Source: published scientific literature (Netzel et al. 2007, Journal of Food Composition and Analysis; Gong et al. 2018, multiple papers). Among Aboriginal groups of the Northern Territory and Western Australia, this small, sour fruit is consumed both fresh and dried. It is employed for its fortifying [tonic] and disease-preventing properties, and is characterised as a 'medicine food' [medicinal foodstuff], reflecting a tradition that does not draw a sharp boundary between food and medicine — a paradigm consistent with traditional pharmacopeias worldwide. maya.source_text: Ritual of the Bacabs (Roys 1965); documented Maya ethnobotany
maya.original: Ix-pom — ku ts'o'okol u yik'nal nabal naab. Ku yilaj ti' máak ku k'iinikil.
maya.translation: Ix-pom (copal) — it extinguishes the burning of the skin [infected wound]. It is used to treat sick persons. Burned as incense in healing ceremonies and applied directly as resin to infected wounds and sores. The Maya specifically distinguished between copal burned as incense (ritual/respiratory use) and copal applied as resin (wound use) — recognising different preparations for different applications.
maya.preparation: Resin applied directly to wounds; burned as incense for respiratory and ritual use
maya.condition: Wound infection, respiratory conditions, ritual healing

cobo.source_text: Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Book VI, cap. CVI — translated in this archive
cobo.original: De las demás especies de copal — eight species of copal-producing trees documented
cobo.translation: Eight distinct copal-producing tree species documented by Cobo across New Spain, each with antimicrobial and medicinal resin. Multiple species independently noted for treating dysentery when dissolved in water and cacao.
cobo.preparation: Resin dissolved in water and cacao (internal); burned as incense (inhalation)
cobo.condition: Dysentery, wound infection, general medicinal

modern_research.key_compound: Boswellic acids (Boswellia — related Burseraceae), alpha-pinene, limonene, incensole acetate
modern_research.summary: Burseraceae resins broadly show antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory activity. Incensole acetate (from frankincense/Boswellia) shows neuroprotective and anxiolytic effects in animal models — may explain ritual calming effects. Boswellic acids (related species) have clinical evidence for osteoarthritis and inflammatory bowel disease.
modern_research.significance: MAXIMUM MESOAMERICAN CONVERGENCE: Maya, Aztec (Badianus + Florentine), and Andean (Cobo) traditions all independently documented Burseraceae resins for wound infection and respiratory use. This represents the strongest within-Americas convergence signal in the archive. The connection to Greek/Roman frankincense (Boswellia, same family) extends the signal globally.

plants.evidence_authority: Boswellic acids — systematic reviews; Boswellia approved in EU as orphan drug for brain tumors
plants.priority_reason: 9 independent civilisations independently documented this · condition burden is critical · compound identified but no clinical trials
