CAPITULO LXXXIV
De la tecoma haca

Este es un árbol que tiene las hojas redondas, y aserradas; lleva un fruto redondo, pequeño y rojo lleno de simientes semejantes a las pepitas del durazno. Es planta mordaz y odorífera, cortando este árbol mana dél una goma como la del copal, muy provechosa, que la suelen usar en lugar de la mirra y en la cura de muchas enfermedades, y principalmente corrige las
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIV
Of the Tecoma Haca

This is a tree with round, serrated leaves; it bears a small, round, red fruit full of seeds resembling the pits of the peach [durazno]. It is a pungent and fragrant plant; when this tree is cut, a gum [resin] flows from it similar to that of copal, which is very beneficial and is commonly used in place of myrrh in the treatment of many ailments. It principally corrects cold imbalances [destemplanzas frías] and fortifies the stomach. This tree grows in the hot lands [tierra caliente] of New Spain.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CV
On Copal

The copal tree is large; its leaves resemble those of the holm oak [encina], except that they are longer; its fruit is round and tends toward red; it has the same flavor as the gum that flows from the tree, which sometimes exudes spontaneously and at other times by making incisions [sajando] in the tree. This congealed resin [licor cuajado] is white and transparent, good for fumigations [sahumerios], by means of which headache is relieved, and it is a remedy for all ailments arising from a cold cause [causa fría]; and all the various kinds of copal, of which there are many, do the same. Ritual of the Bacabs (Roys trans.): 'Ix-pom, ix-cacao, ix-ya-che — copal, cacao tree, sapodilla tree — these are the medicines of the great healers.' Copal (pom) was both ritual and medicinal in Maya culture — a distinction the tradition did not draw as sharply as Western medicine. Medicinal uses documented: antimicrobial wound treatment
corpus_links.translation: Pom (Bursera copallifera / B. bipinnata) — Maya Copal Resin. From the Ritual of the Bacabs (translated by Roys): 'Ix-pom, ix-cacao, ix-ya-che — copal, cacao tree, sapodilla tree — these are the medicines of the great healers.' In Maya culture, copal (pom) served simultaneously as a ritual substance and a medicinal one — a distinction the tradition did not draw as sharply as Western medicine does. Documented medicinal uses include: antimicrobial wound treatment (resin applied directly to infected wounds); pain relief (smoke inhaled for headache); and treatment of respiratory conditions (resin burned in an enclosed space and the smoke inhaled). celtic_norse.source_text: Bald's Leechbook I (Cockayne vol.1, c.900 CE); Lacnunga
celtic_norse.original: Wið untrumnesse, genim þeos wyrt ðe man betonicam nemneþ, gebræd on buteran, smire mid.
celtic_norse.translation: For sickness, take this plant called betonica, cooked in butter, smear with it. For monstrous nocturnal visitors and frightful sights and dreams — betonica applied. For sore of eyes, for sore of ears, for dimness of eyes, for strong blood-running from the nose, for toothache, for sore of side, for sore of belly — betonica used throughout. The Leechbook devotes its entire first chapter to betonica, listing 29 specific medical indications — the most uses attributed to any single plant in the Anglo-Saxon medical tradition.
celtic_norse.preparation: Leaves cooked in butter and applied topically; decocted in ale or water for internal use; dried and powdered
celtic_norse.condition: Head pain, digestive disorders, respiratory, anxiety/nightmares, wound healing (29 documented indications)
celtic_norse.notes: Betony's 29 documented indications in Bald's Leechbook make it the most multi-purpose plant in Anglo-Saxon medicine. The inclusion of anxiety and nightmares among its indications ('monstrous nocturnal visitors') is noteworthy — betony has mild sedative activity that may account for its traditional use for sleep disturbance and anxiety.

greek_roman.original: Betonica — herba salutaris, omnibus morbis medetur.
greek_roman.translation: Betonica — a health-bringing herb, it cures all diseases. Roman soldiers used it as a general tonic and head medicine. Applied for headache, for bites of venomous animals, for fever.
greek_roman.preparation: Dried and powdered in wine; applied as poultice
greek_roman.condition: Headache, fever, snakebite, general tonic

modern_research.summary: Limited modern research. Rosmarinic acid (anti-inflammatory, antioxidant) is shared with rosemary, sage, and other Lamiaceae — likely responsible for some traditional effects. Stachydrine shows cardioprotective activity in animal models. Traditional use for anxiety and sleep disturbance not well studied despite historical prominence.
modern_research.significance: The convergence between Anglo-Saxon and Roman documentation of betony as a multi-purpose medicine — independently identified by two traditions for overlapping conditions — warrants more systematic investigation than it has received. The gap between its historical prominence and modern research attention makes it a priority research candidate.

celtic_norse.source_text: Bald's Leechbook (Cockayne vol.1, c.900 CE); Nine Herbs Charm (Lacnunga)
celtic_norse.original: Ond þu, wegbrade, wyrta modor, eastan openige, innan mihtigu; ofer ðe crætu curran, ofer ðe cwene reodan.
celtic_norse.translation: And you, waybread (plantain), mother of plants, open from the east, mighty within; over you carts have rolled, over you queens have ridden. [Nine Herbs Charm, Lacnunga]. Wound applications: leaves applied directly to wounds to stop bleeding and prevent infection. Leaf poultice for insect stings, burns. Leaf decoction drunk for cough and diarrhea. The Nine Herbs Charm positions waybread as one of the nine most important medicinal plants — alongside mugwort, stinging nettle, and cress.

celtic_norse.condition: Wound infection and bleeding, cough, diarrhea, insect stings

greek_roman.translation: Plantain — cleanses and closes wounds. Leaves applied to old ulcers and wounds hasten healing. Juice drunk for bloody flux and for kidney disease.
greek_roman.preparation: Fresh leaves applied topically; juice extracted
greek_roman.condition: Wound healing, dysentery, kidney conditions

modern_research.summary: Aucubin shows anti-inflammatory activity. Allantoin promotes wound healing (also found in comfrey). Mucilage soothes mucous membranes — validates respiratory use. Multiple studies showing plantain leaf extract reduces wound healing time. Antimicrobial activity against common pathogens.
modern_research.significance: GLOBAL CONVERGENCE: Plantago major spread worldwide with European colonization — Native American peoples called it 'white man's footprint' because it appeared wherever Europeans settled, and then adopted it into their own medicine for identical uses (wound healing, cough). This makes Plantago a unique case: cross-tradition convergence happened in real time and was historically documented, creating a natural experiment confirming the wound-healing effect across independent observers.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXI

Del cacaloxochitl.

Muchos árboles nacen en estas Indias que no llevan otro fruto sino flores muy vistosas. Describiré aquí los más conocidos y estimados por la hermosura de sus flores; que de todos es imposible hacer memoria. Y sea el primero el árbol que produce la flor llamada cacaloxochitl, en la Nueva España; el cual es muy parecido a la adelfa, poco copado, y que no tiene hoja
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXI

On the Cacaloxochitl.

Many trees grow in these Indies that bear no other fruit than very showy flowers. I shall describe here the best known and most prized for the beauty of their blossoms, for it is impossible to record them all. Let the first be the tree that produces the flower called cacaloxochitl in New Spain. It closely resembles the oleander [adelfa], has a sparse crown, and bears leaves only at the growing tips [cogollos]; these leaves are a hand's breadth or more in length and very similar to those of the oleander. The tree is of medium size, like a pomegranate tree; and it is a noteworthy thing that its fruit, so to speak, is the flowering it produces throughout the entire year. Each flower resembles a rose, though considerably smaller, yet larger than a carnation

persian_zoroastrian.source_text: Avesta, Yasna hymns 9-11 (Hom Yasht); Vendidad; Bundahishn
persian_zoroastrian.original: Haoma — yō zaothrābyo paiti.vīsaiti | yō ashāum haomō fravaōiti. (Yasna 9.1) Haoma gave strength, Haoma gave victory, Haoma gave children.
persian_zoroastrian.translation: Haoma — you who come to the libations, you who are sacred haoma. Haoma, pressed by the mortar, mixed with milk and water, drunk in the sacred ritual. Haoma drives away death, gives strength to warriors, gives children to women, gives wisdom to the priest. The Hom Yasht (Yasna 9-11) dedicates three full hymns to haoma — more ritual attention than any other plant in the Avestan corpus. Bundahishn natural history: haoma grows on the mountain Alburz, the cosmic mountain. Its pressing and preparation require specific ritual conditions. Effects documented: increased mental clarity, reduced fatigue, heightened spiritual awareness, physical endurance.
persian_zoroastrian.preparation: Stems pressed by mortar, juice extracted, mixed with milk and water, consumed ritually
persian_zoroastrian.condition: Fatigue, weakness, spiritual purification, fertility, battle preparation
persian_zoroastrian.notes: The identification of haoma as Ephedra is not universal — alternative candidates include Peganum harmala (Syrian rue, containing harmaline — an MAO inhibitor), Sarcostemma species, or Cannabis. The debate mirrors the Vedic Soma controversy (same plant, different linguistic tradition). If haoma = Ephedra, the active compound is ephedrine — a stimulant consistent with the documented effects (energy, endurance, mental clarity). If haoma = Peganum harmala, the MAO-inhibiting beta-carbolines would explain the visionary/spiritual effects. The most pharmacologically satisfying interpretation may be a mixture: Ephedra providing stimulant effects, with MAO-inhibiting additions for the visionary component — a sophisticated empirical discovery paralleling ayahuasca's MAOi combination.

modern_research.key_compound: Ephedrine, pseudoephedrine (if Ephedra); harmaline, harmine (if Peganum harmala)
modern_research.summary: If Ephedra: ephedrine is pharmacologically confirmed as a CNS stimulant and bronchodilator — consistent with documented haoma effects of endurance and clarity. If Peganum harmala: MAO inhibition confirmed, with documented psychoactive effects. Both interpretations are pharmacologically consistent with ancient texts. Modern Ephedra still used in Kampo (maōu) and Chinese medicine.
modern_research.significance: Haoma represents the oldest documented ritual pharmacological plant in the world — the Avestan hymns date to at least 1200 BCE, potentially much older. The pharmacological sophistication implied by haoma's documented effects (regardless of exact species identification) represents knowledge accumulated over millennia of empirical observation at the dawn of recorded civilization.

corpus_links.original: 麻黃：苦，溫，無毒。主中風傷寒頭痛，發表出汗，去邪熱氣，止咳逆上氣。
corpus_links.translation: Mahuang (ephedra): bitter, warm, non-toxic. Principal uses: wind-stroke and cold damage with headache, releases the exterior and promotes sweating, eliminates pathogenic heat qi, stops cough with rebellious qi. Li Shizhen documents ephedra as the primary diaphoretic and bronchodilator — the same application for which ephedrine was isolated and became a pharmaceutical drug in 1924. The isolation of ephedrine from mahuang by Nagayoshi Nagai is one of the most famous traditional medicine → pharmaceutical compound discoveries, and the Bencao Gangmu entry is the definitive traditional documentation of this plant.

Kampo clinical refineme
corpus_links.translation: Ma Huang [麻黄] — Japanese name: Umanokusa [宇末乃久佐]. Flavor: bitter; Temperament: warm. Principal indications: wind-cold [中風傷寒] with headache; warm malaria [温瘧]; promotion of sweating to expel exterior pathogens [發表出汗]; clearing of febrile heat [邪熱気]; arrest of coughing and rebellious rising qi [咳逆上気]; dispelling of alternating cold and heat [寒熱]; and breaking up of hard masses and accumulations [癥堅積聚]. Kampo clinical refinement: The physician Yoshimasu Todo observed that Japanese patients required lower doses than those prescribed in Chinese classical medical texts, and dosing was adjusted empirically over many generations of practice. The alkaloid ephedrine was first isolated from ma huang by the Japanese chemist Nagai Nagayoshi in 1885.

philippine.translation: Ampalaya — leaves and fruit cooked and eaten for diabetes ('sugar in the urine'). Also used for intestinal worms and fever. modern_research.summary: Multiple clinical trials including Philippine PIMS trial showing HbA1c reduction. Polypeptide-p has structural similarity to insulin. Charantin shown to stimulate insulin secretion. WHO traditional medicine guidelines cite ampalaya as having promising anti-diabetic evidence. Multiple meta-analyses: consistent blood glucose lowering effect, though large RCTs needed.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Philippine, Chinese, and Ayurvedic traditions independently documented bitter melon for blood sugar regulation — a triple convergence supporting a genuine pharmacological effect. The Philippine DOH formal registration for Type 2 diabetes represents one of the world's first government-backed traditional medicine approvals for a metabolic disease.

De la coaca

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXV
On the Coaca

The Indians make use of many kinds of herbs for sustenance, which, by a general name, the people of Peru call yayos [yuyos], and the Mexicans call quilites — as if we were to say garden greens or vegetables. Some of these have already been mentioned in the preceding chapters; in what remains of this book, others will be touched upon, of which the coaca is one. This is a herb resembling the sow-thistle [cerraja]; it grows about two cubits in height, more or less. The stalk is as thick as the little finger, round, green, hairy, and sticky. Each plant produces many stalks, and at their tops a great quantity of flowers the size and form of those of chamomile, except that the small petals encircling the bud are yellow. CAPITULO XXXVI
Del soycosoyco

El soycosoyco es una yerba menuda que parece especie de las rosas o davdlinas de las Indias; levántase un codo de la tierra; echa muchos tallos delgados, redondos, lisos, correosos y algún tanto rojos, y pocas hojas; las cuales son tan pequeñas y menudas, que parecen hebrillas de seda cortadas. Produce unas florecitas amarillas que cada una tiene cuatro hojuelas no m
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVI
On the Soycosoyco

The soycosoyco is a small herb that appears to be a species of the roses or carnations [davdlinas, i.e., davelinas/clavellinas] of the Indies. It rises about one cubit [roughly half a meter] above the ground, putting forth many thin, round, smooth, tough, and somewhat reddish stems, and few leaves; these leaves are so small and fine that they resemble little cut threads of silk. It produces small yellow flowers, each having four petals no larger than those of the flower of rue [Ruta graveolens], which emerge from small, elongated buds resembling pine nuts; and after these flowers dry, they end in a tuft of fibers issuing from the same bud. corpus_links.title: On the Cota and the Mullaca plants (Chapters XLIV–XLV)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLIV
De la cota

La cota es una yerba tan pequeña como el ctichuchu, que no parece sino una mancha verde en la tierra; no echa ramas ni tallos; sólo produce sobre la tierra sus hojas y flores; las hojas son semejantes a las del romero, salvo que son algo más larguillas, delgadas y tiernas. Hácense en el suelo grandes manchas de estas yerbas con las hojas y raíces muy juntas y apretadas un
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLIV
On the Cota

The cota is a small herb no larger than the ctichuchu [a small plant], which appears to be nothing more than a green patch on the ground; it puts forth neither branches nor stalks, producing only its leaves and flowers directly upon the earth. The leaves resemble those of rosemary, except that they are somewhat longer, thinner, and more tender. These plants form large patches on the ground, with their leaves and roots very closely and tightly packed together. They produce many flowers resembling in form those of chamomile [manzanilla]; they are a little larger, and the central button is neither as yellow nor as pointed; the small petals surrounding the center are white on the inner side, as in chamomile, and red on the underside. corpus_links.title: On the Misuca and Panti Flowers (Chapters LII–LIII)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LII
De la misuca

La misuca es una flor amarilla de tanto ruedo como un real de a cuatro y de la hechura de la flor de la manzanilla. La mata se levanta un codo de la tierra, echa muchos ramillos delgados, redondos, lisos y verdes; la hoja muy menuda y hendida, semejante a la de la artemisa.

Otra diferencia se halla de misuca muy parecida a ésta, salvo que los vastaguillos son algún tant
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LII
On the Misuca

The misuca is a yellow flower as wide in circumference as a four-real coin [roughly 3–4 cm across], and shaped like the flower of chamomile. The plant rises one cubit [approx. 45 cm] from the ground and puts out many thin, round, smooth, green little branches; the leaf is very small and cleft, resembling that of artemisia [mugwort].

Another variety of misuca is found, very similar to the first, except that the little stems are somewhat reddish and the leaves are like those of verbena, very finely serrated along the sides. The Indians call the first species the female, and the second the male; and with both they customarily dye [cloth or fiber] yellow. These flowers give off no scent whatsoever. In the Aymara language, both the flower and the plant are called mis

corpus_links.title: On the Chaneorama plant
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXVI

De la chaneorama

Esta es una yerba espinosa, cuyos tallos crecen un codo en alto, y son más delgados que el dedo meñique, redondos, macizos, de un verde blanquecino, cubiertos de un corto y delgado vello, que los hace algún tanto ásperos. Las hojas son largas una tercia y anchas un dedo, aserradas por los lados, armadas de espinas cortas, delgadas y agudas, que punzan. En el rema
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXVI

On the Chaneorama

This is a thorny herb whose stems grow to the height of one cubit [approximately 18 inches], and are thinner than the little finger, round, solid, of a whitish green color, covered in a short, fine down that makes them somewhat rough to the touch. The leaves are one-third of a vara [approximately 11 inches] in length and one finger's width wide, serrated along the edges, and armed with short, thin, sharp spines that prick. At the tips of the stems this herb produces white flowers, ten or twelve together on each stem, smaller than those of chamomile [manzanilla]. In the Aymara language this herb is called by this name.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_XXXIX
corpus_links.title: The Incavisa Plant
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXIX
De la incavisa

La incavisa es una mata que se levanta de la tierra tres o cuatro codos; echa muchas varas derechas tan gruesas como un dedo, correosas y algún tanto rojas; sus hojas son semejantes a las del sauce, salvo que son algo más cortas, angostas, tiernas, más gruesas y aserradas. Produce esta planta muchas flores juntas, las cuales son muy parecidas en el tamaño y figura a
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIX
On the Incavisa

The incavisa is a shrub that rises three or four cubits [roughly 4.5–6 feet] from the ground; it puts out many straight stems as thick as a finger, tough and somewhat reddish; its leaves resemble those of the willow, except that they are somewhat shorter, narrow, tender, thicker, and serrated. This plant produces many flowers together, which are very similar in size and shape to the chamomile flower; although the petals [literally: leaves] that encircle the little button are yellow, slightly larger, and not as closely set. This flower has a pleasant fragrance and an agreeable appearance; once it dries, it is succeeded by a thin veil or downy tuft [flocadura] that is carried away by the wind. This plant and its flower are called, in the Aymara language, incavi

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_L
corpus_links.title: The Sunchu plant: description, properties, and uses against snake venom
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO L
Del sunchu

El sunchu es un linaje de flores amarillas, que abraza algunas diferencias dellas muy parecidas todas entre sí en su figura, que es del talle de la flor de la manzanilla, y en la forma de la planta, que es una mata de un estado de alto, aromática y resinosa, la cual echa unas varas delgadas, redondas y algo rojas. Sus hojas son semejantes a las de la yerba-mora, y tocadas co
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER L
On the Sunchu

The sunchu is a genus of yellow-flowered plants, encompassing several varieties that are all very similar to one another in appearance: the shape of the flower resembles that of chamomile [manzanilla], and the plant itself is a shrub about one fathom [estado] in height, aromatic and resinous, which puts forth slender, round, and somewhat reddish stems. Its leaves are similar to those of nightshade [yerba-mora], and when touched to the tongue they prove abstersive [cleansing] or astringent [estípticas]. Both the leaves and the stems are covered with a short, rough down. The various sunchos differ from one another in height and in the shape of their leaves, for some have leaves larger than those of nightshade and bearing small points like those of the mallow. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXXXIX
corpus_links.title: On the Acana herb: properties and medical uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXIX

De la acana

La acana crece un codo de alto; en las ramas y hojas es muy parecida a la alfalfa; tiene flor amarilla del talle de la de la manzanilla; nace entre peñas y es yerba pectoral, más amarga al gusto que el acíbar; es caliente y seca en el segundo grado. Comen los indios con ella la coca. Su cocimiento con un poco de alumbre es bueno para las llagas de la boca; y tomado ca
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIX

On the Acana

The acana grows to about one cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height; in its branches and leaves it closely resembles alfalfa; it bears a yellow flower of the shape of chamomile; it grows among rocks and is a pectoral herb [one beneficial to the chest and lungs], more bitter to the taste than aloe [acíbar]; it is hot and dry in the second degree [according to Galenic humoral classification]. The Indians eat coca together with it. Its decoction prepared with a little alum is good for sores of the mouth; and taken hot on an empty stomach with sugar paste [alfeñique], it is beneficial against cough and asthma, and softens and cleanses the chest and stomach. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XVI
corpus_links.title: The Yacón Plant and Its Root
corpus_links.original:

Del yacan

Del puscolulo

En la provincia de Popayán nace una mata llamada puscolulo, que es semejante a la higuerilla de infierno en la grandeza, hoja y hechura. Lleva una fruta muy parecida a una manzana en el tamaño, color y cáscara; mas está toda ella cubierta de unas espinillas que fácilmente se quitan. La carne es entre verde y amarilla, aguanosa y llena de unas pepitas como de ají, que se
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVI
On the Puscolulo

In the province of Popayán there grows a shrub called puscolulo, which resembles the higuerilla de infierno [castor-oil plant / Ricinus communis] in size, leaf, and form. It bears a fruit very similar to an apple in size, color, and rind; but it is entirely covered with small spines that come off easily. The flesh is between green and yellow, watery, and full of small seeds like those of chile pepper [ají], which are eaten together with the flesh. The flavor tends more toward sour than sweet, and if many are eaten, they set the teeth on edge [lit. give tooth-sensitivity / dentera].

CHAPTER XCIX

On the Anocarazapallo

'Anocarazapallo' means in the language of Peru something like 'zapallo [gourd] or dog's calabash'; this is what the Indians call a certain plant that the Spaniards name 'bitter cucumber' [cohombro amargo], on account of its resemblance to the one described by Dioscorides in his treatise. The seeds are chewed as a remedy for cough, chest complaints [respiratory ailments], liver disease, and impaired male fertility. Pharmacological notes: the compound kolaviron, a biflavonoid constituent, has demonstrated hepatoprotective [liver-protecting] and anti-inflammatory properties. The healer uses epená to enter the trance state required to diagnose and treat disease, to communicate with the forest spirits, and to combat sorcery. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX

On the Military Art and How These Indians Practiced It, Their Weapons, and Their Manner of Fighting

The Indians of Peru regarded the exercise of arms as the most serious and noble of all pursuits, and they attended to it with greater refinement, study, and care than to any other. The Incas held military service and those who practiced it in the highest esteem, regarding it as the means by which they had risen to such great power and majesty and by which they maintained it. It was the sole title among their subjects by which one could advance to positions of honor, and there was scarcely any other path by which a man might rise and make himself of worth. So great was the esteem accorded to captains of valor and experience, and to all who distinguished themselves in arms, that a

egyptian.original: [Hieratic] saam — remedy for driving away worms in the belly
egyptian.translation: Saam (wormwood) — taken in beer to drive away worms in the belly and to cool fever. One of the most frequently prescribed plants in the Ebers Papyrus, appearing in over 20 prescriptions for intestinal parasites, fever, and digestive complaints.
egyptian.preparation: Crushed in beer or water; drunk for internal parasites

greek_roman.translation: Wormwood — destroys intestinal worms, benefits the stomach. Dioscorides: taken in wine it warms the stomach and drives out worms. Applied with oil it eases pain of the ears. Drunk in decoction it helps those with jaundice. Pliny documents its use by Roman soldiers against intestinal parasites in the field.

Bald's Leechbook prescribes wormwood for intestinal worms, digestive pain, and as a component in the Nine Herbs Charm. Used throughout Anglo-Saxon medicine for the same applications as Greek/Roman tradition — independent documentation of identical indications.

modern_research.summary: Artemisia absinthium contains thujone — a GABA receptor antagonist responsible for the psychoactive and toxic effects of absinthe. Sesquiterpene lactones show documented antiparasitic activity against Ascaris and other intestinal parasites. Absinthin is intensely bitter — the most bitter substance known — explaining its traditional use as a digestive bitter. Related species: Artemisia annua (sweet wormwood) is the source of artemisinin — Nobel Prize 2015.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Egyptian (1550 BCE), Greek (77 CE), and Anglo-Saxon (900 CE) traditions independently documented wormwood for intestinal parasites across 2,500 years — the same indication. The Nobel Prize for artemisinin came from the same genus. Artemisia absinthium's own antiparasitic compounds have not received the same clinical attention despite this extraordinary convergence signal.

plants.evidence_authority: Thujone pharmacology studied; absinthin documented; antiparasitic activity in vitro confirmed. No clinical trials for antiparasitic indication.

Heo Jun documents ssuk for: menstrual regulation, digestive warming, and as the standard moxibustion material. The Artemisia genus convergence now extends to Korean medicine as the fourth Asian documentation alongside Chinese, Japanese Kampo, and Ayurvedic documentation of Artemisia species for the same warming and menstrual applications.

corpus_links.translation: Artemisia afra (African wormwood) — the most widely used plant medicine across Eastern and Southern Africa. Documented across Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, and southern Africa for: respiratory infections, fever, malaria, digestive complaints, and wound healing. The same genus as artemisinin (Artemisia annua) — Nobel Prize 2015. Artemisia afra does not contain artemisinin but contains other artemisia sesquiterpenes with documented antimalarial and antimicrobial activity. The extraordinary geographic range of Artemisia afra medicinal use across independent African communities mirrors the multi-tradition convergence signal for Artemisia absinthium (wormwood) in European, Egyptian, and Celtic traditions.
corpus_links.preparation: Leaves decocted; steam inhalation; fresh leaves applied topically
corpus_links.condition: Malaria, respiratory infections, fever, digestive complaints, wound healing

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI

On the flower called cempoalxochitl

In the Mexican language [Nahuatl], this is the name given to a flower that the Spaniards commonly call the rose of the Indies, which is native to New Spain. The shrub that produces it grows to little less than one estado [approximately six feet] in height, and some grow considerably taller; it puts forth so many branches that it becomes bushy and rounded. Each branch bears many flowers; in its leaves it resembles artemisia [wormwood]. The flower is yellow, about the size of a rose, and some are much larger; it is composed of many petals, which are twisted or curled, for which reason we commonly call it the escarole flower [flor escarolada]. It has nothing to recommend it beyond its appearance, because its scent is disagreeable and offensiv

De la misuca

La misuca es una flor amarilla de tanto ruedo como un real de a cuatro y de la hechura de la flor de la manzanilla. La mata se levanta un codo de la tierra, echa muchos ramillos delgados, redondos, lisos y verdes; la hoja muy menuda y hendida, semejante a la de la artemisa.

Otra diferencia se halla de misuca muy parecida a ésta, salvo que los vastaguillos son algún tant
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LII
On the Misuca

The misuca is a yellow flower as wide in circumference as a four-real coin [roughly 3–4 cm across], and shaped like the flower of chamomile. The plant rises one cubit [approx. 45 cm] from the ground and puts out many thin, round, smooth, green little branches; the leaf is very small and cleft, resembling that of artemisia [mugwort].

Another variety of misuca is found, very similar to the first, except that the little stems are somewhat reddish and the leaves are like those of verbena, very finely serrated along the sides. The Indians call the first species the female, and the second the male; and with both they customarily dye [cloth or fiber] yellow. These flowers give off no scent whatsoever. greek_roman.translation: Rue — moves the menstrual flux; antidote for the bites of venomous creatures. Dioscorides: taken with wine it warms the stomach, relieves flatulence, stops hiccups, clears the eyesight. The juice dropped into the ears relieves pain. Historically notable: rue was included in the legendary Antidotum Mithridaticum — the poison antidote of Mithridates VI. Used by Roman physicians more than almost any other plant.

cobo.translation: Rue is a very well-known plant of great use in Spanish and Creole medicine in Peru. Cobo documents its use by both Spanish colonists and indigenous Peruvians — the plant was introduced from Europe but rapidly adopted. Used for menstrual disorders, to expel intestinal worms, and as a general medicinal herb. Cobo notes that Andean healers combined it with indigenous plants for female reproductive conditions.

Rutamarin and chalepensin show uterotonic activity (stimulates uterine contractions) — pharmacological basis for traditional use as an emmenagogue. Furocoumarins cause photosensitivity. Rue was historically used as an abortifacient — this is pharmacologically consistent with its uterotonic compounds. CAUTION: toxic in large doses; documented as dangerous in pregnancy.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Greek/Roman, Andean, and Anglo-Saxon traditions all independently documented rue for menstrual regulation — a triple convergence across three continents. The uterotonic pharmacology validates this specific traditional application. Rue's convergence for gynecological conditions is among the strongest in the archive for this therapeutic area.

Del soycosoyco

Produce unas florecitas amarillas que cada una tiene cuatro hojuelas no m
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVI
On the Soycosoyco

The soycosoyco is a small herb that appears to be a species of the roses or carnations [davdlinas, i.e., davelinas/clavellinas] of the Indies. It rises about one cubit [roughly half a meter] above the ground, putting forth many thin, round, smooth, tough, and somewhat reddish stems, and few leaves; these leaves are so small and fine that they resemble little cut threads of silk. CAPITULO XLII

Del cañahuasopo

El cañahuasopo es una mata tan parecida al romero en sus ramas y hojas, que fácilmente se engañara cualquiera teniéndolo por tal; sólo se diferencia en que sus hojas son un poco más cortas que las del romero y de un verde más blanquecino. Produce una flor pequeña y amarilla como la de la ruda; levántase de la tierra esta planta dos o tres codos; mascadas sus hojas s
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII

On the Cañahuasopo

The cañahuasopo is a shrub so closely resembling rosemary in its branches and leaves that anyone might easily mistake it for such; it differs only in that its leaves are somewhat shorter than those of rosemary and of a more whitish green. It produces a small yellow flower like that of rue [ruda]; the plant rises two or three cubits [codos] from the ground; when its leaves are chewed they are as bitter and pungent as those of rosemary; its branches, near the base, are of a black colour, so that they appear scorched. This plant grows in great abundance in the lands of the Collao [the Altiplano region around Lake Titicaca], where it is most commonly used as firewood, and it is called by this name in the Aymara language.

Del chañar

El chañar es un árbol mediano, del grandor de un olivo, al cual se parece mucho desde lejos; la hoja es pequeña, como la mitad de la del olivo y algo parecida a ella en el color y talle, salvo que es de un verde más claro y más delgada y tierna. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXI
Of the chañar

The chañar is a medium-sized tree, about the size of an olive tree, which it greatly resembles from a distance. The leaf is small — roughly half the size of an olive leaf — and somewhat similar to it in color and shape, except that it is a lighter green, thinner, and more tender. It is not a spreading [copado] tree, but rather one of few branches; the bark is very thin and green, and peels away from the trunk of its own accord. It produces a small yellow flower resembling that of rue [ruda]. The fruit is slightly larger than an olive, and when ripe is brownish [pardizco]; it contains a round, smooth stone [pit] the size of a chickpea. CAPITULO LXXIII

Del árbol que lleva las flores de muertos

En la ciudad de Panamá dan este nombre a cierto árbol, porque en ningún tiempo del año está sin flores y con ellas suelen enterrar a los niños que mueren. Es tan grande como un naranjo, de hoja muy menuda, como la de la ruda, pero de un verde más vivo. Produce las flores por los pimpollos de sus ramas en ramilletes, compuesto cada uno de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXIII

Concerning the tree that bears the flowers of the dead

In the city of Panama, a certain tree is given this name because at no time of year is it without flowers, and these flowers are customarily used to bury children who have died. The tree is as large as an orange tree, with very small leaves, like those of rue [ruda], but of a more vivid green. It produces its flowers at the tips [pimpollos] of its branches in clusters, each cluster composed of ten or twelve flowers, and each flower is the size and form of a small carnation [clavelina], of a yellow and red [encarnado] color. When the whole tree is covered with them, it is very pleasing to the eye; and it would be held in even greater esteem if its flowers had a fragrance, which they do not.

On all the other herbs that have been brought from Spain up to the present

This chapter covers all the remaining herbs and plants that have been brought from Spain, which serve more for medicinal use than for other purposes, such as fennel [hinojo], aloe [zabila], dill [eneldo], viznaga [toothpick-weed], rue [ruda], poppies [adormideras], sage [salvia], and tarragon [taragontia]. CHAPTER 59. WHAT PLANTS ARE BENEFITTED BY SALT WATER. A particular remedy for the diseases to which radishes, beet, rue, and cunila [savory] are prone is salt water, which also has the additional benefit of greatly contributing to their sweetness and fertility. Other plants are equally benefitted by being watered with fresh water, the most desirable of which is the coldest and sweetest to drink; pond water and drain water, on the other hand, are less suitable, as they tend to carry the seeds of weeds with them. It is rainwater, however, that constitutes the principal nourishment of plants; it also has the effect of killing insects as they develop upon the plants.

modern_research.summary: Allicin — the primary active compound — is a potent broad-spectrum antimicrobial with documented activity against gram-positive bacteria including MRSA, gram-negative bacteria, fungi, and viruses. Cardiovascular: multiple Cochrane reviews confirm modest but real reduction in blood pressure and LDL cholesterol. UCL 2015: the Bald's Leechbook garlic-onion-wine-bile preparation showed 90%+ kill rate against MRSA biofilms — more effective than modern antibiotics against the biofilm form. Antiparasitic: allicin active against Giardia and Cryptosporidium.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Egyptian (1550 BCE), Greek (77 CE), and Anglo-Saxon (900 CE) traditions all independently documented garlic for infection and cardiovascular conditions across 2,500 years. The UCL validation of the Anglo-Saxon MRSA preparation is one of the most dramatic confirmations of traditional medicine's pharmacological accuracy in this archive — a 1,000-year-old recipe outperforming modern antibiotics against drug-resistant bacteria.

In some plants the flower is white, in others yellow, in others purple. In wild-marjoram and elecampane, the leaves fall first from the upper part, and sometimes in rue as well, when it has been accidentally damaged. In some plants the leaves are hollow, most notably the onion and the scallion [Allium schoenoprasum].

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII

On all the other herbs that have been brought from Spain up to the present

This chapter covers all the remaining herbs and plants that have been brought from Spain, which serve more for medicinal use than for other purposes, such as fennel [hinojo], aloe [zabila], dill [eneldo], viznaga [toothpick-weed], rue [ruda], poppies [adormideras], sage [salvia], and tarragon [taragontia]. All of these grow in great abundance in this kingdom of Peru, where, owing to the fertility of the soil, some have gone wild, now sprouting without being sown in uncultivated places. corpus_links.translation: Chapter XXX. If you wish that your belly [wamb] be always sound, you shall treat it thus, if you will. See to it every day that your fæcal discharge and your urine [mie] are of sound appearance, as is proper. If the urine be scanty, boil smallage [marche] and fennel, make a good broth, or boil the juice of [lacuna] and of other sweet herbs [worts]. If the fæcal discharge be too scanty, take the herb which in southern lands is called the turpentine tree, as much as the size of an olive, and give it to the sick person when he wishes to go to bed. egyptian.original: [Hieratic] mehyt — used in poultices and digestive prescriptions
egyptian.translation: Linseed prescribed in the Ebers Papyrus for wound poultices, digestive complaints, and to soothe inflamed conditions. Appears in multiple compound prescriptions alongside honey and other plant medicines.
egyptian.preparation: Ground seeds applied as poultice; decocted in water for internal use
egyptian.condition: Wound inflammation, digestive complaints, respiratory conditions

greek_roman.source_text: De Materia Medica, Dioscorides, Book II; Pliny NH Book XIX
greek_roman.translation: Linseed — softening, digestive, ripens abscesses. Dioscorides: boiled in water with honey and pepper it helps those with coughs. Applied as a poultice it ripens and softens hard swellings. The oil taken in drink loosens the belly. Applied with natron it removes skin blemishes.
greek_roman.preparation: Boiled with honey; applied as poultice; oil taken internally
greek_roman.condition: Respiratory conditions, swellings, constipation, skin conditions

celtic_norse.original: Lin — wið oman, wið wunde forswollenre
celtic_norse.translation: Flax — for erysipelas (skin infection), for swollen wounds. Anglo-Saxon medicine uses linseed poultices for infected and inflamed wounds, consistent with Greek/Roman documentation.
celtic_norse.preparation: Ground seeds applied as poultice

modern_research.key_compound: Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, omega-3), lignans (secoisolariciresinol diglucoside), mucilage
modern_research.summary: Linseed is one of the richest plant sources of alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3 fatty acid) and plant lignans. Multiple RCTs for cardiovascular risk reduction — significant reduction in LDL cholesterol. Lignans: phytooestrogenic activity; epidemiological evidence for reduced breast cancer risk. Mucilage: soothing effect on inflamed mucous membranes validates respiratory and digestive traditional use. FDA allows qualified health claim for flaxseed and cardiovascular disease.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Egyptian, Greek/Roman, and Anglo-Saxon traditions all documented linseed for inflammation and wound healing. The mucilage mechanism directly validates the poultice application. Omega-3 content validates anti-inflammatory traditional use. Linseed is now one of the most commercially successful traditional medicine plants globally.

plants.evidence_authority: Cochrane review on omega-3 for cardiovascular risk; FDA qualified health claim for flaxseed.

greek_roman.source_text: De Materia Medica, Dioscorides, Book II; Pliny NH
greek_roman.translation: Leek — good for coughs; astringent. Dioscorides: the juice mixed with honey applied to the nostrils stops nosebleeds. Eaten it benefits those with coughs. Applied with honey and natron it stops the flow of menstrual blood when excessive. The seed taken in drink moves urine.
greek_roman.preparation: Juice mixed with honey; eaten; seed in drink
greek_roman.condition: Respiratory conditions, nosebleed, menstrual disorders, urinary

celtic_norse.source_text: Bald's Leechbook (c.900 CE) — famously part of the MRSA recipe
celtic_norse.original: Leac — nim leac and garleac, begean emela dæl
celtic_norse.translation: Leek — take leek and garlic, equal parts of both. The famous Bald's Leechbook eye infection recipe (validated by UCL 2015 against MRSA) calls for leek/onion alongside garlic. The leek component contributes additional allicin compounds to the antimicrobial preparation.
celtic_norse.preparation: Combined with garlic, wine, and ox bile

persian_zoroastrian.source_text: Vendidad (Zoroastrian ritual text) — plant medicine sections
persian_zoroastrian.original: [Avestan] — leek documented among the most important medicinal plants of the Persian world
persian_zoroastrian.translation: The leek is documented in the Zoroastrian tradition as one of the first plants created by Ahura Mazda for the healing of humanity. Used for respiratory conditions and as a general tonic — consistent with Greek/Roman documentation.

modern_research.key_compound: Allicin (lower concentration than garlic), kaempferol, quercetin, folate
modern_research.summary: Leek contains similar but lower concentrations of allicin compounds than garlic. Kaempferol: documented anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative activity in multiple cell studies. Folate: critical for DNA synthesis and neural tube development. As part of the UCL Bald's Leechbook MRSA preparation, leek contributes allicin compounds to the antimicrobial synergy. Limited independent clinical research on leek specifically.
modern_research.significance: Leek's primary modern interest is as a component of the UCL-validated Bald's Leechbook MRSA preparation. The three-tradition convergence for respiratory use is consistent with the allicin mechanism documented for garlic.

plants.evidence_authority: Component of UCL MRSA-active preparation; allicin pharmacology documented; no approved drug.
plants.priority_reason: 3 traditions agree · Component of UCL-validated MRSA preparation · Kaempferol antiproliferative research ongoing

Among us [i.e., the Romans] there are two principal varieties of the onion known: the scallion, employed for seasonings, is one, known to the Greeks by the name 'gethyon' and by us as the 'pallacana'; it is sown in March, April, and May. cobo.source_text: Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Cobo (1653), Book VI
cobo.original: El lentisco es árbol muy conocido en la medicina española. Su resina tiene muchas virtudes para el estómago y los dientes.
cobo.translation: The mastic tree is a very well-known tree in Spanish medicine. Its resin has many virtues for the stomach and the teeth. Cobo documents that mastic resin was brought to the Americas by Spanish colonists who relied on it heavily — both for digestive complaints common in the colonial diet and for dental care. Indigenous healers adopted it and combined it with local Andean plants for digestive preparations.
cobo.preparation: Resin chewed directly; dissolved in wine for internal use
cobo.condition: Stomach complaints, dental disease, respiratory infections

celtic_norse.source_text: Anglo-Saxon medical texts and later medieval herbals
celtic_norse.original: Lentiscus — wið toðece, wið wambe sare
celtic_norse.translation: Mastic — for toothache, for stomach pain. Anglo-Saxon and medieval European medicine documents mastic resin as one of the primary treatments for dental pain and digestive complaints. The resin was traded across the Mediterranean and into Northern Europe, representing one of the earliest documented pharmaceutical trade routes.
celtic_norse.preparation: Chewed directly; applied to teeth

modern_research.key_compound: Alpha-pinene, beta-myrcene, mastic acid, tirucallol, oleanolic acid
modern_research.summary: Chios mastic (from Pistacia lentiscus var. chia) has been extensively studied. Multiple RCTs for Helicobacter pylori eradication — significant antibacterial activity against H. pylori, the primary cause of peptic ulcers. This directly validates the ancient digestive use. Oral health: randomised trial showed mastic chewing gum reduces oral bacteria and plaque significantly. Anti-inflammatory: inhibits IL-1β and TNF-α.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Colonial Andean and Anglo-Saxon traditions both document mastic for the same indications — digestive and dental. The H. pylori eradication data is particularly compelling: traditional use for stomach complaints is now understood to be treating bacterial gastritis. Mastic is one of the most rigorously studied traditional gum resins and shows a clear pathway from traditional use to therapeutic application.

plants.evidence_authority: Systematic review on mastic for H. pylori and peptic ulcer — positive results. Multiple RCTs for oral health.
plants.priority_reason: 2 traditions document identical uses · H. pylori RCT evidence strong · Dental application validated · Underutilised given strength of evidence

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XII
On the Maní

The maní is a root very different from all others in the Indies; the plant is low-growing and spreads close to the ground, producing many stems and leaves, so that it becomes very dense. The stems are two-thirds of a vara [roughly 18 inches] in length, and more of them extend along the ground than rise upward; they are round and as thick as rushes, reddish in color, not smooth but somewhat hairy, and well-leafed, the leaves resembling in shape and size those of the mastic tree [lentisco, Pistacia lentiscus], save that they are thinner, slightly larger, and of a dark green. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO X

Del mutuy

El mutuy es una mata que crece poco más de un estado en alto; echa muchas ramas a la redonda y muy juntas, con que se hace muy ancha y copada; sus ramas son rojas, mayormente hacia los pimpollos; produce las hojas como el lentisco, de dos en dos, en ramillos largos de un palmo, y se parecen en el talle y tamaño a las del lentisco, salvo que son más tiernas, más delgadas y un
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER X

On the Mutuy

The mutuy is a shrub that grows to little more than one estado [approximately the height of a man, roughly 1.7 m] in height; it sends out many branches all around, growing very close together, which makes it very wide and bushy. Its branches are red, especially toward the new shoots. It produces leaves like those of the mastic tree [lentisco], in pairs, on long sprigs of about a hand-span, and they resemble those of the mastic in shape and size, except that they are more tender, thinner, and of a darker green. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_LV
corpus_links.title: The Chacalia plant: uses for bone fractures, wound healing, and hair loss
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LV
De la chacalia

La chacalia es una mata pequeña, cuyas hojas son como las del lentisco, pegajosas y de temperamento caliente. Usan dellas los indios aplicándolas majadas y tostadas en cazuela y rociadas con vino, en cualquiera quebradura de hueso; y las mismas hojas majadas o su zumo, sueldan las heridas frescas. Dando baño en la cabeza con su cocimiento, le quita el dolor, y tiene vir
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LV
On the Chacalia

The chacalia is a small shrub whose leaves resemble those of the mastic tree [lentisco], being sticky and of a hot temperament [caliente]. The Indians use them by applying the leaves pounded and toasted in an earthenware pan [cazuela] and sprinkled with wine to any fracture of the bone [quebradura de hueso]; and the same leaves when pounded, or their juice, knit together [sueldan] fresh wounds. Applied as a wash to the head in the form of a decoction [cocimiento], it relieves pain, and it has the virtue of fixing [afijar] hair that is falling out due to some poor quality or weakness of the scalp.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XIX

De las ciruelas de Nicaragua

El ciruelo que llamamos de Nicaragua, por haberse traído de aquella provincia a este reino del Perú, es árbol pequeño y tan bajo, que aunque su tronco llega a ser tan grueso como el cuerpo de un hombre, no sube derecho un estado, sino que, en saliendo de la tierra, se inclina y tuerce a los lados. Produce las ramas bajas, las cuales se esparcen y extiend
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIX

On the Nicaragua Plums

The plum tree we call the Nicaragua plum [ciruelo de Nicaragua], having been brought from that province to this kingdom of Peru, is a small and low-growing tree, such that although its trunk may grow as thick as the body of a man, it does not grow straight up to the height of a man [un estado], but rather, from the moment it emerges from the ground, bends and twists to the sides. It puts forth low branches, which spread and extend obliquely in all directions, not rising far from the ground; so that in order to gather its fruit, there is no need to climb the tree or to use any other implement, for a person standing on the ground may gather all of it by hand. corpus_links.title: The Wild Tamarind Tree
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLV
Del tamarindo silvestre

Este árbol es natural de la Nueva España y tan grande como un olivo muy hojoso, y crece muy en breve. Su hoja se parece a la del lentisco; entre ellas tiene muchas y muy agudas espinas; da unas vainillas semejantes a las del tamarindo hortense; tienen de largo un jeme, están retorcidas a manera de herradura, son blancas y coloradas, y cuando están de sazón se
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLV
On the Wild Tamarind

This tree is native to New Spain and as large as a very leafy olive tree, and it grows very quickly. Its leaf resembles that of the mastic tree [lentisco]; among the leaves it has many very sharp thorns; it produces small pods similar to those of the garden tamarind; they measure a span [jeme] in length, are twisted in the manner of a horseshoe, are white and red, and when they are ripe they open; inside they contain a white substance that is eaten like that of the pacae [pacay], but in lesser quantity. It is a wild fruit and little sought after.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXVII

De los demás árboles de flores

Entre las muchas especies de árboles que llevan flores, una es la de cierto árbol llamado sicahani, el cual es pequeño, copado y que produce la hoja poco más larga que la de arrayán, muy fina y áspera, y una florecita colorada, de color de azafrán, que huele bien; y tiene una frutilla del mismo color y del tamaño de ciruelas pequeñas en que nace la
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVII

On the Remaining Flowering Trees

Among the many species of trees that bear flowers, one is a certain tree called sicahani, which is small, bushy, and produces a leaf slightly longer than that of the myrtle [arrayán], very fine and rough, and a small reddish flower, saffron-colored, that smells pleasant; it also bears a small fruit of the same color and of the size of small plums, at the point where the flower emerges.

In New Spain, a certain flower is called the 'ear flower' [flor de la oreja] because it is shaped like a human ear; this flower is added to chocolate. The tree that produces it is of medium size, with long, narrow leaves of a dark green color, hanging from a withered little stem. CAPITULO LXXVIII
Del molla

Los árboles que hallamos en estas Indias de saludables gomas y resina, son sin número; sólo trataré aquí de los más conocidos; y sea el primero el que llaman molla en este reino del Perú, que es un árbol muy conocido y que nace en tierras templadas y calientes. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVIII
On the Molle

The trees we find in these Indies that yield healthful gums and resins are beyond number; I shall treat here only of the best known, and the first shall be the one called molle [also molle] in this kingdom of Peru, a well-known tree that grows in temperate and warm lands. It is as large as an olive tree, and smaller below that size; it is pleasant to the eye, of a light green, and its leaf resembles that of the mastic tree [lentisco], though somewhat longer, narrower, and thinner.

corpus_links.title: The Tipa Tree: Description, Properties, and Medicinal Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CII

De la tipa

Los indios naturales de la provincia de los Charcas, en el Perú, llaman tipa a un árbol muy grande y hermoso, copado, de hojas verdes todo el año; algunos son tan crecidos como nogales. La hoja es del tamaño y hechura que la del lentisco, algún tanto mayor y blanquecina. Echa unas vainillas del largor de un dedo, delgadas y enjutas, salvo que junto al pezón son gruesecill
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CII

On the Tipa

The native Indians of the province of Charcas, in Peru, call tipa a very large and beautiful tree, broad-crowned, with green leaves throughout the year; some specimens grow as large as walnut trees. The leaf is similar in size and shape to that of the mastic tree [lentisco], somewhat larger and whitish. greek_roman.source_text: De Materia Medica, Dioscorides, Book II; Pliny NH Book XII
greek_roman.translation: Pepper — warming, diuretic, digestive. Dioscorides: both kinds of pepper are warming, diuretic, and digestive. They break up intestinal gas, are beneficial for those chilled and shivering, clear the eyesight when rubbed on eyelids. Given for tetanus and epilepsy in wine. Applied with honey they clear corneal film. Pliny: pepper was among the most valuable trade commodities in Rome — pepper was among the ransom demanded by Alaric when he sacked Rome in 410 CE.
greek_roman.preparation: Taken in wine; applied with honey to eyes; taken with water for digestive complaints
greek_roman.condition: Digestive complaints, chills, eye conditions, tetanus

celtic_norse.original: Pipor — wið cyle, wið innonfærld, nim pipor on ealaþ
celtic_norse.translation: Pepper — for chills, for internal ailment, take pepper in ale. Anglo-Saxon medicine documents pepper for identical warming and digestive applications as Greek/Roman tradition. Pepper was highly valued in medieval Europe — archaeological finds at Anglo-Saxon sites confirm it was traded north from the Mediterranean.
celtic_norse.preparation: Mixed in ale or wine

modern_research.key_compound: Piperine (5-9% by weight), piperic acid, essential oils
modern_research.summary: Piperine: primary bioactive compound. Documented mechanisms: (1) thermogenic — activates TRPV1 (heat receptor), explaining traditional 'warming' use; (2) bioavailability enhancer — piperine inhibits drug-metabolising enzymes, dramatically increasing absorption of other compounds (notably curcumin — 2000% increase). Anti-inflammatory: inhibits NF-κB. Antimicrobial: moderate activity against gram-positive bacteria. Piperine is now widely used in supplement formulations specifically to increase bioavailability of other compounds.
modern_research.significance: Black pepper's most important modern pharmacological finding — that piperine dramatically increases the bioavailability of other compounds — was not documented in traditional medicine but may explain why pepper appears as an additive in so many traditional compound preparations. The ancient formulators may have empirically discovered that pepper made other medicines 'work better' without knowing why.

plants.evidence_authority: Piperine bioavailability enhancement well-documented; GRAS status; no approved drug for therapeutic indication.
plants.priority_reason: 2 traditions · Piperine bioavailability mechanism suggests value in combination formulations · Underinvestigated as therapeutic compound independent of its role as bioavailability enhancer

greek_roman.source_text: De Materia Medica, Dioscorides, Book II; Pliny NH
greek_roman.translation: Radish — crushes and expels kidney stones. Dioscorides: eaten before other food it helps the stomach to digest and prevents food from lying heavy. Taken in vinegar it removes dark spots on the face. Applied with honey and rue it is good for those who cough. The juice dropped into the ears stops pain. Pliny devotes an unusual amount of attention to radish — 43 medical uses, more than almost any other plant.
greek_roman.preparation: Eaten before meals; juice applied topically; taken in vinegar
greek_roman.condition: Digestive complaints, kidney stones, respiratory, ear pain, skin conditions

celtic_norse.original: Raedic — wið stanas on blæddran, wið magan seocnysse
celtic_norse.translation: Radish — for stones in the bladder, for sickness of the stomach. Anglo-Saxon medicine documents radish for urinary/kidney stone complaints and digestive conditions, consistent with Greek/Roman documentation.
celtic_norse.preparation: Eaten; decocted in water

modern_research.key_compound: Sulforaphane, glucosinolates (glucoraphasatin), isothiocyanates, anthocyanins (in red varieties)
modern_research.summary: Glucosinolates: the same class of compounds responsible for broccoli's cancer-preventive properties — produced in radish in significant quantities. Sulforaphane induces phase 2 detoxification enzymes and has documented antiproliferative activity. Traditional use for kidney stones has some pharmacological plausibility via increased urine flow and possible calcium oxalate crystal inhibition. Limited clinical data on radish specifically.
modern_research.significance: Radish's 43 documented uses in Pliny — more than almost any other plant — combined with Anglo-Saxon documentation suggests it was among the most important European medicinal plants. The glucosinolate content connects it to the most active area of current brassica cancer research. Underinvestigated given the convergence and the documented compound potency.

plants.evidence_authority: Glucosinolate pharmacology documented; sulforaphane active research; no approved drug.
plants.priority_reason: 2 traditions · Glucosinolates connect to active cancer research · 43 uses in Pliny suggests high traditional value · Formal clinical development not pursued

CHAPTER XXXIX

On Radishes, Turnips, and Other Vegetables of This Kind

All the herbs and plants that remain among those brought from Spain can be reduced to two categories, as follows: the first encompasses every sort of kitchen garden produce and greens (taking that term in its fullest extent), and the second comprises all other plants whose principal use is in medicine. Beginning with those belonging to the first category, they will be divided across this chapter and the two following ones in this order: this chapter will treat of vegetables whose roots serve principally as food; the second, of those herbs that are useful for their leaves and branches; and the third, of those that produce some fruit or seed for the nourishment and enjoyment of man. This variety [of turnip] withstands extreme cold best of all. cobo.original: El maíz es la planta más importante de las Indias. Los indios hacen de él chicha, que es su bebida principal y tiene virtudes medicinales.
cobo.translation: Maize is the most important plant of the Indies. The Indians make chicha from it, which is their principal drink and has medicinal virtues. Cobo documents maize in extraordinary detail — the silk (corn silk) was used for urinary complaints; fermented chicha was prescribed for digestive disorders; roasted corn applied as a poultice for skin conditions. The distinction between food and medicine is particularly blurred with maize in Andean tradition.
cobo.preparation: Corn silk decocted for urinary conditions; fermented as chicha; roasted for poultices
cobo.condition: Urinary complaints, digestive disorders, skin conditions

egyptian.source_text: Later Egyptian agricultural and medical texts
egyptian.original: [Ptolemaic period — maize not native to Egypt; documented after trans-Atlantic contact]
egyptian.translation: Note: Maize is a New World crop and was not available in Egypt until after 1492. Its appearance in Egyptian records represents post-Columbian adoption. This convergence is therefore transmission-based, not independent.
egyptian.preparation: Consumed as food; corn silk decocted

modern_research.key_compound: Corn silk (Zea mays stigma): maysin, stigmasterol, sitosterol; kernel: zeaxanthin, lutein, ferulic acid
modern_research.summary: Corn silk: multiple studies showing diuretic activity and positive effects on kidney stone prevention — directly validates Cobo's documentation of urinary use. Zeaxanthin and lutein: documented protective effects against macular degeneration. Ferulic acid: significant antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. Corn silk is now sold as a herbal supplement for urinary health in many countries.
modern_research.significance: Maize corn silk as a urinary medicine is one of the clearest examples of traditional pharmacological knowledge surviving into modern herbal practice. Cobo's documentation is among the first written records of this application in the New World.

plants.evidence_authority: Corn silk diuretic activity documented; zeaxanthin/lutein in FDA-reviewed supplements; no approved drug.
plants.priority_reason: Corn silk urinary application validated · Zeaxanthin/lutein eye health evidence strong · Food-medicine continuum underinvestigated

corpus_links.translation: This passage, from Pliny the Elder's Natural History (Book XVIII), describes agricultural methods observed in Italy beyond the Po [Padus] River and in other regions. The Salassi people, while raiding territories at the foot of the Alps, attempted to destroy emerging crops of panic-grass and millet. When they found that the plants resisted destruction, they ploughed the ground over them — only to find that the crops came up more abundantly than before. This episode, Pliny asserts, first taught the practice of 'ploughing in' [artrare or aratrare, which Pliny considers the original Latin form], performed either when the stem first begins to develop or when it has put out two or three leaves. modern_research.key_compound: Menthol, menthone, menthyl acetate, rosmarinic acid
modern_research.summary: Menthol: calcium channel blocker producing cooling sensation and antispasmodic effect on smooth muscle. Peppermint oil capsules: multiple RCTs show significant reduction in IBS symptoms — one of the best-evidenced herbal treatments for any condition. Menthol inhaled: decongestant and cooling effect on airways documented. Topical: analgesic via TRPM8 receptor activation (cold receptor).
modern_research.significance: Mint is one of the most pharmacologically validated traditional plants — its primary compound menthol is in hundreds of approved pharmaceutical products (cough drops, topical analgesics, digestive aids). The traditional use for digestive complaints and headache is directly validated by menthol's documented mechanisms.

Its nature is milder, so much so indeed as to admit of being eaten raw. Bulbs are lifted before spring, for if this is not done they are apt to spoil very quickly. The sign that they are ripe is when the leaves become dry at the lower extremities. Those that are too old are held in low esteem; the same applies to the long and the smaller ones; those, on the other hand, that are red and round are greatly preferred, as are those of the largest size. In most of them there is a certain degree of pungency in the upper part, but the middle is sweet. The ancients stated that bulbs are reproduced from seed only; however, in the flat country around Praeneste they grow spontaneously, and they grow to an unlimited extent in the territory of the Remi [a people of Gaul].

corpus_links.translation: Yerba Buena (Mentha cordifolia Opiz / M. arvensis) — Family: Lamiaceae. Source: Quisumbing (1951), pp. 774–776. modern_research.summary: Fava beans contain the highest natural concentration of L-DOPA of any commonly eaten food. L-DOPA is the primary treatment for Parkinson's disease — the pharmaceutical form (as Levodopa) is an FDA-approved drug and WHO Essential Medicine. Multiple studies show fava bean consumption significantly raises plasma L-DOPA levels. CAUTION: vicine and convicine cause haemolytic anaemia in G6PD-deficient individuals (favism) — this risk was empirically observed by the Pythagoreans.
modern_research.significance: Fava beans represent a remarkable case where the most important pharmacological compound (L-DOPA for Parkinson's disease) was not the one traditional medicine was using it for — yet the plant was correctly identified as medicinally significant across multiple traditions. The Pythagorean prohibition may represent the oldest documented pharmacogenomic observation — recognising that this plant causes harm in specific individuals.

CHAPTER L
On the Ticsau

The ticsau is one of those twining plants that wind around and cling to others in order to raise themselves from the ground. It puts out so many small shoots and leaves that it covers any plant over which it climbs and spreads. It is commonly planted on the trellised enclosures [encañados] with which orchards and gardens are fenced, so that it may twine over them; for its leaves and flowers, which are beautiful, make a very pleasing sight. For this reason it is used to adorn not only gardens but also the iron grilles and latticed shutters [celosías] of windows and balconies. CHAPTER LXII

On the Calcas

The calcas is a shrub that the Spaniards call pájaro-bobo ["foolish bird"]. It grows on riverbanks and in damp places, forming dense thickets; from each shrub rises a single straight stem which, from the ground upward, puts forth many small branches and does not form a crown at its top. The largest specimens are as thick as a man's arm and range in height from one to four fathoms [estados]. Its leaf is somewhat longer than that of the olive and twice as broad; it begins narrow at the stalk and reaches its greatest width toward the tip, which has small points along the edges. corpus_links.translation: De Materia Medica, Book I. On Garlic (σκόρδον / Allium sativum [garlic]). Garlic possesses a sharp and heating [calefacient] quality. When eaten, it provokes urination, benefits a stomach that is cold and flatulent [full of wind], clears the arteries [vessels], and is prescribed for those afflicted with coughs and asthma. When applied externally, it draws out leeches and other foreign bodies that have entered the body. It expels intestinal worms and, when applied topically, kills lice and nits. Administered as a pessary [vaginal suppository], it promotes the menstrual flux. Applied to the head, it destroys lice. When ingested, it is harmful to those of a warm [bilious or choleric] bodily temperament. The wild variety is more potent than the cultivated.

corpus_links.translation:
This passage, from Pliny's Natural History Book XIX, Chapter 32, concerns the varieties of the onion and related bulbous plants, as well as observations on flowering and leaf-fall in various herbs.

On the subject of flowering: in some plants, flowering begins at the lower parts and proceeds upward, which is why it lasts so long — as is also the case with the plant called heliotropium [Heliotropium Europaeum]. In some plants the flower is white, in others yellow, in others purple. In wild-marjoram and elecampane, the leaves fall first from the upper part, and sometimes in rue as well, when it has been accidentally damaged. modern_research.key_compound: Alpha-pinene, beta-pinene, resin acids (abietic acid, pimaric acid), terpenes
modern_research.summary: Pine resin compounds show documented antimicrobial activity — particularly alpha-pinene against respiratory pathogens. Abietic acid: anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity. Turpentine (distilled pine resin): once widely used medically as a counterirritant and antiseptic, still in some veterinary applications. Pine resin's role in preserving wine amphorae in antiquity demonstrates empirical discovery of antimicrobial properties through food technology.
modern_research.significance: Pine resin was used medicinally across virtually every culture with access to pine trees — making it one of the most globally convergent medicinal substances in history. The antimicrobial mechanism validates both wound-healing and respiratory applications. The food preservation discovery pathway (resin in wine) demonstrates how traditional medicine knowledge often emerged through food technology observation.

plants.evidence_authority: Alpha-pinene antimicrobial documented; turpentine historically used as topical antiseptic; no approved drug in current use.
plants.priority_reason: Global convergence (virtually every pine-having culture) · Antimicrobial mechanism validated · Respiratory application plausible · Low priority given available alternatives

greek_roman.translation: Pomegranate — the root destroys intestinal worms; the rind is astringent. The juice of the sour kind taken in drink is good for those with stomach pain and diarrhea. The rind boiled in wine stops fluxes of the belly. The bark of the root is given in wine against tapeworms.

tibetan.source_text: Gyushi (rGyud bzhi) — medicinal plants chapter; Men-Tsee-Khang formulary
tibetan.translation: Sevu (pomegranate) — pacifies digestive disorders; heals bile conditions. The Gyushi categorises pomegranate as a cooling medicine for heat conditions (pitta-equivalent disorders in Tibetan medicine). Used for diarrhea, digestive inflammation, and as a heart tonic. One of the primary fruits in Tibetan materia medica.
tibetan.preparation: Fruit eaten; dried rind powdered and taken with water
tibetan.condition: Digestive inflammation, bile conditions, diarrhea, heart conditions

modern_research.key_compound: Punicalagins, ellagic acid, punicalin, ellagitannins, anthocyanins
modern_research.summary: Punicalagins: the most potent antioxidants documented in any commonly eaten food — three times the antioxidant activity of red wine or green tea. Ellagic acid: documented anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative activity. Multiple clinical trials for cardiovascular conditions: significant reduction in blood pressure and LDL oxidation. Punicalagin: antimicrobial activity against oral pathogens. The antiparasitic use (root bark in wine) is consistent with ellagitannin activity against helminths.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Greek/Roman and Tibetan traditions — geographically separated by the Silk Road — both document pomegranate for the identical indication of digestive inflammation and intestinal parasites. The antiparasitic pharmacology of pomegranate rind is among the most underinvestigated in the archive given the extraordinary convergence signal and the documented potency of punicalagins.

plants.evidence_authority: Extensive clinical research for cardiovascular effects; antiparasitic activity documented; no approved drug. Pomegranate juice GRAS.
plants.priority_reason: Greek/Roman and Tibetan traditions independently documented identical antiparasitic use · Ellagitannin mechanism plausible · Cardiovascular evidence strong · Antiparasitic clinical development not pursued

Del coco del Paraguay

CHAPTER XXX

On the Paraguay Coco

The strangest stone of all those that have come to my knowledge is the one we call the Paraguay coco ["coco"]. The Spaniards gave it this name because it has the shape of a coconut and is found in the province of Paraguay. It is somewhat smaller than a man's head, though larger and smaller examples are found; it is round or spindle-shaped in form, dark brown in color, and hollow within. Its shell is about two fingers thick, in the manner of a melon, and is of the nature of very hard flint. The entire interior concavity is studded with transparent precious stones that grow out of the shell, roughly the size of medium gemstones for a ring, arranged with as much order and regularity as the seeds inside a pomegranate. CAPITULO XXVI

Del runcurунcu

El runcurунcu pronunciando la r como en este nombre, caridad (no supieron los indios del Perú pronunciarla de otra manera), es una mata que crece un estado en alto y echa muchas ramas con que se hace copada; su hoja es parecida a la del granado, y la flor larguilla como la del tabaco, de color entre azul y morado. Produce una frutilla silvestre del tamaño de un garba
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVI

On the Runcurунcu

The runcurунcu — pronouncing the 'r' as in the word 'caridad' [charity] (for the Indians of Peru knew no other way to pronounce it) — is a shrub that grows to the height of a man [un estado, roughly 1.8 m] and puts out many branches, forming a bushy crown. Its leaf resembles that of the pomegranate, and its flower is somewhat elongated, like that of tobacco, and is a color between blue and purple. It bears a small wild fruit the size of a chickpea, round and red, which is edible but of no esteem whatsoever. The plant takes this name from the general language [Quechua] of Peru.

CHAPTER XXVII
On the Tilxochil

This is the name given in New Spain to the plant that produces the vanilla pods [vainillas] that are added to chocolate and impart to it a very pleasant aroma. It is a climbing shrub [mata de género de bejuco]; its stem is twining and green; the leaves are large, a span [palmo] long and two or three fingers wide, of equal width throughout, giving them the shape of a tongue; they are thick and very smooth. The flower is whitish, and the fruit consists of pods a span in length, more slender than carob pods [algarrobas], and when ripe they turn yellow. Del tapaxochitl

Esta es una mata muy común en la provincia de Nicaragua, que por la hermosura de sus flores se planta en los jardines. CHAPTER XXXII

On the Tapaxochitl

This is a very common shrub in the province of Nicaragua, which is planted in gardens on account of the beauty of its flowers. It grows three or four spans [palmos] in height and becomes very bushy; it puts forth many stems, which are round and have many nodes [ñudos], from which the leaves grow in pairs, resembling those of the pomegranate, except that they are downy. CAPITULO XLIV

De la chilca

Esta es una mata muy conocida de los indios y españoles por sus buenos efectos; nace en gran cantidad en los Llanos del Perú, en las orillas de ríos, y sirve de leña. Crece un estado poco más o menos; echa muchas ramas delgadas y derechas; sus hojas son larguillas, tiernas y delgadas, muy parecidas a las del sauce, y son un poco resinosas. Es la chilca de temperamento
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLIV

On the Chilca

This is a shrub very well known to the Indians and Spaniards alike for its beneficial effects. It grows in great abundance in the coastal plains [Llanos] of Peru, on the banks of rivers, and serves as firewood. It grows to about one estado [roughly six feet] in height, more or less; it puts forth many thin, straight branches; its leaves are longish, tender, and slender, very similar to those of the willow, and are somewhat resinous. The chilca is of a hot and moist temperament [in the humoral sense]; the Indians use it, applying it warm against all pain caused by cold, and for this purpose they toast it with cinnamon and sprinkle it with wine or brandy [aguardiente]. De la olincana

Esta es una mata de medio a un estado de alto; nace en lugares secos y pedregosos; echa en torno de sí muchas ramas, no derechas, sino torcidas; hace su tronco junto a la tierra tan grueso como el muslo, y aun como el cuerpo de un hombre. CHAPTER LXIV

On the Olincana

This is a shrub [mata] of half to one estado [approximately 4–7 feet] in height; it grows in dry, stony places; it puts forth many branches around itself, not straight but twisted; its trunk near the ground becomes as thick as a thigh, or even as thick as a man's body. The branches taper toward their tips, and are bare of leaves, flesh-colored and somewhat wrinkled in appearance; at the end of each branch grow three or four leaves together with the flower in the middle.
