corpus_links.title: The Ataranca Plant
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXX
De la ataranca

Esta es una planta muy parecida al runcú-Tuncu. Levántase de la tierra como un estado; produce muchas ramas todas llenas de unas espinas blanquecinas tan grandes como las del naranjo; su hoja es algo semejante a la del granado, sólo que es un poco más angosta. En la lengua quichua se llama esta mata ataranca.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXX
Of the Ataranca

This is a plant very similar to the runcú-tuncu. It rises from the ground to about the height of a man [un estado]; it produces many branches all covered with whitish thorns as large as those of the orange tree; its leaf is somewhat similar to that of the pomegranate, except that it is a little narrower. In the Quechua language this shrub is called ataranca.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVIII
On the Jasmines of the Indies

The Mexican Indians call a shrub 'acuilt' to which the Spaniards give the name 'jasmines of the Indies'; it is native to New Spain. It is a twining plant that grows in damp places and tends to trail along the ground or to wind itself around nearby trees, being of the ivy family [género de hiedra]. Two species of this plant are found, which differ only in the color of their flowers and the size of their leaves: one bears white flowers, and the other, yellow. Both send out many round, smooth, and slender shoots; the leaf resembles that of the pomegranate, though more pointed, and is very much marked by small veins that arise from the stalk and run along its length. CAPITULO IX
Del mamey

El nombre de mamey es tomado de la isla Española, y comprende al árbol y a la fruta. Hállanse cuatro diferencias de mameyes: el uno es general, y los otros particulares de varias provincias donde se hallaron. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX
On the Mamey

The name mamey is taken from the island of Hispaniola and refers to both the tree and its fruit. Four varieties of mamey are found: one is common and widespread, and the others are particular to the various provinces where they were discovered. The common and ordinary mamey is a large tree, comparable in size to a medium walnut tree, very well formed, full-crowned, green, and of very pleasant appearance. Its leaf resembles that of the orange tree, but is smoother and stiffer, and of a lighter green on the outside than on the inside. The fruit is round and about the size of a medium pomegranate; the rind is a dark amber tending toward brown [pardo], somewhat thinner and stiffer than that of a pomegranate. Inside it contains one or two seeds [huesos, lit. 'stones'] s

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_X
corpus_links.title: Mamey de Cartagena, Níspero, and Lúcuma: Descriptions and Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO X

Del mamey de Cartagena

El mamey de Cartagena, que dondequiera que se da conserva este nombre, por haberse llevado de aquella provincia, aunque es muy parecido al mamey del capítulo pasado, se distingue de él en especie. Es este árbol el más hermoso y de mejor parecer de cuantos yo he visto propios de las Indias. Es de la grandeza de un nogal, muy poblado de hoja, bien hecho y copado.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER X

On the Mamey of Cartagena

The mamey of Cartagena [Mammea americana or Pouteria sapota, var.], which wherever it grows retains this name on account of having been brought from that province, although it greatly resembles the mamey of the preceding chapter, is nonetheless a distinct species. This tree is the most beautiful and handsome of all those I have seen native to the Indies. It is the size of a walnut tree [nogal], very full of leaves, well-formed and spreading. The leaf is also very beautiful, somewhat resembling that of the citron [cidra], but better proportioned; it measures a span in length and five fingers in width, flat, with very little channeling, stiff and very smooth, thick, covered with small white dots that run from the midrib to the margins; the upper surface

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_LXXl
corpus_links.title: On the Cacaloxochitl (Plumeria) and a related white-flowered tree
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXI

Del cacaloxochitl.

Muchos árboles nacen en estas Indias que no llevan otro fruto sino flores muy vistosas. Describiré aquí los más conocidos y estimados por la hermosura de sus flores; que de todos es imposible hacer memoria. Y sea el primero el árbol que produce la flor llamada cacaloxochitl, en la Nueva España; el cual es muy parecido a la adelfa, poco copado, y que no tiene hoja
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXI

On the Cacaloxochitl.

Many trees grow in these Indies that bear no other fruit than very showy flowers. I shall describe here the best known and most prized for the beauty of their blossoms, for it is impossible to record them all. Let the first be the tree that produces the flower called cacaloxochitl in New Spain. It closely resembles the oleander [adelfa], has a sparse crown, and bears leaves only at the growing tips [cogollos]; these leaves are a hand's breadth or more in length and very similar to those of the oleander. The tree is of medium size, like a pomegranate tree; and it is a noteworthy thing that its fruit, so to speak, is the flowering it produces throughout the entire year. Each flower resembles a rose, though considerably smaller, yet larger than a carnation

corpus_links.title: Various Flowering Trees of the Americas
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXVII

De los demás árboles de flores

Entre las muchas especies de árboles que llevan flores, una es la de cierto árbol llamado sicahani, el cual es pequeño, copado y que produce la hoja poco más larga que la de arrayán, muy fina y áspera, y una florecita colorada, de color de azafrán, que huele bien; y tiene una frutilla del mismo color y del tamaño de ciruelas pequeñas en que nace la
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVII

On the Remaining Flowering Trees

Among the many species of trees that bear flowers, one is a certain tree called sicahani, which is small, bushy, and produces a leaf slightly longer than that of the myrtle [arrayán], very fine and rough, and a small reddish flower, saffron-colored, that smells pleasant; it also bears a small fruit of the same color and of the size of small plums, at the point where the flower emerges.

In New Spain, a certain flower is called the 'ear flower' [flor de la oreja] because it is shaped like a human ear; this flower is added to chocolate. The tree that produces it is of medium size, with long, narrow leaves of a dark green color, hanging from a withered little stem. The flower smells pleasant, and its leaves are purple on the inner side and gre

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XCIX
corpus_links.title: The Sogue Tree (Peruvian Willow): Uses and Preparations
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCIX
Del sogue

Al árbol que los indios del Perú llaman sogue, los españoles le dan nombre de sauce, porque se le parece. Sus hojas, corteza y flores son estípticas; el cocimiento de las hojas con vino aprovecha para llagas de pierna, y cocido con leche y con ella dado baño, quita los dolores y los nudos de la gota. Y el cocimiento de las dichas hojas, mezclado con zumo de granadas y acei
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCIX
On the Sogue

The tree that the Indians of Peru call sogue is given the name sauce [willow] by the Spaniards, because it resembles that tree. Its leaves, bark, and flowers are astringent [estípticas]; a decoction of the leaves with wine is beneficial for leg sores, and when boiled with milk and used as a bath, it relieves pains and the nodules of gout. A decoction of the said leaves, mixed with pomegranate juice and oil, relieves earache when a few warm drops are instilled into the ears. A decoction made with a little alum [alumbre] of the leaves, bark, and flowers strengthens the teeth and gums, and is used against chilblains [sabañones] when applied as a bath. The powdered leaves are effective against burns; and the seed in powder form, taken with the flower of dried roses o

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_CIV
corpus_links.title: The Pepper of Tabasco
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CIV
De la pimienta de Tabasco

El árbol que da esta pimienta nace en la provincia de Tabasco, en la Nueva España; es grande, con las hojas como las del naranjo; la flor roja, a manera de la del granado, que huele como azahar, y también las hojas del árbol son olorosas. Echa la fruta en racimos, la cual es redonda; al principio está verde, luego se pone leonada, y últimamente inclina a col
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CIV
On the Pepper of Tabasco

The tree that yields this pepper grows in the province of Tabasco, in New Spain. It is large, with leaves like those of the orange tree; its flower is red, resembling that of the pomegranate, and it smells like orange blossom; likewise, the leaves of the tree are fragrant. It bears its fruit in clusters; the fruit is round — at first it is green, then it turns tawny [leonado], and finally it tends toward black. It is of pleasant aroma and sharp [mordaz] to the taste. It can serve as a substitute when pepper is lacking. It fortifies the stomach and the heart, and produces other beneficial effects.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_CXI
corpus_links.title: The Higüero Tree (Calabash Tree)
corpus_links.original:
CAPÍTULO CXI
Del higüero

Higüero se llama en la lengua que tenían los indios de la isla Española un árbol mediano como un granado. Es de mucha hoja, la cual se parece a la del granado, salvo que es más ancha y luenga y lo ancho lo tiene en el remate, de donde va ensangostando hasta el pezón; es lisa, tiesa y retorcida o crespa. La madera de este árbol es recia y correosa, parecida a la del granad
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXI
On the Higüero

"Higüero" is the name given in the language of the Indians of Hispaniola [isla Española] to a medium-sized tree resembling a pomegranate tree. It has abundant foliage, which resembles that of the pomegranate, except that the leaves are wider and longer, with their greatest width at the tip, from which they taper down to the stalk [pezón]; they are smooth, stiff, and twisted or curly. The wood of this tree is hard and tough, similar to that of the pomegranate; from it many things are made, particularly saddle-frames [fustes de sillas]. Its fruit consists of small gourds [calabazas] with very thin shells, some round and others elongated. The largest are commonly about the size of a man's head, and from there downward to no larger than a hen's egg. Many things are

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XXIX
corpus_links.title: On the Capulíes and Other Cherry-like Fruits of the Indies
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXIX
De los capulíes

Asimismo hállanse en esta tierra algunas frutas que se parecen a nuestras guindas y cerezas; por lo cual solemos llamarlas cerezas de las Indias. La fruta deste género que tiene mayor semejanza y parentesco con nuestras cerezas son los capulíes. El árbol es de mediana grandeza, derecho, con ramas largas; las hojas como las del almendro, medianamente aserradas; la flo
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIX
On the Capulíes

Likewise, in this land one finds certain fruits that resemble our sour cherries [guindas] and sweet cherries [cerezas]; for which reason we commonly call them cherries of the Indies. The fruit of this kind that most closely resembles and is most akin to our cherries is the capulí. The tree is of middling size, upright, with long branches; the leaves are like those of the almond tree, moderately serrated; the flower is white and small, consisting of five slender little petals hanging in clusters, from which the fruit proceeds—these are small berries very similar to cherries in size, color, and form, and also in their pits and flavor, except that the taste leans somewhat toward that of blackberries. Each berry grows individually on a very short stem, which is th

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_LXXXII
corpus_links.title: On Balsam: Three or Four Species of Balsam-Yielding Trees in the Indies
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXII
Del bálsamo

El árbol que destila el bálsamo en estas Indias no de sola una especie, sino de tres o cuatro. Es este licor muy semejante al bálsamo de Siria, y no inferior a él en olor y facultades. La una especie de árboles que lo dan y de mayor grandeza, nace en la diócesis de Guatemala, donde yo lo vi, y en otras tierras calientes; crece más que un moral, y hace un tronco grueso
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXII
On Balsam

The tree that yields balsam in these Indies is not of a single species, but of three or four. This liquor is very similar to the balsam of Syria, and in no way inferior to it in fragrance or properties. One species—the largest of those that produce it—grows in the diocese of Guatemala, where I myself saw it, and in other warm lands. It grows taller than a mulberry tree and forms a thick trunk of fragrant and very hard wood, so strong that it serves for purposes requiring very sturdy timber, such as axles for sugar mills and similar uses. The leaves are like those of the almond tree, somewhat larger, rounder, and more pointed; the flowers are yellow at the tips of the branches, appearing at first in the form of long pouches [bolsillos], with certain seeds that are

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::X::cap_XVII
corpus_links.title: On Pomegranates in the New World
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XVII
De las granadas

Aunque alcancé yo a conocer y tratar muchos españoles de los antiguos que se acordaban del tiempo en que comenzaron a dar en este reino las primeras frutas de todas las especies que se han traído de España, con todo eso no he podido averiguar quién haya traído cada género destas plantas en particular. Y la razón es porque las más vinieron juntamente con los primeros
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVII
On Pomegranates

Although I was fortunate enough to know and converse with many of the old Spaniards who remembered the time when the first fruits of all the species brought from Spain began to bear in this kingdom, I have nonetheless been unable to ascertain who brought each particular kind of plant. The reason is that most of them came together with the first Spaniards who entered this kingdom, or so shortly thereafter, that within ten or twelve years of its pacification, most of the fruits and vegetables that are grown now were already being produced; and as for those planted since then, the person responsible for introducing many of them is unknown, since they were private individuals, and such plants spread quickly throughout the whole land. Only those [lettuces] produced from white seed are capable of being blanched; and even then, as soon as they begin to grow, sand from the sea-shore should be spread over them, taking care to tie the leaves together as soon as they begin to reach any appreciable size.

CHAPTER 40. BEET: FOUR VARIETIES OF IT.

Beet is the smoothest of all garden plants. The Greeks distinguish two kinds of beet by colour: the black and the white. The latter, which is the variety generally preferred, produces very little seed and is commonly known as the Sicilian beet — just as it is the white lettuce that is held in the highest esteem. egyptian.original: [Hieratic] khesbed — applied to eyes; used in compound preparations for infection
egyptian.translation: Lapis lazuli ground into powder and applied to the eyes for eye conditions. Used in compound mineral prescriptions for skin infections and general health. The Ebers Papyrus includes mineral medicines alongside plant medicines — lapis lazuli was highly valued both medicinally and as a pigment.

tibetan.translation: Lapis lazuli (béru) — beneficial for eye diseases; beneficial for difficulties of the mind. Tibetan mineral medicine places lapis lazuli among the most important mineral medicines for eye conditions and mental disturbances. The characteristic blue colour was associated with the sky and with calming properties in Tibetan cosmology.
tibetan.preparation: Ground fine; taken internally in small quantities; applied topically

modern_research.key_compound: Lazurite (Na₈[AlSiO₄]₆(SO₄,S,Cl)₂), pyrite, calcite — trace sulphur compounds
modern_research.summary: Lapis lazuli contains trace sulphur compounds from pyrite inclusions. Some antimicrobial activity documented for sulphur compounds generally. The eye application has no obvious modern pharmacological validation — the use likely reflected the traditional doctrine of signatures (blue colour associated with sky/clarity/vision) rather than active compound pharmacology. The convergence between Egyptian and Tibetan traditions for eye use may reflect transmission of doctrine rather than independent pharmacological discovery.
modern_research.significance: Lapis lazuli is one of several mineral medicines in this archive that document the early integration of geology and medicine. The Egyptian-Tibetan convergence for eye conditions is intriguing but likely represents the global application of the doctrine of signatures (blue = eye/sky/clarity) rather than a pharmacological signal. Mineral medicines require separate evaluation criteria from plant medicines.

plants.evidence_authority: Sulphur antimicrobial activity documented generally; no specific clinical evidence for lapis lazuli.
plants.priority_reason: Convergence may reflect doctrine of signatures rather than pharmacological activity · Mineral medicine — different evaluation criteria · Low priority

On the second day the head was anointed with Fish-oil. On the third day with Hippopotamus Oil. On the fourth day with abra-oil [an unidentified oil of Egyptian origin]. After this course of intensive treatment, if the Eczema still persisted, the affected scalp was smeared daily with Bread-meal and dressed with 'Rotted Cereals.'

CHAPTER XVI: DISEASES OF THE EYES

Nine pages of the original papyrus are devoted to eye conditions, a fact which should surprise no one acquainted with that country, even across the thousands of years separating us from that remote period. north_american_indigenous.original: [Documented oral tradition — Iroquois, Ojibwe, Micmac, Penobscot]
north_american_indigenous.translation: Goldthread (Coptis trifolia) — roots used by multiple Eastern Woodlands nations for sore mouths and throats, digestive complaints, and as a bitter tonic. The intensely yellow root (from berberine content) was recognisable and distinctive. Iroquois: root tea for sore throat and fever. Ojibwe: root for eye infections. The bright yellow colour functioned as a natural identification marker — healers across independent nations identified the same useful compound by the same visual signal.
north_american_indigenous.preparation: Root decocted as tea; applied topically to sores
north_american_indigenous.condition: Sore throat, eye infections, digestive complaints, fever

tibetan.source_text: Gyushi (rGyud bzhi) — medicinal plants; Men-Tsee-Khang formulary
tibetan.translation: Tig ta (Coptis/gentian bitter) — heals bile disorders; beneficial for eye diseases. The Gyushi categorises tig ta as a bitter medicine for heat conditions (pitta disorders). Used for jaundice, liver conditions, eye infections, and as a general antimicrobial. Berberine-containing plants (Coptis and Berberis) occupy overlapping positions in Tibetan materia medica.
tibetan.preparation: Root powdered and taken in water; applied as eye wash
tibetan.condition: Liver/bile conditions, eye infections, digestive inflammation

modern_research.key_compound: Berberine (primary alkaloid — same as goldenseal), coptisine, palmatine
modern_research.summary: Berberine — the primary alkaloid — is one of the most extensively studied plant compounds. Documented antimicrobial (including MRSA-active), antifungal, antiparasitic. Multiple clinical trials: berberine comparable to metformin for Type 2 diabetes blood glucose management. Anti-inflammatory: inhibits NF-κB pathway. Neurological: emerging evidence for Alzheimer's disease (inhibits acetylcholinesterase). The yellow colour of berberine-containing roots allowed independent cultures to identify the same pharmacologically active compound.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: North American (Coptis trifolia) and Tibetan (Coptis japonica) traditions independently documented different Coptis species for infection and digestive complaints — the same genus on opposite sides of the globe, identified for the same uses. Berberine is also the active compound in North American goldenseal (MMA-042) and Ayurvedic/Chinese Berberis. Four independent traditions discovered the same compound in related plants — the most dramatic example of parallel pharmacological discovery in the archive.

plants.evidence_authority: Cochrane and systematic reviews on berberine for Type 2 diabetes — positive results. Multiple RCTs. Berberine widely sold as supplement.
plants.priority_reason: Four independent traditions discovered berberine across Coptis, Berberis, and Hydrastis species · Diabetes evidence comparable to metformin · Antibiotic resistance application · Full clinical development not pursued

corpus_links.title: Huanglian (Coptis) — the bitter cold detoxifier
corpus_links.original: 黃連：味苦，寒。主熱氣目痛，眥傷泣出，明目，腸澼腹痛下利，婦人陰中腫痛。久服令人不忘。
corpus_links.translation: Huanglian (Coptis/goldthread): flavor bitter, cold. Principally treats hot-type eye pain, damage to the inner corner of the eye with tearing, brightens the eyes, intestinal dysentery with abdominal pain and diarrhea, and female genital swelling and pain. Long-term use prevents forgetting. This is the same Coptis genus as MMA-068 (Coptis/Goldthread) — documented in North American and Tibetan traditions. The Shennong documentation adds Chinese traditional medicine as a fourth independent tradition recognizing the same plant genus for infection and inflammation.
corpus_links.preparation: Decoction; powder; Huanglian Jiedu Tang (compound with other bitter cold herbs)
corpus_links.condition: Eye infections, dysentery, intestinal infections, inflammatory conditions

corpus_links.label: NAM.Goldenseal
corpus_links.title: Goldenseal — berberine in the Eastern Woodlands
corpus_links.original: [Hydrastis canadensis — Cherokee, Iroquois, Ojibwe documentation in Moerman]
corpus_links.translation: Goldenseal (Hydrastis canadensis) is documented by Cherokee, Iroquois, and Ojibwe nations for: eye infections, mouth conditions, digestive complaints, and as a general antimicrobial. The Cherokee specifically used goldenseal root tea for eye inflammation — the same application as Coptis/goldthread (MMA-068) documented in North American and Tibetan traditions. Both plants share berberine as the primary active compound — the same compound now studied for Type 2 diabetes (comparable to metformin in RCTs). This entry extends the berberine convergence to include goldenseal as a distinct North American species alongside Coptis trifolia, creating a documented five-species, five-tradition berberine convergence.
corpus_links.preparation: Root tea for eye infections (eyewash); root decoction for internal conditions; root powder applied topically
corpus_links.condition: Eye infections, mouth conditions, digestive complaints, skin infections

corpus_links.title: Oren (Coptis) — Properties, Uses, and Preparations
corpus_links.original: 黄連 (Oren / Huang Lian) — Coptis japonica / C. chinensis. Honzo Wamyo: 黄連、和名 加加美久佐。苦、寒。主熱気目痛、眥傷泣出、明目、腸澼腹痛下痢、婦人陰中腫痛。Oren, Japanese name Kakamikusa. Bitter, cold. Primary: heat conditions with eye pain and lacrimation, brightens vision, intestinal flux with abdominal pain and diarrhea, women's internal swelling and pain. Active compound: berberine (ベルベリン) — antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, blood glu
corpus_links.translation: Oren [黄連; Chinese: Huang Lian] — Japanese name: Kakamikusa [加加美久佐]. Taste: bitter. Thermal quality: cold. Primary indications: heat conditions accompanied by eye pain and damage to the canthi [眥傷] with lacrimation; brightens the eyes [明目]; intestinal flux [腸澼] with abdominal pain and diarrhea; internal genital swelling and pain in women [婦人陰中腫痛]. The active compound, berberine, has demonstrated antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and blood glucose-regulating properties. The compound formula Oren-gedoku-to [黄連解毒湯; 'Coptis Detoxifying Decoction'] is widely employed in Japanese traditional medicine for inflammatory conditions. Modern clinical research indicates that berberine exhibits efficacy comparable to metformin in the management of blood glucose in Type 2 diabetes.

corpus_links.original: [Cross-archive analysis]
corpus_links.translation: Coptis species (goldthread/huanglian) now documented in four independent traditions: North American Indigenous (MMA-068), Tibetan (MMA-068), Kampo/Japanese, and now Shennong/Chinese. All four traditions independently identified Coptis species for infection and inflammation — the same pharmacological activity now attributed to berberine, the primary alkaloid. Combined with Ayurvedic documentation of Berberis (same berberine-containing family), this creates a five-tradition convergence for berberine-class compounds across independent medical systems globally.

Li Shizhen devotes more space to huanglian than almost any other plant — correcting earlier texts on dosage, preparation, and appropriate versus inappropriate use. celtic_norse.translation: Dock — for when one is burned by nettle, then take dock leaf. The famous folk remedy for nettle stings — applying dock leaf to reduce the burning and itching — is documented in Anglo-Saxon medicine. Also used for skin conditions and digestive complaints.

modern_research.key_compound: Anthraquinone glycosides (emodin, chrysophanol), tannins, oxalic acid
modern_research.summary: Emodin: laxative activity (same mechanism as senna and rhubarb anthraquinones) — validates traditional laxative use. Tannins: astringent activity — validates traditional use of seeds for diarrhea (opposite to root's laxative effect). The dock leaf nettle sting folk remedy: mechanistic explanation debated — the cooling effect of the moist leaf may be more important than specific compounds. Oxalic acid: can form kidney stones at high doses. Limited clinical research on dock specifically.
modern_research.significance: Dock represents a fascinating case where the same plant's root and seed have opposite therapeutic effects — an empirical observation made by Greek/Roman physicians and consistent with the anthraquinone (laxative, in root) vs tannin (astringent, in seed) pharmacology. The Anglo-Saxon nettle sting remedy is one of the oldest documented and most widely practised folk remedies in Northern Europe.

modern_research.summary: Sparteine: potent cardiac antiarrhythmic and oxytocic alkaloid — directly affects cardiac conduction. Historically used as an antiarrhythmic drug (sparteine sulfate) before being replaced by safer alternatives. Cytisine: partial nicotinic agonist — currently in clinical trials as a smoking cessation aid (less expensive than varenicline/Chantix). Traditional emetic/diuretic use is consistent with sparteine's cardiovascular effects. CAUTION: toxic in high doses — can cause cardiac arrest.
modern_research.significance: Broom's active compound cytisine is currently in clinical trials for smoking cessation — representing an active research pathway from traditional plant to modern pharmaceutical. Sparteine's cardiac activity directly validates the traditional use for dropsy (edema from heart failure). The convergence between Greek/Roman and Anglo-Saxon traditions for cardiac-related edema is pharmacologically consistent.

plants.evidence_authority: Cytisine in Phase 3 trials for smoking cessation; sparteine historically approved but now withdrawn; cardiac activity well-documented.

modern_research.summary: Pinocamphone: antispasmodic effect on bronchial smooth muscle — pharmacological basis for respiratory traditional use. Limited clinical research on hyssop specifically despite extensive traditional documentation.
modern_research.significance: Hyssop's convergence between Greek/Roman and Anglo-Saxon traditions for respiratory use is consistent with the antispasmodic bronchodilatory mechanism of pinocamphone. The antiviral activity against herpes is an interesting modern finding not predicted by traditional medicine but emerging from the antimicrobial investigation.

greek_roman.translation: Frankincense — astringent, warming, digestive. The resin applied to wounds stops bleeding and draws them together. Taken in drink with wine it helps those who vomit blood. The smoke of frankincense is good for those who have weak sight, when applied as a fumigation. Applied with egg white it fills out the hollow areas of wounds. Pliny: frankincense was among the most valuable traded commodities in the ancient world, second only to pepper in value.

modern_research.key_compound: Boswellic acids (AKBA, KBA), incensole acetate, alpha-boswellic acid
modern_research.summary: Boswellic acids: potent 5-LOX inhibitors (leukotriene synthesis inhibitors) — documented anti-inflammatory mechanism. Multiple RCTs for osteoarthritis and inflammatory bowel disease — positive results. EU approved Boswellia extract (Casperome) for brain tumours as an orphan drug. Incensole acetate: psychoactive — activates TRPV3 channel, may explain emotional/spiritual effects of burning frankincense. AKBA: documented antiproliferative activity against cancer cell lines.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Frankincense (Boswellia) is documented in the same Burseraceae family as copal/pom — the Maya/Aztec/Andean healing resin (MMA-033). Three traditions (Greek/Roman, Anglo-Saxon, and the entire Mesoamerican complex) independently identified Burseraceae resins as medicinally significant. The boswellic acid anti-inflammatory mechanism is one of the strongest validated mechanisms in the archive for an uninvestigated-for-drug-development traditional plant.

plants.evidence_authority: Systematic reviews on Boswellia for osteoarthritis and IBD — positive results. EU orphan drug approval for brain tumour adjunct therapy.
plants.priority_reason: 2 traditions · Cochrane evidence for arthritis and IBD · EU orphan drug approval · Convergence with Burseraceae family documented in Mesoamerican traditions · Anti-cancer research ongoing

CHAPTER XCI
On the Espinco

This is a fragrant herb so similar to clover that it is undoubtedly a species thereof. Its leaf and flowers are like those of clover, except that it does not rise from the ground, and it bears small round spines like tiny medals [medecillas]. It is a warm and moist herb, and from it the Indians make a paste with which they form very fragrant black beads that, when strung, they wear around the neck. The powders of this herb, mixed with powders of incense [frankincense] and given in wine, render even the most severe torments unfelt. The Indians assert that its paste, made with sage and resin of molle and placed upon the navel, makes barren women fertile; and that by carrying the aforesaid beads on one's person, one is kept safe from vipers and venomous animals. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXI
On the Quina-Quina

In Peru they give this name to a large and handsome tree resembling a quince or an olive; its leaf is the size and shape of the Ceuti [Moroccan] lemon leaf; the trunk is somewhat reddish, resinous, and aromatic. The tree is [humorally] hot in the second degree, astringent [estíptico], dry, and of a pleasant smell. It bears small seeds [pepitas] the size of almonds, yellow in color and of an oily substance, which smell agreeably fragrant; these too are hot and astringent in the second degree, and dry beyond the first. When the trunk and branches are scored [sajando], they exude a fragrant resin that congeals so thoroughly it can be ground to powder, at which point it becomes a pale black color; this resin is hot and drier than the seeds. CAPITULO CIII
Del incienso de Quito

En la provincia de Quito, en el Perú, se halla un árbol que destila una resina parecida al incienso, por la cual la llaman los españoles árbol de incienso. Es pequeño, de hasta dos estados de alto; sus ramas son cortas, de suerte que no se copa, sino que viene a ser ahusado; y su hoja es muy parecida a la del olivo. Por las ramas destila una resina en granitos
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CIII
On the Incense Tree of Quito

In the province of Quito, in Peru, there is found a tree that exudes a resin resembling frankincense [incienso], on account of which the Spaniards call it the incense tree [árbol de incienso]. It is small, reaching up to two estados [approximately 10–11 feet] in height; its branches are short, so that it does not spread into a broad crown but rather tapers to a point [comes to be spindle-shaped]. Its leaf closely resembles that of the olive. Along the branches it exudes a resin in small, round granules that smell of frankincense, and the tree itself smells the same, such that when anyone passes near it, the scent they perceive makes them think that frankincense is being burned somewhere close by.

[Continuation of the discussion of flavours in plants:] centaury [taury] is bitter; cucumbers, gourds, and lettuces are watery; parsley, anise, and fennel are pungent and odoriferous. The salt flavour is the only one not found in plants, with the sole exception of the chicheling vetch [Lathyrus sativus], and even there it is found only on the exterior surface of the plant, in the form of a kind of dust that settles upon it.

Ritual of the Bacabs (Roys trans.): 'Ix-pom, ix-cacao, ix-ya-che — copal, cacao tree, sapodilla tree — these are the medicines of the great healers.' Copal (pom) was both ritual and medicinal in Maya culture — a distinction the tradition did not draw as sharply as Western medicine. Medicinal uses documented: antimicrobial wound treatment
corpus_links.translation: Pom (Bursera copallifera / B. bipinnata) — Maya Copal Resin. From the Ritual of the Bacabs (translated by Roys): 'Ix-pom, ix-cacao, ix-ya-che — copal, cacao tree, sapodilla tree — these are the medicines of the great healers.' In Maya culture, copal (pom) served simultaneously as a ritual substance and a medicinal one — a distinction the tradition did not draw as sharply as Western medicine does. Documented medicinal uses include: antimicrobial wound treatment (resin applied directly to infected wounds); pain relief (smoke inhaled for headache); and treatment of respiratory conditions (resin burned in an enclosed space and the smoke inhaled). modern_research.key_compound: Cinnamaldehyde (65-80% of essential oil), coumarin (cassia), eugenol, procyanidins
modern_research.summary: Cinnamaldehyde: insulin-sensitising activity — multiple clinical trials showing significant reduction in fasting blood glucose in Type 2 diabetes. TRPA1 agonist explaining warming sensation. Antimicrobial: broad-spectrum activity including anti-biofilm effects against oral pathogens. Coumarin (in cassia specifically): anticoagulant — present at levels that may cause liver toxicity at high doses. Ceylon cinnamon (C. verum) has much lower coumarin than cassia. Multiple meta-analyses confirm blood glucose lowering effect.
modern_research.significance: CONVERGENCE: Egyptian and Anglo-Saxon traditions document cinnamon for warming and digestive conditions. The blood glucose lowering mechanism — not known to traditional medicine as 'diabetes treatment' — validates the traditional description of cinnamon as beneficial for 'thirst' and 'weakness' (classic diabetes symptoms). Cinnamon is one of the most commercially studied traditional medicines for Type 2 diabetes globally.

plants.evidence_authority: Cochrane review and multiple meta-analyses for cinnamon in Type 2 diabetes — positive results. CAUTION: cassia variety contains hepatotoxic coumarin at high doses.

CHAPTER XXXIX
On Cassia Fistula

Besides the cassia fistula [caña fistola] that, brought from the East Indies, has been planted and grows abundantly in many parts of these West Indies—being the variety dispensed in apothecaries [boticas]—there is found in certain provinces another wild kind, native to the land, which appears to be of the same lineage as that of India, though distinct in species. The tree that produces this wild cassia fistula is much larger than that of the other variety. The leaf of the one and the other is the same; however, the pods of this wild kind, although they are the same color and shape as those of the Indian cassia fistula, are much longer, thicker, and hollow on the inside, lacking the pulp [pulpa] that the good cassia fistula possesses. Del hicaco

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI
On the Hicaco

This is a tree that grows along the seacoasts, so small that it rises no more than one or two fathoms [estados] from the ground; it is of pleasing appearance, and its leaf resembles that of the strawberry tree [madroño, Arbutus unedo]. The fruit it bears is like an apricot [albaricoque], more pleasing to the eye than to the taste, for it has the color of a flushed apple; the skin is like that of an apple, and the flesh is white and spongy, not at all appetizing, for it is a wild and coarse fruit; it has a very large stone [pit] in proportion to its size.

corpus_links.original: Cassia and Cinnamon are warming, digestive, and diuretic. Taken in drink they help those bitten by serpents and those with pain in the sides. They move the menstrual flux. They benefit those with cold and moist stomachs. Applied with oil to the face they remove spots and blemishes. Taken in drink with wine they warm those who are cold. Cinnamon is more powerful than cassia in all these uses — it i
corpus_links.translation: Cassia and Cinnamon are warming [calefacient], digestive [peptic], and diuretic. Taken as a drink, they aid those bitten by serpents [snakebite antidote] and those suffering from pain in the sides [pleurisy or flank pain]. They promote the menstrual flux [emmenagogue]. They are beneficial for those with cold and moist stomachs [atonic or phlegmatic digestive conditions]. Applied to the face with oil, they remove spots and blemishes [topical depilatory/clarifying use]. Taken in drink with wine, they warm those who suffer from cold [constitutional coldness or chills]. Cinnamon surpasses cassia in all of these virtues — it is more warming and more fragrant.

Wild cucumber, boiled in vinegar, is employed in fomentations [warm topical applications] for gout, and its juice is used as a remedy for toothache. When dried and mixed with resin, the root is a cure for impetigo [a contagious skin infection] and the skin diseases known as 'psora' [itch-scab] and 'lichen' [a scabrous skin condition resembling moss or lichen in appearance]. It is also beneficial for abscesses [imposthumes] of the parotid glands and inflammatory tumours [pani], and it restores the natural colour of the skin after a scar [cicatrix] has formed. The juice of the leaves, mixed with vinegar, is used as an ear injection in cases of deafness.

cobo.source_text: Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Cobo (1653), Books V–VI — most frequently mentioned Andean medicinal plant
cobo.original: El arrayán es árbol muy medicinal. Su corteza y hojas cocidas en agua sirven para lavar heridas, llagas y apostemas. Las hojas mascadas confortan las encías y aprietan los dientes flojos.
cobo.translation: The arrayán (myrtle) is a very medicinal tree. Its bark and leaves boiled in water serve to wash wounds, sores, and abscesses. The leaves chewed strengthen the gums and tighten loose teeth. Cobo documents arrayán as the single most-mentioned medicinal plant in his Andean observations — appearing in 15 separate therapeutic contexts. Used for wound washing, dental health, digestive complaints, and respiratory conditions. Indigenous Andean healers used it systematically across all these applications.
cobo.preparation: Bark and leaves decocted for wound washing; leaves chewed for dental conditions; decoction drunk for digestive complaints
cobo.condition: Wound infection, dental disease, digestive complaints, respiratory conditions
cobo.notes: Arrayán's prominence in Cobo — 15 mentions, more than any other Andean plant except cinchona — suggests it was the most versatile and widely used plant in the indigenous Andean pharmacopoeia that Cobo documented. The fact that it appears consistently across wound care, dental medicine, and digestive applications across different indigenous communities suggests genuine pharmacological value rather than localised traditional practice.

modern_research.summary: Myrtaceae family plants consistently show antimicrobial activity from essential oil components. Myricetin: documented antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. Eugenol: the same compound responsible for clove's dental application — directly validates the traditional dental use of arrayán. Multiple studies on South American Myrtaceae species showing antimicrobial activity against wound pathogens. Cobo's wound-washing application is consistent with the antimicrobial essential oil content.
modern_research.significance: The most-documented Andean plant in Cobo's archive with 15 mentions — yet almost entirely absent from modern pharmacological research. The Myrtaceae family's antimicrobial properties are well-established globally (tea tree oil is the most commercially developed example); the South American arrayán species represent an under-investigated branch of the same family with likely similar antimicrobial mechanisms.

plants.evidence_authority: Myrtaceae essential oil antimicrobial activity well-documented; eugenol dental application validated (also in clove); no clinical trials for arrayán specifically.
plants.priority_reason: Most-mentioned plant in Cobo's entire archive · Eugenol dental mechanism validated · Wound antimicrobial application consistent with Myrtaceae pharmacology · Zero clinical research despite 15 documented uses

On the Herb Called Pencácuc

CHAPTER LXX
On the plant called Suelda Consuelda ["mend-and-heal"]

The plant called by the Spaniards suelda consuelda is named by the Indians of Peru, in the general language [Quechua], chuleorrhuko, and in Cochabamba, in the diocese of Charcas, auquilagna, which means "father of herbs." The shrub is small and its stems very similar to vine shoots [sarmientos], except that they are more tender. Its leaf is likewise very similar to that of the grapevine, but smaller and more greasy than it, and both leaves and stems are very tender and tart like vinegar. It produces a small, purple, and showy flower that gives off no fragrance whatsoever. De la mullupachay

La mullupachay es una mata de tres o cuatro codos de alto; echa muchas ramas delgadas, armadas de unas espinas blanquecinas, delgadas y agudas; la hoja es tan pequeña como la del arrayán. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXV
On the mullupachay

The mullupachay is a shrub three or four cubits [codos] in height; it puts forth many slender branches, armed with whitish, thin, and sharp thorns; its leaf is as small as that of the myrtle [arrayán]. It produces small white flowers, no larger than those of the cabbage, with a small yellow button in the center. It bears a small fruit the size and shape of an olive stone [hueso de aceituna], which, once ripe, turns a dark red verging on black, and is edible, though wild and by no means appetizing. This plant is called, in the Quechua tongue of Peru, mullupachay.

The cantuta is a shrub that puts forth many branches all around, giving it a bushy, rounded crown. It commonly grows to about two fathoms [estados] in height and is thickly set with leaves resembling those of myrtle [arrayán], though somewhat larger, more slender, and more tender. This plant produces no other fruit than the flowers that share its name; some of these are purple of a vivid, glowing hue, and others are yellow—the purple ones being the finer and more pleasing in appearance. The stem or little neck [cuellecito] is hollow, about the thickness of a carnation's [clavellina's] stem and somewhat longer; both it and the petals of the flower are of the same substance, very fine, thin, and uniform in color. De la tola

Los que dan al sopo nombre de tok, llaman a esta planta, tola menor, a diferencia de la otra; y ésta es una mata que nace en regiones frías, de uno a cuatro codos en alto, muy poblada de ramas y hojas, que la hacen tan copada como una hermosa mata de albahaca. Chapter XLIII

On the Tola

Those who give the name 'tok' to the sopo call this plant 'lesser tola,' to distinguish it from the other; and this is a shrub that grows in cold regions, from one to four cubits [codos] in height, very densely covered in branches and leaves, which make it as full and bushy as a fine clump of basil [albahaca]. Its leaves are a dark green, the size of those of the myrtle [arrayán], which, beginning very narrow at the petiole [pecíolo], gradually widen toward the tip and terminate in three small points, the middle one being slightly longer than those on either side. CAPITULO XLVI
De la paucarcancha

Esta es una mata de hasta un estado de alto; produce muchas ramas leñosas de color pardo, cuyos cogollos están muy poblados de hojas, la cual es pequeña, menor que la del arrayán, muy tiesa, lisa, acanalada y en la punta una espinilla delgada y dura con que se ponen estas hojas tan espinosas como las de la coscoja. En la cumbre y remate de cada tallo nace una flor
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI
On the Paucarcancha

This is a shrub [mata] of up to one estado [approximately 1.7 meters, or roughly the height of a man] tall; it produces many woody branches of a brownish color, whose shoot-tips [cogollos] are very densely furnished with leaves. The leaf is small—smaller than that of the myrtle [arrayán]—very stiff, smooth, channeled, and terminating at the tip in a thin, hard spine, which renders these leaves as prickly as those of the kermes oak [coscoja]. At the crown and apex of each stem there grows a red flower as long as half a finger of the hand and only slightly thinner than the finger itself; this flower is composed of many small leaflets [hojitas, i.e., petals or tepals] that emerge together from the stalk [pezón], as narrow as the thickness of a grain of barley

CAPITULO XC

Del espingo

Los indios gentiles de las provincias de los Andes, en el Perú, suelen sacar a los pueblos de su frontera unas vainillas como algarrobas, de color leonado oscuro, cuya sustancia, cuajada, es como sangre de drago, aunque reluciente y tirante a negra, y de suave y profundo olor. Produce estas vainas un árbol que nace en aquella tierra, llamado espingo. Sacan los indios bárb
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XC

On the Espingo

The pagan Indians of the Andean provinces of Peru are accustomed to bringing out to the frontier towns certain small pods resembling carob [algarroba], of a dark tawny color, whose coagulated substance is like dragon's blood [sangre de drago], though lustrous and tending toward black, with a gentle and deep fragrance. These pods are produced by a tree that grows in that land, called the espingo. These barbarous Indians bring out the pods as a precious commodity, trading them for knives, scissors, and other small items that they value greatly; this they easily obtain from the Spaniards, for these pods are held to be highly medicinal. Specifically, their powders, taken on an empty stomach in water or diluted wine, cure bloody dysentery [camaras de sangre]; and tak

corpus_links.title: The Sogue Tree (Peruvian Willow): Uses and Preparations
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCIX
Del sogue

Al árbol que los indios del Perú llaman sogue, los españoles le dan nombre de sauce, porque se le parece. Sus hojas, corteza y flores son estípticas; el cocimiento de las hojas con vino aprovecha para llagas de pierna, y cocido con leche y con ella dado baño, quita los dolores y los nudos de la gota. Y el cocimiento de las dichas hojas, mezclado con zumo de granadas y acei
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCIX
On the Sogue

The tree that the Indians of Peru call sogue is given the name sauce [willow] by the Spaniards, because it resembles that tree. Its leaves, bark, and flowers are astringent [estípticas]; a decoction of the leaves with wine is beneficial for leg sores, and when boiled with milk and used as a bath, it relieves pains and the nodules of gout. A decoction of the said leaves, mixed with pomegranate juice and oil, relieves earache when a few warm drops are instilled into the ears. A decoction made with a little alum [alumbre] of the leaves, bark, and flowers strengthens the teeth and gums, and is used against chilblains [sabañones] when applied as a bath. The powdered leaves are effective against burns; and the seed in powder form, taken with the flower of dried roses o

corpus_links.translation: Some measures have been put in place by those who govern to curb the drunkenness of the Indians; but who could restrain them if they cannot keep their own mouths shut? The story I shall now relate illustrates well how far the violent passion that drives them to this vice can go. In the city of Cuzco, a friar had charge of a confraternity of Indians, and as his brothers were to go out on the night of Holy Thursday in penitential procession [disciplinándose, i.e., flagellating themselves], he had a large pot of wine set to boil with myrtle and rosemary, so that the penitents might be tended to [their wounds dressed] once the procession was finished, leaving two or three Indians behind to keep the fire going under the wine. corpus_links.label: DMM.Book5.Wines
corpus_links.title: Book V — Wines, vinegar, and minerals
corpus_links.original: Περὶ οἴνων καὶ μεταλλικῶν — οἶνοι ἐπὶ ζωμοὺς τιθέμενοι
corpus_links.translation: On wines and minerals — wines prepared by infusing plants. Dioscorides Book V documents pharmaceutical wine preparations — essentially the Roman equivalent of tinctures and extracts. This represents the Greek/Roman pharmacy's primary delivery system for plant medicines. Key medicinal wines documented: wormwood wine, rose wine, myrtle wine, pine resin wine (resinated wine), and juniper berry wine. Each represents a specific therapeutic plant dissolved into a preservation medium — the prototype for modern pharmaceutical tinctures.

tradition_names.egyptian: Kyphi (kp.t) — Ebers Papyrus and temple records

plants.modern_botanical: [Compound: frankincense, myrrh, juniper, raisins, honey, wine + 10 more ingredients]

egyptian.source_text: Ebers Papyrus; temple records at Edfu and Philae listing Kyphi formulae
egyptian.original: [Hieratic] kp.t — recipe from Philae temple: 16 ingredients including honey, wine, raisins, myrrh, frankincense, juniper.
egyptian.translation: Kyphi — the sacred compound incense of ancient Egypt, used as ritual offering and medicine simultaneously. Burned for respiratory complaints; dissolved in wine for liver and kidney conditions. Plutarch describes kyphi as composed of things that delight most in the night — documenting its use for sleep and anxiety. The most sophisticated compound pharmaceutical preparation in the ancient world.
egyptian.preparation: Burned as fumigation for respiratory and ritual use; dissolved in wine for internal conditions
egyptian.condition: Respiratory conditions, sleep disturbance, anxiety, liver and kidney complaints

modern_research.key_compound: Boswellic acids (frankincense), terpenoids (myrrh), juniperone (juniper), polyphenols (raisins, honey)
modern_research.summary: Kyphi as compound not systematically studied. Individual ingredients have documented activities — boswellic acids (anti-inflammatory, EU orphan drug), myrrh terpenoids (antimicrobial), honey (antimicrobial). Incensole acetate in frankincense: anxiolytic effects in mice — potentially explaining ritual and sleep applications.
modern_research.significance: Kyphi is the world's oldest documented compound pharmaceutical formulation — 16 ingredients prepared according to specific protocols. Pharmacological evaluation of ancient compound formulations is an emerging field. Kyphi is the most sophisticated example in this archive of traditional medicine understanding synergistic multi-ingredient pharmacology.

plants.evidence_authority: Individual ingredient pharmacology documented; kyphi as compound unstudied; incensole acetate psychoactive activity documented.
plants.priority_reason: World's oldest documented compound pharmaceutical · Individual ingredients validated · Synergistic combination unstudied · Historical significance

greek_roman.source_text: De Materia Medica, Dioscorides, Book II; Hippocratic corpus — barley gruel (ptisane)
greek_roman.original: κριθή — ἡ πτισάνη τρέφει, οὐρεῖ, λύει κοιλίαν
greek_roman.translation: Barley — the barley gruel (ptisane) nourishes, promotes urine, loosens the bowels. Hippocrates prescribed barley gruel as the primary therapeutic food for fever and acute illness — ptisane is the most frequently mentioned therapeutic preparation in the entire Hippocratic corpus. Applied as a poultice it softens and reduces swellings. The grain fermented produces a drink good for those with urinary complaints. Dioscorides: barley meal mixed with fenugreek applied as a poultice ripens abscesses.
greek_roman.preparation: Grain boiled as gruel (ptisane); applied as poultice with other plants; fermented as medicinal drink
greek_roman.condition: Fever (primary Hippocratic remedy), digestive complaints, urinary conditions, wound swellings
greek_roman.notes: Barley ptisane — barley gruel — was Hippocrates' universal fever remedy. The Hippocratic text On Regimen in Acute Diseases is essentially a treatise on when and how to administer barley gruel. This makes barley the most important single therapeutic substance in the foundation document of Western medicine.

modern_research.key_compound: Beta-glucan (7-15% of grain), tocols, phenolic acids, avenanthramides
modern_research.summary: Beta-glucan: FDA qualified health claim for cardiovascular risk reduction — lowers LDL cholesterol and blood glucose. Multiple RCTs confirming beta-glucan efficacy for Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. The mechanism validates the traditional observation that barley 'nourishes' during fever — beta-glucan's slow-release energy and immune-modulating properties are consistent with Hippocratic fever management. Beta-glucan also documented to stimulate immune function.
modern_research.significance: Barley is the foundation of the Western medical tradition's most important therapeutic food — Hippocratic ptisane. The beta-glucan mechanism now validates the nutritional and metabolic rationale for barley-based fever therapy. FDA has granted a qualified health claim for beta-glucan cardiovascular benefit, making barley one of the few traditional therapeutic foods with formal regulatory recognition.

plants.evidence_authority: FDA qualified health claim for barley beta-glucan and cardiovascular disease risk reduction. Beta-glucan in USP. EFSA approved health claim in EU.

cobo.source_text: Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Cobo (1653), Book V
cobo.original: El molle es árbol muy estimado de los indios por sus muchas virtudes medicinales. Con su resina curan heridas y apostemas. Sus hojas cocidas en agua son buenas para lavar heridas viejas y úlceras.
cobo.translation: The molle is a tree greatly esteemed by the Indians for its many medicinal virtues. With its resin they cure wounds and abscesses. Its leaves boiled in water are good for washing old wounds and ulcers. The fruit is used to make chicha de molle — a fermented drink used both as food and medicine. The bark decocted is used for toothache and as a purgative. Cobo describes molle as one of the most versatile medicinal trees in Andean medicine — comparable to the European oak in the breadth of its applications.
cobo.preparation: Resin applied to wounds; leaves decocted for wound washing; fruit fermented as medicinal chicha; bark decocted for dental pain
cobo.condition: Wound infection, dental pain, digestive complaints, respiratory conditions, as purgative
cobo.notes: Schinus molle (Peruvian pepper tree) is now globally distributed — planted as an ornamental and shade tree across Southern Europe, Africa, and California. The medicinal uses documented by Cobo for Andean communities have since been documented independently by multiple African communities who adopted the introduced tree — an interesting case of post-colonial convergence where an introduced plant's medicinal properties were independently rediscovered.

modern_research.key_compound: Alpha-phellandrene, beta-phellandrene, myrtenal, bornyl acetate, cardanol (anacardic acid in fruit)
modern_research.summary: Multiple studies confirming antimicrobial activity of Schinus molle essential oil — particularly against Staphylococcus aureus, E. coli, and Candida. Anacardic acids in the fruit show significant antimicrobial activity consistent with traditional wound-healing use. Anti-inflammatory activity documented. The plant is now studied by Brazilian and Peruvian researchers actively. Dental application: essential oil shows activity against oral pathogens consistent with traditional toothache use.
modern_research.significance: Schinus molle is one of the most pharmacologically validated Andean plants with active modern research, yet virtually absent from international pharmaceutical development pipelines. The convergence between Cobo's 17th-century documentation and modern antimicrobial research is direct and mechanistically coherent. This plant represents the archive's clearest example of an Andean medicine with genuine drug development potential that has received no serious clinical investment.

plants.evidence_authority: Multiple antimicrobial studies published in peer-reviewed journals; anti-inflammatory activity documented; no clinical trials.
plants.priority_reason: 7 mentions in Cobo · Antimicrobial activity confirmed in multiple studies · Drug-resistant pathogen activity documented · No clinical development despite strong preclinical evidence

corpus_links.title: On the Guaki and Chapichapi plants: medicinal uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXII
De la guaki

Llaman guahi los indios peruanos a una raíz muy conocida y estimada dellos; es muy amarga y de profundo olor no enfadoso; su temperamento es caliente y seco. Es tan parecida esta yerba a la que Dioscórides llama aristoquia luenga, que no parece distinguirse della. Usan los indios de su raíz para muchas enfermedades; con ella, mascada, se refriegan cualquiera parte del cu
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXII
On the Guaki

The Peruvian Indians call by the name guahi a root that is very well known and esteemed among them. It is very bitter and has a deep but not unpleasant smell; its temperament [complexion] is hot and dry. This herb so closely resembles what Dioscorides calls aristolochia longa [long birthwort] that it seems indistinguishable from it. The Indians use its root for many ailments; when chewed, they rub it on any painful part of the body. Its decoction [cocimiento] dispels all flatulence [ventosidad], cleanses the bowels, and warms cold parts of the body; drunk regularly, it cures jaundice [ictericia]. A decoction made from the root of this herb together with guaiacum [palo santo], polypody [polipodio], and some senna leaves [hojas de sen], drunk regularly, relieves al

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXXIII
corpus_links.title: On the Chuquicañilla plant: uses for headache, fever, asthma, and gout
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXIII
De la chuquicañilla

La chuquicañilla es una yerba pequeñuela, espinosa, que se levanta del suelo como cuatro dedos y echa de sí un olor que no enfada. Su temperamento es caliente y seco. Usan de su sahumerio los indios para dolores de cabeza y calenturas, y dan su cocimiento para que suden con él los tales enfermos y expelen la calentura, porque es esta yerba muy provocativa de su
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXIII
On the Chuquicañilla

The chuquicañilla is a small, thorny herb that rises from the ground about four fingers' height and gives off an odor that is not unpleasant. Its temperament [complexion] is hot and dry. The Indians use its smoke [fumigation] for headaches and fevers, and they give its decoction so that the sick may sweat with it and expel the fever, because this herb is a very powerful promoter of perspiration. Its decoction, taken hot and with sugar, benefits asthmatics and those with a constricted chest [tight-chested]; and when this herb is boiled together with molle, tola, and a large quantity of salt and used as a bath, it dries out gouty and swollen legs.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XCI
corpus_links.title: The Espinco plant: properties, preparations, and uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCI
Del espinco

Esta es una yerba olorosa y tan parecida al trébol, que sin duda es especie suya; su hoja y flores son como las del trébol, salvo que no se levanta de la tierra y tienen unas espinillas redondas como medecillas. Es caliente y húmeda yerba, y della hacen los indios una pasta de que forman unas cuentas negras muy olorosas, que, ensartadas, las traen al cuello. Los polvos de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCI
On the Espinco

This is a fragrant herb so similar to clover that it is undoubtedly a species thereof. Its leaf and flowers are like those of clover, except that it does not rise from the ground, and it bears small round spines like tiny medals [medecillas]. It is a warm and moist herb, and from it the Indians make a paste with which they form very fragrant black beads that, when strung, they wear around the neck. The powders of this herb, mixed with powders of incense [frankincense] and given in wine, render even the most severe torments unfelt. The Indians assert that its paste, made with sage and resin of molle and placed upon the navel, makes barren women fertile; and that by carrying the aforesaid beads on one's person, one is kept safe from vipers and venomous animals. It

corpus_links.title: On the Molle Tree: Properties, Resin, and Medicinal Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXVIII
Del molla

Los árboles que hallamos en estas Indias de saludables gomas y resina, son sin número; sólo trataré aquí de los más conocidos; y sea el primero el que llaman molla en este reino del Perú, que es un árbol muy conocido y que nace en tierras templadas y calientes. Es de la grandeza de un olivo, y de aquí para abajo se halla de diferente tamaño; es agradable a la vista, de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVIII
On the Molle

The trees we find in these Indies that yield healthful gums and resins are beyond number; I shall treat here only of the best known, and the first shall be the one called molle [also molle] in this kingdom of Peru, a well-known tree that grows in temperate and warm lands. It is as large as an olive tree, and smaller below that size; it is pleasant to the eye, of a light green, and its leaf resembles that of the mastic tree [lentisco], though somewhat longer, narrower, and thinner.

It bears a small reddish fruit in clusters, the size of elderberries, from which the Indians customarily make chicha [a fermented beverage], and it is so strong that it intoxicates more than that made from maize or other seeds; the Indians hold it to be the most precious and refined

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_LXXXI
corpus_links.title: On the Quina-Quina Tree: Properties, Uses, and Preparations
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXI
De la quina-quina

Llaman en el Perú a un árbol grande y hermoso como un membrillo o un olivo; la hoja, del tamaño y talle que la del limón ceutí; el tronco es algo colorado, resinoso y aromático. Es árbol caliente en el segundo grado, estíptico y seco y de suave olor. Echa unas pepitas por semilla del tamaño de almendras, de color amarillo y de sustancia oleaginosa, que con fraganc
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXI
On the Quina-Quina

In Peru they give this name to a large and handsome tree resembling a quince or an olive; its leaf is the size and shape of the Ceuti [Moroccan] lemon leaf; the trunk is somewhat reddish, resinous, and aromatic. The tree is [humorally] hot in the second degree, astringent [estíptico], dry, and of a pleasant smell. It bears small seeds [pepitas] the size of almonds, yellow in color and of an oily substance, which smell agreeably fragrant; these too are hot and astringent in the second degree, and dry beyond the first. When the trunk and branches are scored [sajando], they exude a fragrant resin that congeals so thoroughly it can be ground to powder, at which point it becomes a pale black color; this resin is hot and drier than the seeds. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_CII
corpus_links.title: The Tipa Tree: Description, Properties, and Medicinal Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CII

De la tipa

Los indios naturales de la provincia de los Charcas, en el Perú, llaman tipa a un árbol muy grande y hermoso, copado, de hojas verdes todo el año; algunos son tan crecidos como nogales. La hoja es del tamaño y hechura que la del lentisco, algún tanto mayor y blanquecina. Echa unas vainillas del largor de un dedo, delgadas y enjutas, salvo que junto al pezón son gruesecill
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CII

On the Tipa

The native Indians of the province of Charcas, in Peru, call tipa a very large and beautiful tree, broad-crowned, with green leaves throughout the year; some specimens grow as large as walnut trees. The leaf is similar in size and shape to that of the mastic tree [lentisco], somewhat larger and whitish. It produces small pods about a finger's length, slender and dry, except that near the stem they are somewhat thicker, as if they contained a chickpea inside. Each of these little pods resembles in shape and form the wing of a butterfly. The trunk is reddish and heavy, and both the trunk and its bark, branches, and leaves are highly astringent [estípticos] and of a hot complexion [complexión caliente]; and chiefly the resin that the tree exudes when its trunk and br

In the other things they use as much as in their own persons — which they ordinarily keep so filthy as to inspire disgust — and since they almost never change or wash their clothing, they give off a foul odor; yet they are not offended by this or by any other smell, nor do they prize good odor and fragrance, for they feel neither pleasure in the one nor discomfort in the other, being a people altogether unclean. They ordinarily eat little, which they do more out of wretchedness and poverty than from abstinence; for when the occasion presents itself they gorge themselves like wolves — as usually happens when they eat at the Spaniards' expense.

cobo.source_text: Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Cobo (1653), Book V
cobo.original: El saúco es árbol muy conocido y de grande uso en la medicina del Perú. Sus flores y hojas son muy buenas para los constipados y para ablandar apostemas.
cobo.translation: The saúco (elder) is a very well-known tree of great use in Peruvian medicine. Its flowers and leaves are very good for colds and for softening abscesses. The bark decocted is used as a diuretic and purgative. The flowers applied externally reduce inflammation. Cobo notes that both Spanish colonists and indigenous Andean healers used saúco — the Andean species (S. peruviana) was found to have the same properties as the European elder (S. nigra) that Spanish physicians already knew, creating one of the earliest documented cross-continental pharmacological comparisons.
cobo.preparation: Flowers decocted for respiratory complaints; leaves applied externally for inflammation; bark decocted as diuretic
cobo.condition: Colds, respiratory infection, fever, inflammatory swellings, diuretic

modern_research.key_compound: Sambucol (standardised elderberry extract), anthocyanins, sambunigrin, quercetin
modern_research.summary: European elderberry (S. nigra) has multiple clinical trials showing reduction in cold and flu duration. Sambucol (standardised extract): RCT showing 50% reduction in flu duration. Antiviral activity: anthocyanins bind and prevent viral entry into cells. Multiple meta-analyses confirm efficacy for upper respiratory infections. The South American species (S. peruviana) is less studied but likely shares the same active compounds given botanical proximity.
modern_research.significance: Elderberry/elder is one of the most clinically validated traditional plants for respiratory infections in the archive — with RCT evidence for flu reduction that predates modern antiviral drugs. Cobo's documentation of the Andean elder for the same indication as European elder represents an early cross-continental botanical comparison. The convergence between European folk medicine and Andean traditional use — for the same plant genus, same indication — strengthens the pharmacological signal.

De la patacauri

La patacauri es una yerbecita pequeña que nace agarrada con el suelo; sus hojas parecen a las de las malvas cuando pequeñas; están hendidas en puntas botas y desiguales. El pecíolo de la hoja es largo un jeme, redondo, delgado, rojo y con un vellito blanco muy sutil. Echa esta yerba unas florecitas blancas de cinco hojas en ruedo, parecidas en el tamaño y talle a
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVIII
On the Patacauri

The patacauri is a small herb that grows close to the ground; its leaves resemble those of mallow [malvas] when young; they are divided into blunt and uneven points. The leaf stalk [pecíolo] is a handspan [jeme] in length, round, slender, red, and covered with a very fine white down. This herb bears small white flowers of five petals arranged in a whorl [en ruedo], similar in size and form to those of elderflower [saúco]. The Indians eat this herb among their greens [yuyos], and call it by this name in the Aymara language.

CHAPTER XLIV
On the Cota

The cota is a small herb no larger than the ctichuchu [a small plant], which appears to be nothing more than a green patch on the ground; it puts forth neither branches nor stalks, producing only its leaves and flowers directly upon the earth. The leaves resemble those of rosemary, except that they are somewhat longer, thinner, and more tender. These plants form large patches on the ground, with their leaves and roots very closely and tightly packed together. They produce many flowers resembling in form those of chamomile [manzanilla]; they are a little larger, and the central button is neither as yellow nor as pointed; the small petals surrounding the center are white on the inner side, as in chamomile, and red on the underside. De la ullaulla

La Ullaulla es una florecita llamada así en la lengua aimará, de color entre blanco y morado, del tamaño y talle de la del saúco, algún tanto mayor; compónese de cinco hojitas en rueda, las cuales tienen las puntas botas; nacen a manojitos de ocho a diez florecillas cada uno. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LIV
On the Ullaulla

The Ullaulla is a small flower called by this name in the Aymara language, of a color between white and purple, of the size and form of the elderflower [saúco], though somewhat larger; it is composed of five small petals arranged in a wheel [i.e., radially], whose tips are blunt [botas]. They grow in small clusters of eight to ten florets each. They have a fragrance that is pleasing and lively to the sense of smell, and they are among the most fragrant flowers produced by the mountain ranges [sierras] of Peru, where they grow in great abundance and greatly beautify the fields. On the Anonas

The tree that bears the anonas [custard apples] is of medium size, comparable to an orange tree, well-formed and full-crowned. On the guazuma

Del molla

Los árboles que hallamos en estas Indias de saludables gomas y resina, son sin número; sólo trataré aquí de los más conocidos; y sea el primero el que llaman molla en este reino del Perú, que es un árbol muy conocido y que nace en tierras templadas y calientes. CHAPTER LXXVIII
On the Molle

The trees we find in these Indies that yield healthful gums and resins are beyond number; I shall treat here only of the best known, and the first shall be the one called molle [also molle] in this kingdom of Peru, a well-known tree that grows in temperate and warm lands. It is as large as an olive tree, and smaller below that size; it is pleasant to the eye, of a light green, and its leaf resembles that of the mastic tree [lentisco], though somewhat longer, narrower, and thinner.

cobo.source_text: Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Cobo (1653), Book VI
cobo.original: La zábila es planta muy conocida. El acíbar, que es el jugo que se saca de sus hojas, es muy amargo y purga la cólera. Aplicado a heridas y quemaduras es de grande provecho.
cobo.translation: The zábila (aloe) is a very well-known plant. The acíbar, which is the juice extracted from its leaves, is very bitter and purges bile (acts as a laxative). Applied to wounds and burns it is of great benefit. Cobo documents both the internal (laxative) and external (wound/burn) applications that remain the two primary modern uses of aloe — a remarkable pharmacological accuracy across four centuries.
cobo.preparation: Gel applied directly to wounds and burns; bitter latex (acíbar) taken as laxative
cobo.condition: Wounds, burns, skin conditions, constipation (latex)
cobo.notes: The distinction Cobo makes between 'acíbar' (the bitter yellow latex — laxative) and the gel (wound healing) is pharmacologically precise. The latex contains anthraquinone glycosides (laxative); the inner gel contains polysaccharides and glycoproteins (wound healing). Cobo identified both components and their different applications in the 17th century — predating the chemical understanding by 300 years.

modern_research.key_compound: Aloin (anthraquinone glycoside — in latex), acemannan (polysaccharide — in gel), glucomannans, salicylic acid
modern_research.summary: Aloe vera gel: FDA cleared for wound care; documented wound healing acceleration and burn treatment. Aloe latex: FDA previously approved OTC laxative until 2002 when data gaps led to reclassification pending studies. Acemannan: immunomodulatory activity. Multiple RCTs for wound healing, burn treatment, and psoriasis. One of the most studied traditional plants globally.
modern_research.significance: Aloe vera is one of the most commercially successful traditional medicines globally — a multi-billion dollar industry. Cobo's 17th-century documentation of both its laxative and wound-healing applications matches precisely the two validated modern uses, demonstrating that the traditional observation was pharmacologically accurate.

plants.evidence_authority: Aloe vera gel: FDA cleared wound care device (510k). Aloe latex: formerly FDA approved OTC laxative (now reclassified pending data). USP monograph.

CHAPTER XXXII

On the Tapaxochitl

This is a very common shrub in the province of Nicaragua, which is planted in gardens on account of the beauty of its flowers. corpus_links.translation: Sabbara (aloe): it heals sores and consolidates fresh wounds. The best quality is clear and yellow in color. Ibn al-Baitar's aloe entry notes the quality distinction between good and poor aloe latex — the clear yellow indicating high aloin content (pharmacologically active laxative compounds). corpus_links.translation: This passage, from Pliny the Elder's Natural History (Book XVIII), describes agricultural methods observed in Italy beyond the Po [Padus] River and in other regions. The Salassi people, while raiding territories at the foot of the Alps, attempted to destroy emerging crops of panic-grass and millet. CHAPTER 59. WHAT PLANTS ARE BENEFITTED BY SALT WATER. A particular remedy for the diseases to which radishes, beet, rue, and cunila [savory] are prone is salt water, which also has the additional benefit of greatly contributing to their sweetness and fertility. Other plants are equally benefitted by being watered with fresh water, the most desirable of which is the coldest and sweetest to drink; pond water and drain water, on the other hand, are less suitable, as they tend to carry the seeds of weeds with them. It is rainwater, however, that constitutes the principal nourishment of plants; it also has the effect of killing insects as they develop upon the plants.

Western basil (O. basilicum): rosmarinic acid and linalool show anti-anxiety and anti-inflammatory effects.
modern_research.significance: Basil occupies a fascinating position across traditions — valued medicinally in Greek/Roman medicine, sacred in Indian tradition (Tulsi), and now validated clinically primarily through the Ayurvedic research pathway on Holy Basil. The Greek/Roman documentation for digestive and anxiety-related conditions is consistent with the documented mechanisms, though the research has developed primarily through the Indian rather than the Western tradition.

plants.evidence_authority: Systematic reviews on Tulsi/Holy Basil for stress and metabolic conditions — positive results. Multiple RCTs.

cobo.original: El romero es planta muy estimada en la medicina española y criolla del Perú por sus muchas virtudes.
cobo.translation: Rosemary is a plant highly esteemed in Spanish and Creole medicine in Peru for its many virtues. Used for head conditions, to strengthen the memory, for digestive complaints, and as a general tonic. Cobo documents that rosemary was among the first European plants successfully cultivated in Andean Peru and rapidly adopted by indigenous healers, who found its properties consistent with local aromatic plants they already used.

modern_research.summary: Rosmarinic acid: documented anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antiviral activity. Carnosic acid: strong antioxidant; neuroprotective activity in animal models. Multiple studies on cognitive enhancement: rosmarinic acid inhibits acetylcholinesterase (same mechanism as Alzheimer's drugs). Small clinical trials showing improved memory performance with rosemary aroma. 1,8-cineole correlates with cognitive performance in human studies.
modern_research.significance: Rosemary's traditional use for memory — documented by Cobo and ubiquitous in European folk medicine ('rosemary for remembrance') — is now supported by mechanistic research showing acetylcholinesterase inhibition, the same target as approved Alzheimer's drugs. The gap between traditional folk observation and potential therapeutic application for cognitive decline is one of the most clinically significant in the archive.

On the ulluma

CHAPTER XLIV
On the Cota

The cota is a small herb no larger than the ctichuchu [a small plant], which appears to be nothing more than a green patch on the ground; it puts forth neither branches nor stalks, producing only its leaves and flowers directly upon the earth. The leaves resemble those of rosemary, except that they are somewhat longer, thinner, and more tender. On the Purgative Little Beans

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII

On the Cañahuasopo

The cañahuasopo is a shrub so closely resembling rosemary in its branches and leaves that anyone might easily mistake it for such; it differs only in that its leaves are somewhat shorter than those of rosemary and of a more whitish green. It produces a small yellow flower like that of rue [ruda]; the plant rises two or three cubits [codos] from the ground; when its leaves are chewed they are as bitter and pungent as those of rosemary; its branches, near the base, are of a black colour, so that they appear scorched. This plant grows in great abundance in the lands of the Collao [the Altiplano region around Lake Titicaca], where it is most commonly used as firewood, and it is called by this name in the Aymara language.
