corpus_links.translation: Multiple sage species (Salvia and Artemisia) are documented across 19+ nations for both medicinal and ceremonial purposes — the distinction between them being culturally variable. White sage (Salvia apiana) is used for purification ceremonies across Southwest nations; common sage (Salvia officinalis) for digestive and respiratory conditions across Eastern nations; sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) across Great Basin nations for fever and respiratory. The medicinal applications — antimicrobial, digestive, respiratory — are consistent across all sage species and connect to Mediterranean sage (Salvia officinalis) in the Greek/Roman tradition for the same applications.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXX
On the plant called Suelda Consuelda ["mend-and-heal"]

The plant called by the Spaniards suelda consuelda is named by the Indians of Peru, in the general language [Quechua], chuleorrhuko, and in Cochabamba, in the diocese of Charcas, auquilagna, which means "father of herbs." The shrub is small and its stems very similar to vine shoots [sarmientos], except that they are more tender. Its leaf is likewise very similar to that of the grapevine, but smaller and more greasy than it, and both leaves and stems are very tender and tart like vinegar. It produces a small, purple, and showy flower that gives off no fragrance whatsoever. cobo.translation: The granadilla (passionfruit) is highly esteemed. Its juice calms heart palpitations. The Indians use it specifically for anxiety and palpitations — one of the earliest written records of Passiflora's anxiolytic properties.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIV
Of the Tumbo

The tumbo is another species of apincoya [passion flower relative], more similar to the granadilla of the Quijos [people] than to the common one. Its stem is square, with four corners; the leaf is heart-shaped, a hand-span [jeme] in length and slightly less in width; it is smooth, stiffer than the leaf of the granadilla, yet not as channeled as that of the Quijos variety, and of a darker green than either. From the midrib of the leaf, very distinct and clearly marked veins extend outward to the margins. The flower is of the same form as that of the granadilla, except that it is more purple, and the bracts [hojas] surrounding the flower are likewise purple. De la vadea

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XV
On the vadea

In the city and province of Guayaquil, in the diocese of Quito, the Spaniards call vadea a species of passionflower vine [apincolia, sic] that grows there, very similar in its leaves, flower, and fruit to the tumbo. It is as large as a medium-sized gourd, about one-third of a vara [roughly 11 inches] in length, and some are larger; it is oval in shape, yellow on the exterior, with a tender rind like that of a citron [cidra], two fingers thick, in the manner of a melon, with white and tender flesh, containing many seeds inside like those of a granadilla [passionfruit], but somewhat larger, and a watery, sweet juice with a hint of a pleasant tartness [agrete sabroso], amounting to about a quartillo [roughly a quarter pint]. CAPITULO XVIII
De las piñuelas

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVIII
On the Piñuelas

The plant that bears the piñuelas belongs to the genus of the maguey [agave], under which genus there are comprehended as many species as there are in that of the cardones [columnar cacti], all of them agreeing in having leaves like those of the zabila [aloe], some larger and thicker than others, of different colors, with a stalk in the middle more or less thick and tall according to the variety of maguey. This shrub of the piñuelas rises three or four cubits from the ground; its leaves [pencas] are of a whitish green, armed along the edges with sharp spines, on account of which they are used in some places to enclose [fence] gardens. CAPITULO LXXX
Del ñorbo

El ñorbo es una mata voluble de casta de bejuco; echa muchos vástagos delgados, que se revuelven a otras plantas o a los encañados y los pueblan de hojas y flores. La hoja es de singular hechura y que no he visto otra semejante a ella en ninguna planta: es ni más ni menos que la mitad de la hoja del naranjo, cortada por medio la parte que cae hacia la punta, con que viene
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXX
On the Ñorbo

The ñorbo is a twining shrub of the vine [bejuco] kind; it puts forth many slender shoots that wind themselves around other plants or around trellises [encañados], which they cover with leaves and flowers. The leaf is of a singular form unlike any I have seen on any other plant: it is neither more nor less than half the leaf of an orange tree, cut through the middle at the part toward the tip, so that this leaf ends up resembling the other half still attached to the stalk. The flower is white and purple, fragrant, and of a lovely appearance, shaped like that of the puchipiichi, and its span is about that of a two-real coin [real de a dos]; in it one can see the same emblems of the Passion of Our Redeemer as in the flower of the granadilla [passionflower], for thi

CAPITULO XXXIV

Del puchipuchi

Esta es una frutilla silvestre, cuya mata es voluble, crece sobre árboles o se extiende por el suelo; echa un vástago delgado como un cañón de escribir, redondo, verde y velloso; su hoja es parecida a la de las malvas, es blanquecina, vellosa y algo pegajosa; la fruta que lleva esta planta es del tamaño y figura de un huevo de paloma, con un hollejito delgado, tiern
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIV

On the Puchipuchi

This is a small wild fruit whose plant is a climber [voluble]; it grows over trees or spreads along the ground. It sends out a slender stem, like a writing quill [cañón de escribir], round, green, and hairy. Its leaf resembles that of the mallow [malva]: it is whitish, hairy, and somewhat sticky. The fruit borne by this plant is the size and shape of a pigeon's egg, with a thin, tender, and tough little skin [hollejito]. The edible substance within consists of small black seeds the size of linseed [linaza], covered in a whitish, watery liquid that is sweet with a hint of tartness. CAPITULO XXIII
De las orugas

Las orugas que nacen en las legumbres y en todo linaje de plantas, son unos gusanos que se engendran de las hojas verdes y se mantienen della: verdadera pestilencia de las huertas; los cuales crecen en tanta cantidad en las tierras calientes y templadas destas Indias, que a tiempos suelen destruir las plantas. Hállanse diferencias de orugas cuantas son las especies de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIII
On Caterpillars

The caterpillars [orugas] that appear on vegetables and on all manner of plants are worms [gusanos] generated from green leaves, upon which they also feed: a true pestilence of gardens. They multiply in such quantities in the warm and temperate lands of these Indies that at times they are wont to destroy the plants entirely. There are as many varieties of caterpillar as there are species of vegetables and plants; for I have at times observed that all those bred on different kinds of vegetables and trees differ from one another. On the leaf of the granadilla [passion fruit vine] are found the smallest I have ever seen, for they are tiny black worms, almost as thin as a thread and no longer than a pine nut.

cobo.translation: The lemon and lime are very medicinal. Their juice cuts fevers and prevents weakness on long voyages — implicit scurvy prevention, documented almost a century before Lind's 1747 trial. Juice mixed with salt kills lice and cures mange.

CAPITULO PRIMERO

De los nombres destas Indias Occidentales y Nuevo Mundo

CHAPTER ONE

On the Names of These West Indies and the New World

I begin this second book with the two last parts of the earth, which we call América and the Austral Land [Tierra Austral] (and which are the proper subject of this history). CAPITULO V

Del segundo Inca, llamado Cinchi-Roca

Muerto Manco-Cápac, fue obedecido en rey su hijo mayor Cinchi-Roca, el cual era ya hombre de más de veinte años. Quedó tan bien industriado por su padre en las cosas del gobierno y república, y procedía con tan gran prudencia, que alcanzó ser amado de todos no menos que su padre, por el buen tratamiento que les hacía. Por principio de su reinado v
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER V

On the Second Inca, Called Cinchi-Roca

Upon the death of Manco-Cápac, his eldest son Cinchi-Roca was obeyed as king; he was already a man of more than twenty years of age. He had been so well instructed by his father in matters of government and statecraft [república], and conducted himself with such great prudence, that he came to be loved by all no less than his father had been, on account of the good treatment he showed them. At the outset of his reign he visited the settlements and villages of the valley of Cuzco, which were by then greatly enlarged and grown in buildings and people; and in the course of this visit he commanded that all should cultivate whatever lands they might need for sowing their potatoes [papas]; and thus cultivation spread as far as Cinga, which is a

The men and women of each nation and province had their own marks and [divisas] [insignia] by which they were known, and they were not permitted to go about without them nor to exchange them for those of another nation, under severe penalties. These they wore on their clothing in different stripes and colors; and the men wore another mark more prominently on the head, with each nation distinguished by its headdress [tocado]. For although all of them went about with long hair, some wore it cut below the ears and others very long; some braided and others loose, and most bound or wrapped with various kinds of ties [ligaduras]. Del maguey del vino

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX

On the Military Art and How These Indians Practiced It, Their Weapons, and Their Manner of Fighting

The Indians of Peru regarded the exercise of arms as the most serious and noble of all pursuits, and they attended to it with greater refinement, study, and care than to any other. The Incas held military service and those who practiced it in the highest esteem, regarding it as the means by which they had risen to such great power and majesty and by which they maintained it. It was the sole title among their subjects by which one could advance to positions of honor, and there was scarcely any other path by which a man might rise and make himself of worth. modern_research.significance: Alexanders represents a plant that fell out of medical use not because of inefficacy but because of cultural displacement by celery — a fascinating case of therapeutic continuity through botanical substitution. The limited modern research means this plant is genuinely unknown territory.

De la hopahopa.

Llaman hopahopa los indios a ciertas lentejuelas que se dan encima del agua encharcada y en los totorales o juncales; son algo coloradas y de complexión templada, con muy poca estipticidad; majada esta yerba y puesta en la muela que duele, quita el dolor; y asimismo, puesta sobre las quebraduras o fracturas de huesos con un poco de sal y polvos de muña, las restaura
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXI
On the hopahopa.

The Indians call hopahopa certain small lentil-like [plants] that grow on the surface of stagnant water and in reed beds or rush beds [totorales o juncales]. They are somewhat reddish and of a temperate complexion [temperament], with very little astringency [estipticidad]. This herb, ground [majada] and applied to the aching molar, relieves the pain; and likewise, applied over fractures or broken bones together with a little salt and powdered muña, it restores them. Its decoction taken with wine and alum [alumbre], drunk frequently, heals mouth sores [llagas de la boca] and firms the teeth.

At Babylon, however, they cut the blade twice and then allow the cattle to graze upon it a third time, for otherwise the crop would run entirely to leaf. CHAPTER 59. WHAT PLANTS ARE BENEFITTED BY SALT WATER. A particular remedy for the diseases to which radishes, beet, rue, and cunila [savory] are prone is salt water, which also has the additional benefit of greatly contributing to their sweetness and fertility. It is rainwater, however, that constitutes the principal nourishment of plants; it also has the effect of killing insects as they develop upon the plants.

modern_research.summary: Apiol: documented uterotonic activity — validates traditional use as emmenagogue and for menstrual regulation. CAUTION: apiol is toxic at high doses — parsley seed oil was historically used as an abortifacient with documented fatalities. Diuretic activity: consistent with traditional use for urinary conditions. Luteolin: anti-inflammatory and antioxidant. Vitamin K: highest concentration of any common herb — relevant for anticoagulant interactions. Myristicin: mild psychoactive properties at high doses.
modern_research.significance: Parsley's traditional use as a menstrual regulator is pharmacologically validated by apiol's uterotonic activity — the same mechanism explains both its therapeutic use for delayed menstruation and its historical use as an abortifacient. This is one of the clearest cases in the archive of traditional medicine correctly identifying a uterotonic mechanism centuries before the pharmacology was understood. CAUTION: potentially dangerous in pregnancy.

CHAPTER ONE

On the shrubs found in these Indies of the same species as those of Spain

corpus_links.translation: A mixture composed of onion crushed in honey and taken in beer was prescribed [for itch]. corpus_links.original: Several remedies for 'Hotness in the Eyes,' a condition which without doubt must have been visited rather frequently on those driven for various reasons to place themselves under the care and treatment of an Oculist of the Pharaohonic period. As an eye-cooler, 'Baked Ox-liver, placed carefully thereon' does not sound very hopeful, but Soda-from-Upper-Egypt (even when dissolved in Spring-water) sou
corpus_links.translation: Several remedies are given for 'Hotness in the Eyes' [ocular inflammation], a condition that must have been quite common among those who sought the care of an oculist during the Pharaonic period. As an eye-cooler, 'Baked Ox-liver, placed carefully thereon' does not sound very hopeful; and Soda-from-Upper-Egypt [natron], even when dissolved in spring-water, sounds positively alarming, despite the scribe's special marginal note appended to the prescription reading: 'It Heats It!' The third remedy, however, shows more promise and reveals once again the ancient physicians' belief in the homœopathic doctrine of like curing like: ANOTHER [REMEDY] TO DRIVE OUT HOTNESS IN THE EYES: Tallow from the jawbone of an ass. Mix in cool water and let the patient apply it to his temples so that he may be he

tradition_names.egyptian: Documented in Ebers Papyrus compound prescriptions

egyptian.original: [Hieratic] — caraway seed in digestive compound prescriptions
egyptian.translation: Caraway seed documented in the Ebers Papyrus as a component in compound medicines for digestive complaints — used for flatulence, abdominal pain, and as a digestive stimulant. Among the oldest documented culinary-medicinal plants, with evidence of use in ancient Egypt dating to at least 1550 BCE and archaeological finds suggesting use as far back as 5000 BCE.
egyptian.preparation: Seeds decocted or chewed; incorporated into compound preparations

modern_research.key_compound: Carvone (50-85% of essential oil), limonene, carveol
modern_research.summary: Carvone (same compound as in dill): antispasmodic activity on gastrointestinal smooth muscle — directly validates traditional digestive use. European Commission E monograph approves caraway for dyspeptic complaints. Multiple clinical studies confirming efficacy for functional dyspepsia and irritable bowel symptoms. One of the most clearly validated traditional digestive herbs in European regulatory frameworks.
modern_research.significance: Caraway has one of the clearest regulatory validations among traditional digestive plants — Commission E approval, ESCOP monograph, and documented antispasmodic mechanism. The 5,000-year documented use (archaeological) combined with modern regulatory recognition makes it one of the most time-tested validated plant medicines in the archive.

plants.evidence_authority: EU Commission E approved for dyspeptic complaints; ESCOP monograph; clinical evidence for functional dyspepsia.

corpus_links.label: CS.Chik.1.3
corpus_links.title: Brahmi Rasayana — cognition and memory
corpus_links.original: ब्राह्मी मेध्या स्मृतिकरी आयुष्या रसायनी।
corpus_links.translation: Brahmi enhances intelligence, improves memory, is longevity-promoting, and is a rasayana. Bacopa monnieri (Brahmi) is Ayurveda's primary cognitive medicine — documented by Charaka for memory, learning, intelligence, and longevity. The specific claim that brahmi improves memory in children and reverses cognitive decline in older patients is among the most precisely stated therapeutic claims in the Charaka Samhita. Multiple modern RCTs have since validated these claims.
corpus_links.preparation: Brahmi ghrita (brahmi-infused clarified butter); also brahmi juice with honey
corpus_links.condition: Poor memory, cognitive decline, epilepsy, anxiety, insanity

corpus_links.label: CS.Chik.3
corpus_links.title: Jvarachikitsa — fever treatment
corpus_links.original: सर्वरोगाणाम् अग्रणी ज्वरः। गुडूची ज्वरघ्नी।
corpus_links.translation: Fever is foremost among all diseases. Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia) destroys fever. The Charaka fever chapter documents a hierarchy of fever treatment — from simple fasting and rest to complex multi-herb decoctions. Guduchi is the primary anti-fever plant. The pippali (long pepper) + ginger + black pepper combination (Trikatu) is documented for digestive fever. Neem (nimba) is documented for malarial fever types — one of the earliest documented antimalarial treatments.
corpus_links.preparation: Guduchi decoction; Trikatu (long pepper + ginger + black pepper) for digestive fever
corpus_links.condition: Fever (all types), malarial fever, digestive fever, fever with ama (toxins)

corpus_links.label: CS.Chik.5
corpus_links.title: Gulma Chikitsa — abdominal tumors and digestive masses
corpus_links.original: हिङ्ग्वादयः गुल्मघ्नाः। अग्निमान्द्यहरा वायुलोमाः।
corpus_links.translation: Asafoetida (hingu) and others destroy abdominal masses. They overcome sluggish digestion and promote downward movement of wind. Asafoetida (Ferula asafoetida) is documented as the primary medicine for gulma — abdominal masses, which may correspond to tumors, cysts, or severe digestive disorders. The antispasmodic and carminative properties of asafoetida are well-established. This chapter also documents long pepper for digestive complaints and haritaki for constipation-related gulma.
corpus_links.preparation: Asafoetida compound preparations in sesame oil; taken after meals
corpus_links.condition: Abdominal masses, digestive disorders, flatulence, constipation

corpus_links.label: CS.Chik.14
corpus_links.title: Apasmara Chikitsa — epilepsy treatment
corpus_links.original: ब्राह्म्याः सर्पिर्मेध्यं। वचा संज्ञाप्रदा।
corpus_links.translation: Brahmi ghrita (brahmi in ghee) is the cognitive treatment [for epilepsy]. Vacha (Acorus calamus) restores consciousness. The Charaka epilepsy chapter is one of the most pharmacologically interesting — brahmi (Bacopa) and vacha (Acorus) are both documented for neurological conditions. Vacha (calamus root) contains asarone — a compound with documented anticonvulsant activity. The combination of these plants in Saraswatarishta and other classical preparations is still used in Ayurvedic practice today.
corpus_links.preparation: Brahmi ghrita; Saraswatarishta (fermented preparation with brahmi, vacha, ashwagandha)
corpus_links.condition: Epilepsy, psychosis, cognitive disorders, loss of consciousness

corpus_links.label: CS.Plant.Shatavari
corpus_links.title: Shatavari — Ayurvedic women's medicine
corpus_links.original: शतावरी बल्या वृष्या रसायनी स्तन्यजननी।
corpus_links.translation: Shatavari gives strength, is aphrodisiac, is a rasayana, and promotes milk production. Asparagus racemosus (shatavari — literally 'who has a hundred husbands') is Ayurveda's primary women's medicine — documented by Charaka for: lactation support, menstrual regulation, fertility, menopausal symptoms, and as a general women's tonic. Multiple modern RCTs have confirmed lactation-promoting activity (galactagogue effect).
corpus_links.preparation: Root powder in warm milk; shatavari ghrita; shatavari kalpa
corpus_links.condition: Lactation, menstrual disorders, infertility, menopause, general women's health

corpus_links.label: CS.Plant.Neem
corpus_links.title: Nimba (Neem) — the universal purifier
corpus_links.original: निम्बः सर्वज्वरघ्नः। कुष्ठघ्नः। कृमिघ्नः।
corpus_links.translation: Neem destroys all fevers. It destroys skin diseases. It destroys worms/parasites. Neem (Azadirachta indica) is documented throughout Charaka for an extraordinary range of conditions — fever, skin diseases, parasites, diabetes, wound healing, and as a general antimicrobial. The three-fold claim (anti-fever, anti-skin disease, anti-parasitic) is directly validated by modern research: nimbidin (anti-inflammatory), azadirachtin (antiparasitic — the most studied natural pesticide), and gedunin (antimalarial).
corpus_links.preparation: Neem leaf decoction; neem oil topically; neem bark decoction
corpus_links.condition: Fever (all types), skin diseases, intestinal parasites, diabetes, wound infection

corpus_links.label: CS.Plant.Guduchi
corpus_links.title: Guduchi — the immunity plant
corpus_links.original: गुडूची सर्वज्वरघ्नी। रसायनी। मेध्या।
corpus_links.translation: Guduchi destroys all fevers. It is a rasayana. It enhances intelligence. Tinospora cordifolia (guduchi/giloy) is documented in Charaka for an exceptional range of conditions. Modern research has confirmed: (1) immunomodulatory activity — stimulates macrophage activity; (2) xanthine oxidase inhibition for gout; (3) anti-malarial activity; (4) hepatoprotective effects. During COVID-19, guduchi received significant attention in India as a potential immune support supplement.
corpus_links.preparation: Guduchi sattva (starch extract); guduchi decoction; guduchi ghrita
corpus_links.condition: Fever, gout, liver conditions, immunity, diabetes, general health

corpus_links.label: CS.Plant.LongPepper
corpus_links.title: Pippali (Long Pepper) — Ayurveda's most prescribed spice-medicine
corpus_links.original: पिप्पली कासश्वासहरी। दीपनी। रसायनी।
corpus_links.translation: Long pepper destroys cough and asthma. It kindles digestive fire. It is a rasayana. Pippali (Piper longum) is arguably the most frequently mentioned plant in the Charaka Samhita — appearing in Trikatu (with ginger and black pepper), in respiratory formulas, digestive preparations, and rasayana compounds. Piperine in long pepper is the same bioavailability-enhancing compound as in black pepper but at higher concentration. Piperlongumine — a compound unique to long pepper — shows documented anticancer activity.
corpus_links.preparation: Trikatu (long pepper + ginger + black pepper); pippali rasayana in honey and ghee
corpus_links.condition: Asthma, chronic cough, poor digestion, obesity, respiratory infections

corpus_links.label: SBC.Superior.1
corpus_links.title: Renshen (Ginseng) — first among superior plants
corpus_links.original: 人參：味甘，微寒。主補五臟，安精神，定魂魄，止驚悸，除邪氣，明目，開心益智。久服輕身延年。
corpus_links.translation: Renshen (ginseng): flavor sweet, slightly cold. Principally tonifies the five organs, calms the spirit, stabilizes the ethereal and corporeal souls, stops palpitations, eliminates pathogenic qi, brightens the eyes, opens the heart and benefits wisdom. Long-term use lightens the body and extends the years. Ginseng is the first plant listed among the superior drugs — the position of highest honor. The properties documented (tonifies five organs, calms spirit, benefits cognition, extends lifespan) correspond exactly to the modern clinical evidence: adaptogenic, immunomodulatory, cognitive-enhancing, anti-fatigue.
corpus_links.preparation: Decoction; powder in hot water; red ginseng (steamed and dried)
corpus_links.condition: Fatigue, cognitive decline, immune weakness, cardiovascular, general tonification

corpus_links.label: SBC.Superior.2
corpus_links.title: Huangqi (Astragalus) — the great immune tonic
corpus_links.original: 黃芪：味甘，微溫。主癰疽，久敗瘡，排膿止痛，大風癩疾，五痔鼠瘻，補虛，小兒百病。
corpus_links.translation: Huangqi (astragalus): flavor sweet, slightly warm. Principally treats abscesses and festering sores, expels pus and stops pain, major wind conditions and leprosy, hemorrhoids and scrofula, supplements deficiency, and the hundred diseases of children. Astragalus membranaceus is documented for wound healing, immunodeficiency conditions, and pediatric conditions — a range now validated by modern immunology research showing astragalus polysaccharides are among the most potent plant-derived immune modulators known.
corpus_links.preparation: Decoction; combined with other tonics in compound preparations
corpus_links.condition: Immune deficiency, wound healing, fatigue, pediatric conditions, abscesses

corpus_links.label: SBC.Superior.4
corpus_links.title: Gouqi (Goji Berry) — vision and longevity
corpus_links.original: 枸杞子：味苦，寒。主五內邪氣，熱中消渴，周痹。久服堅筋骨，輕身不老。
corpus_links.translation: Goji berry: flavor bitter, cold. Principally treats pathogenic qi in the five organs, internal heat and wasting thirst (diabetes), and painful obstruction throughout the body. Long-term use strengthens tendons and bones, lightens the body, and prevents aging. The 'wasting thirst' (xiaoke) documented here corresponds to diabetes — one of the earliest documented plant treatments for what we now call diabetes. Modern research: betaine and polysaccharides show blood glucose lowering activity.
corpus_links.preparation: Berries eaten; decoction; infusion in rice wine
corpus_links.condition: Diabetes (wasting thirst), eye conditions, longevity, fatigue, bone weakness

corpus_links.label: SBC.Superior.5
corpus_links.title: Huanglian (Coptis) — the bitter cold detoxifier
corpus_links.original: 黃連：味苦，寒。主熱氣目痛，眥傷泣出，明目，腸澼腹痛下利，婦人陰中腫痛。久服令人不忘。
corpus_links.translation: Huanglian (Coptis/goldthread): flavor bitter, cold. Principally treats hot-type eye pain, damage to the inner corner of the eye with tearing, brightens the eyes, intestinal dysentery with abdominal pain and diarrhea, and female genital swelling and pain. Long-term use prevents forgetting. This is the same Coptis genus as MMA-068 (Coptis/Goldthread) — documented in North American and Tibetan traditions. The Shennong documentation adds Chinese traditional medicine as a fourth independent tradition recognizing the same plant genus for infection and inflammation.
corpus_links.preparation: Decoction; powder; Huanglian Jiedu Tang (compound with other bitter cold herbs)
corpus_links.condition: Eye infections, dysentery, intestinal infections, inflammatory conditions

corpus_links.label: SBC.Superior.6
corpus_links.title: Dang Gui (Angelica) — women's blood medicine
corpus_links.original: 當歸：味甘，溫。主咳逆上氣，溫瘧，寒熱洗洗在皮膚中，婦人漏下，絕子，諸惡瘡瘍金瘡。
corpus_links.translation: Dang gui: flavor sweet, warm. Principally treats cough with rebellious qi, malarial fever, chills and heat sensation in the skin, uterine bleeding, infertility, various malignant sores and metal wounds. Angelica sinensis (dang gui / Chinese angelica) is the most important women's blood medicine in Chinese materia medica — documented here alongside wound healing, which connects to Greek/Roman use of related Angelica species for the same wound indication.
corpus_links.preparation: Decoction; Si Wu Tang compound (four substances decoction)
corpus_links.condition: Menstrual disorders, uterine bleeding, infertility, wound healing, anemia

corpus_links.label: SBC.Superior.7
corpus_links.title: Gegen (Kudzu root) — cardiovascular and fever
corpus_links.original: 葛根：味甘，平。主消渴，身大熱，嘔吐，諸痹，起陰氣，解諸毒。
corpus_links.translation: Kudzu root: flavor sweet, neutral. Principally treats wasting thirst (diabetes), great heat in the body, vomiting, various painful obstructions, raises yin qi, and resolves all toxins. Kudzu root (Pueraria lobata) is documented for diabetes, fever, and as an antitoxin. Modern research: puerarin (kudzu isoflavone) shows significant cardiovascular effects — one of the few traditional Chinese plants with FDA-investigated potential for alcohol dependence treatment.
corpus_links.preparation: Decoction; powder; Ge Gen Tang compound
corpus_links.condition: Diabetes, fever, cardiovascular conditions, alcohol dependence, neck stiffness

corpus_links.label: SBC.Middle.2
corpus_links.title: Huangqi (Scutellaria) — the fever and infection herb
corpus_links.original: 黃芩：味苦，平。主諸熱，黃疸，腸澼泄利，逐水，下血閉，惡瘡疽蝕，火瘍。
corpus_links.translation: Huangqin (Scutellaria baicalensis): flavor bitter, neutral. Principally treats all heat conditions, jaundice, intestinal dysentery and diarrhea, drives out water retention, disperses blood obstruction, malignant sores and tissue decay, and fire-type wounds. Skullcap root (Scutellaria baicalensis) is documented for fever, infections, and jaundice — the same indications as the modern research showing baicalein and wogonin have documented anti-inflammatory, antiviral, and hepatoprotective activity.
corpus_links.preparation: Decoction; Huang Lian Jie Du Tang compound
corpus_links.condition: Fever, jaundice, respiratory infections, intestinal infections, liver conditions

corpus_links.label: SBC.Middle.5
corpus_links.title: Gancao (Licorice Root) — the harmonizer
corpus_links.original: 甘草：味甘，平。主五臟六腑寒熱邪氣，堅筋骨，長肌肉，倍力，金瘡腫，解毒。久服輕身延年。
corpus_links.translation: Gancao (licorice root): flavor sweet, neutral. Principally treats pathogenic cold and heat qi in the five organs and six bowels, strengthens tendons and bones, increases muscle mass, doubles strength, treats metal wound swellings, resolves toxins. Long-term use lightens the body and extends the years. Glycyrrhiza uralensis (Chinese licorice) — the same genus as the licorice documented in Egyptian, Greek/Roman, Persian, and Ayurvedic traditions. With the Shennong documentation, licorice now has the strongest multi-tradition convergence of any plant in the archive: five independent medical traditions across four continents.
corpus_links.preparation: Appears in approximately 70% of all classical Chinese herbal formulas as harmonizing ingredient
corpus_links.condition: Digestive complaints, respiratory conditions, wound healing, toxin resolution, general tonic

corpus_links.label: BGM.Fuling
corpus_links.title: Fuling (Poria) — calming the spirit through the earth
corpus_links.original: 茯苓：甘，平，無毒。主胸脅逆氣，憂恚驚邪恐悸，心下結痛，寒熱煩滿，咳逆⋯
corpus_links.translation: Fuling (Poria): sweet, neutral, non-toxic. Principal uses: counterflow qi in the chest and flanks, anxiety, fright, fear, and palpitations, knotted pain below the heart, chills and heat with vexation and fullness, cough with rebellious qi... Poria cocos (a polypore mushroom growing on pine roots) is one of the most frequently used substances in Chinese herbal medicine — appearing in approximately 10% of all classical formulas. Li Shizhen documents its primary action as calming the heart-spirit, which is consistent with modern research showing Poria polysaccharides have documented sedative and anxiolytic activity.
corpus_links.preparation: Powder in hot water; combined in Si Jun Zi Tang (Four Gentlemen Decoction)
corpus_links.condition: Anxiety, insomnia, palpitations, digestive weakness, urinary conditions

corpus_links.label: BGM.Yimucao
corpus_links.title: Yimucao (Motherwort) — women's life herb
corpus_links.original: 益母草：辛苦，微寒，無毒。主瘀血，月水不通，產後血暈。益母之名，以功而名。
corpus_links.translation: Yimucao (motherwort): acrid and bitter, slightly cold, non-toxic. Principal uses: static blood, menstrual obstruction, postpartum blood dizziness. The name 'Benefit Mother Herb' comes from its function. Leonurus japonicus (Chinese motherwort) is the primary gynecological herb in classical Chinese medicine — documented by Li Shizhen specifically for menstrual regulation and postpartum conditions. Modern research has confirmed uterotonic activity from leonurine — directly validating the traditional 'moves the uterus' mechanism. This connects to the archive's documentation of rue (MMA-046) for the same gynecological application via a different but parallel uterotonic mechanism.
corpus_links.preparation: Decoction; Yi Mu Cao Gao (syrup)
corpus_links.condition: Menstrual irregularity, dysmenorrhea, postpartum hemorrhage, uterine conditions

corpus_links.label: BGM.Banlangen
corpus_links.title: Banlangen (Isatis root) — the viral fever herb
corpus_links.original: 板藍根：苦，寒，無毒。清熱解毒，涼血利咽。
corpus_links.translation: Banlangen (Isatis root): bitter, cold, non-toxic. Clears heat and resolves toxins, cools the blood and benefits the throat. Li Shizhen documents Isatis tinctoria root for epidemic fevers and throat infections — the same plant used as an indigo dye source. During multiple viral epidemics in China (SARS 2003, H1N1 2009, COVID-19 2020), banlangen was among the most widely distributed Chinese herbal medicines. In vitro antiviral activity has been documented against multiple respiratory viruses including influenza.
corpus_links.preparation: Banlangen granules (most common OTC Chinese herbal product); decoction
corpus_links.condition: Viral fever, sore throat, epidemic diseases, inflammatory throat conditions

corpus_links.original: 半夏：辛，溫，有毒。消心腹胸膈痰熱，咳嗽上氣，心下急痛堅痞。
corpus_links.translation: Banxia (Pinellia): acrid, warm, toxic. Disperses phlegm and heat in the heart, abdomen, chest, and diaphragm; cough with rebellious qi; acute pain and hardness below the heart. Li Shizhen's expanded entry on Pinellia (first documented in Shennong Bencaojing) details the processing methods required to reduce toxicity and the specific preparations for different manifestations: Ban Xia Hou Po Tang for globus hystericus (throat constriction), Xiao Ban Xia Tang for morning sickness, Er Chen Tang for phlegm conditions.
corpus_links.preparation: Always processed (processed with ginger or alum); Ban Xia Hou Po Tang; Xiao Ban Xia Tang
corpus_links.condition: Nausea, morning sickness, chemotherapy nausea, phlegm conditions, globus hystericus

De la copaquira

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIV
On Copaquira

The Indians of Peru, in the Aymara language, call verdigris [cardenillo] 'copaquiri,' and because of the resemblance that the stone I describe here bears to it, they give it the same name. The Spaniards, corrupting the word, call it copaquira and 'stone of the Lipes' [piedra de los Lipes], because it is found only in the province of the Lipes, which falls under the archbishopric of Charcas. Copaquira is a blue-green and transparent stone, which is extracted from a deposit found in the said province of the Lipes, whose veins are no thicker than a finger, although there are sometimes found pockets filled with medium-sized pieces weighing four or more pounds. corpus_links.translation: The flower of copper [verdigris, i.e., basic copper acetate or copper carbonate patina] being applied stops the flow of blood from wounds and cleanses foul ulcers. When applied with honey, it draws together the edges of wounds. Used as an eye salve, it sharpens the sight. Beaten fine and applied, it arrests excessive menstrual flow. Washed copper [i.e., copper that has been rinsed or purified] applied with vinegar removes eruptions of the skin and dandruff. Copper vessels used for water storage prevent the water from putrefying.

Oil of worms

Mouse oil
Cat's oil

WHAT TO DO TO DRAW OUT SPLINTERS FROM THE FLESH
[Remedy 1:] The per-baibait bird [an unidentified Egyptian bird] with Honey. Apply thereto.

[Remedy 2:] Worms' blood, cooked and crushed in Oil; Mole, killed, cooked, and drained in Oil; Ass's dung, mixed in Fresh Milk. Apply to the opening.

[Remedy 3:] Male-and-Female-Semen [i.e., combined human semen]. Apply thereto.

[Remedy 4:] Skull of the Shadfish [a species of fish], cooked in Oil. Apply to the point of the splinter. Thereby it comes out.

[Remedy 5:] Incense, Dough, Sea-salt, Wasp's dung

corpus_links.translation: Regarding the body, the Scribe set down several remedies. One internal remedy was compounded of Figs, Grapes, and Onions, Bread-of-the-Zizyphus-Lotus [bread made from the fruit of Ziziphus lotus], Blossoms-of-the-Cucumber, Incense, Wine, and Sweet Beer. Irregularities of the 'met' [the Egyptian concept of bodily channels or vessels] were treated by having the patient chew 'uwah-grain' while simultaneously applying a poultice of Goose's eggs to his buttocks — yet another illustration of the Scribe's adherence to the doctrine of like-curing-like [similia similibus curantur]. corpus_links.translation: The ancient physician was at a loss when confronted with the so-called 'wood-like uha-disease' [Egyptian: uha, possibly a stiffening or sclerotic condition] occurring in isolation. cobo.source_text: Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Cobo (1653), Book IV
cobo.original: La papa es el principal sustento de los indios del Perú. Además de servir de comida, tiene uso medicinal: cocida y aplicada en cataplasma sirve para calmar el ardor y la inflamación.
cobo.translation: The potato is the principal sustenance of the Indians of Peru. Besides serving as food, it has medicinal use: cooked and applied as a poultice it serves to calm burning and inflammation. Cobo is among the first European writers to systematically document the potato's medicinal as well as nutritional role. Indigenous Andean communities distinguished between dozens of potato varieties with different medicinal properties — a pharmacological knowledge system of extraordinary sophistication.
cobo.preparation: Cooked and applied as poultice for inflammation; eaten for nutritional conditions; raw juice applied topically
cobo.condition: Inflammatory conditions (topical), nutritional deficiencies, digestive complaints

modern_research.key_compound: Solanine (in skin/green parts — toxic), chlorogenic acid, resistant starch, vitamin C, potassium
modern_research.summary: Potato skin: solanine (toxic at high doses) and chlorogenic acid (anti-inflammatory, antioxidant). Resistant starch in cooled cooked potato: documented prebiotic effect. Raw potato juice: anti-ulcer activity documented in small trials (alkaline pH buffers gastric acid; anti-inflammatory compounds). Topical use validated by anti-inflammatory compound profile. The enormous genetic diversity of Andean potatoes (over 3,000 varieties) represents an underexplored pharmacogenomic resource.
modern_research.significance: Cobo's documentation of the potato's dual food-medicine role captures one of the most important Andean contributions to global nutrition. The medicinal applications — particularly the topical anti-inflammatory use and the raw juice gastric protection — are consistent with the documented chemistry. The 3,000+ Andean potato varieties represent a genetic library of Solanaceae diversity that modern pharmacology has barely begun to explore.

CHAPTER VIII
On the Batata

The batata [sweet potato] is a root well known not only throughout all the Indies, but also in Spain, and it was one of the most esteemed foods the Indians had. CHAPTER XIII
On Potatoes

Throughout the highland and cold lands of Peru, where neither maize nor the other seeds and legumes that grow in temperate and warm regions are harvested, the ordinary crops that the Indians cultivate are certain roots called papas [potatoes], of the size and shape of truffles [criadillas de tierra]. Both fresh and dried, these are so universally consumed in Peru that half the Indians there have nothing else to eat. The plant grows to a height of two hand-spans [palmos]; its leaves are so continuous and closely set along the stem that they appear to be a single leaf with many points, which points somewhat resemble the leaves of lemon balm [toronjil]. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIV
On the Ocas

The ocas are edible roots that grow in the cold lands where the potatoes grow. The plant of this root is called xibico; it is of the sorrel family [linaje de acederas], small, about one third of a vara [roughly 11 inches] in height, more or less; its branches are gathered close together, giving it a bushy appearance; the leaves are very small, arranged in threes, like those of the sorrel. The roots of this plant are somewhat elongated, about half a jeme [roughly 3–4 inches] in length, not smooth but uneven and knotted; some are white, others purple, and of other colors, like the potatoes; they are very tender and floury. The Indians eat them green, roasted, and boiled; they also split them lengthwise and dry them in the sun for storage. Dried in this manner they ar

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol2::IV::cap_V
corpus_links.title: Reign and Death of Cinchi-Roca, the Second Inca
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO V

Del segundo Inca, llamado Cinchi-Roca

Muerto Manco-Cápac, fue obedecido en rey su hijo mayor Cinchi-Roca, el cual era ya hombre de más de veinte años. Quedó tan bien industriado por su padre en las cosas del gobierno y república, y procedía con tan gran prudencia, que alcanzó ser amado de todos no menos que su padre, por el buen tratamiento que les hacía. Por principio de su reinado v
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER V

On the Second Inca, Called Cinchi-Roca

Upon the death of Manco-Cápac, his eldest son Cinchi-Roca was obeyed as king; he was already a man of more than twenty years of age. He had been so well instructed by his father in matters of government and statecraft [república], and conducted himself with such great prudence, that he came to be loved by all no less than his father had been, on account of the good treatment he showed them. At the outset of his reign he visited the settlements and villages of the valley of Cuzco, which were by then greatly enlarged and grown in buildings and people; and in the course of this visit he commanded that all should cultivate whatever lands they might need for sowing their potatoes [papas]; and thus cultivation spread as far as Cinga, which is a

For this reason, there always resided in that city and court Indians from every province of the kingdom, occupied in the keeping and ministry of their idols, where they learned the customs and usages of the court; and as they rotated through their mitas [obligatory labor turns] and shifts, upon returning to their homeland they preserved and taught their own people all that they had seen and learned at court.

cobo.source_text: Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Cobo (1653), Book V
cobo.original: La muña es hierba muy olorosa que los indios usan mucho para los males del estómago y para conservar las papas.
cobo.translation: Muña is a very fragrant herb that the Indians use greatly for stomach ailments and for preserving potatoes. Cobo documents two distinct uses: medicinal (digestive complaints, respiratory conditions) and food preservation — the practice of storing potatoes with muña to prevent insect damage and spoilage. This dual use as food preservative and medicine is consistent with the documented antimicrobial properties.
cobo.preparation: Leaves chewed or decocted for digestive complaints; used as fumigation for respiratory; placed with stored food as preservative
cobo.condition: Digestive complaints, respiratory conditions, altitude sickness (soroche), food preservation
cobo.notes: Muña is one of the few plants in the archive documented simultaneously as medicine and food preservative — a dual use that reflects a sophisticated empirical understanding of its antimicrobial properties. Modern research has validated both applications.

modern_research.summary: Muña essential oil shows potent antimicrobial activity — particularly against food spoilage organisms, validating the traditional potato preservation use. Carvacrol and thymol (also in oregano and thyme) show broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity including against drug-resistant pathogens. Anti-parasitic: documented activity against Giardia in vitro. Altitude sickness (soroche): muña is traditionally used by Andean communities for altitude adaptation; limited pharmacological research on this specific application.
modern_research.significance: Muña's dual documentation as medicine and food preservative in Cobo is one of the clearest examples of empirical antimicrobial discovery in traditional practice — healers identified the same plant as useful for preventing food spoilage and treating internal infections, both consistent with the documented carvacrol/thymol antimicrobial mechanism.

plants.evidence_authority: Antimicrobial activity documented in multiple Peruvian studies; carvacrol/thymol pharmacology well-established; no clinical trials.
plants.priority_reason: Dual food-preservative and medicinal use consistent with antimicrobial mechanism · Drug-resistant pathogen activity · Active research in Peru · No international clinical development

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XIX
corpus_links.title: On the ulluma root: properties, uses, and preparations
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XIX
De la ulluma

La ulluma es cierta raíz muy parecida a la oca; hállanse de tan diferentes colores como las ocas; son de temperamento frío y algo ventoso y muy mucilaginoso; bebiendo una buena porción del cocimiento destas raíces, junto con la muña, facilita el parto, y el mismo efecto dicen los indios que hacen ellas comidas solas en buena cantidad. Ultra desto, hecho lamedor del cocim
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIX
On the ulluma

The ulluma is a certain root very similar to the oca [Oxalis tuberosa]; roots of it are found in as many different colors as the oca. They are of a cold and somewhat flatulent [ventoso] temperament and highly mucilaginous [mucilaginoso]. Drinking a good portion of the decoction of these roots together with muña facilitates childbirth, and the Indians say that eating them alone in a sufficient quantity produces the same effect. Beyond this, a lincture [lamedor] made from the decoction of these roots with the requisite amount of sugar, and given frequently to those with penetrating wounds [heridos penetrantes], causes them to expectorate with ease the blood extravasated [extravenada] in the chest. And when these roots are boiled with rosemary and the resulting wate

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XXXIX
corpus_links.title: On the Herb Payco (Epazote / Wormseed)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXIX
Del payco

Es el payco una yerba muy medicinal; sus hojas son menudas, crespas y de muchas puntas, y sus raíces, como hilos; es de temperamento caliente. Echan los indios esta yerba en sus guisados. Sus hojas, aplicadas en forma de emplasto sobre cualquier tumor, lo resuelven; asimismo resuelven las ventosidades; para cuyo efecto, sintiéndose con ellas los indios, comen estas hojas:
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIX
On Payco

Payco is a highly medicinal herb; its leaves are small, curly, and with many points, and its roots are like threads; it is of a hot temperament [i.e., hot in the humoral sense]. The Indians add this herb to their stews. Its leaves, applied in the form of a poultice over any tumor, dissolve it; they likewise dispel flatulence [ventosidades]; for this purpose, when the Indians suffer from it, they eat these leaves. The same effect is achieved by its decoction taken with muña [a Andean herb], drunk hot on an empty stomach with a little chili pepper [ají]. The decoction of payco, with a good quantity of salt, reduces swelling in the legs. This herb is called, in the language of Peru, payco, and in the Mexican tongue, pizote.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXXXI
corpus_links.title: On the hopahopa (aquatic lentil-like plant)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXI
De la hopahopa.

Llaman hopahopa los indios a ciertas lentejuelas que se dan encima del agua encharcada y en los totorales o juncales; son algo coloradas y de complexión templada, con muy poca estipticidad; majada esta yerba y puesta en la muela que duele, quita el dolor; y asimismo, puesta sobre las quebraduras o fracturas de huesos con un poco de sal y polvos de muña, las restaura
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXI
On the hopahopa.

The Indians call hopahopa certain small lentil-like [plants] that grow on the surface of stagnant water and in reed beds or rush beds [totorales o juncales]. They are somewhat reddish and of a temperate complexion [temperament], with very little astringency [estipticidad]. This herb, ground [majada] and applied to the aching molar, relieves the pain; and likewise, applied over fractures or broken bones together with a little salt and powdered muña, it restores them. Its decoction taken with wine and alum [alumbre], drunk frequently, heals mouth sores [llagas de la boca] and firms the teeth.

cobo.source_text: Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Cobo (1653), Book VI
cobo.original: Las malvas son de grande uso en la medicina española y criolla del Perú.
cobo.translation: Mallows are of great use in Spanish and Creole medicine in Peru. Cobo documents mallow for digestive complaints, respiratory conditions, and wound treatment — extending the existing Greek/Roman and Anglo-Saxon documentation for mallow (MMA-077) to a third tradition via adoption in colonial Peru.
cobo.preparation: Leaves decocted; applied as poultice
cobo.condition: Digestive complaints, respiratory conditions, wound healing, inflammation

modern_research.summary: See MMA-077 for full pharmacological summary. This Cobo entry adds a third independent documentation tradition for mallow — Spanish colonial Peru adopting European mallow for the same applications, demonstrating the plant's consistent therapeutic recognition across cultures.
modern_research.significance: Extends mallow convergence (MMA-077) to three independent documentation contexts: Greek/Roman, Anglo-Saxon, and colonial Andean. Post-colonial adoption by Andean healers represents independent empirical validation of European mallow medicine.

plants.evidence_authority: See MMA-077. Mucilage soothing mechanism validated; ESCOP monograph; no approved drug.
plants.priority_reason: Extends mallow to three documentation traditions including independent Andean adoption · Mucilage mechanism validated

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XXXVIII
corpus_links.title: The Patacauri Plant
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXVIII
De la patacauri

La patacauri es una yerbecita pequeña que nace agarrada con el suelo; sus hojas parecen a las de las malvas cuando pequeñas; están hendidas en puntas botas y desiguales. El pecíolo de la hoja es largo un jeme, redondo, delgado, rojo y con un vellito blanco muy sutil. Echa esta yerba unas florecitas blancas de cinco hojas en ruedo, parecidas en el tamaño y talle a
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVIII
On the Patacauri

The patacauri is a small herb that grows close to the ground; its leaves resemble those of mallow [malvas] when young; they are divided into blunt and uneven points. The leaf stalk [pecíolo] is a handspan [jeme] in length, round, slender, red, and covered with a very fine white down. This herb bears small white flowers of five petals arranged in a whorl [en ruedo], similar in size and form to those of elderflower [saúco]. The Indians eat this herb among their greens [yuyos], and call it by this name in the Aymara language.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XC
corpus_links.title: On the Copana plant and its uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XC
De la copana

La copana es una yerba que produce las hojas cortas, espinosas y aparradas por el suelo; sus raíces son unas pequeñas cebollas mucilaginosas por extremo, de temperamento caliente y húmedo. Úsan dellas las indias para aderezarse y engomarse el cabello. Majadas estas cebollas con malvas y unto sin sal, valen para madurar cualquiera apostema.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XC
On the copana

The copana is an herb that produces short, spiny leaves that spread low along the ground; its roots are small bulbs that are extremely mucilaginous, of a hot and moist temperament [in the Galenic sense]. The Indian women use them to dress and set their hair. These bulbs, pounded together with mallows and lard without salt, are efficacious for ripening [i.e., bringing to a head] any abscess [apostema].

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_XXIV
corpus_links.title: The Quelluquellu Plant
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXIV
Del quelluquellu

El quelluquellu es una mata silvestre buena para leña; crece un estado en alto; produce muchas ramas o varas a la redonda, de color rojo; su hoja, en la figura, es muy semejante a la de la malva. Echa en pequeños manojitos una florecilla colorada mucho menor que la del olivo, a la cual sucede una frutilla también colorada, redonda, del tamaño de garbanzos, que, aunq
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIV
On the Quelluquellu

The quelluquellu is a wild shrub [mata silvestre] good for firewood; it grows to the height of one estado [approximately one fathom, or the height of a man]; it produces many branches or stems spreading outward, red in color; its leaf, in shape, is very similar to that of the mallow. It puts forth, in small clusters, a little red flower much smaller than that of the olive tree, which is followed by a small fruit, likewise red, round, and the size of chickpeas, which, though insipid, the Indians commonly eat. The roots of this plant are red and medicinal, for they have the property of constricting and binding [i.e., astringent action]. This plant is called by this name in the Aymara language.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_L
corpus_links.title: The Sunchu plant: description, properties, and uses against snake venom
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO L
Del sunchu

El sunchu es un linaje de flores amarillas, que abraza algunas diferencias dellas muy parecidas todas entre sí en su figura, que es del talle de la flor de la manzanilla, y en la forma de la planta, que es una mata de un estado de alto, aromática y resinosa, la cual echa unas varas delgadas, redondas y algo rojas. Sus hojas son semejantes a las de la yerba-mora, y tocadas co
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER L
On the Sunchu

The sunchu is a genus of yellow-flowered plants, encompassing several varieties that are all very similar to one another in appearance: the shape of the flower resembles that of chamomile [manzanilla], and the plant itself is a shrub about one fathom [estado] in height, aromatic and resinous, which puts forth slender, round, and somewhat reddish stems. Its leaves are similar to those of nightshade [yerba-mora], and when touched to the tongue they prove abstersive [cleansing] or astringent [estípticas]. Both the leaves and the stems are covered with a short, rough down. The various sunchos differ from one another in height and in the shape of their leaves, for some have leaves larger than those of nightshade and bearing small points like those of the mallow. The flo

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XXXIV
corpus_links.title: The Puchipuchi: A Wild Climbing Fruit
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXIV

Del puchipuchi

Esta es una frutilla silvestre, cuya mata es voluble, crece sobre árboles o se extiende por el suelo; echa un vástago delgado como un cañón de escribir, redondo, verde y velloso; su hoja es parecida a la de las malvas, es blanquecina, vellosa y algo pegajosa; la fruta que lleva esta planta es del tamaño y figura de un huevo de paloma, con un hollejito delgado, tiern
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIV

On the Puchipuchi

This is a small wild fruit whose plant is a climber [voluble]; it grows over trees or spreads along the ground. It sends out a slender stem, like a writing quill [cañón de escribir], round, green, and hairy. Its leaf resembles that of the mallow [malva]: it is whitish, hairy, and somewhat sticky. The fruit borne by this plant is the size and shape of a pigeon's egg, with a thin, tender, and tough little skin [hollejito]. The edible substance within consists of small black seeds the size of linseed [linaza], covered in a whitish, watery liquid that is sweet with a hint of tartness. The flesh of this fruit closely resembles that of the granadilla [passion fruit], which will be discussed in the following book; likewise its flower in shape and form is very sim

corpus_links.title: On Tacú: Andean Medicinal Clay and Its Varieties
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO IX

Del Tacú

Tacú llaman los indios del Perú, en la lengua aimará, a la tierra que propiamente es Bolo Arménico y por tal se suele administrar, a la cual podemos llamar con propiedad Bolo Indico. Hállase el tacú en el cerro rico de Potosí y en otras minas de metales, en especial de hierro, en tres diferencias: la primera, es una tierra colorada como sangre, de que usan los pintores y, pr
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX

On Tacú

The Indians of Peru, in the Aymara language, call tacú a substance that is properly Armenian Bole [Bolo Arménico] and is commonly administered as such; we may fittingly call it Indian Bole [Bolo Indico]. Tacú is found in the rich mountain of Potosí and in other metal mines, especially iron mines, and comes in three varieties: the first is a blood-red earth, used by painters and, principally, by gilders; the second is liver-colored; and the third, most common and most used by the Indians for curing certain ailments, is yellow. This last variety the Indians sell in the marketplaces in loaves and cakes, and they make use of it to treat bloody dysentery [cámaras de sangre], its powder being drunk dissolved in chicha, which is their wine. This earth is also useful, especial

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LIX
corpus_links.title: Chapter LIX: On the Choclla (two species of cebadilla)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LIX

De la choclla

Dos especies se hallan en estas Indias de cierta yerba que los españoles llaman cebadilla, por la semejanza que tienen con la cebada: la una es natural de la Nueva España, y la otra, deste reino del Perú. La primera echa una espiga parecida a la del trigo, larga un palmo y más; su caña es asimismo como la del trigo, algo más gruesa, parda y maciza, de un estado de alto
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LIX

On the Choclla

Two species are found in these Indies of a certain herb that the Spaniards call cebadilla [little barley], on account of its resemblance to barley. One is native to New Spain and the other to this kingdom of Peru. The first puts forth a spike resembling that of wheat, a handspan or more in length; its stalk is likewise similar to that of wheat, somewhat thicker, brownish, and solid, about a man's height tall; it grows wild in the savannas without being sown. The grains are black, somewhat smaller than those of barley, and when ground they kill the worms [maggots] in the sores [saddle-galls] of beasts of burden, and likewise the chigoe fleas [niguas] that burrow into persons.

The other species of cebadilla is called choclla in the Aymara language; it is a prize

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXX
corpus_links.title: On the plant called Suelda Consuelda
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXX
De la suelda consuelda

A la planta llamada de los españoles suelda consuelda, nombran los indios del Perú, en la lengua general, chuleorrhuko, y en Cochabamba, diócesis de Charcas, auquilagna, que quiere decir padre de las yerbas. La mata es pequeña y sus tallos muy parecidos a los sarmientos, salvo que son más tiernos. Su hoja asimismo es muy semejante a la de la vid, sino que es me
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXX
On the plant called Suelda Consuelda ["mend-and-heal"]

The plant called by the Spaniards suelda consuelda is named by the Indians of Peru, in the general language [Quechua], chuleorrhuko, and in Cochabamba, in the diocese of Charcas, auquilagna, which means "father of herbs." The shrub is small and its stems very similar to vine shoots [sarmientos], except that they are more tender. Its leaf is likewise very similar to that of the grapevine, but smaller and more greasy than it, and both leaves and stems are very tender and tart like vinegar. It produces a small, purple, and showy flower that gives off no fragrance whatsoever. En algunas partes preparan la palta verde hecha pequeñas tajadas y echadas en salmuera, para suplir la falta de aceitunas. In some places the unripe palta is prepared by cutting it into small slices and placing them in brine, to serve as a substitute for olives. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_CII
corpus_links.title: The Tipa Tree: Description and Medical Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CII

De la tipa

Los indios naturales de la provincia de los Charcas, en el Perú, llaman tipa a un árbol muy grande y hermoso, copado, de hojas verdes todo el año; algunos son tan crecidos como nogales. La hoja es del tamaño y hechura que la del lentisco, algún tanto mayor y blanquecina. Echa unas vainillas del largor de un dedo, delgadas y enjutas, salvo que junto al pezón son gruesecill
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CII

Of the Tipa

The native Indians of the province of Charcas, in Peru, call tipa a very large and beautiful tree, full-crowned, with green leaves throughout the year; some specimens grow as tall as walnut trees. The leaf is the size and shape of that of the mastic tree [lentisco], somewhat larger and whitish. It produces small pods about a finger's length, slender and dry, except near the stem where they are slightly thickened as if a chickpea were contained within. Each of these pods resembles in shape and form a butterfly's wing. The trunk is reddish and heavy, and both it and its bark, branches, and leaves are very astringent [estípticos] and of a hot complexion [complexión caliente]; most notably the resin that the tree exudes when its trunk and branches are incised, which t

cobo.translation: Celery is very medicinal. Its seed and root boiled in water are good for kidney complaints and for provoking urine. Also documented for blood pressure and digestive antispasmodic conditions.

corpus_links.title: On the camina plant: its properties and medicinal uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXVIII
De la camina

La camina es una yerba de un codo en alto, cuyas hojas son muy parecidas a las del apio. Echa unas flores como las del eneldo; huele esta planta con fragancia como la del apio. Su temperamento es caliente y seco. Mascada esta yerba, tiene partes sutiles, pica la lengua y la deja áspera por un buen rato. Tiene virtud de resolver, y su zumo mundifica las llagas. Su coci
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXVIII
On the camina

The camina is an herb about one cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height, whose leaves closely resemble those of celery [apio]. It produces flowers like those of dill [eneldo]; the plant smells fragrant, much like celery. Its temperament [complexion, in Galenic humoral terms] is hot and dry. When this herb is chewed, it has subtle [penetrating] properties, stings the tongue, and leaves it rough for a good while. It has the virtue of resolving [dispersing humors], and its juice cleanses [mundifies] wounds. A decoction of it with a little honey from bees, given to drink on an empty stomach, breaks kidney stones and bladder stones; and bathing with a decoction of its roots for sciatica resolves the humor [disperses the accumulated fluid or morbid matter] and rel

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXXX
corpus_links.title: On the Higuana plant: properties, wound treatment, and poisonous use
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXX

De la higuana

La higuana es una planta muy pareja a la yerba de la estrella; son sus hojas como las del apio: echa una flor marina en forma de estrella; sus raíces son largas y delgadas. Es yerba de temperamento caliente, a cuya causa, el zumo della es un cáustico fuerte que abrasa las partes do llega y puesto en moderada cantidad mundifica las llagas viejas con presteza, aunque es
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXX

On the Higuana

The higuana is a plant very similar to the herb of the star [yerba de la estrella]; its leaves resemble those of celery [apio]; it puts forth a sea-like [marina] flower in the shape of a star; its roots are long and slender. It is an herb of hot temperament [temperamento caliente], by reason of which its juice [zumo] is a powerful caustic [cáustico fuerte] that burns the parts it touches; yet applied in moderate quantity it cleanses [mundifica] old wounds [llagas viejas] with speed, even when they are very foul and fetid. The Indians were accustomed to use the powders of this herb mixed into drink in order to poison their enemies.

CAPITULO C

Del chamico

La yerba que los indios llaman chamico crece un codo, poco más o menos; tiene las hojas mayores algo que los dedos, con unas puntas a los lados; echa una flor blanca de hechura de campanilla, pequeña, que se convierte en unas cabezuelas del tamaño de las adormideras, cubiertas de agudas espinas, en cuya cavidad se encierra la semilla, que es como de rábano, la cual dicen q
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER C

On the Chamico

The herb that the Indians call chamico grows to about one cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height, more or less. Its leaves are somewhat larger than one's fingers, with pointed tips along the sides. It produces a small white flower in the shape of a little bell, which turns into small heads the size of poppy capsules, covered with sharp spines, within whose cavity the seed is enclosed; the seed resembles that of the radish, and is said to be as cooling [in humoral temperament] as celery. A decoction of it taken internally dulls the senses. The Indians use it to intoxicate themselves, and if a large quantity is consumed, it deprives a person of their senses in such a way that, though their eyes remain open, they neither see nor recognize anything. CAPITULO LXXXIX

De la acana

La acana crece un codo de alto; en las ramas y hojas es muy parecida a la alfalfa; tiene flor amarilla del talle de la de la manzanilla; nace entre peñas y es yerba pectoral, más amarga al gusto que la acíbar; es caliente y seca en el segundo grado. Comen los indios con ella la coca. Su cocimiento con un poco de alumbre es bueno para las llagas de la boca; y tomado ca
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIX

On the Acana

The acana grows to a cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height; in its branches and leaves it closely resembles alfalfa; it bears a yellow flower of the shape of that of camomile; it grows among rocks and is a pectoral herb [i.e., beneficial to the chest and lungs], more bitter to the taste than aloes [acíbar]; it is hot and dry in the second degree [following Galenic humoral classification]. The Indians eat coca with it. A decoction of it with a little alum is good for sores of the mouth; and taken warm on an empty stomach with sugar candy [alfeñique], it is beneficial against cough and asthma, and softens and cleanses the chest and stomach. Beyond this, the decoction applied to the face removes freckles from it, and if prepared with wine, it removes cataract

CAPITULO LXXVIII
Del molla

Los árboles que hallamos en estas Indias de saludables gomas y resina, son sin número; sólo trataré aquí de los más conocidos; y sea el primero el que llaman molla en este reino del Perú, que es un árbol muy conocido y que nace en tierras templadas y calientes. Es de la grandeza de un olivo, y de aquí para abajo se halla de diferente tamaño; es agradable a la vista, de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVIII
On the Molle

The trees we find in these Indies that yield healthful gums and resins are beyond number; I shall treat here only of the best known, and the first shall be the one called molle [also molle] in this kingdom of Peru, a well-known tree that grows in temperate and warm lands. It is as large as an olive tree, and smaller below that size; it is pleasant to the eye, of a light green, and its leaf resembles that of the mastic tree [lentisco], though somewhat longer, narrower, and thinner.

It bears a small reddish fruit in clusters, the size of elderberries, from which the Indians customarily make chicha [a fermented beverage], and it is so strong that it intoxicates more than that made from maize or other seeds; the Indians hold it to be the most precious and refined

CAPITULO LXXXIX

De la vilca

En el Perú llaman vilca a un árbol de la grandeza de un olivo, de hoja menuda, muy parecida a la del guarango, de verde más oscuro. Es árbol copado y de buen parecer. Produce unas vainas enjutas, como algarrobas, de una tercia de largo y dos dedos de ancho, y en ellas una pepita del tamaño y delgadeza de medio real, la cáscara lisa, de un color leonado oscuro y muy de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIX

On the Vilca

In Peru, the name vilca is given to a tree of the size of an olive tree, with small leaves very similar to those of the guarango [Caesalpinia spinosa], but of a darker green. It is a broad-crowned, handsome tree. It produces dry pods, like carob pods, one third of a vara in length and two fingers in width, and within them a seed [pepita] the size and thinness of half a real [a small silver coin], with a smooth husk of a dark tawny color and very thin. The substance inside these seeds is yellow and bitter like aloe [acíbar]. The Indians hold them in great esteem on account of their medicinal properties. cobo.translation: The citron is a healthy and medicinal fruit. Its candied rind is good for the stomach and for those with corruption in the mouth (oral infection). Cobo documents citron for digestive complaints, oral infection, and as a general health tonic — consistent with its role as the oldest cultivated citrus in ancient Mediterranean medicine.
cobo.preparation: Rind candied or decocted; juice drunk; applied topically
cobo.condition: Digestive complaints, oral infection, skin conditions, general tonic

modern_research.summary: Citron is the oldest cultivated citrus — ancestor of all other citrus species. Diosmin (citrus flavonoid derivative): approved pharmaceutical drug in France for venous insufficiency. Hesperidin: capillary-strengthening, anti-inflammatory. Limonene: antimicrobial, antifungal.
modern_research.significance: Citron's position as the ancestor of all modern citrus gives it particular historical significance. Diosmin derived from citrus flavonoids is an approved European pharmaceutical, making citrus one of the most commercially developed traditional medicine plant families.

plants.evidence_authority: Diosmin (citrus flavonoid derivative) approved as drug in France for venous insufficiency; hesperidin pharmacology documented.

corpus_links.label: BGM.Qingpi
corpus_links.title: Citrus peel medicines — the Chen Pi and Qing Pi distinction
corpus_links.original: 陳皮：苦辛，溫，無毒。主胸中瘕熱，逆氣，利水穀，下氣止嗽，除膀胱留熱，下停水，五淋，利小便。
corpus_links.translation: Chen pi (aged tangerine peel): bitter and acrid, warm, non-toxic. Principal uses: masses and heat in the chest, counterflow qi, promotes digestion, descends qi and stops cough, eliminates bladder heat, disperses retained water, five types of painful urination, promotes urination. Li Shizhen documents the distinction between fresh green peel (qing pi — more potent, liver-moving) and aged orange peel (chen pi — gentler, stomach-harmonizing). This botanical pharmacological distinction — that the same plant's peel changes therapeutic properties as it ages — is one of the most sophisticated observations in the Bencao Gangmu.
corpus_links.preparation: Er Chen Tang (Two Aged Herbs Decoction); added to most digestive formulas
corpus_links.condition: Digestive qi stagnation, nausea, cough with phlegm, abdominal distension

Del tumbo

El tumbo es otra especie de apincoya, más parecida a la granadilla de los Quijos que a la común; tiene el vástago cuadrado de cuatro esquinas, la hoja en figura de corazón, de un jeme de largo y poco menos de ancho; es lisa, más tiesa que la hoja de la granadilla, ni tan acanalada como la de los Quijos, y de un verde más escuro que entrambas. Del lomo della salen a las márg
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIV
Of the Tumbo

The tumbo is another species of apincoya [passion flower relative], more similar to the granadilla of the Quijos [people] than to the common one. Its stem is square, with four corners; the leaf is heart-shaped, a hand-span [jeme] in length and slightly less in width; it is smooth, stiffer than the leaf of the granadilla, yet not as channeled as that of the Quijos variety, and of a darker green than either. From the midrib of the leaf, very distinct and clearly marked veins extend outward to the margins. The flower is of the same form as that of the granadilla, except that it is more purple, and the bracts [hojas] surrounding the flower are likewise purple. The fruit is the size of a medium citron [cidra], oval in shape, somewhat smaller than an ostrich egg; its ri

CAPITULO XV
De la vadea

En la ciudad y provincia de Guayaquil, diócesis de Quito, llaman los españoles vadea a una especie de apincolia [sic] que allí nace, muy parecida en sus hojas, flor y fruto al tumbo. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XV
On the vadea

In the city and province of Guayaquil, in the diocese of Quito, the Spaniards call vadea a species of passionflower vine [apincolia, sic] that grows there, very similar in its leaves, flower, and fruit to the tumbo. It is as large as a medium-sized gourd, about one-third of a vara [roughly 11 inches] in length, and some are larger; it is oval in shape, yellow on the exterior, with a tender rind like that of a citron [cidra], two fingers thick, in the manner of a melon, with white and tender flesh, containing many seeds inside like those of a granadilla [passionfruit], but somewhat larger, and a watery, sweet juice with a hint of a pleasant tartness [agrete sabroso], amounting to about a quartillo [roughly a quarter pint]. The entire fruit is edible, but the most pr

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XII_part1
corpus_links.title: On Zapotes: Varieties, Tree, and Fruit Description
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XII
De los zapotes.

Los zapotes son propios de la Nueva España, adonde se hallan cinco diferencias dellos; los mejores son los colorados. El árbol que los lleva es grande y copado como el mamey, con los cogollos muy poblados de hoja; ésta es larga un palmo, lisa, tiesa, de un verde oscuro y más ancha al cabo que en medio. La fruta es del tamaño de un membrillo y aun como una grande cidra
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XII
On Zapotes.

The zapotes are native to New Spain, where five varieties of them are found; the best are the red ones [colorados]. The tree that bears them is large and spreading [copado], like the mamey, with the young shoots [cogollos] very densely leafed; the leaf is a palm's length [approx. 8 inches] long, smooth, stiff, of a dark green, and wider at the tip than in the middle. The fruit is the size of a quince and even as large as a big citron [cidra], spindle-shaped [ahusada], with a thin and tender skin; the flesh is very red and soft [text breaks off].

CAPITULO XXXVI
Del soycosoyco

El soycosoyco es una yerba menuda que parece especie de las rosas o davdlinas de las Indias; levántase un codo de la tierra; echa muchos tallos delgados, redondos, lisos, correosos y algún tanto rojos, y pocas hojas; las cuales son tan pequeñas y menudas, que parecen hebrillas de seda cortadas. Produce unas florecitas amarillas que cada una tiene cuatro hojuelas no m
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVI
On the Soycosoyco

The soycosoyco is a small herb that appears to be a species of the roses or carnations [davdlinas, i.e., davelinas/clavellinas] of the Indies. It rises about one cubit [roughly half a meter] above the ground, putting forth many thin, round, smooth, tough, and somewhat reddish stems, and few leaves; these leaves are so small and fine that they resemble little cut threads of silk. It produces small yellow flowers, each having four petals no larger than those of the flower of rue [Ruta graveolens], which emerge from small, elongated buds resembling pine nuts; and after these flowers dry, they end in a tuft of fibers issuing from the same bud. This herb gives off a somewhat aromatic odor. It is hot in the second degree and moist in the first [according to Galen

corpus_links.title: Three Flowers of the Indies: Cempoalxochitl, Rose of the Indies, and Velvet Flower
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLVI

De la flor llamada cempoalxochitl

En la lengua mexicana tiene este nombre una flor que los españoles suelen llamar rosa de las Indias, la cual es natural de la Nueva España. La mata que la produce crece poco menos de un estado, y algunas, mucho más; echa tantas ramas, que se hace copada. Y cada una da muchas flores; es parecida en la hoja a la artemisa. La flor es amarilla, de la g
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI

On the flower called cempoalxochitl

In the Mexican language [Nahuatl], this is the name given to a flower that the Spaniards commonly call the rose of the Indies, which is native to New Spain. The shrub that produces it grows to little less than one estado [approximately six feet] in height, and some grow considerably taller; it puts forth so many branches that it becomes bushy and rounded. Each branch bears many flowers; in its leaves it resembles artemisia [wormwood]. The flower is yellow, about the size of a rose, and some are much larger; it is composed of many petals, which are twisted or curled, for which reason we commonly call it the escarole flower [flor escarolada]. It has nothing to recommend it beyond its appearance, because its scent is disagreeable and offensiv

corpus_links.title: On Several Other Cardones (Cacti): Pullapulla and Hachacana
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO IX
De los demás cardones

De las muchas diferencias de cardones que yo he visto, no deben de quedar más que tres o cuatro, mas no dudo sino que habrá otros de que yo no tenga noticias. Uno de los más pequeños es el que se dice pullapulla, el cual no se levanta de la tierra más que, cuando mucho, un jeme. Hácese una mata redonda algo ahusada, que no parece sino un montoncillo de peras o de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX
On the Other Cardones [cacti]

Of the many varieties of cardones [columnar or globose cacti] that I have seen, there remain no more than three or four to describe, though I do not doubt that there are others of which I have no knowledge. One of the smallest is the one called pullapulla, which rises from the ground no more than, at most, one span [jeme: the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the index finger, roughly 7–8 cm]. It forms a round, somewhat tapering clump that looks like nothing so much as a little pile of pears or prickly-pear pads [tunas] arranged very close together in orderly fashion, their crowns pointing upward; for instead of branches or broad leaves [pencas], this plant produces small stems or joints [pezoncilos o trocillos] the size and shape of
