corpus_links.title: The Mutuy plant: description, uses, and medicinal preparations
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO X

Del mutuy

El mutuy es una mata que crece poco más de un estado en alto; echa muchas ramas a la redonda y muy juntas, con que se hace muy ancha y copada; sus ramas son rojas, mayormente hacia los pimpollos; produce las hojas como el lentisco, de dos en dos, en ramillos largos de un palmo, y se parecen en el talle y tamaño a las del lentisco, salvo que son más tiernas, más delgadas y un
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER X

On the Mutuy

The mutuy is a shrub that grows to little more than one estado [approximately the height of a man, roughly 1.7 m] in height; it sends out many branches all around, growing very close together, which makes it very wide and bushy. Its branches are red, especially toward the new shoots. It produces leaves like those of the mastic tree [lentisco], in pairs, on long sprigs of about a hand-span, and they resemble those of the mastic in shape and size, except that they are more tender, thinner, and of a darker green. corpus_links.title: Two Nicaraguan and Guatemalan ornamental plants: Tapaxochitl and the Grafted Flower
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXII

Del tapaxochitl

Esta es una mata muy común en la provincia de Nicaragua, que por la hermosura de sus flores se planta en los jardines. Crece tres o cuatro palmos en alto y se hace muy copada; echa muchos tallos, que son redondos y con muchos ñudos; de los cuales nacen las hojas de dos en dos y son parecidas a las del granado, salvo que son vellosas. En la cumbre de los vástagos na
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXII

On the Tapaxochitl

This is a very common shrub in the province of Nicaragua, which is planted in gardens on account of the beauty of its flowers. It grows three or four spans [palmos] in height and becomes very bushy; it puts forth many stems, which are round and have many nodes [ñudos], from which the leaves grow in pairs, resembling those of the pomegranate, except that they are downy. At the top of the shoots the flower grows; it is a dark crimson tending toward purple, very striking, somewhat resembling the pink [clavellina], except that it is round in the manner of a button, the size of a hazelnut, composed of very small, hard, rough, and pointed little leaves [bracts], which are almost all spiny when touched with the hand, among which small white points emerge that ar

corpus_links.title: On the Cantuta and the Muña: Two Peruvian Plants
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXVII

De la cantuta

La cantuta es una mata que echa muchas ramas alrededor, con que se viene a hacer copada; crece comúnmente dos estados; está muy poblada de hojas, la cual es como la del arrayán, algún tanto mayor y más delgada y tierna. No produce otro fruto esta planta más que flores del mismo nombre, las cuales son purpúreas de color encendido y otras amarillas; las mejores y de m
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVII

On the Cantuta

The cantuta is a shrub that puts forth many branches all around, giving it a bushy, rounded crown. It commonly grows to about two fathoms [estados] in height and is thickly set with leaves resembling those of myrtle [arrayán], though somewhat larger, more slender, and more tender. This plant produces no other fruit than the flowers that share its name; some of these are purple of a vivid, glowing hue, and others are yellow—the purple ones being the finer and more pleasing in appearance. The stem or little neck [cuellecito] is hollow, about the thickness of a carnation's [clavellina's] stem and somewhat longer; both it and the petals of the flower are of the same substance, very fine, thin, and uniform in color. Near the tip or mouth of the flower, the stem o

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_XLVII
corpus_links.title: Two Peruvian shrubs: the Ujuta and the Urcu-urcu
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLVII

De la ujuta

Los indios del Perú llaman ujuta al calzado que usan, y dan el mismo nombre a una flor, por tener, como tiene, la figura del dicho calzado. La mata que la produce crece dos o tres codos y echa muchas ramas o varas delgadas, pardas, redondas, lisas y correosas. Su hoja se parece a la del almendro, salvo que es un poco menor y más tierna. Es la flor amarilla de muy fino
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVII

Of the Ujuta

The Indians of Peru call ujuta the footwear [sandal] they use, and they give the same name to a flower because it has, as indeed it does, the shape of said footwear. The shrub that produces it grows two or three cubits tall and puts out many branches or thin stems, brownish, round, smooth, and tough [correosas]. Its leaf resembles that of the almond tree, except that it is somewhat smaller and more tender. The flower is yellow of a very fine color, of handsome appearance, though without fragrance; it has no more than a single petal [hoja] in the shape of a small gourd, a little shorter than a finger, thickest where it is about as wide as the ball of the thumb, tapering toward the stalk [pezón], and hollow within. The little buds of this flower, before opening,

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_LXXXI
corpus_links.title: The Chinchircuma Plant
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXI
De la chinchircuma

Esta es una mata voluble, que nace en tierras frías; produce un vástago delgado como un junco mediano, redondo, blanquecino, muy tierno y quebradizo; la hoja es larga medio jeme y no más ancha que la longitud de un grano de trigo; echa una flor naranjada de muy vivo color, semejante a la clavellina en la hechura, salvo que tiene un poco más grueso el pezón y no e
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXI
On the Chinchircuma

This is a twining shrub that grows in cold lands. It produces a thin stem like a medium-sized rush [junco], round, whitish, very tender and brittle. The leaf is half a [jeme — the span from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the index finger, roughly 3–4 inches] long and no wider than the length of a grain of wheat. It puts forth a vivid orange-colored flower, similar in form to the carnation [clavellina], except that its stalk [pezón] is somewhat thicker and is not smooth but rather scaly, composed of small, somewhat purplish leaflets arranged in the manner of scales. The petals of the flower are numerous and narrower than those of the carnation. This flower has a pleasing appearance but no scent, and its name derives from the Aymara language.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_LXXl
corpus_links.title: On the Cacaloxochitl (Plumeria) and a related white-flowered tree
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXI

Del cacaloxochitl.

Muchos árboles nacen en estas Indias que no llevan otro fruto sino flores muy vistosas. Describiré aquí los más conocidos y estimados por la hermosura de sus flores; que de todos es imposible hacer memoria. Y sea el primero el árbol que produce la flor llamada cacaloxochitl, en la Nueva España; el cual es muy parecido a la adelfa, poco copado, y que no tiene hoja
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXI

On the Cacaloxochitl.

Many trees grow in these Indies that bear no other fruit than very showy flowers. I shall describe here the best known and most prized for the beauty of their blossoms, for it is impossible to record them all. Let the first be the tree that produces the flower called cacaloxochitl in New Spain. It closely resembles the oleander [adelfa], has a sparse crown, and bears leaves only at the growing tips [cogollos]; these leaves are a hand's breadth or more in length and very similar to those of the oleander. The tree is of medium size, like a pomegranate tree; and it is a noteworthy thing that its fruit, so to speak, is the flowering it produces throughout the entire year. Each flower resembles a rose, though considerably smaller, yet larger than a carnation

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_LXXIII
corpus_links.title: The Tree Called 'Flowers of the Dead' (Panama)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXIII

Del árbol que lleva las flores de muertos

En la ciudad de Panamá dan este nombre a cierto árbol, porque en ningún tiempo del año está sin flores y con ellas suelen enterrar a los niños que mueren. Es tan grande como un naranjo, de hoja muy menuda, como la de la ruda, pero de un verde más vivo. Produce las flores por los pimpollos de sus ramas en ramilletes, compuesto cada uno de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXIII

Concerning the tree that bears the flowers of the dead

In the city of Panama, a certain tree is given this name because at no time of year is it without flowers, and these flowers are customarily used to bury children who have died. The tree is as large as an orange tree, with very small leaves, like those of rue [ruda], but of a more vivid green. It produces its flowers at the tips [pimpollos] of its branches in clusters, each cluster composed of ten or twelve flowers, and each flower is the size and form of a small carnation [clavelina], of a yellow and red [encarnado] color. When the whole tree is covered with them, it is very pleasing to the eye; and it would be held in even greater esteem if its flowers had a fragrance, which they do not.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_LXXVII
corpus_links.title: Various Flowering Trees of the Americas
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXVII

De los demás árboles de flores

Entre las muchas especies de árboles que llevan flores, una es la de cierto árbol llamado sicahani, el cual es pequeño, copado y que produce la hoja poco más larga que la de arrayán, muy fina y áspera, y una florecita colorada, de color de azafrán, que huele bien; y tiene una frutilla del mismo color y del tamaño de ciruelas pequeñas en que nace la
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVII

On the Remaining Flowering Trees

Among the many species of trees that bear flowers, one is a certain tree called sicahani, which is small, bushy, and produces a leaf slightly longer than that of the myrtle [arrayán], very fine and rough, and a small reddish flower, saffron-colored, that smells pleasant; it also bears a small fruit of the same color and of the size of small plums, at the point where the flower emerges.

In New Spain, a certain flower is called the 'ear flower' [flor de la oreja] because it is shaped like a human ear; this flower is added to chocolate. The tree that produces it is of medium size, with long, narrow leaves of a dark green color, hanging from a withered little stem. The flower smells pleasant, and its leaves are purple on the inner side and gre

cobo.source_text: Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Cobo (1653), Book IV
cobo.original: La chácara es tubérculo muy estimado de los indios del Perú después de la papa.
cobo.translation: The chácara (oca) is a tuber highly esteemed by the Indians of Peru after the potato. Cobo documents oca as a food-medicine — the sour varieties used for digestive conditions, the sweet varieties as a general food. Used medicinally for kidney complaints, urinary conditions, and digestive complaints. The high oxalic acid content explains the sour taste and traditional use for acidic digestive conditions.
cobo.preparation: Tubers eaten cooked or freeze-dried (chuno method); applied as poultice
cobo.condition: Digestive complaints, kidney conditions, general nutrition

modern_research.key_compound: Oxalic acid, anthocyanins (in red varieties), vitamin C, starch
modern_research.summary: Oca is the second most important Andean tuber after potato. Oxalic acid: explains sour taste; at high concentrations can cause kidney stones. Anthocyanins in red oca: anti-inflammatory and antioxidant. Vitamin C: high content. The freeze-drying technology (chuño) developed by Andean civilizations for oca and potato preservation represents one of the most sophisticated food preservation techniques in pre-industrial history.
modern_research.significance: Oca represents another example of the Andean food-medicine continuum. The chuño freeze-drying technique developed for oca and potato preservation is one of the most sophisticated food technologies in pre-industrial history — and created a reliable pharmaceutical supply chain for plant medicines in the Inca empire.

plants.evidence_authority: Anthocyanin anti-inflammatory documented; Vitamin C well-established; oxalic acid kidney stone risk at high doses.

CAPITULO XVIII
De la isaña

La isaña es una raíz, que los indios comen, del tamaño y forma de la oca; unas, son amarillas exterior e interiormente, y otras, coloradas. La mata es muy parecida a la de los frísoles; cuando topa otras plantas donde asirse, trepa y se encarama sobre ellas; el vástago es redondo, verde y liso; la hoja es tan grande como la palma de la mano hendida en cinco puntas botas
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVIII
On the Isaña

The isaña is a root that the Indians eat, of the size and shape of the oca [Oxalis tuberosa]; some are yellow both on the outside and inside, and others are red. The plant is very similar to that of the bean [fríjol]; when it encounters other plants to cling to, it climbs and clambers over them. The stem is round, green, and smooth; the leaf is as large as the palm of the hand and is divided into five blunt points [lobes]; its petiole [pezón] is slender, round, and about one third of a vara in length. The flower is somewhat elongated, about half a finger long, in the shape of a small bell [campanilla]; it terminates in five small petals arranged around it, three of which are yellow and the other two, along with the rest of the flower, are red. When the isaña — w

corpus_links.title: On the ulluma root: properties, uses, and preparations
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XIX
De la ulluma

La ulluma es cierta raíz muy parecida a la oca; hállanse de tan diferentes colores como las ocas; son de temperamento frío y algo ventoso y muy mucilaginoso; bebiendo una buena porción del cocimiento destas raíces, junto con la muña, facilita el parto, y el mismo efecto dicen los indios que hacen ellas comidas solas en buena cantidad. Ultra desto, hecho lamedor del cocim
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIX
On the ulluma

The ulluma is a certain root very similar to the oca [Oxalis tuberosa]; roots of it are found in as many different colors as the oca. They are of a cold and somewhat flatulent [ventoso] temperament and highly mucilaginous [mucilaginoso]. Drinking a good portion of the decoction of these roots together with muña facilitates childbirth, and the Indians say that eating them alone in a sufficient quantity produces the same effect. Beyond this, a lincture [lamedor] made from the decoction of these roots with the requisite amount of sugar, and given frequently to those with penetrating wounds [heridos penetrantes], causes them to expectorate with ease the blood extravasated [extravenada] in the chest. And when these roots are boiled with rosemary and the resulting wate

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XCV
corpus_links.title: The María Tree and Its Medicinal Oil
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCV
Del árbol llamado María

El árbol llamado María en estas Indias es muy alto, derecho, con la hoja grande y redonda; produce unos granillos inútiles como uvas; es admirable para árboles o mástiles de navios, porque su pie es muy derecho y cimbrea y no quiebra; su madera es roja y no tan buena para tablas, porque se raja fácilmente. Sajando este árbol, destila una resina tan medicinal c
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCV
Of the tree called María

The tree called María in these Indies is very tall and straight, with large, round leaves; it produces small, useless berries resembling grapes. It is admirable for the yards or masts of ships, because its trunk is very straight, bends [cimbrea] without breaking; its wood is red and not so well suited for planks, as it splits easily. When this tree is scored [sajando], it exudes a resin as medicinal as it is universally known, under the name of oil of María [aceite de María], with which wounds are healed with remarkable results. I myself once heard the confession of a man who had just been stabbed in the chest, and the surgeon told me the wound was mortal, because breath was escaping through it; he treated it with this oil, and within a few days the ma

corpus_links.translation: It is evident how absolute a lord the Inca was over everything his subjects possessed, for no one was permitted to hold a chácara [small farm or plot] or estate, nor even dominion over a single span of land as private property, except by special grant [merced] of the Inca; and outside of this title, there was no other means by which to acquire ownership of real property [bienes raíces]. Del convento de Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe de frailes Franciscos

La tercera casa de San Francisco tiene por tutelar Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe; está comenzada a edificar con nombre de colegio, y por estorbos que se han ofrecido se ha interrumpido mucho tiempo la obra. CHAPTER XIII

On the Convent of Our Lady of Guadalupe of the Franciscan Friars

The third house of Saint Francis has as its patron Our Lady of Guadalupe. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CIII
Del incienso de Quito

En la provincia de Quito, en el Perú, se halla un árbol que destila una resina parecida al incienso, por la cual la llaman los españoles árbol de incienso. Es pequeño, de hasta dos estados de alto; sus ramas son cortas, de suerte que no se copa, sino que viene a ser ahusado; y su hoja es muy parecida a la del olivo. Por las ramas destila una resina en granitos
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CIII
On the Incense Tree of Quito

In the province of Quito, in Peru, there is found a tree that exudes a resin resembling frankincense [incienso], on account of which the Spaniards call it the incense tree [árbol de incienso]. It is small, reaching up to two estados [approximately 10–11 feet] in height; its branches are short, so that it does not spread into a broad crown but rather tapers to a point [comes to be spindle-shaped]. Its leaf closely resembles that of the olive. Along the branches it exudes a resin in small, round granules that smell of frankincense, and the tree itself smells the same, such that when anyone passes near it, the scent they perceive makes them think that frankincense is being burned somewhere close by.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol2::IV::cap_XXXI_part1
corpus_links.title: The Royal Roads Built by the Incas Across Their Kingdom
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXI

De los caminos que hicieron los Incas por todo su reino, y la contribución de gente que para aderezarlos daban las provincias

Tenían hechos los Incas dos caminos reales que tomaban todo el largo de su reino desde la provincia de Quito hasta el reino de Chile, que son novecientas leguas, el uno por los Llanos y costa de la mar, y el otro la tierra adentro por las provincias de la Si
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXI

Concerning the roads that the Incas built throughout their kingdom, and the contribution of labor that the provinces provided for their upkeep

The Incas had constructed two royal roads [caminos reales] that ran the entire length of their kingdom, from the province of Quito to the kingdom of Chile—a distance of nine hundred leagues [leguas]. One road ran along the lowlands [los Llanos] and the sea coast, and the other ran inland through the provinces of the highlands [la Sierra], set back from the coast by as much as thirty leagues in some places and five in others.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XCVII
corpus_links.title: The Fever Tree and the Dysentery Tree: Two Medicinal Barks from the Diocese of Quito
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCVII
Del árbol de calenturas

En los términos de la ciudad de Loja, diócesis de Quito, nace cierta casta de árboles grandes, que tienen la corteza como de canela, un poco más gruesa, y muy amarga; la cual, molida en polvos, se da a los que tienen calenturas y con sólo este remedio se quitan. Hánsede tomar estos polvos en cantidad del peso de dos reales en vino o en cualquiera otro licor
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCVII
Of the Fever Tree

Within the territory of the city of Loja, diocese of Quito, there grows a certain kind of large tree whose bark resembles that of cinnamon, though somewhat thicker and very bitter. This bark, ground into powder, is given to those suffering from fevers [calenturas], and by this remedy alone they are cured. The powder is to be taken in a quantity equal in weight to two reales [approximately 6–7 grams], dissolved in wine or any other liquid, shortly before the onset of the chill [el frío]. These powders are already so well known and highly esteemed, not only throughout the Indies but also in Europe, that they are urgently sent for as far as Rome.

De la naranjillas

En la provincia de Quito nace una mata de un estado, poco más o menos; su hoja es del talle de la higuerilla de infierno, un poco mayor, y espinosa por las venas. A la fruta que lleva dan nombre de naranjillas, por tener alguna semejanza con las naranjas. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIII
On the Naranjillas

In the province of Quito there grows a shrub of about one estado [approximately six feet] in height, more or less. Its leaf is shaped like that of the castor-oil plant [higuerilla de infierno], somewhat larger, and spiny along the veins. The fruit it bears is called naranjillas [little oranges] on account of its resemblance to oranges. It is the size of a medium peach, round, and orange in color; in its rind and substance it resembles tomatoes. The interior is a watery substance with a bittersweet flavor; it contains many seeds inside, as the tomato does, and has a pleasant taste.

CHAPTER LXIII
On the Spiny Vicura

In New Spain the Indians call this little animal huitztlacuatzin, which is much the same as saying 'spiny hahuatzin,' because it is the size and shape of the vicura [a small rodent]. It is black in color and is covered with hollow, sharp quills nearly a hand-span [jeme] in length, very similar to those of the porcupine. It has some white hairs mixed in, resembling fine fur, except on the head, where they end in black. When this animal finds itself cornered, it hurls its quills at those who pursue it, embedding them in the flesh, where they work their way in little by little and cannot be removed by any means. The two richest and most important parts of Peru — namely the Lowlands [Llanos] and the Highlands [Sierra] — are subject to two plagues and calamities most burdensome, which are wont to bring notable harm to their inhabitants. culpeper_gerard.original: Millefolium. Yarrow. Meanly cold and binding, an healing herb for wounds, stanches bleeding.
culpeper_gerard.translation: Culpeper (1653) describes yarrow as cooling and binding, calling it “an healing herb for wounds” that “stanches bleeding.” He notes the folk name Nose-bleed came from the belief that the fresh juice, snuffed up the nose, would induce bleeding rather than stop it -- the opposite of its usual wound-binding use -- and attributes its discovery to Achilles, taught by Chiron the Centaur. Gerard's earlier Herball (1597), the standard English reference of its century, documents yarrow for toothache (chewed), headache (leaves placed in the nose), dysentery (as a decoction), and wound care -- broadly consistent with Culpeper's later account and with the wound-healing use recorded across the Celtic/Norse, Greek/Roman, and North American traditions in this archive.

celtic_norse.translation: Ribwort (narrow-leaved plantain) — for cough, for spitting of blood. Anglo-Saxon medicine documents ribwort plantain as a specific for respiratory conditions — cough and respiratory bleeding — distinguished from the broader waybread (P. major) used for wounds. The distinction between the two Plantago species in Anglo-Saxon medicine is pharmacologically significant: P. lanceolata has higher concentration of mucilage and aucubin than P. major, making it more suitable for respiratory applications.

modern_research.summary: Aucubin: anti-inflammatory and antibronchospasm activity. Mucilage: soothing effect on irritated respiratory mucosa. Multiple studies confirming respiratory benefit of P. lanceolata. ESCOP and Commission E approve ribwort for respiratory catarrh. Clinical trial showing significant reduction in cough frequency.
modern_research.significance: Ribwort plantain's Anglo-Saxon use specifically for respiratory conditions (cough, haemoptysis) is pharmacologically validated by aucubin's anti-inflammatory and mucilage's soothing mechanisms. The Anglo-Saxon distinction between P. major (wound/digestive) and P. lanceolata (respiratory) reflects genuine pharmacological differences between the two species.

celtic_norse.original: Netele — wið wunda, wið naedran slite
celtic_norse.translation: Nettle — for wounds, for snake bite. Dead nettle (Lamium) documented alongside stinging nettle (Urtica) in Anglo-Saxon medicine. Red dead nettle specifically documented for wound healing and as an antiseptic application. Also used for respiratory conditions and female health.
celtic_norse.preparation: Leaves applied to wounds; decocted for internal use
celtic_norse.condition: Wound infection, respiratory complaints, menstrual conditions

modern_research.summary: White dead nettle (L. album) has documented anti-inflammatory and antispasmodic activity. European Pharmacopoeia includes L. album for leucorrhoea and menstrual conditions. Limited research on red dead nettle specifically. Tannins: astringent wound-healing activity consistent with traditional application.
modern_research.significance: Dead nettle's wound-healing application in Anglo-Saxon medicine is consistent with documented tannin astringency. The white dead nettle species has European Pharmacopoeia recognition for gynecological applications — validating the traditional menstrual use.

plants.evidence_authority: European Pharmacopoeia includes Lamium album for gynecological conditions; tannin astringency documented.
plants.priority_reason: Anglo-Saxon wound application consistent with tannin mechanism · L. album pharmacopoeia recognition · Limited research for red variety specifically

celtic_norse.original: Everthroat — wið toðece, wið heafodece
celtic_norse.translation: Everthroat (pellitory) — for toothache, for headache. An Anglo-Saxon name for pellitory, documented for the same dental and head pain applications as the Greek/Roman tradition. The name 'everthroat' refers to the burning sensation produced when the root is chewed — the same property that makes it effective for dental pain.
celtic_norse.preparation: Root chewed for dental pain; applied topically

modern_research.summary: Pellitorine: alkamide producing numbing/tingling sensation via TRPV1/TRPA1 receptor activation. This directly validates the traditional dental pain application — the same class of compounds in Echinacea and the toothache plant (Spilanthes).
modern_research.significance: See MMA-069 (Pellitory). This entry documents the same plant under its Anglo-Saxon name 'Everthroat' — the burning throat sensation of the root chewed is the same alkamide mechanism validated for dental analgesia.

plants.evidence_authority: Pellitorine numbness mechanism documented; alkamide pharmacology studied; no approved drug.
plants.priority_reason: Duplicate documentation of MMA-069 under Anglo-Saxon name · Alkamide numbing mechanism validated

celtic_norse.translation: Horehound — for blood-running (haemoptysis), for internal erysipelas. Bald's Leechbook documents horehound for respiratory conditions including cough and blood-spitting. Also used for digestive complaints and fever. One of the most consistently mentioned plants in Anglo-Saxon medicine for respiratory conditions.
celtic_norse.preparation: Decocted in water or ale; taken in honey for respiratory

modern_research.summary: Marrubiin: potent expectorant and antispasmodic activity on bronchial smooth muscle. FDA approved horehound as an OTC cough suppressant ingredient until 1989 when reformulation of OTC drug categories was required (lack of current data, not safety concerns). European Commission E approves horehound for cough. Multiple pharmacological studies confirming expectorant mechanism.
modern_research.significance: Horehound for cough was validated enough to receive FDA OTC approval before regulatory changes required new data submissions. The Anglo-Saxon documentation for respiratory conditions is directly validated by marrubiin's expectorant mechanism.

plants.evidence_authority: FDA formerly approved as OTC cough suppressant ingredient; EU Commission E approved for cough; marrubiin expectorant mechanism well-documented.

tradition_names.celtic_norse: Pipor (Old English — black pepper traded into Anglo-Saxon England)

celtic_norse.source_text: Bald's Leechbook (c.900 CE) — pepper appears in multiple compound preparations
celtic_norse.original: Pipor — in manegum lacnungum. Wið cyle, wið fefor, wið innonfærld.
celtic_norse.translation: Pepper — in many remedies. For chills, for fever, for internal ailments. Bald's Leechbook includes pepper in multiple compound preparations — primarily as a warming ingredient for digestive and respiratory complaints. Archaeological finds confirm pepper was traded to Anglo-Saxon England despite its distant origin, demonstrating how highly valued it was as a medicinal ingredient.
celtic_norse.preparation: Ground and mixed in ale or wine; added to compound preparations
celtic_norse.condition: Chills, fever, digestive warming, respiratory conditions

modern_research.key_compound: Piperine (5-9% by weight), piperic acid, essential oils
modern_research.summary: See MMA-052 (Black Pepper) for full research summary. This entry documents the Anglo-Saxon tradition's adoption of black pepper as a key medicinal ingredient — adding a third documentation context (alongside Dioscorides' Greek/Roman and Cobo's Andean documentation).
modern_research.significance: Anglo-Saxon use of pepper as a warming and digestive medicine is pharmacologically consistent with piperine's TRPV1 activation (heat receptor) and bioavailability-enhancing properties. The fact that pepper was traded to distant Anglo-Saxon England despite its cost demonstrates the high value placed on it as a medicine.

plants.evidence_authority: See MMA-052. Piperine TRPV1 activation documented; bioavailability enhancement well-established; GRAS.
plants.priority_reason: Third independent documentation for pepper · Piperine bioavailability mechanism suggests value in combination formulations

corpus_links.label: CS.Plant.LongPepper
corpus_links.title: Pippali (Long Pepper) — Ayurveda's most prescribed spice-medicine
corpus_links.original: पिप्पली कासश्वासहरी। दीपनी। रसायनी।
corpus_links.translation: Long pepper destroys cough and asthma. It kindles digestive fire. It is a rasayana. Pippali (Piper longum) is arguably the most frequently mentioned plant in the Charaka Samhita — appearing in Trikatu (with ginger and black pepper), in respiratory formulas, digestive preparations, and rasayana compounds. Piperine in long pepper is the same bioavailability-enhancing compound as in black pepper but at higher concentration. Piperlongumine — a compound unique to long pepper — shows documented anticancer activity.
corpus_links.preparation: Trikatu (long pepper + ginger + black pepper); pippali rasayana in honey and ghee
corpus_links.condition: Asthma, chronic cough, poor digestion, obesity, respiratory infections

corpus_links.label: SA.Warburgia
corpus_links.title: Warburgia (Pepper-bark tree) — the fever and malaria medicine
corpus_links.original: [Zulu: isibhaha; Tswana: sennetse — documented by Hutchings and Van Wyk]
corpus_links.translation: Warburgia salutaris (pepper-bark tree) — the single most important fever and malaria medicine across Zulu, Xhosa, and Tswana traditions. The bark produces an intensely hot, burning sensation from warburganal and muzigadial (sesquiterpene dialdehydes) — active compounds with documented antimalarial, antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory activity. The tree is now critically endangered due to over-harvesting for traditional medicine — one of the most serious examples of medicinal plant unsustainability in Africa. This creates an urgent case for synthetic production of warburganal.
corpus_links.preparation: Bark decoction drunk for fever; bark chewed for respiratory; applied topically for skin infections
corpus_links.condition: Malaria, fever, respiratory infections, skin infections — CRITICALLY ENDANGERED

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CIV
On the Pepper of Tabasco

The tree that yields this pepper grows in the province of Tabasco, in New Spain. It is large, with leaves like those of the orange tree; its flower is red, resembling that of the pomegranate, and it smells like orange blossom; likewise, the leaves of the tree are fragrant. It bears its fruit in clusters; the fruit is round — at first it is green, then it turns tawny [leonado], and finally it tends toward black. It is of pleasant aroma and sharp [mordaz] to the taste. It can serve as a substitute when pepper is lacking. It fortifies the stomach and the heart, and produces other beneficial effects.

Applied with honey they clear corn
corpus_links.translation: From De Materia Medica by Pedanius Dioscorides (77 CE), Book I. On Pepper (Greek: κόσκινον; Latin: Piper nigrum and Piper longum). Both varieties of pepper possess warming [calorific], diuretic, and digestive [peptic] properties. They dissolve and expel intestinal flatulence, and are of benefit to those suffering from chills and shivering fits. When rubbed upon the eyelids, they sharpen the eyesight; they draw down [attract] moisture from the head; and when administered in wine, they are prescribed for tetanus [opisthotonos] and epilepsy [the falling sickness]. When applied together with honey, they disperse opacity [leucoma] of the cornea. Long pepper [Piper longum] is more heating in its action than round pepper [Piper nigrum]. Chapter 62. Piperitis, Libanotis, and Smyrnium.

[Continuation of the discussion of flavours in plants:] centaury [taury] is bitter; cucumbers, gourds, and lettuces are watery; parsley, anise, and fennel are pungent and odoriferous. The salt flavour is the only one not found in plants, with the sole exception of the chicheling vetch [Lathyrus sativus], and even there it is found only on the exterior surface of the plant, in the form of a kind of dust that settles upon it.

In order to arrive at a full understanding here, as elsewhere, of how unfounded the notions commonly held tend to be, I shall take this opportunity to remark that panax has the flavour of pepper, and siliquastrum [pepper-wort] even more so — a circumstance to which it owes its name piperitis ["pepper-plant"]. Here are clear signs of disorders and sicknesses of the stomach [wamb], and how a man shall cure the evil humours of the stomach. When stomach disease is present, the signs are these: the stomach turns itself, is fevered, and feels sore when the man eats food; there are prickings [sharp pains] and loss of appetite. When a man observes these signs, the first remedy [leechdom] is a day's fasting, so that by it he may cleanse the stomach and make it lighter. corpus_links.translation: 1. Concerning the nature of the tree called Gokaren, it is stated in revelation that on the first day the tree called Gokaren grew in the deep mud within the wide-formed ocean; it is indispensable as the agent of the renovation of the universe, for immortality is prepared from it. 2. The evil spirit has placed among its opponents a lizard in that deep water, so that it may harm the Haoma. 3. To ward off that lizard, Ohrmazd created ten Kar fish there, which at all times continually circle around the Haoma, such that the head of one of those fish is always directed toward the lizard. 4. Both the lizard and those fish are sustained spiritually—that is, no physical food is necessary for them—and until the renovation of the universe they remain in contention. 5. corpus_links.translation: 1. Regarding the three-legged ass, they say that it stands in the midst of the wide-formed ocean; its feet number three, its eyes six, its mouths nine, its ears two, and its horn one; its body is white, its sustenance spiritual, and it is a righteous creature. 2. Of its six eyes, two are in the normal position of eyes, two are on the top of the head, and two are in the position of the hump; by the keenness of those six eyes it overcomes and destroys [evil]. 3. Of the nine mouths, three are in the head, three in the hump, and three in the inner part of the flanks; each mouth is roughly the size of a cottage, while the creature itself is as large as Mount Alvand. 4. corpus_links.translation: 1. corpus_links.translation: The Religious Calendar. 1. Concerning matters of religion, it is stated in revelation as follows: 'The creatures of the world were created by me complete in three hundred and sixty-five days' — that is, the six periods of the Gahambars [sacred festival seasons], which are completed in the course of one year. 2. It is always necessary to count the day first and the night afterwards, for the day departs first and then the night follows. 3. corpus_links.translation: On the Evil-Doing of Ahriman and the Demons. 1. corpus_links.translation: Section I, Verse 1: Hail, O bounteous bull! Hail to thee, O beneficent bull! Hail to thee, who causest increase! Hail to thee, who causest growth! corpus_links.translation: ...going out in search of food, leaving their dwelling unattended — which was a small hut they had built for shelter — and that, sustaining themselves on roots and herbs, they suffered great want and hunger for some time. But one day, returning to their hut from the search for food, exhausted and worn out with fatigue, they found it very well stocked with diverse dishes and an abundance of chicha [maize beer], without knowing from where or from whom such a notable benefit and gift had come. Greatly astonished by this, they searched diligently to see whether anyone was in the vicinity, wishing to know by whose hand they had been aided in such a time of great distress; and finding no trace of any person, they sat down to eat and relieved their hunger for the time being. Los indios de la provincia de Anemarca, distrito del Cuzco, tenían la fábula siguiente: Refieren que cuando quiso venir el diluvio, un mes antes las llamas o carneros de la tierra mostraron tan gran tristeza, que de día no comían y las noches se les pasaban mirando a las estrellas, hasta tanto que, reparando en ell
corpus_links.translation:
…whom the Cañares [people] worshipped as a god in their paganism [gentilidad], in memory of the aforementioned legend.

The Indians of the province of Anemarca, in the district of Cuzco, held the following legend: They relate that one month before the Flood came, the llamas or sheep of the land [carneros de la tierra, i.e., llamas] displayed such great sadness that during the day they would not eat, and their nights were spent gazing at the stars. A shepherd, taking notice of this, asked them the cause of their sorrow. They replied that he should look upon a certain grouping of stars they pointed out to him, which were in assembly and deliberation over the fact that the world was to be destroyed by water. corpus_links.translation: Chapter III — [concerning] those who venerated as a celebrated shrine [adoratorio insigne] the cave of Pacaritampu, because their ancestors had there escaped the destruction of the world; and they believed that the earth had been peopled from those ancestors, and that all peoples were descended from them. They also disagreed among themselves on this point, for some say that God placed there in that cave the Incas who emerged from it; others deny this, saying rather that when the flood came, they entered the cave and sealed its door fast, and so escaped the waters. These and other similar absurdities were recounted both by the Incas and by the other nations of this realm; I do not set them all down here in order to avoid prolixity, since those already mentioned are sufficient for my purpose

corpus_links.translation:
Myths of Yima [Jamshed], Part I.

§1. Zarathushtra asked Ahura Mazda: 'O Ahura Mazda, most beneficent Spirit, Maker of the material world, thou Holy One! Who was the first mortal, before myself, Zarathushtra, with whom thou, Ahura Mazda, didst converse [lit. 'on the Religion,' per the commentary], and whom thou didst teach the Religion of Ahura — the Religion of Zarathushtra?'

§2. Ahura Mazda answered: 'The fair Yima [Jamshed], the good shepherd [the commentary explains: 'his being a good shepherd means that he held in good condition herds of men and herds of animals'], O holy Zarathushtra! He was the first mortal, before thee, Zarathushtra, with whom I, Ahura Mazda, did converse, and whom I taught the Religion of Ahura — the Religion of Zarathushtra.'

corpus_links.translation: In cereals generally, it is the thicker end of the seed that produces the root, and the thinner end the shoot [blossom]; whereas in other seeds both root and shoot emerge from the same part. During winter, grain [corn] remains in the blade; but in spring, winter grain sends up a tall stem. Millet and panic-grass grow with jointed and grooved stalks, while sesame has a stem resembling that of giant-fennel [Ferula]. The fruit of all these seeds is either borne in an ear — as in wheat and barley, for instance, where it is protected from birds and small animals by a prickly beard [awn] bristling like a row of palisades — or enclosed in pods, as in the leguminous plants, or in capsules, as in sesame and the poppy. corpus_links.translation: This passage, from Pliny the Elder's Natural History (Book XVIII), describes agricultural methods observed in Italy beyond the Po [Padus] River and in other regions. The Salassi people, while raiding territories at the foot of the Alps, attempted to destroy emerging crops of panic-grass and millet. When they found that the plants resisted destruction, they ploughed the ground over them — only to find that the crops came up more abundantly than before. This episode, Pliny asserts, first taught the practice of 'ploughing in' [artrare or aratrare, which Pliny considers the original Latin form], performed either when the stem first begins to develop or when it has put out two or three leaves. It is a well-known fact that some lands require more seed than others, from which circumstance first arose a superstition common among the peasantry: they believe that when the ground demands seed with greater avidity than usual, it is famished and is devouring the grain. It is reasonable to sow seed in humid soil sooner than elsewhere, to prevent the grain from rotting in the rain; on dry spots it should be sown later, and just before a shower falls, so that it may not lie long without germinating and thus come to nothing. When seed is put in early it should be sown thickly, as it takes a considerable time to germinate; but when put in later, it should be sown thinly, lest it be suffocated. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI
Of the Racacha

In the Quechua language of this kingdom, the name racacha is given to a plant whose root is edible and very similar to the achira [Canna edulis]. The bush stands three hand-spans [palmos] tall, very full-crowned and densely leafed, the leaves being dark green and all springing directly from the root. Their petiole or stalk is one cubit [codo] in length, as thick as a medium-sized rush [junco], smooth, and marked along its length with small reddish streaks or veins; it is entirely hollow like a tube, and at its tip grow three leaves, each with three or four deeply cut points longer than those of nettles. CHAPTER LX

On the Guachanca

Because the roots of this herb resemble potatoes [papas], the Spaniards call it 'purgative little potato' [popillas de purga]. The guachanca grows to a hand's breadth [palmo] in height; it produces branches as slender as, or more so than, the stalk of a grape leaf, round, smooth, and tender, with few leaves up to the top, where it puts forth three or four together, which in size and shape resemble those of clover. Its flower is as small as that of clover or mustard, followed by seeds that are small triangular granules, about the size of coriander seeds. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXII

On the Calcas

The calcas is a shrub that the Spaniards call pájaro-bobo ["foolish bird"]. It grows on riverbanks and in damp places, forming dense thickets; from each shrub rises a single straight stem which, from the ground upward, puts forth many small branches and does not form a crown at its top. The largest specimens are as thick as a man's arm and range in height from one to four fathoms [estados]. corpus_links.original: [Amharic] kosso — yezar tera, yefit tera — used universally against tapeworm
corpus_links.translation: Kosso (Hagenia abyssinica) — the female flowers used universally across Ethiopia for tapeworm (Taenia species). The preparation: dried female flowers mixed with tej (honey wine) and drunk fasting. Ethiopia has historically had among the highest rates of Taenia tapeworm infection globally, and kosso was the standard treatment across virtually all Ethiopian communities for centuries. European physicians who encountered Ethiopian medicine in the 19th century introduced kosso to Western pharmacy — it appeared in the London Pharmacopoeia (1867) and was used in Europe until anthelmintic drugs replaced it in the 1950s.
corpus_links.preparation: Dried female flowers mixed with tej (honey wine); drunk fasting in large doses
corpus_links.condition: Tapeworm (Taenia saginata and T. solium) — the primary traditional anthelmintic across the Ethiopian highlands

corpus_links.label: SA.Buchu
corpus_links.title: Buchu — the urinary medicine of the Cape
corpus_links.original: [Khoikhoi / Cape Malay oral tradition — documented from 1650s Dutch colonial records]
corpus_links.translation: Buchu (Agathosma betulina / A. crenulata) — used by the Khoikhoi people of the Cape for urinary tract conditions, digestive complaints, and as an antiseptic. The distinctive anise-blackcurrant smell of buchu made it recognizable to Dutch colonists who adopted it and exported it to Europe in the 17th century. Buchu became a listed medicine in the British Pharmacopoeia (1821) and was prescribed specifically for urinary tract infections — making it one of the few indigenous African plants that entered the European pharmacopoeia. Modern research confirms diosphenol (buchu camphor) has significant antimicrobial activity against urinary tract pathogens.
corpus_links.preparation: Leaves infused in brandy (buchu brandy) — both medicinal and commercial; leaves decocted in water
corpus_links.condition: Urinary tract infections, digestive complaints, antiseptic wound treatment

corpus_links.translation: The mixture was to be drunk from a cool flask. If the patient was a boy, he had to drink it from a hennu-vessel [a specific Egyptian liquid measure or vessel]. A curious remedy was prescribed for urinary retention in a child: REMEDY FOR A CHILD TO CLEAR THE ACCUMULATION OF URINE IN HIS BODY — An Old Book [discarded papyrus] cooked in Oil; smear on his Body. Here, 'An Old Book' refers to a discarded papyrus scroll, the medicinal virtue of which was considered to be enhanced by the writing fluid absorbed into it. Both 'drugs'—the paper and the ink—were as standard a part of the pharmacopoeia of the time as red lead or honey or numerous other substances, and were frequently prescribed for a variety of ailments. Another remedy for a child experiencing difficulty urinating deserves mention here

corpus_links.label: CS.Sutra.25
corpus_links.title: Yajjah Purushiya — the plant kingdom as medicine
corpus_links.original: न तत् किञ्चिद् द्रव्यं यद् भेषजं न स्यात्।
corpus_links.translation: There is no substance in the world that cannot be used as a medicine. This foundational Ayurvedic principle — that everything in the natural world has potential therapeutic application — underpins the entire Charaka pharmacopoeia. The implication is that the physician's task is knowledge, not scarcity: every plant, mineral, and animal product is potentially medicinal when properly understood and applied.

corpus_links.label: IBB.Intro
corpus_links.title: Ibn al-Baitar's scope — the largest pre-modern pharmacopoeia
corpus_links.original: كتاب الجامع لمفردات الأدوية والأغذية — أكبر موسوعة دوائية في التاريخ الإسلامي
corpus_links.translation: The Compendium of Simple Medicaments and Foods — the largest pharmaceutical encyclopedia in Islamic history. Ibn al-Baitar (1197–1248) travelled extensively across North Africa, Spain, Syria, and Egypt collecting plants personally — a field approach anticipating modern pharmacognosy. His compendium documents 1,400 plants, 300 of which are not in any earlier Arabic source. He critically evaluated earlier sources (Ibn Sina, Dioscorides, Al-Razi) and corrected numerous errors. The work supersedes the Canon of Medicine in raw botanical scope and represents the peak of classical Arabic pharmacobotany.

corpus_links.label: IBB.NewPlants
corpus_links.title: Ibn al-Baitar's 300 new plants — undocumented species
corpus_links.original: [Al-Baitar documents approximately 300 plants not found in earlier Arabic or Greek sources]
corpus_links.translation: Ibn al-Baitar documented approximately 300 plants not previously described in the pharmacological literature — primarily plants from the Iberian Peninsula (Al-Andalus), the Maghreb (North Africa), and sub-Saharan plants known through trans-Saharan trade. These include endemic Iberian plants that were never incorporated into the mainstream European pharmacopoeia despite their documented medicinal use by Arabic-speaking physicians in Spain. The loss of this botanical knowledge during the Reconquista represents one of the greatest undocumented pharmacological losses in history. Key plants include specific Andalusian lavender varieties, endemic Iberian Cistus species, and Atlas Mountain medicinal plants.

corpus_links.label: NAM.Moerman
corpus_links.title: Moerman's database — 4,029 uses across 291 nations
corpus_links.original: [Moerman, D.E. 1998. Native American Ethnobotany. Timber Press.]
corpus_links.translation: Daniel Moerman's Native American Ethnobotany database documents 4,029 medicinal plant uses across 291 indigenous North American nations — the most comprehensive documented indigenous pharmacopoeia in the world. Key statistical finding: plants used by more than five independent nations show significantly higher rates of confirmed pharmacological activity in modern research (Moerman, 1996) — validating the archive's convergence methodology. The most widely documented plants across the most nations: yarrow (46 nations), elderberry (27 nations), wild bergamot (21 nations), sage (19 nations), and echinacea (13 nations). These represent the highest-convergence indigenous North American plants.

corpus_links.translation: Melaleuca alternifolia — Tea Tree. This is a published ethnobotanical record with documented involvement of the Bundjalung community. Sources: Lassak & McCarthy, Australian Medicinal Plants (1983), and Brophy et al., CSIRO Plant Industry. The Bundjalung people of northern New South Wales crushed the leaves and used them as an inhalant [inhalant therapy] for coughs, colds, and headaches. Crushed leaves were also applied as a poultice [topical compress] to wounds, cuts, burns, and skin infections. Bathing in streams and pools where Melaleuca trees grew was recognised as therapeutic — these were understood to be healing waters. Traditional preparation methods: fresh leaves crushed between the hands and inhaled directly; alternatively, leaves were wrapped around the wound site. Note: This docu

corpus_links.label: SA.Intro
corpus_links.title: Southern African traditional medicine — izinyanga, izangoma, and the San
corpus_links.original: [Zulu oral tradition — documented by A. Hutchings]
corpus_links.translation: Southern African traditional medicine operates across three distinct practitioner types: izinyanga (herbalists — plant medicine specialists), izangoma (diviners — spiritual healers who may also use plants), and the San (Bushmen) healers who represent the oldest continuous healing tradition in the world, dating to at least 40,000 BCE. The San pharmacopoeia is particularly significant — a population that has lived continuously in southern Africa longer than any other human group, with accumulated plant knowledge across tens of thousands of years. Key source: Watt & Breyer-Brandwijk's Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of Southern and Eastern Africa (1962) — the most comprehensive documentation of the region, covering 4,500 plant uses.

Del cayú

El cayú es árbol natural de tierra caliente, como lo son casi todas las frutas naturales de Indias; es de la grandeza de un crecido naranjo; la hoja, de buen parecer, algo mayor que la del naranjo; la fruta que lleva es muy parecida en lo exterior a un pero grande, muy tierna, dulce, aguanosa y de muy buen sabor. Su pezón es otra fruta distinta, y media entre árbol y la fr
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVII
On the Cayú

The cayú is a tree native to warm lands, as are nearly all the fruits indigenous to the Indies. It is as large as a well-grown orange tree; its leaf is of handsome appearance, somewhat larger than that of the orange tree. The fruit it bears closely resembles in outward appearance a large pear [pero]; it is very tender, sweet, watery, and of excellent flavor. Its stem [pezón] is another distinct fruit, intermediate between the tree and the cayú fruit itself; it is the size and shape of a chestnut. This stem is eaten roasted, and its inner flesh [meollo] is like that of a chestnut.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXI

On Stones That Form from Wood and Other Things

Beyond the stones that the earth produces within its bowels and cavities, we find in this New World others of a very particular kind, whose formation is quite different and constitutes, as it were, an exception to the common and ordinary manner in which the rest are produced. Chief among these must be reckoned that most singular stone found in the Río de la Plata and in other places, which is transformed from the branches of a certain tree called the capirona [Calycophyllum spruceanum or related sp.]. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CXXVII
De la capirona

En la provincia del Paraguay y en otras tierras calientes de este reino del Perú nace cierto árbol, que en la gobernación de Yaguarsongo, diócesis de Quito, llaman capirona, el cual es de madera recia, y de tan particular naturaleza, que metido en el agua por tiempo, se convierte en piedra; y como nazca comúnmente en las orillas de los ríos, las ramas que caen dentr
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXXVII
Of the Capirona

In the province of Paraguay and in other warm lands of this kingdom of Peru there grows a certain tree, which in the governorship of Yaguarsongo, diocese of Quito, they call capirona. It is of hard wood and of so particular a nature that, when submerged in water for a period of time, it turns to stone. And since it commonly grows along the banks of rivers, the branches that fall into the water, with part remaining above the surface, have turned to stone in that portion covered by the water, while the rest remains wood as it was before. This stone is so hard, dense, and tough that it serves as a flint [pedernal], and when struck with a steel [eslabón], it gives off many sparks.

CHAPTER XXV
On the Haquimasci

The stone called in Peru haquimasci resembles in some ways the one that Dioscorides calls the Judaica [lapis judaicus], although it is softer and lacks those small raised portions shaped like acorns that give the Judaica stone its characteristic points. This stone is found in abundance in many parts of Peru, as there are entire hillsides of it, and the Indians recognize it with ease. Running through it are many fine, wavy, somewhat brownish veins. The Indians use this stone, ground up and taken in water or in chicha [fermented maize beer], to stanch [loose] bowel complaints [cámaras] and the excessive blood that flows in women who have recently given birth, or on account of an excess of the menses. CAPITULO LXI

De la Cunturire

Los indios del Perú llaman cunturire a la raíz nombrada de los españoles contrayerba. Nace esta yerba en las provincias de Tomina y Mizque; echa un ramillo pequeño con cuatro o cinco hojas cada uno, las cuales son tan largas como las del naranjo, pero más angostas y de más escuro verde. Sus raíces son pequeñas, menores que un dedo de la mano, ñudosas y muy semejantes
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXI

On the Cunturire

The Indians of Peru call cunturire the root known among the Spaniards as contrayerba [counterherb / antidote herb]. This plant grows in the provinces of Tomina and Mizque; it puts forth small branches bearing four or five leaves each, which are as long as those of the orange tree, but narrower and of a darker green. Its roots are small, no larger than a finger of the hand, knotted, and very similar to ginger; they are of a hot and dry temperament in the second degree [humoral classification], of aromatic scent, somewhat bitter and mordant [biting to the taste]; they are effective against all poisons, for which reason both the Indians and the Spaniards regard them as the theriac [universal antidote] of Peru. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIII
On the Lodestone [Piedra Imán]

The lodestone deposits in Peru are so numerous that by reason of their abundance the stone has neither value nor esteem there; for one finds very large hills composed entirely of this stone, from which pieces of whatever size one desires may be extracted, to be carried to Spain and other places. I have observed certain things concerning the nature of this stone, the first being that, although it has the power to attract iron on all sides, it does not do so with equal force, but tends to be more active on one side than on another. De la Cunturire

Los indios del Perú llaman cunturire a la raíz nombrada de los españoles contrayerba. Nace esta yerba en las provincias de Tomina y Mizque; echa un ramillo pequeño con cuatro o cinco hojas cada uno, las cuales son tan largas como las del naranjo, pero más angostas y de más escuro verde. Sus raíces son pequeñas, menores que un dedo de la mano, ñudosas y muy semejantes
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXI

On the Cunturire

The Indians of Peru call cunturire the root known among the Spaniards as contrayerba [counterherb / antidote herb]. This plant grows in the provinces of Tomina and Mizque; it puts forth small branches bearing four or five leaves each, which are as long as those of the orange tree, but narrower and of a darker green. Its roots are small, no larger than a finger of the hand, knotted, and very similar to ginger; they are of a hot and dry temperament in the second degree [humoral classification], of aromatic scent, somewhat bitter and mordant [biting to the taste]; they are effective against all poisons, for which reason both the Indians and the Spaniards regard them as the theriac [universal antidote] of Peru. During times of contagious illness, they cast them i

corpus_links.title: The Guayroro Tree and Its Seeds
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCI

Del guayroro

El guayroro es un árbol muy grande, que se halla en las provincias de los Andes, en el Perú. Echa unas vainas o canutos al modo de los de la cañafístola, en cuya cavidad se hallan unas pepitas más redondas, aunque llanas y lisas, de color de un fino coral; tiene cada una, una mancha negra que la hermosea. Estiman mucho estas pepitas los indios, afirmando valer contra el
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCI

On the Guayroro

The guayroro is a very large tree, found in the provinces of the Andes, in Peru. It produces pods or tubes in the manner of those of the cassia fistula [cañafístola], in whose cavity are found seeds that are rather round, though flat and smooth, the color of fine coral; each one bears a black spot that adorns it. The Indians hold these seeds in high esteem, asserting that they are effective against heart ailments and melancholy, the powder being taken in wine or orange-blossom water in a dose of just over half a dram [sic]. Beyond this, they say that wearing a string of them around the neck so that it rests upon the chest is beneficial against sorrows of the heart, and that they strengthen the sight and the brain.

CAPITULO XXX

Del coco del Paraguay

La piedra más extraña de cuantas han venido a mi noticia es la que llamamos coco del Paraguay; hanle puesto este nombre los españoles por tener figura de coco y criarse en la provincia del Paraguay. Es poco menor que la cabeza de un hombre, aunque se hallan mayores y menores; de figura redonda o ahusada, de color pardo oscuro, y por de dentro, hueco; tiene de g
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXX

On the Paraguay Coco

The strangest stone of all those that have come to my knowledge is the one we call the Paraguay coco ["coco"]. The Spaniards gave it this name because it has the shape of a coconut and is found in the province of Paraguay. It is somewhat smaller than a man's head, though larger and smaller examples are found; it is round or spindle-shaped in form, dark brown in color, and hollow within. Its shell is about two fingers thick, in the manner of a melon, and is of the nature of very hard flint. The entire interior concavity is studded with transparent precious stones that grow out of the shell, roughly the size of medium gemstones for a ring, arranged with as much order and regularity as the seeds inside a pomegranate. These stones are pointed and angular, pyr

corpus_links.title: On the Viñaygnayna plant (Ever-Young herb)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXIV
De la Viñaygnayna

Viñaygnayna quiere decir en la lengua de los indios peruanos, siempre mozo, y dan este nombre a una yerba de tallos y hojas pequeñas y raíces coloradas, la cual es de complexión templada y consta de partes algo estípticas. Sus raíces, majadas, tienen facultad de consolidar las heridas frescas, y si el zumo de las hojas se mezcla con aguardiente, mundifica y deseca
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXIV
On the Viñaygnayna

Viñaygnayna means in the language of the Peruvian Indians 'ever-young' [siempre mozo], and they give this name to an herb with small stems and leaves and red roots, which is of a temperate complexion [complexión templada] and consists of somewhat astringent [estípticas] parts. Its roots, when pounded, have the power to consolidate [consolidar] fresh wounds; and if the juice of the leaves is mixed with aguardiente [distilled spirits], it cleanses [mundifica] and dries out moist sores [llagas húmedas]. When the roots are held in the mouth, they strengthen the teeth; and the water in which they have been boiled, taken regularly as a drink, strengthens the stomach and stanches blood that customarily passes by way of the urine.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLIV

De la chilca

Esta es una mata muy conocida de los indios y españoles por sus buenos efectos; nace en gran cantidad en los Llanos del Perú, en las orillas de ríos, y sirve de leña. Crece un estado poco más o menos; echa muchas ramas delgadas y derechas; sus hojas son larguillas, tiernas y delgadas, muy parecidas a las del sauce, y son un poco resinosas. Es la chilca de temperamento
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLIV

On the Chilca

This is a shrub very well known to the Indians and Spaniards alike for its beneficial effects. It grows in great abundance in the coastal plains [Llanos] of Peru, on the banks of rivers, and serves as firewood. It grows to about one estado [roughly six feet] in height, more or less; it puts forth many thin, straight branches; its leaves are longish, tender, and slender, very similar to those of the willow, and are somewhat resinous. The chilca is of a hot and moist temperament [in the humoral sense]; the Indians use it, applying it warm against all pain caused by cold, and for this purpose they toast it with cinnamon and sprinkle it with wine or brandy [aguardiente]. It removes and dispels all flatulence [ventosidad] and is [used] against flank pain [ijada], ap

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LII
De la pupa

La pupa, y por otro nombre hamillo, es una mata de un estado de alto; tiene los ramos verdes y la hoja como de verdolagas, tantico más angosta y larguilla; es muy tierna, hoja y cogollo; da una florecilla colorada y muy delgada, de hechura de la cantuta, y unos granillos ni más ni menos que los de la yerba-mora, sólo que no los echa en racimos, sino cada uno de por sí pega
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LII
On the Pupa

The pupa, also known by another name as hamillo, is a shrub about one estado [roughly one fathom, approximately six feet] in height; it has green branches and leaves like those of purslane [verdolagas], only somewhat narrower and more elongated; both leaf and shoot are very tender. It produces a small, slender reddish flower shaped like that of the cantuta [cantuta flower], and tiny berries exactly like those of nightshade [yerba-mora], except that it does not bear them in clusters but each one separately, attached to the small branches. From this plant the Indians extract birdlime for catching birds, and it is as good as that of Spain. The distilled water of its flowers, taken by the alembic [alquitara], is a singular remedy — taken each morning in doses of two or

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_LX
corpus_links.title: On the Large Coconut Palms
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LX

De las palmas de cocos grandes

Innumerables son las diferencias de palmas que se hallan en estas Indias, así en tierras calientes como en las templadas y frías, como no lleguen a tener temple de páramo, y mucho más las que nacen en las islas Filipinas, porque me han certificado personas prácticas de aquella tierra, que se cuentan más de cincuenta géneros dellas. Sólo describiré aquí
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LX

On the Large Coconut Palms

Innumerable are the varieties of palms to be found in these Indies, both in hot lands and in temperate and cold ones, so long as they do not reach the climate of the high moorland [páramo], and still more so among those that grow in the Philippine Islands, for persons of practical experience in that land have assured me that more than fifty kinds of them are counted. I shall describe here only those we find in this America of which I have knowledge, and indeed personal acquaintance by sight with the greater part of them. It must be noted above all that not all of them grow everywhere, because, being of different natures and qualities, they require different climates [temples]. De las costumbres más generales en que se conforman todos los indios

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VII

On the most general customs shared by all Indians

Peoples so thoroughly subjected and surrendered to the father of lies and cruel enemy of the human race—who caused them to render the honor and worship due to the Creator alone to himself—it is not difficult to understand what manner of instruction in errors, cruelties, and every kind of vice they would have learned from so perverse a master. They were all idolaters, given over to endless superstitions and omens, with the exception here and there of some nation of men so coarse and savage that, being of a purely brutish nature, they recognized no deity in heaven or on earth, nor had any form of worship whatsoever. CAPITULO IV
De la sal

Así como este reino del Perú es el más abundante de metales, mayormente de plata, de cuantos sabemos hoy en el mundo, así también lo es de salinas naturales; que parece proveyó Dios de ellas con tanta abundancia donde tan necesaria es la sal para beneficiar los metales de plata, en que se consume una cantidad increíble de sal; y no hay provincia ni ciudad que padezca falta d

On Salt

Just as this kingdom of Peru is the most abundant in metals — above all in silver — of any known to us in the world today, so too is it in natural salt deposits [salinas]; for it seems God provided them in such abundance in a place where salt is so necessary for the processing [beneficio] of silver ores, in which an incredible quantity of salt is consumed. De la batata

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VIII
On the Batata

The batata [sweet potato] is a root well known not only throughout all the Indies, but also in Spain, and it was one of the most esteemed foods the Indians had. The plant is small, and its branches spread along the ground without rising very high; each plant [mata] produces many shoots or stems, which are round, smooth, and purple, and grow to about two-thirds of a vara [roughly 18 inches] lying along the ground. The leaf grows from the shoot on a petiole [pezón] as long as that of a grape-vine leaf, but thinner and more tender, and purple in color; the leaf is broader near the petiole than elsewhere, and ends in three points, the two lateral ones somewhat shorter than the middle one; the small veins of the leaf are green on the upper surface and purple on the u

corpus_links.title: The Liren Root (Chapter IX)
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX
Of the Liren

In the language of the island of Hispaniola, the name 'lirenes' is given to certain roots the size of dates, and somewhat larger, or like small bergamot pears [perillas cermeñas], which on the outside are brownish [pardas], with a soft, thin, hairy skin [cáscara vellosa y delgada] that comes off easily once they are cooked; and on the inside they are white, and when cooked they are of good flavor. These little roots are attached to thin runners [vaguetas delgadas] like those of the sweet potato [batatas]; the plant is small and spreads its branches over the ground like the sweet potato plant, to which it is so similar that it appears to be a particular variety [especie] of it.

CAPITULO XII
Del maní

El maní es una raíz muy diferente de todas las demás de Indias; la mata és baja y muy aparrada con la tierra; produce muchos tallos y hojas, de manera que se viene a hacer muy cerrada. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XII
On the Maní

The maní is a root very different from all others in the Indies; the plant is low-growing and spreads close to the ground, producing many stems and leaves, so that it becomes very dense. The stems are two-thirds of a vara [roughly 18 inches] in length, and more of them extend along the ground than rise upward; they are round and as thick as rushes, reddish in color, not smooth but somewhat hairy, and well-leafed, the leaves resembling in shape and size those of the mastic tree [lentisco, Pistacia lentiscus], save that they are thinner, slightly larger, and of a dark green. CAPITULO XLIII
Del suhigi

En la provincia de Santa Cruz de la Sierra nace un árbol llamado suhigi. Es muy alto y de hojas grandes y anchas; da unas vainas grandes y en ellas una fruta muy parecida al maní o a piñones.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLIII
On the Suhigi

In the province of Santa Cruz de la Sierra there grows a tree called suhigi. It is very tall and has large, broad leaves; it produces large pods, and within them a fruit very similar to peanuts [maní] or pine nuts [piñones].

corpus_links.title: The Añutaya (Skunk): Natural History, Behavior, and Medicinal Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXI
De la añutaya

La añutaya es un animal pequeño, de casta y hechura de zorra, manchado de pardo, blanco y negro, con el pelo tan blanco y largo como de gato; el hocico agudo y la cola como de zorra, del tamaño de un pequeño gozque. Es el animal de más profundo y pestífero hedor que se conoce en el mundo, principalmente sus orines; inficiona el aire por donde pasa, de modo que por su he
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXI
On the Añutaya

The añutaya is a small animal of the fox family and form, spotted with brown, white, and black, with fur as white and long as a cat's; with a pointed snout and a tail like a fox's, and about the size of a small lap-dog [gozque]. It is the animal with the most profound and pestilential stench known in the world, principally on account of its urine; it contaminates the air wherever it passes, such that one can detect where it is by its foul smell from more than five hundred paces away. It is well understood that its defensive weapons consist in the execrable odor of its urine, and it defends itself therewith against any who would do it harm; for when it finds itself cornered by dogs, it discharges its urine, spraying it onto their snouts, whereby it drives them of

CAPITULO VIII
De la batata

La batata es raíz muy conocida no sólo en todas las Indias, sino también en España, y una de las más regaladas comidas que los indios tenían. La planta es pequeña, y sus ramas se extienden sobre el suelo sin levantarse mucho; produce cada mata muchos vástagos o tallos, los cuales son redondos, lisos y morados, y crecen como dos tercias tendidos sobre la tierra. Nace la
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VIII
On the Batata

The batata [sweet potato] is a root well known not only throughout all the Indies, but also in Spain, and it was one of the most esteemed foods the Indians had. The plant is small, and its branches spread along the ground without rising very high; each plant [mata] produces many shoots or stems, which are round, smooth, and purple, and grow to about two-thirds of a vara [roughly 18 inches] lying along the ground. The leaf grows from the shoot on a petiole [pezón] as long as that of a grape-vine leaf, but thinner and more tender, and purple in color; the leaf is broader near the petiole than elsewhere, and ends in three points, the two lateral ones somewhat shorter than the middle one; the small veins of the leaf are green on the upper surface and purple on the u

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LIX

De la choclla

Dos especies se hallan en estas Indias de cierta yerba que los españoles llaman cebadilla, por la semejanza que tienen con la cebada: la una es natural de la Nueva España, y la otra, deste reino del Perú. La primera echa una espiga parecida a la del trigo, larga un palmo y más; su caña es asimismo como la del trigo, algo más gruesa, parda y maciza, de un estado de alto
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LIX

On the Choclla

Two species are found in these Indies of a certain herb that the Spaniards call cebadilla [little barley], on account of its resemblance to barley. One is native to New Spain and the other to this kingdom of Peru. The first puts forth a spike resembling that of wheat, a handspan or more in length; its stalk is likewise similar to that of wheat, somewhat thicker, brownish, and solid, about a man's height tall; it grows wild in the savannas without being sown. The grains are black, somewhat smaller than those of barley, and when ground they kill the worms [maggots] in the sores [saddle-galls] of beasts of burden, and likewise the chigoe fleas [niguas] that burrow into persons.

The other species of cebadilla is called choclla in the Aymara language; it is a prize

corpus_links.title: On Fleas and Chigoe Fleas (Niguas): Natural History, Medical Effects, and a Notable Case
corpus_links.original:
CAPÍTULO XXVI
De las pulgas y niguas

Todas las tierras yuncas y medianamente calientes deste Nuevo Mundo son muy infestadas de pulgas, de las cuales se hallan dos diferencias: las unas son las comunes, que aunque son molestas, no tan ofensivas como las segundas. Engéndrase a tiempos tanta copia dellas, aun en tierras templadas, que dan mucha molestia así a los hombres como a los animales caseros,
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVI
On Fleas and Chigoe Fleas [niguas]

All the lowland [yunca] and moderately warm regions of this New World are greatly infested with fleas, of which two varieties are found: the first are the common kind, which, though troublesome, are not as harmful as the second. At times such a multitude of them breeds, even in temperate lands, that they cause great annoyance to men as well as to domestic and even wild animals. For they are harbored not only by cats, dogs, mice, and domesticated guanacos, but also by wild rats and field mice; and the abundance produced by these wild hosts further swells the populations born in settled areas.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXIV
De la yerba de Santa María

Nace esta yerba en la costa de la mar del Sur de la Nueva España y allí le dan este nombre; crece un estado en alto; su hoja es de forma de corazón y mayor que la palma de la mano; echa unos botoncillos largos y delgados, muy semejantes a los canelones de disciplina. Tiene su hoja olor y sabor de hinojo, y puesta en la cabeza, es buena para el dolor dell
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIV
On the Herb of Santa María

This herb grows on the coast of the South Sea [Pacific coast] of New Spain, where it is given this name. It grows to the height of one estado [approximately one fathom, or the height of a man]; its leaf is heart-shaped and larger than the palm of the hand. It puts forth long, slender little buds very similar to the lashes [tails] of a discipline whip [flagellant's scourge]. Its leaf has the smell and taste of fennel, and when placed on the head it is good for headache caused by the sun.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXV
De la coaca

Usan los indios por mantenimiento muchos géneros de yerbas que, con nombre general, las llaman los del Perú, yayos, y los mexicanos, quilites, como si dijésemos hortaliza o verdura; de algunas queda ya hecha mención en los capítulos pasados; en lo que resta deste libro se irán tocando otras, de las cuales es una la coaca. Esta es una yerba parecida a la cerraja; crece do
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXV
On the Coaca

The Indians make use of many kinds of herbs for sustenance, which, by a general name, the people of Peru call yayos [yuyos], and the Mexicans call quilites — as if we were to say garden greens or vegetables. Some of these have already been mentioned in the preceding chapters; in what remains of this book, others will be touched upon, of which the coaca is one. This is a herb resembling the sow-thistle [cerraja]; it grows about two cubits in height, more or less. The stalk is as thick as the little finger, round, green, hairy, and sticky. Each plant produces many stalks, and at their tops a great quantity of flowers the size and form of those of chamomile, except that the small petals encircling the bud are yellow. These flowers are fragrant and pleasant in appear
