corpus_links.title: Two Andean herbs: Soycosoyco and Siqui
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXVI
Del soycosoyco

El soycosoyco es una yerba menuda que parece especie de las rosas o davdlinas de las Indias; levántase un codo de la tierra; echa muchos tallos delgados, redondos, lisos, correosos y algún tanto rojos, y pocas hojas; las cuales son tan pequeñas y menudas, que parecen hebrillas de seda cortadas. Produce unas florecitas amarillas que cada una tiene cuatro hojuelas no m
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVI
On the Soycosoyco

The soycosoyco is a small herb that appears to be a species of the roses or carnations [davdlinas, i.e., davelinas/clavellinas] of the Indies. It rises about one cubit [roughly half a meter] above the ground, putting forth many thin, round, smooth, tough, and somewhat reddish stems, and few leaves; these leaves are so small and fine that they resemble little cut threads of silk. It produces small yellow flowers, each having four petals no larger than those of the flower of rue [Ruta graveolens], which emerge from small, elongated buds resembling pine nuts; and after these flowers dry, they end in a tuft of fibers issuing from the same bud. This herb gives off a somewhat aromatic odor. It is hot in the second degree and moist in the first [according to Galen

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XLIV
corpus_links.title: On the Cota and the Mullaca plants (Chapters XLIV–XLV)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLIV
De la cota

La cota es una yerba tan pequeña como el ctichuchu, que no parece sino una mancha verde en la tierra; no echa ramas ni tallos; sólo produce sobre la tierra sus hojas y flores; las hojas son semejantes a las del romero, salvo que son algo más larguillas, delgadas y tiernas. Hácense en el suelo grandes manchas de estas yerbas con las hojas y raíces muy juntas y apretadas un
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLIV
On the Cota

The cota is a small herb no larger than the ctichuchu [a small plant], which appears to be nothing more than a green patch on the ground; it puts forth neither branches nor stalks, producing only its leaves and flowers directly upon the earth. The leaves resemble those of rosemary, except that they are somewhat longer, thinner, and more tender. These plants form large patches on the ground, with their leaves and roots very closely and tightly packed together. They produce many flowers resembling in form those of chamomile [manzanilla]; they are a little larger, and the central button is neither as yellow nor as pointed; the small petals surrounding the center are white on the inner side, as in chamomile, and red on the underside. These flowers grow no taller than

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXXXVI
corpus_links.title: On the Chaneorama plant
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXVI

De la chaneorama

Esta es una yerba espinosa, cuyos tallos crecen un codo en alto, y son más delgados que el dedo meñique, redondos, macizos, de un verde blanquecino, cubiertos de un corto y delgado vello, que los hace algún tanto ásperos. Las hojas son largas una tercia y anchas un dedo, aserradas por los lados, armadas de espinas cortas, delgadas y agudas, que punzan. En el rema
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXVI

On the Chaneorama

This is a thorny herb whose stems grow to the height of one cubit [approximately 18 inches], and are thinner than the little finger, round, solid, of a whitish green color, covered in a short, fine down that makes them somewhat rough to the touch. The leaves are one-third of a vara [approximately 11 inches] in length and one finger's width wide, serrated along the edges, and armed with short, thin, sharp spines that prick. At the tips of the stems this herb produces white flowers, ten or twelve together on each stem, smaller than those of chamomile [manzanilla]. In the Aymara language this herb is called by this name.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXXXIX
corpus_links.title: On the Acana plant: properties, preparations, and medical uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXIX

De la acana

La acana crece un codo de alto; en las ramas y hojas es muy parecida a la alfalfa; tiene flor amarilla del talle de la de la manzanilla; nace entre peñas y es yerba pectoral, más amarga al gusto que la acíbar; es caliente y seca en el segundo grado. Comen los indios con ella la coca. Su cocimiento con un poco de alumbre es bueno para las llagas de la boca; y tomado ca
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIX

On the Acana

The acana grows to a cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height; in its branches and leaves it closely resembles alfalfa; it bears a yellow flower of the shape of that of camomile; it grows among rocks and is a pectoral herb [i.e., beneficial to the chest and lungs], more bitter to the taste than aloes [acíbar]; it is hot and dry in the second degree [following Galenic humoral classification]. The Indians eat coca with it. A decoction of it with a little alum is good for sores of the mouth; and taken warm on an empty stomach with sugar candy [alfeñique], it is beneficial against cough and asthma, and softens and cleanses the chest and stomach. Beyond this, the decoction applied to the face removes freckles from it, and if prepared with wine, it removes cataract

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_XXVII
corpus_links.title: Tilxochil (Vanilla) and Hubo de Lagarto (Manchineel or related toxic fruit tree)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXVII
Del tilxochil

Llámase así en la Nueva España la planta que produce las vainillas que se echan en el chocolate y le dan muy agradable olor. Es una mata de género de bejuco; su tallo voluble y verde; las hojas, grandes, largas un palmo y dos o tres dedos de ancho, y por todas partes es igual su ancho, con que hace figura de lengua; es gruesa y muy lisa. La flor es blanquilla, y el fr
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVII
On the Tilxochil

This is the name given in New Spain to the plant that produces the vanilla pods [vainillas] that are added to chocolate and impart to it a very pleasant aroma. It is a climbing shrub [mata de género de bejuco]; its stem is twining and green; the leaves are large, a span [palmo] long and two or three fingers wide, of equal width throughout, giving them the shape of a tongue; they are thick and very smooth. The flower is whitish, and the fruit consists of pods a span in length, more slender than carob pods [algarrobas], and when ripe they turn yellow. Once harvested from the plant, they are cured in the sun with great care, and after curing they become the color of raisins, tough and juicy, like them. Inside they are filled with tiny black granules no larger t

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_XXXIX
corpus_links.title: The Incavisa Plant
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXIX
De la incavisa

La incavisa es una mata que se levanta de la tierra tres o cuatro codos; echa muchas varas derechas tan gruesas como un dedo, correosas y algún tanto rojas; sus hojas son semejantes a las del sauce, salvo que son algo más cortas, angostas, tiernas, más gruesas y aserradas. Produce esta planta muchas flores juntas, las cuales son muy parecidas en el tamaño y figura a
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIX
On the Incavisa

The incavisa is a shrub that rises three or four cubits [roughly 4.5–6 feet] from the ground; it puts out many straight stems as thick as a finger, tough and somewhat reddish; its leaves resemble those of the willow, except that they are somewhat shorter, narrow, tender, thicker, and serrated. This plant produces many flowers together, which are very similar in size and shape to the chamomile flower; although the petals [literally: leaves] that encircle the little button are yellow, slightly larger, and not as closely set. This flower has a pleasant fragrance and an agreeable appearance; once it dries, it is succeeded by a thin veil or downy tuft [flocadura] that is carried away by the wind. This plant and its flower are called, in the Aymara language, incavi

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_L
corpus_links.title: The Sunchu plant: description, properties, and uses against snake venom
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO L
Del sunchu

El sunchu es un linaje de flores amarillas, que abraza algunas diferencias dellas muy parecidas todas entre sí en su figura, que es del talle de la flor de la manzanilla, y en la forma de la planta, que es una mata de un estado de alto, aromática y resinosa, la cual echa unas varas delgadas, redondas y algo rojas. Sus hojas son semejantes a las de la yerba-mora, y tocadas co
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER L
On the Sunchu

The sunchu is a genus of yellow-flowered plants, encompassing several varieties that are all very similar to one another in appearance: the shape of the flower resembles that of chamomile [manzanilla], and the plant itself is a shrub about one fathom [estado] in height, aromatic and resinous, which puts forth slender, round, and somewhat reddish stems. Its leaves are similar to those of nightshade [yerba-mora], and when touched to the tongue they prove abstersive [cleansing] or astringent [estípticas]. Both the leaves and the stems are covered with a short, rough down. The various sunchos differ from one another in height and in the shape of their leaves, for some have leaves larger than those of nightshade and bearing small points like those of the mallow. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XXIV
corpus_links.title: The Land Apple (Manzano de la Tierra) of New Spain
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXIV
De las manzanas de la tierra

El árbol que llamamos manzano de la tierra sólo se halla en la Nueva España. Es pequeño y muy parecido en todo al manzano de Castilla, salvo que es mucho mayor y de hojas más pequeñas, aunque de la misma hechura. El fruto que produce son unas manzanillas pequeñas, redondas y amarillas, de tamaño y hechura de níspero. Es fruta silvestre y desabrida; tiene
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIV
On the Land Apples

The tree we call the land apple [manzano de la tierra] is found only in New Spain. It is small and very similar in every respect to the apple tree of Castile [manzano de Castilla], except that it is much larger and has smaller leaves, though of the same shape. The fruit it produces consists of small, round, yellow little apples [manzanillas], of the size and shape of a medlar [níspero]. It is a wild and insipid fruit; each one contains three seeds inside shaped like pine nuts [piñones], and so hard that they cannot be broken with the teeth. The Spaniards use these apples to make preserves [conservas]; and Castilian apples graft well onto this tree.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XVI
corpus_links.title: The Yacón Plant and Its Root
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XVI
Del yacan

La planta que produce la raíz llamada yacan es de un estado de alto, poco más o menos; echa un vástago o caña tan gruesa y más que el dedo pulgar de color verde, áspera y vellosa; por de dentro, hueca y con ñudos a trechos que dividen los cañutos, que son largos de a palmo, y por los ñudos echan tres ramas más delgadas. La hoja es de particular hechura: nace del tallo o cañ
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVI
On the Yacán

The plant that produces the root called yacán stands approximately one estado [roughly six feet] tall; it sends up a stalk or cane as thick as, or thicker than, the thumb, green in color, rough and hairy; hollow on the inside, with nodes spaced at intervals that divide the internodes, which are about a handspan in length, and from these nodes spring three thinner branches. The leaf is of a peculiar form: from the stalk or cane there grows a green leafstalk as thick as a goose quill, about a handspan long, which is flanked on either side by a small leaflet about a finger's breadth wide, running lengthwise from the same stalk; at the end of this stalk is attached the leaf itself, which is shaped like a harpoon—perfectly triangular—and measures one third [of a vara]

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XXXI
corpus_links.title: On the Tempesquisti and the Manzanilla (Manchineel Tree)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXI

Del tempesquisti

El tempesquisti es un árbol grande y hermoso con los extremos de las ramas muy pobladas de hoja, la cual es reluciente, en lo cual y en el pezón de la misma hoja es muy parecida a la del peral, salvo que es más larga y puntiaguda. Esparcen estas hojas en las iglesias, por adorno, en lugar de juncias. Produce este árbol una fruta negra y dulce como higo, que se come
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXI

On the Tempesquisti

The tempesquisti is a large and handsome tree whose branch tips are very densely covered with leaves. The leaf is shiny, and in this respect—as well as in its petiole [leaf-stalk]—it greatly resembles that of the pear tree, except that it is longer and more pointed. These leaves are strewn in churches as decoration, in place of rushes [juncias]. The tree produces a black, sweet fruit resembling a fig, which is eaten.

CHAPTER XXXII

On the Manzanilla

On many coasts of these Indies there grows a certain tree whose fruit the Spaniards call manzanilla [little apple], because it resembles a small apple. The tree stands low, about two or three fathoms [estados] in height, very leafy and handsome in appearance, with a leaf like that of the pear tree. It bears

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEPTIMO::cap_XLVIII
corpus_links.title: On the sharks and shark-like fishes of the Peruvian coast
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLVIII
De los cazones

En toda la costa deste reino del Perú se cría gran copia de cazones de todas especies conocidas en España y aún de otras propias de las Indias, y son conocidos por los nombres siguientes: cazón pique; otro se llama cazón negrito; otros canahotas, dentudo, guayas, que llaman en España albariños. A éstos, que son propios cazones, se reducen otros peces por alguna seme
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVIII
On the Sharks [cazones]

Along the entire coast of this kingdom of Peru there grows a great abundance of sharks [cazones] of all the species known in Spain, and also of others native to the Indies. They are known by the following names: cazón pique; another is called cazón negrito; others are canahotas, dentudo, guayas — which in Spain they call albariños. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XL
corpus_links.title: On the Bledos (Amaranths) of the Indies
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XL
De los bledos de las Indias

Fuera de los bledos de una especie de los de España, se hallan en esta tierra otros distintos, que para diferenciarlos de los comunes los llamamos de las Indias. Es una mata de a dos estados de alto, con muchas ramas que esparce a la redonda, tan gruesas como tres dedos, y el pie es como la muñeca de la mano. Tiene las hojas del talle de los bledos, pero ta
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XL
On the Bledos [amaranths] of the Indies

Besides the bledos [amaranths] of the same species as those of Spain, there are found in this land other distinct ones, which, to differentiate them from the common kind, we call the bledos of the Indies. It is a shrub of about two estados [approximately ten to twelve feet] in height, with many branches that spread out all around, as thick as three fingers, and the trunk is as thick as a wrist. Its leaves are of the same form as those of the bledos, but so much larger that they exceed those of the plantain [llantén, Plantago spp.]; they are smooth, green, and of pleasing appearance; and they serve as food in exactly the same way as the bledos. This plant produces a fruit which, when ripe, closely resembles a mulberry [mora del moral] in b

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_LXIV
corpus_links.title: On the Olincana plant and its toxic properties
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXIV

De la olincana

Esta es una mata de medio a un estado de alto; nace en lugares secos y pedregosos; echa en torno de sí muchas ramas, no derechas, sino torcidas; hace su tronco junto a la tierra tan grueso como el muslo, y aun como el cuerpo de un hombre. Las ramas van adelgazando hacia la punta, las cuales están desnudas de hojas, de color de carne y como arrugadas; al remate de cad
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXIV

On the Olincana

This is a shrub [mata] of half to one estado [approximately 4–7 feet] in height; it grows in dry, stony places; it puts forth many branches around itself, not straight but twisted; its trunk near the ground becomes as thick as a thigh, or even as thick as a man's body. The branches taper toward their tips, and are bare of leaves, flesh-colored and somewhat wrinkled in appearance; at the end of each branch grow three or four leaves together with the flower in the middle. The leaf has three points cleft nearly to the petiole [pezón], so that they form a bird's foot; each point is the size and shape of the leaf of the bledo [Amaranthus spp.], the middle point somewhat larger than those on the sides; the petiole smooth and slender like that of a vine leaf, though

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_LXIX
corpus_links.title: The Fire Plant
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXIX

De la planta del fuego

Esta especie de mata nace en la Nueva España, y yo la he visto en las huertas de México. Es un arbolillo de uno o dos estados de alto, mal poblado de hoja, la cual es espinosa, grande y de hechura de la de los bledos: hoja, tronco y ramas son de un color rojo como de fuego, lo cual y el efecto que obra le dan el nombre que tiene; porque si una persona la toca
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXIX

On the Fire Plant

This species of shrub grows in New Spain, and I have myself seen it in the gardens of Mexico [City]. It is a small tree of one or two fathoms [estados] in height, sparsely leaved, the leaves being spiny, large, and shaped like those of the bledo [pigweed/amaranth]. The leaf, trunk, and branches are all of a fiery red color, and it is from this appearance and from the effect it produces that the plant takes its name; for if a person touches it with the hand or with any bare part of the body, such as an arm or a leg, it causes a terrible burning sensation, and the part touched becomes inflamed and reddened as though afflicted with Saint Lazarus's disease [mal de San Lázaro, i.e., leprosy or a leprous-like skin condition]. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LI
Del vilcu

El vilcu es una planta muy semejante al ticsau en sus hojas, flores y en ser voluble; produce los vástagos delgados como un junco, redondos, verdes, con unas venillas rojas, tiernos y correosos, y a trechos echa las hojas y flores. La hoja es poco menor que la palma de la mano, de hechura de la de la vid, hendida hasta cerca del pezón, con cinco o siete puntas, la de enmedio
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LI
On the Vilcu

The vilcu is a plant very similar to the ticsau in its leaves, flowers, and in being a climber [voluble]; it produces slender stems like a rush [junco], round, green, with small red veins, tender and tough, and it puts forth leaves and flowers at intervals along them. The leaf is slightly smaller than the palm of the hand, shaped like that of the grapevine, lobed nearly to the petiole [pezón], with five or seven points, the middle one being the largest, and the lateral ones progressively smaller the farther they are from the middle one. The flowers are yellow, entirely without scent, and on account of their shape the Spaniards call them 'little birds' [pajaritos]; they are small like those of the broom [retama], having two petals larger than the rest that resemble

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_LXI
corpus_links.title: The Añaguaya shrub of the Collao region
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXI
De la añaguaya

La añaguaya es una mata espinosa a la canilla; levántase de la tierra de uno a dos codos; la hoja es de la forma que la de la sabina y algo más menuda; las espinas son menores que las del naranjo, derechas, agudas y blanquiscas. Da una florecita amarilla de ningún olor, del talle que la de la retama, un poquito menor. Nace esta planta en las provincias del Collao, en t
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXI
On the añaguaya

The añaguaya is a thorny shrub of slender [cane-like] form; it rises from the ground one to two cubits [roughly 18 to 36 inches]; the leaf is shaped like that of the savin [juniper] and somewhat smaller; the thorns are smaller than those of the orange tree, straight, sharp, and whitish. It produces a small yellow flower of no scent, in shape like that of the broom plant [retama], though a little smaller. This plant grows in the provinces of the Collao [the altiplano region around Lake Titicaca], in very cold country, and serves only as firewood.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_LXV
corpus_links.title: On the Pinco-Pinco Plant: Properties and Medical Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXV
Del pinco-pinco

Esta es una mata de tres o cuatro codos en alto; echa muchas varillas juntas delgadas y parejas como las de la retama; son macizas, leñosas y desnudas de hojas, y aunque lisas, de trecho a trecho ñudosas. Nace por los suelos una frutilla colorada del tamaño de garbanzos, con dos granitos negros dentro poco menores que los de la linaza. Es muy estimada esta planta en e
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXV
On the Pinco-Pinco

This is a shrub three or four cubits [codos] in height; it puts forth many slender and even stems together, like those of the broom plant [retama]; they are solid, woody, and bare of leaves, and although smooth, knotted at intervals. At ground level it produces a small red fruit the size of chickpeas, containing two small black seeds inside, somewhat smaller than those of flaxseed. This plant is highly esteemed in Peru for its many and marvelous effects. It is hot and dry with a manifest astringency [estipticidad]. Its leaves or branches, pounded and applied to fresh wounds, draw them together, dry them, and heal them. Its powders, mixed with those of alum, have the power to dry out any sore or ulcer. CAPITULO LVII

Del itapallo y chichicaste

El itapallo es una yerba que en sus efectos parece especie de ortiga, aunque realmente se distingue della en esto: levántase de la tierra un codo; sus tallos son verdes, redondos, tiernos y no más gruesos que un delgado junco; produce desde el pie muchas hojas, las cuales son de un verde oscuro, largas un jeme, y por donde más anchas, tienen tres dedos; v
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LVII

On the Itapallo and the Chichicaste

The itapallo is an herb that in its effects resembles a species of nettle [ortiga], though it is truly distinct from it in the following respects: it rises from the ground about one cubit [codo] in height; its stems are green, round, tender, and no thicker than a slender reed; from the base it produces many leaves, which are of a dark green color, a hand-span [jeme] in length, and at their widest about three fingers broad; from near the stalk they narrow progressively until they end in slender points; they are deeply cut along the sides into many points. This herb puts forth a flower of a fine crimson color, very handsome, though entirely without scent; it is composed of five small petals so closely joined to one another that they appear t

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XVI
corpus_links.title: The Yacón Plant and Its Root
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XVI
Del yacan

La planta que produce la raíz llamada yacan es de un estado de alto, poco más o menos; echa un vástago o caña tan gruesa y más que el dedo pulgar de color verde, áspera y vellosa; por de dentro, hueca y con ñudos a trechos que dividen los cañutos, que son largos de a palmo, y por los ñudos echan tres ramas más delgadas. La hoja es de particular hechura: nace del tallo o cañ
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVI
On the Yacán

The plant that produces the root called yacán stands approximately one estado [roughly six feet] tall; it sends up a stalk or cane as thick as, or thicker than, the thumb, green in color, rough and hairy; hollow on the inside, with nodes spaced at intervals that divide the internodes, which are about a handspan in length, and from these nodes spring three thinner branches. The leaf is of a peculiar form: from the stalk or cane there grows a green leafstalk as thick as a goose quill, about a handspan long, which is flanked on either side by a small leaflet about a finger's breadth wide, running lengthwise from the same stalk; at the end of this stalk is attached the leaf itself, which is shaped like a harpoon—perfectly triangular—and measures one third [of a vara]

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XXIX
corpus_links.title: Chapter XXIX: On the Zapallo (American Squash/Pumpkin)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXIX
Del zapallo

Es el zapallo una especie de calabaza muy distinta de la referida en el capítulo antecedente; la mata se extiende por el suelo o sobre árboles, como la de la calabaza; echa un vástago que al principio no es más grueso que un dedo de la mano, redondo, verde y áspero por un vello que tiene como el de la borraja, y va creciendo hasta ponerse tan grueso como la muñeca de la
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIX
On the Zapallo

The zapallo is a species of gourd [calabaza] very distinct from the one described in the preceding chapter. The plant spreads along the ground or over trees, as the gourd does. It puts forth a stem which at first is no thicker than a finger, round, green, and rough with a down [vello] resembling that of the borage plant, and it grows until it becomes as thick as the wrist of a child's hand. The leaf is similar to that of the gourd, except that it is more downy and rough, as is also the stalk [pezón], with three slightly indented points, from each of which to the stalk measures about a hand's span [palmo], more or less, depending on the size of the leaf. There are many varieties of zapallo to be found; but the plant of all of them is very similar in leaf and flo

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXIV
De la guariconca

Esta es una yerba cabelluda de color blanco y de temperamento caliente y húmedo. Usan los indios de su cocimiento cuando les aflige la tos, tomándolo caliente en cantidad con azúcar en ayunas y después de cenar. Facilita el escupir en los que tienen dolor de costado, y principalmente si de su cocimiento se hace lamedor y se toma a menudo; y tomado este cocimiento c
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXIV
On the Guariconca

This is a hairy herb, white in color, and of a hot and moist temperament [complexion]. The Indians use its decoction when they are afflicted by a cough, taking it hot and in quantity with sugar, on an empty stomach and after supper. It facilitates expectoration in those suffering from pleurisy [dolor de costado, lit. 'side pain'], and especially if a syrup [lamedor] is made from its decoction and taken frequently. Taken as a decoction with honey, or made into a syrup thereof, it is effective against asthma and cleanses the sores [ulcers] of the lungs. Boiled together with maidenhair fern [culantrillo de pozo] and made into a syrup with sugar, it eases the chest and eradicates a chronic cough. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_XLI
corpus_links.title: The Sopo (Tola) shrub: description, habitat, and medicinal uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLI
Del sopo

Esta es una mata que crece tres o cuatro codos de alto; sus ramas son de color pardisco; no produce hojas, sino que en su cumbre echa muchos ramillos delgados que unos nacen de otros, verdes y no más gruesos que hilo de acarreto; no son lisos, sino ásperos o escamosos, a causa de unas puntillas que nacen por todo el tallo unas sobre otras, como escamas, que son más verdes qu
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLI
On the Sopo

This is a shrub that grows three or four cubits [codos] tall; its branches are brownish in color; it does not produce leaves, but at its crown it puts forth many thin small branchlets that spring one from another, green and no thicker than pack-thread [hilo de acarreto]; they are not smooth but rough or scaly, owing to small points that arise all along the stem one above another like scales, which are greener than the exposed portion of the stem, which is very little and rather whitish. This shrub grows in the very cold high moorlands [páramos], and the Indians say that vicuñas grazing upon it thereby produce bezoar stones [piedras bezares]; it bears neither flower nor any fruit; it makes excellent firewood and is commonly burned in the provinces of the Collao, and

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::NOVENO::cap_LVIII
corpus_links.title: Chapter LVIII: On the Vicuña
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LVIII

De la vicuña

La vicuña es un animal silvestre menor que la llama, y muy parecido a ella en su disposición y hechura; es del tamaño de una cabra, más delgada y crecida de piernas, pati-hendida, de pescuezo largo y delgado, y la parte alta del cuerpo y mayor parte dél de un color rubio que tira a leonado claro, con el vientre blanco y parte inferior del pecho. Son todas las vicuñas
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LVIII

On the Vicuña

The vicuña is a wild animal smaller than the llama, and very similar to it in its constitution and form. It is the size of a goat [cabra], slender and long-legged, cloven-hoofed, with a long, thin neck, and the upper part of the body—and the greater part of it—is a tawny color tending toward a light leonine hue, with a white belly and lower chest. All vicuñas are this color. They travel in herds, though they are often seen grazing singly. They are found only in the mountain ranges of Peru, in the coldest high plateaus [páramos], among the snow-covered cordilleras. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXX
De la suelda consuelda

A la planta llamada de los españoles suelda consuelda, nombran los indios del Perú, en la lengua general, chuleorrhuko, y en Cochabamba, diócesis de Charcas, auquilagna, que quiere decir padre de las yerbas. La mata es pequeña y sus tallos muy parecidos a los sarmientos, salvo que son más tiernos. Su hoja asimismo es muy semejante a la de la vid, sino que es me
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXX
On the plant called Suelda Consuelda ["mend-and-heal"]

The plant called by the Spaniards suelda consuelda is named by the Indians of Peru, in the general language [Quechua], chuleorrhuko, and in Cochabamba, in the diocese of Charcas, auquilagna, which means "father of herbs." The shrub is small and its stems very similar to vine shoots [sarmientos], except that they are more tender. Its leaf is likewise very similar to that of the grapevine, but smaller and more greasy than it, and both leaves and stems are very tender and tart like vinegar. It produces a small, purple, and showy flower that gives off no fragrance whatsoever. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXXXI
corpus_links.title: On the hopahopa (aquatic lentil-like plant)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXI
De la hopahopa.

Llaman hopahopa los indios a ciertas lentejuelas que se dan encima del agua encharcada y en los totorales o juncales; son algo coloradas y de complexión templada, con muy poca estipticidad; majada esta yerba y puesta en la muela que duele, quita el dolor; y asimismo, puesta sobre las quebraduras o fracturas de huesos con un poco de sal y polvos de muña, las restaura
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXI
On the hopahopa.

The Indians call hopahopa certain small lentil-like [plants] that grow on the surface of stagnant water and in reed beds or rush beds [totorales o juncales]. They are somewhat reddish and of a temperate complexion [temperament], with very little astringency [estipticidad]. This herb, ground [majada] and applied to the aching molar, relieves the pain; and likewise, applied over fractures or broken bones together with a little salt and powdered muña, it restores them. Its decoction taken with wine and alum [alumbre], drunk frequently, heals mouth sores [llagas de la boca] and firms the teeth.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXXXIX
corpus_links.title: On the Acana plant: properties, preparations, and medical uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXIX

De la acana

La acana crece un codo de alto; en las ramas y hojas es muy parecida a la alfalfa; tiene flor amarilla del talle de la de la manzanilla; nace entre peñas y es yerba pectoral, más amarga al gusto que la acíbar; es caliente y seca en el segundo grado. Comen los indios con ella la coca. Su cocimiento con un poco de alumbre es bueno para las llagas de la boca; y tomado ca
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIX

On the Acana

The acana grows to a cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height; in its branches and leaves it closely resembles alfalfa; it bears a yellow flower of the shape of that of camomile; it grows among rocks and is a pectoral herb [i.e., beneficial to the chest and lungs], more bitter to the taste than aloes [acíbar]; it is hot and dry in the second degree [following Galenic humoral classification]. The Indians eat coca with it. A decoction of it with a little alum is good for sores of the mouth; and taken warm on an empty stomach with sugar candy [alfeñique], it is beneficial against cough and asthma, and softens and cleanses the chest and stomach. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XCIII
corpus_links.title: The Tarco Tree: Properties and Medicinal Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCIII
Del tarco

Tarco llaman en el Perú a un árbol mediano, cuyas flores son entre azules y moradas, y así ellas como el árbol son de temperatura caliente y seco en el segundo grado. Tienen las flores cierta parte laxativa con que purgan la flema y melancolía, según dicen los indios; hacen de ellas una conserva que obra el mismo efecto de purgar. Demás de esto, los polvos, así de las hoj
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCIII
Of the Tarco

In Peru, the name tarco is given to a medium-sized tree whose flowers are between blue and purple; both the flowers and the tree itself are of a hot and dry temperament [complexion] in the second degree. The flowers possess a certain laxative quality by which they purge [phlegm] and melancholy [black bile], according to the Indians; a preserve [conserva] is made from them that produces the same purgative effect. Beyond this, the powders made from both the leaves and the bark of the tree have the property of drying any moist wound [llaga húmeda], and they dry up and consume hemorrhoids [almorranas]; a decoction of the same, prepared with a little linseed [linaza], softens them. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_CII
corpus_links.title: The Tipa Tree: Description and Medical Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CII

De la tipa

Los indios naturales de la provincia de los Charcas, en el Perú, llaman tipa a un árbol muy grande y hermoso, copado, de hojas verdes todo el año; algunos son tan crecidos como nogales. La hoja es del tamaño y hechura que la del lentisco, algún tanto mayor y blanquecina. Echa unas vainillas del largor de un dedo, delgadas y enjutas, salvo que junto al pezón son gruesecill
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CII

Of the Tipa

The native Indians of the province of Charcas, in Peru, call tipa a very large and beautiful tree, full-crowned, with green leaves throughout the year; some specimens grow as tall as walnut trees. The leaf is the size and shape of that of the mastic tree [lentisco], somewhat larger and whitish. It produces small pods about a finger's length, slender and dry, except near the stem where they are slightly thickened as if a chickpea were contained within. Each of these pods resembles in shape and form a butterfly's wing. corpus_links.original: [Achillea millefolium — documented across 46 independent nations by Moerman]
corpus_links.translation: Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) is documented by 46 independent North American nations — more than any other plant in the Moerman database. Applications span: wound healing and hemostasis (most common), fever reduction, respiratory infections, digestive complaints, and ceremonial use. The Navajo, Ojibwe, Cherokee, Cheyenne, and Blackfoot nations — geographically separated by thousands of miles — all independently documented yarrow for wound bleeding. This represents the archive's single highest documented convergence for any one plant: 46 independent North American nations plus Celtic/Norse (Bald's Leechbook) plus Greek/Roman (the genus named for Achilles) — potentially 48+ independent traditions for one therapeutic application.

CAPITULO LV
De la qixeaquea

La qixeaquea se llama así en la lengua aimará. Es una yerba pequeña; echa los ramillos largos un palmo, delgados, verdes y vellosos; sus hojas son como las del poleo, más puntiagudas, las cuales y los ramillos son pegajosos; produce unas florecicas blancas del tamaño y forma que las de la patacauri.
Dejo otras infinitas flores silvestres que nacen en diversas partes de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LV
On the qixeaquea

The qixeaquea is so called in the Aymara language. It is a small herb; it puts forth slender branches about a hand's span [palmo] in length, thin, green, and hairy; its leaves resemble those of pennyroyal [poleo], though more pointed, and both the leaves and the branches are sticky; it produces small white flowers of the same size and form as those of the patacauri.
I leave aside the countless other wildflowers that grow in various parts of this land, for it would be an endless task to attempt to enumerate them all — for those alone that during the season of the garúas [coastal drizzle-fogs] clothe the hills and slopes surrounding this city of Lima, and those that the Indian women sell in the plaza of Mexico City in carefully arranged bouquets, are beyond all n

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCIV
De la quinta-Laura

La quinta-Laura es una yerba muy parecida a la romaza; tiene las hojas largas de un palmo y anchas como dos dedos, y las raíces tan gruesas como un dedo. El cocimiento destas raíces y hojas, tomado en ayunas, ablanda el vientre del que está estreñido. El agua de las hojas, sacada por la alquitara, bebida en ayunas con un poco de canela, vale contra los dolores de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCIV
On the quinta-Laura

The quinta-Laura is an herb very similar to dock [romaza]; its leaves are a hand-span long and two fingers wide, and its roots are as thick as a finger. A decoction [cocimiento] of these roots and leaves, taken on an empty stomach, loosens the bowels of one who is constipated. The water of the leaves, extracted by alembic [alquitara], drunk on an empty stomach with a little cinnamon, is effective against stomach pains; and taken with sugar, it is used against bile disorders [cólera] and against jaundice [ictericia]. The leaves, pounded and made into a poultice [emplasto] with maize flour and salt, reduces the swelling of the belly and legs of those suffering from dropsy [hidrópicos]; and the seed of this herb, toasted and taken in red wine in the quantity

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXIX
De la caña fistola

Fuera de la caña fistola que, traída de la India oriental, se ha plantado y nace con abundancia en muchas partes destas Indias occidentales, que es la que se administra en las boticas, se halla en algunas provincias otra silvestre propia de la tierra, que parece del mismo linaje que la de la India, aunque distinta en especie. El árbol que produce esta caña fistol
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIX
On Cassia Fistula

Besides the cassia fistula [caña fistola] that, brought from the East Indies, has been planted and grows abundantly in many parts of these West Indies—being the variety dispensed in apothecaries [boticas]—there is found in certain provinces another wild kind, native to the land, which appears to be of the same lineage as that of India, though distinct in species. The tree that produces this wild cassia fistula is much larger than that of the other variety. The leaf of the one and the other is the same; however, the pods of this wild kind, although they are the same color and shape as those of the Indian cassia fistula, are much longer, thicker, and hollow on the inside, lacking the pulp [pulpa] that the good cassia fistula possesses. CAPITULO XXIX
Del zapallo

Es el zapallo una especie de calabaza muy distinta de la referida en el capítulo antecedente; la mata se extiende por el suelo o sobre árboles, como la de la calabaza; echa un vástago que al principio no es más grueso que un dedo de la mano, redondo, verde y áspero por un vello que tiene como el de la borraja, y va creciendo hasta ponerse tan grueso como la muñeca de la
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIX
On the Zapallo

The zapallo is a species of gourd [calabaza] very distinct from the one described in the preceding chapter. The plant spreads along the ground or over trees, as the gourd does. It puts forth a stem which at first is no thicker than a finger, round, green, and rough with a down [vello] resembling that of the borage plant, and it grows until it becomes as thick as the wrist of a child's hand. The leaf is similar to that of the gourd, except that it is more downy and rough, as is also the stalk [pezón], with three slightly indented points, from each of which to the stalk measures about a hand's span [palmo], more or less, depending on the size of the leaf. There are many varieties of zapallo to be found; but the plant of all of them is very similar in leaf and flo

CAPITULO XXXIV

De la coginoa, ayangue, peje-chapín, pejesapo, peje-tamboril y peje-perro

La coginoa es un pescado muy parecido a la palometa. El ayanque es propio destas Indias, de dos palmos de largo, poco más o menos; tiene la boca grande y colorada y agudos dientes, y se cuenta entre los pescados regalados. El pece llamado de los pescadores chapín, por ser parecido en la figura a un chapín, t
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIV

On the coginoa, ayanque, peje-chapín, pejesapo, peje-tamboril, and peje-perro

The coginoa is a fish very similar to the palometa [pompano]. The ayanque is native to these Indies, roughly two hand-spans in length, more or less; it has a large, red mouth and sharp teeth, and is counted among the prized [regalados] fish. The fish called by fishermen the chapín [slipper-fish], because its shape resembles a chapín [a platform shoe or clog], is a palm and a half in length and more than six fingers in height; it has no scales, but rather a shell-like covering; its flesh is white, like chicken breast, and of good flavor. corpus_links.title: On Clams, Mussels, and Shellfish of the American Coasts
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO II
De las almejas y chuchas

Debajo del nombre de almejas se comprenden muchas y varias conchas que se crían en las costas de los mares así del Sur como del Norte; convienen todas en ser corvadas o tumbadas, y diferéncianse en la hechura, color y tamaño. En la costa del Panamá, entre la arena de la playa que baña la mar, se cría gran suma de ellas, a las cuales, en aquella provincia, llam
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER II
On Clams and Chuchas

Under the name of clams [almejas] are comprised many and various shells that grow along the coasts of the seas, both of the South [Pacific] and the North [Atlantic/Caribbean]; they all share in being curved or rounded, and they differ in shape, color, and size. Along the coast of Panama, amid the sand of the beach washed by the sea, a great number of them are found, which in that province are called chuchas. Somewhat smaller than these, and blacker, they exist in great quantities along many parts of the coast of Peru; and in the port of Callao and on the island of that port [San Lorenzo Island] others are found as large as the palm of the hand, with flesh very white and smooth. Among these, some are oblong and others round, and some are larger than others.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::XIV::cap_LIX
corpus_links.title: On the Rhea (American Ostrich) of Peru and surrounding provinces
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LIX
Del avestruz

En los páramos y punas de la Sierra del Perú, y mucho más en las provincias del Cuyo, Tucumán y Santa Cruz de la Sierra, se crían gran suma de avestruces. Son las mayores aves de toda la América, y no de tan finas plumas como ellos, a cuya causa no se aprovechan dellas los españoles en esta tierra para plumajes, sino que las gastan en hacer curiosos quitasoles y plumeros
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LIX
On the Rhea [avestruz, "ostrich"]

In the moorlands [páramos] and high plateaus [punas] of the Andean range of Peru, and still more abundantly in the provinces of Cuyo, Tucumán, and Santa Cruz de la Sierra, great numbers of rheas [avestruces] are raised. They are the largest birds in all of America, though their feathers are not so fine as those of the [Old World] ostrich, for which reason the Spaniards in this land do not use them as plumes for adornment; rather, they employ them to make curious parasols [quitasoles] and feather-dusters for sweeping the altars and removing dust from religious images, for which purpose they are extremely good and highly prized. corpus_links.translation: Panax quinquefolius — American Ginseng. Cherokee uses: general tonic [restorative], aphrodisiac, and treatment of headache. Iroquois uses: fever reduction, digestive complaints, and female [gynecological] disorders. Ojibwe uses: tonic for the weak and elderly. Meskwaki uses: menstrual cramps. Multiple clinical trials have demonstrated: positive results for blood sugar regulation in Type 2 diabetes; modest positive results for cognitive function; and immune modulation. CAPITULO VII
De la achuma

La achuma es cierta especie de cardón de los del segundo género; crece un estado de alto y a veces más; es tan grueso como la pierna, cuadrado y de color de zabila; produce unas pitahayas pequeñas y dulces. Es ésta una planta con que el demonio tenía engañados a los indios del Perú en su gentilidad; de la cual usaban para sus embustes y supersticiones. Bebido el zumo del
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VII
On the Achuma

The achuma is a certain species of cardón [columnar cactus] of the second genus; it grows to the height of one estado [approximately 1.7 meters] and sometimes more; it is as thick as a man's leg, four-sided [ribbed], and the color of aloe [zabila]. It produces small, sweet pitahayas [cactus fruits]. This is a plant by which the Devil had deceived the Indians of Peru in their heathendom, and which they used in their trickery and superstitions. When its juice is drunk, it deprives one of one's senses in such a way that those who drink it are left as if dead; and some have even been seen to die from the great coldness that the brain receives. Transported by this drink, the Indians would dream a thousand absurdities and believed them as if they were truths. Its tempe

corpus_links.title: On Several Other Cardones (Cacti): Pullapulla and Hachacana
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO IX
De los demás cardones

De las muchas diferencias de cardones que yo he visto, no deben de quedar más que tres o cuatro, mas no dudo sino que habrá otros de que yo no tenga noticias. Uno de los más pequeños es el que se dice pullapulla, el cual no se levanta de la tierra más que, cuando mucho, un jeme. Hácese una mata redonda algo ahusada, que no parece sino un montoncillo de peras o de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX
On the Other Cardones [cacti]

Of the many varieties of cardones [columnar or globose cacti] that I have seen, there remain no more than three or four to describe, though I do not doubt that there are others of which I have no knowledge. One of the smallest is the one called pullapulla, which rises from the ground no more than, at most, one span [jeme: the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the index finger, roughly 7–8 cm]. It forms a round, somewhat tapering clump that looks like nothing so much as a little pile of pears or prickly-pear pads [tunas] arranged very close together in orderly fashion, their crowns pointing upward; for instead of branches or broad leaves [pencas], this plant produces small stems or joints [pezoncilos o trocillos] the size and shape of

corpus_links.title: The Avacollay and Other Columnar Cacti
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO VI
Del avacollay y otros cardones

El cardón llamado avacollay es el mayor de los de esta segunda clase, en que se ponen todos los demás que son verdes, espinosos, acanalados y que no dan madera de provecho; y deben de pasar de diez o doce suertes dellos. El avacollay crece unas veces levantado y derecho, y otras, tendido por el suelo, que no parece sino culebra verde. Tiene de cuatro a s
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VI
On the Avacollay and Other Cardones [columnar cacti]

The cardón [columnar cactus] called avacollay is the largest of those in this second class, which comprises all the rest that are green, spiny, ribbed, and yield no useful timber; and there must be more than ten or twelve varieties of them. The avacollay grows sometimes upright and erect, and at other times sprawling along the ground, where it looks for all the world like a green serpent. It has four to six ribs [lit. corners]; in its form it resembles a candle with many wicks. It is as thick as an arm and between one and two fathoms [estados] in length. At its crown it bears a white flower entirely without scent, two or three times larger than a lily, which the Indians eat cooked. There are many varieties of cardones lying b

CAPITULO X

Del mutuy

El mutuy es una mata que crece poco más de un estado en alto; echa muchas ramas a la redonda y muy juntas, con que se hace muy ancha y copada; sus ramas son rojas, mayormente hacia los pimpollos; produce las hojas como el lentisco, de dos en dos, en ramillos largos de un palmo, y se parecen en el talle y tamaño a las del lentisco, salvo que son más tiernas, más delgadas y un
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER X

On the Mutuy

The mutuy is a shrub that grows to little more than one estado [approximately the height of a man, roughly 1.7 m] in height; it sends out many branches all around, growing very close together, which makes it very wide and bushy. Its branches are red, especially toward the new shoots. It produces leaves like those of the mastic tree [lentisco], in pairs, on long sprigs of about a hand-span, and they resemble those of the mastic in shape and size, except that they are more tender, thinner, and of a darker green. This plant bears many small yellow flowers with no fragrance, composed of four or five petals, spreading about as wide as a carnation [clavellina]; the entire shrub becomes covered with these flowers, which greatly beautify it, and where it is not scorched by

corpus_links.title: On the Siga Tree and Its Resin
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CI
De la siga

La siga es cierto árbol que nace en el reino del Perú, del grandor de un [naranjo], que echa unas flores amarillas. Herido este árbol, destila una resina que los españoles llaman de Santa Cruz, por traerse de la provincia de Santa Cruz de la Sierra. Tiene esta resina el olor del árbol y es caliente en el grado tercero con vigor y fuerza de tal, y algo olorosa. Aprovecha, ap
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CI
On the Siga

The siga is a certain tree that grows in the kingdom of Peru, of the size of an [orange tree], and bears yellow flowers. When this tree is wounded, it exudes a resin that the Spaniards call [resin] of Santa Cruz, because it is brought from the province of Santa Cruz de la Sierra. This resin carries the scent of the tree; it is hot in the third degree [of the classical humoral scale], with vigour and force befitting that grade, and is somewhat fragrant. Applied in the form of a plaster, it is beneficial against all pain arising from a cold cause, in whatever part of the body it may be located, and against pain of the flank [colic/kidney pain]. Applied in the same manner together with powders of spearmint, mastic, and aromatic rose [compound] upon a stomach weakened b

CAPITULO LXXXIII
Del pica

Este es un árbol mediano, del grandor de un olivo; su hoja, redonda, y tan grande como la palma de la mano; echa una frutilla silvestre no comestible, colorada y redonda, del tamaño de pequeñas manzanas. Destila de este árbol una goma o resina de color de oro y muy reluciente, parecida en el olor y color al incienso, aunque tira algo su olor al de la almáciga. Quémanla e
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIII
On the Pica

This is a medium-sized tree, as large as an olive tree; its leaf is round and as large as the palm of the hand; it bears a small wild fruit that is not edible, red and round, the size of small apples. From this tree there distils a gum or resin of a golden colour and very lustrous, resembling incense in smell and colour, although its scent tends somewhat toward that of mastic [almáciga]. It is burned in place of incense in the provinces of the Collao, in Peru. The pica grows in the provinces of the Andes, and there is a great abundance of these trees throughout the Andean zone encompassing the provinces of Caraguaya and Larecaja—the first belonging to the diocese of Cuzco, the second to that of Chuquiabo [La Paz]. Del mutuy

El mutuy es una mata que crece poco más de un estado en alto; echa muchas ramas a la redonda y muy juntas, con que se hace muy ancha y copada; sus ramas son rojas, mayormente hacia los pimpollos; produce las hojas como el lentisco, de dos en dos, en ramillos largos de un palmo, y se parecen en el talle y tamaño a las del lentisco, salvo que son más tiernas, más delgadas y un
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER X

On the Mutuy

The mutuy is a shrub that grows to little more than one estado [approximately the height of a man, roughly 1.7 m] in height; it sends out many branches all around, growing very close together, which makes it very wide and bushy. Its branches are red, especially toward the new shoots. It produces leaves like those of the mastic tree [lentisco], in pairs, on long sprigs of about a hand-span, and they resemble those of the mastic in shape and size, except that they are more tender, thinner, and of a darker green. This plant bears many small yellow flowers with no fragrance, composed of four or five petals, spreading about as wide as a carnation [clavellina]; the entire shrub becomes covered with these flowers, which greatly beautify it, and where it is not scorched by

CAPITULO XXXVII

De la cantuta

La cantuta es una mata que echa muchas ramas alrededor, con que se viene a hacer copada; crece comúnmente dos estados; está muy poblada de hojas, la cual es como la del arrayán, algún tanto mayor y más delgada y tierna. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVII

On the Cantuta

The cantuta is a shrub that puts forth many branches all around, giving it a bushy, rounded crown. It commonly grows to about two fathoms [estados] in height and is thickly set with leaves resembling those of myrtle [arrayán], though somewhat larger, more slender, and more tender. This plant produces no other fruit than the flowers that share its name; some of these are purple of a vivid, glowing hue, and others are yellow—the purple ones being the finer and more pleasing in appearance. The stem or little neck [cuellecito] is hollow, about the thickness of a carnation's [clavellina's] stem and somewhat longer; both it and the petals of the flower are of the same substance, very fine, thin, and uniform in color. CAPITULO XXVI

Del runcurунcu

El runcurунcu pronunciando la r como en este nombre, caridad (no supieron los indios del Perú pronunciarla de otra manera), es una mata que crece un estado en alto y echa muchas ramas con que se hace copada; su hoja es parecida a la del granado, y la flor larguilla como la del tabaco, de color entre azul y morado. Produce una frutilla silvestre del tamaño de un garba
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVI

On the Runcurунcu

The runcurунcu — pronouncing the 'r' as in the word 'caridad' [charity] (for the Indians of Peru knew no other way to pronounce it) — is a shrub that grows to the height of a man [un estado, roughly 1.8 m] and puts out many branches, forming a bushy crown. Its leaf resembles that of the pomegranate, and its flower is somewhat elongated, like that of tobacco, and is a color between blue and purple. It bears a small wild fruit the size of a chickpea, round and red, which is edible but of no esteem whatsoever. The plant takes this name from the general language [Quechua] of Peru.

CAPITULO XXXII

Del tapaxochitl

Esta es una mata muy común en la provincia de Nicaragua, que por la hermosura de sus flores se planta en los jardines. Crece tres o cuatro palmos en alto y se hace muy copada; echa muchos tallos, que son redondos y con muchos ñudos; de los cuales nacen las hojas de dos en dos y son parecidas a las del granado, salvo que son vellosas. En la cumbre de los vástagos na
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXII

On the Tapaxochitl

This is a very common shrub in the province of Nicaragua, which is planted in gardens on account of the beauty of its flowers. It grows three or four spans [palmos] in height and becomes very bushy; it puts forth many stems, which are round and have many nodes [ñudos], from which the leaves grow in pairs, resembling those of the pomegranate, except that they are downy. At the top of the shoots the flower grows; it is a dark crimson tending toward purple, very striking, somewhat resembling the pink [clavellina], except that it is round in the manner of a button, the size of a hazelnut, composed of very small, hard, rough, and pointed little leaves [bracts], which are almost all spiny when touched with the hand, among which small white points emerge that ar

corpus_links.title: The Ataranca Plant
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXX
De la ataranca

Esta es una planta muy parecida al runcú-Tuncu. Levántase de la tierra como un estado; produce muchas ramas todas llenas de unas espinas blanquecinas tan grandes como las del naranjo; su hoja es algo semejante a la del granado, sólo que es un poco más angosta. En la lengua quichua se llama esta mata ataranca.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXX
Of the Ataranca

This is a plant very similar to the runcú-tuncu. It rises from the ground to about the height of a man [un estado]; it produces many branches all covered with whitish thorns as large as those of the orange tree; its leaf is somewhat similar to that of the pomegranate, except that it is a little narrower. In the Quechua language this shrub is called ataranca.

CAPITULO XLVI

De la flor llamada cempoalxochitl

En la lengua mexicana tiene este nombre una flor que los españoles suelen llamar rosa de las Indias, la cual es natural de la Nueva España. La mata que la produce crece poco menos de un estado, y algunas, mucho más; echa tantas ramas, que se hace copada. Y cada una da muchas flores; es parecida en la hoja a la artemisa. La flor es amarilla, de la g
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI

On the flower called cempoalxochitl

In the Mexican language [Nahuatl], this is the name given to a flower that the Spaniards commonly call the rose of the Indies, which is native to New Spain. The shrub that produces it grows to little less than one estado [approximately six feet] in height, and some grow considerably taller; it puts forth so many branches that it becomes bushy and rounded. Each branch bears many flowers; in its leaves it resembles artemisia [wormwood]. The flower is yellow, about the size of a rose, and some are much larger; it is composed of many petals, which are twisted or curled, for which reason we commonly call it the escarole flower [flor escarolada]. CAPITULO L
Del sunchu

El sunchu es un linaje de flores amarillas, que abraza algunas diferencias dellas muy parecidas todas entre sí en su figura, que es del talle de la flor de la manzanilla, y en la forma de la planta, que es una mata de un estado de alto, aromática y resinosa, la cual echa unas varas delgadas, redondas y algo rojas. Sus hojas son semejantes a las de la yerba-mora, y tocadas co
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER L
On the Sunchu

The sunchu is a genus of yellow-flowered plants, encompassing several varieties that are all very similar to one another in appearance: the shape of the flower resembles that of chamomile [manzanilla], and the plant itself is a shrub about one fathom [estado] in height, aromatic and resinous, which puts forth slender, round, and somewhat reddish stems. Its leaves are similar to those of nightshade [yerba-mora], and when touched to the tongue they prove abstersive [cleansing] or astringent [estípticas]. Both the leaves and the stems are covered with a short, rough down. The various sunchos differ from one another in height and in the shape of their leaves, for some have leaves larger than those of nightshade and bearing small points like those of the mallow. CAPITULO LII
De la pupa

La pupa, y por otro nombre hamillo, es una mata de un estado de alto; tiene los ramos verdes y la hoja como de verdolagas, tantico más angosta y larguilla; es muy tierna, hoja y cogollo; da una florecilla colorada y muy delgada, de hechura de la cantuta, y unos granillos ni más ni menos que los de la yerba-mora, sólo que no los echa en racimos, sino cada uno de por sí pega
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LII
On the Pupa

The pupa, also known by another name as hamillo, is a shrub about one estado [roughly one fathom, approximately six feet] in height; it has green branches and leaves like those of purslane [verdolagas], only somewhat narrower and more elongated; both leaf and shoot are very tender. It produces a small, slender reddish flower shaped like that of the cantuta [cantuta flower], and tiny berries exactly like those of nightshade [yerba-mora], except that it does not bear them in clusters but each one separately, attached to the small branches. From this plant the Indians extract birdlime for catching birds, and it is as good as that of Spain. CAPITULO LVI

De la casigua

Esta es una mata pequeña semejante al romero así en las ramillas delgadas como en el tamaño de las hojas, son algo puntiagudas, espinosas y más gruesas; si se tratan entre las manos, son algo pegajosas y dulces al principio, pero al fin de mascarlas, dejan algún género de amargo. Es caliente y seca; su cocimiento con culantrillo y anís es contra la tos; y con mayor fue
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LVI

On the casigua

This is a small shrub resembling rosemary both in its slender little branches and in the size of its leaves; the leaves are somewhat pointed, thorny, and rather thick. If handled between the fingers, they are somewhat sticky and sweet at first, but after chewing them they leave a certain bitterness in the mouth. It is hot and dry in temperament [in the Galenic sense]. A decoction of it made with maidenhair fern [culantrillo] and anise is used against cough; and it takes effect with greater force if a syrup [lamedor, a lick-medicine] is prepared from the decoction and taken frequently.

On the cilla-cilla

CAPITULO LXVI
Del mío

En las provincias de Tucumán y Paraguay nace una mata que los indios llaman mío, que es como decir yerba ponzoñosa, la cual se parece mucho en las hojas y altor al romero; es de tal calidad, que si los caballos la comen, al punto se comienzan a hinchar y dentro de un cuarto de hora mueren sin remedio. A cuya causa, los que caminan por donde hay esta planta, el remedio que ha
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXVI
Of the Mío

In the provinces of Tucumán and Paraguay there grows a shrub that the Indians call mío, which is as much as to say 'poisonous herb' [yerba ponzoñosa]. It closely resembles rosemary in its leaves and height. It is of such a nature that if horses eat it, they immediately begin to swell and within a quarter of an hour they die without remedy. For this reason, those who travel through areas where this plant grows resort to rubbing it on the muzzles of their horses, which prevents the animals from eating it.

CHAPTER LXVII
Of the Flor de la Trinidad [Flower of the Trinity]

CAPITULO LXXXII
Del bálsamo

El árbol que destila el bálsamo en estas Indias no de sola una especie, sino de tres o cuatro. Es este licor muy semejante al bálsamo de Siria, y no inferior a él en olor y facultades. La una especie de árboles que lo dan y de mayor grandeza, nace en la diócesis de Guatemala, donde yo lo vi, y en otras tierras calientes; crece más que un moral, y hace un tronco grueso
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXII
On Balsam

The tree that yields balsam in these Indies is not of a single species, but of three or four. This liquor is very similar to the balsam of Syria, and in no way inferior to it in fragrance or properties. One species—the largest of those that produce it—grows in the diocese of Guatemala, where I myself saw it, and in other warm lands. It grows taller than a mulberry tree and forms a thick trunk of fragrant and very hard wood, so strong that it serves for purposes requiring very sturdy timber, such as axles for sugar mills and similar uses. corpus_links.original: आमलकी विभीतकं हरीतकी च — त्रयो मध्यस्था। त्रिफला रसायनी।
corpus_links.translation: Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica), vibhitaka (Terminalia bellirica), and haritaki (Terminalia chebula) — these three are moderate in nature. Triphala is a rasayana. Triphala — the combination of three fruits — is the single most prescribed compound in Ayurvedic medicine. Charaka documents it for: constipation, eye conditions, liver conditions, skin diseases, diabetes, obesity, and as a general rasayana. All three fruits are individually significant — haritaki is Ayurveda's single most important medicinal plant (documented in 49 chapters of Charaka).

corpus_links.original: 上藥一百二十種為君，主養命以應天。中藥一百二十種為臣，主養性以應人。下藥一百二十五種為佐使，主治病以應地。
corpus_links.translation: The 120 superior drugs are like rulers — they nourish life and correspond to Heaven. The 120 middle drugs are like ministers — they nourish nature and correspond to Humanity. The 125 inferior drugs are like assistants — they treat disease and correspond to Earth. The Shennong Bencaojing classifies 365 substances (matching the days of the year) into three grades: Superior (non-toxic, taken long-term for longevity), Middle (some toxicity, taken for conditions with care), and Inferior (toxic or potent, for acute treatment only). This three-tier classification is the foundation of Chinese pharmaceutical theory.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO L

Del guarango

En el Perú tienen nombre de guarango cinco o seis especies de árboles muy parecidos entre sí, que casi todos echan unas vainas como algarrobas. Al que produce las mejores llaman los españoles algarrobo de las Indias, el es de diferente casta que el algarrobo de España. Es árbol mediano, del grandor de un olivo; la hoja es muy menuda, la cual en tamaño y hechura es parecid
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER 50

On the Guarango

In Peru, the name guarango is given to five or six species of trees that closely resemble one another, nearly all of which produce pods similar to carob [algarrobas]. The one that bears the finest pods the Spaniards call the 'algarrobo of the Indies' [carob of the Indies]; it is of a different kind from the algarrobo of Spain. It is a medium-sized tree, about the size of an olive tree; its leaf is very small, and in size and shape closely resembles the leaf of a fern or of a savin [juniper]. The fruit of the guarango consists of pods like carobs, though not as wide and long, whose seeds, in color and smoothness, resemble those of our carobs, except that they have many spines. This fruit is good to eat, and the Indians in some places make flour and bread from it

Del copal

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CV
On Copal

The copal tree is large; its leaves resemble those of the holm oak [encina], except that they are longer; its fruit is round and tends toward red; it has the same flavor as the gum that flows from the tree, which sometimes exudes spontaneously and at other times by making incisions [sajando] in the tree. This congealed resin [licor cuajado] is white and transparent, good for fumigations [sahumerios], by means of which headache is relieved, and it is a remedy for all ailments arising from a cold cause [causa fría]; and all the various kinds of copal, of which there are many, do the same. CAPITULO X

Del mamey de Cartagena

El mamey de Cartagena, que dondequiera que se da conserva este nombre, por haberse llevado de aquella provincia, aunque es muy parecido al mamey del capítulo pasado, se distingue de él en especie. Es este árbol el más hermoso y de mejor parecer de cuantos yo he visto propios de las Indias. Es de la grandeza de un nogal, muy poblado de hoja, bien hecho y copado.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER X

On the Mamey of Cartagena

The mamey of Cartagena [Mammea americana or Pouteria sapota, var.], which wherever it grows retains this name on account of having been brought from that province, although it greatly resembles the mamey of the preceding chapter, is nonetheless a distinct species. CHAPTER LXXVIII
On the Molle

The trees we find in these Indies that yield healthful gums and resins are beyond number; I shall treat here only of the best known, and the first shall be the one called molle [also molle] in this kingdom of Peru, a well-known tree that grows in temperate and warm lands. It is as large as an olive tree, and smaller below that size; it is pleasant to the eye, of a light green, and its leaf resembles that of the mastic tree [lentisco], though somewhat longer, narrower, and thinner.

De la espigua

CHAPTER CVII
Of the Espigua

This is a tree of the size of a mulberry tree, tall and spreading, with abundant foliage, which resembles that of the orange tree; it puts forth its leaves as the walnut does, on small stems growing from the branch with two rows of paired leaves on either side. Its fruit consists of small balls or berries in the manner of those borne by the chinaberry tree [árbol del paraíso]; they are the size of large grapes, with a thin green rind on the outside, which when it dries turns yellow and wrinkled. Beneath this rind is a black, round seed, of the size mentioned, so smooth, lustrous, and hard that rosaries are made from them. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXIV
De la tecoma haca

Este es un árbol que tiene las hojas redondas, y aserradas; lleva un fruto redondo, pequeño y rojo lleno de simientes semejantes a las pepitas del durazno. Es planta mordaz y odorífera, cortando este árbol mana dél una goma como la del copal, muy provechosa, que la suelen usar en lugar de la mirra y en la cura de muchas enfermedades, y principalmente corrige las
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIV
Of the Tecoma Haca

This is a tree with round, serrated leaves; it bears a small, round, red fruit full of seeds resembling the pits of the peach [durazno]. It is a pungent and fragrant plant; when this tree is cut, a gum [resin] flows from it similar to that of copal, which is very beneficial and is commonly used in place of myrrh in the treatment of many ailments. It principally corrects cold imbalances [destemplanzas frías] and fortifies the stomach. This tree grows in the hot lands [tierra caliente] of New Spain.

De los duraznos, priscos, albérchigos, melocotones y albaricoques

Estas cinco castas de fruta, por el parentesco que entre sí tienen, piden un mismo temple. Danse copiosamente en los valles templados de la Sierra deste reino y en los de los Llanos; pero con esta diferencia: que en los Llanos, aunque los árboles echan mucha flor, dan poco fruto, por caerse la mayor parte antes de cuaj

CAPITULO CXV

Del guachapelí

El guachapelí es un árbol que sólo nace en tierras calientes; no crece muy alto, porque no sube derecho, sino que echa el tronco torcido y encorvado y muchas y muy gruesas ramas. Su hoja es pequeña como la de la alfalfa. Es árbol silvestre infructífero, pero de muy buena madera para labrar, de la cual se hacen comúnmente los corvatones y costillas de los navíos; y par
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXV

On the Guachapelí

The guachapelí is a tree that grows only in warm lowland regions [tierras calientes]. It does not grow very tall, because it does not rise straight up; rather, it sends out its trunk twisted and curved, with many very thick branches. Its leaf is small, like that of alfalfa. It is a wild tree that bears no fruit, but yields very good timber for working. From this timber, the knees [corvatones] and ribs of ships are commonly made. In order to obtain pieces suitable for this purpose, the trunk is cut one or two varas [a vara being roughly 33 inches] above the ground, and from that junction together with an equal length of the root, a ship's knee is fashioned. The wood of this tree is very hard, tough, and does not split, which is why blocks [motones] and pulley

corpus_links.title: The Amatinca: A Venomous Viper of Vilcabamba
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLI
De la amatinca

Llaman los indios peruanos amatinca a cierta especie de víboras que se crían en la provincia de Vilcabamba, diócesis de la ciudad de Cuzco; son pequeñas y verdes, y tienen en la frente una punta como aguja; las cuales desde los árboles, donde andan ordinariamente, se arrojan a cualquier animal que pasa, y con más velocidad que una saeta, lo clavan, quedando la venenosa
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLI
On the Amatinca

The Peruvian Indians give the name amatinca to a certain species of viper found in the province of Vilcabamba, in the diocese of the city of Cuzco. They are small and green, and bear on their forehead a point like a needle. From the trees, where they ordinarily dwell, they hurl themselves at any animal that passes by, and with greater speed than an arrow they impale it — the venomous serpent dying in the act, as does the wounded animal, which likewise perishes.

CAPITULO CII

De la tipa

Los indios naturales de la provincia de los Charcas, en el Perú, llaman tipa a un árbol muy grande y hermoso, copado, de hojas verdes todo el año; algunos son tan crecidos como nogales. La hoja es del tamaño y hechura que la del lentisco, algún tanto mayor y blanquecina. Echa unas vainillas del largor de un dedo, delgadas y enjutas, salvo que junto al pezón son gruesecill
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CII

On the Tipa

The native Indians of the province of Charcas, in Peru, call tipa a very large and beautiful tree, broad-crowned, with green leaves throughout the year; some specimens grow as large as walnut trees. The leaf is similar in size and shape to that of the mastic tree [lentisco], somewhat larger and whitish. It produces small pods about a finger's length, slender and dry, except that near the stem they are somewhat thicker, as if they contained a chickpea inside. Each of these little pods resembles in shape and form the wing of a butterfly. CAPITULO CXV

Del guachapelí

El guachapelí es un árbol que sólo nace en tierras calientes; no crece muy alto, porque no sube derecho, sino que echa el tronco torcido y encorvado y muchas y muy gruesas ramas. Su hoja es pequeña como la de la alfalfa. Es árbol silvestre infructífero, pero de muy buena madera para labrar, de la cual se hacen comúnmente los corvatones y costillas de los navíos; y par
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXV

On the Guachapelí

The guachapelí is a tree that grows only in warm lowland regions [tierras calientes]. It does not grow very tall, because it does not rise straight up; rather, it sends out its trunk twisted and curved, with many very thick branches. Its leaf is small, like that of alfalfa. It is a wild tree that bears no fruit, but yields very good timber for working. From this timber, the knees [corvatones] and ribs of ships are commonly made. In order to obtain pieces suitable for this purpose, the trunk is cut one or two varas [a vara being roughly 33 inches] above the ground, and from that junction together with an equal length of the root, a ship's knee is fashioned. CHAPTER II

On the trees found in these Indies of the same genera as those of Spain

CAPITULO VI

Del mamón

En la isla Española llaman mamón a otro árbol y fruta parecida a la anona. Es el mamón árbol mediano, del grandor de un durazno, de muy buen parecer; su hoja es semejante a la del aliso, algo mayor y más acanalada y de un verde muy claro, que hermosea mucho el árbol; la fruta tiene el mismo nombre, la cual, cuando está pequeña y verde, parece alcachofa, por la cáscara muy d
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VI

On the Mamón

On the island of Hispaniola they call mamón another tree and fruit resembling the anona [custard apple]. The mamón is a medium-sized tree, about the size of a peach tree [durazno], and of very pleasing appearance; its leaf resembles that of the alder [aliso], being somewhat larger and more channeled, and of a very light green that greatly beautifies the tree. The fruit bears the same name; when it is small and unripe, it resembles an artichoke [alcachofa] on account of its very uneven surface, as though composed of green scales layered one upon another.

De Manco-Cápac, primer rey de los Incas

Apoderado el Inca Manco-Cápac del mando de aquella corta comunidad y república de hombres bárbaros, se portó con ellos más con humanidad y llaneza de hermano, que con autoridad de superior. Empleaba toda su industria en procurar el bien y acrecentamiento de los suyos.

CHAPTER IX

Concerning the sixth king of Peru, called Inca Roca

The sixth king of this land was Inca Roca, of whom the Indians say he began the faction [parcialidad] of Hanan-Cusco. De los dos últimos meses, y las fiestas que hacían en ellos

Llamaban al undécimo mes Tomaraymi piichayquiz, en el cual se hacía el sacrificio ordinario de los cien carneros; y si faltaba el agua en este mes, ponían atado en un llano un carnero escogido de los del sol, que fuese todo negro, y derramaban alrededor dél cantidad de chicha con ciertas ceremonias. No le daban de comer cos
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXX

Concerning the last two months and the festivals celebrated in them

They called the eleventh month Tomaraymi piichayquiz [Tomaraymi piichayquiz], in which the ordinary sacrifice of one hundred llamas [carneros] was performed. If water [rain] was lacking during this month, they would tie a chosen llama belonging to the Sun—one that was entirely black—in an open plain, and they would pour around it a quantity of chicha [maize beer] with certain ceremonies. They gave it nothing to eat until it rained, saying that out of pity for seeing it suffer, the Sun would cause rain to fall. CAPITULO XCVII
Del árbol de calenturas

En los términos de la ciudad de Loja, diócesis de Quito, nace cierta casta de árboles grandes, que tienen la corteza como de canela, un poco más gruesa, y muy amarga; la cual, molida en polvos, se da a los que tienen calenturas y con sólo este remedio se quitan. Háuse de tomar estos polvos en cantidad del peso de dos reales en vino o en cualquiera otro licor
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCVII
Of the Fever Tree

In the territory of the city of Loja, diocese of Quito, there grows a certain kind of large tree whose bark resembles cinnamon bark, somewhat thicker, and very bitter. This bark, ground into powder, is given to those suffering from fevers, and by this remedy alone the fevers are cured. The powder should be taken in a quantity equivalent to the weight of two reales [a small silver coin unit, roughly 6–7 grams], in wine or in any other liquid, shortly before the onset of the chills. These powders are now so well known and esteemed not only throughout the Indies but in Europe as well, that they are urgently requested and sent for even in Rome.
