The men and women of each nation and province had their own marks and [divisas] [insignia] by which they were known, and they were not permitted to go about without them nor to exchange them for those of another nation, under severe penalties. These they wore on their clothing in different stripes and colors; and the men wore another mark more prominently on the head, with each nation distinguished by its headdress [tocado]. CAPITULO XXXII

De los tambos y chasquis, y el tributo que en servirlos daban los indios

Los dos caminos reales de Sierra y Llanos que habemos dicho pasaban por las poblaciones mayores del reino, que eran cabezas de provincias, como Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas y otros lugares de la Sierra, y de los Llanos Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha y otros pueblos grandes, estacionados dichos pueblos por el c
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXII

On the tambos [way-stations] and chasquis [relay runners], and the tribute that the Indians rendered in serving them

The two royal roads of the Sierra [highlands] and the Llanos [coastal plains] that we have described passed through the largest settlements of the kingdom, which were the principal towns of the provinces — such as Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas, and other places in the Sierra, and on the Llanos: Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha, and other large towns. These towns were spaced along the highland road at intervals of twenty to thirty leagues from one another, more or less depending on the stretch, and along the coastal road there was one in each of the principal valleys. De las gallinas

Pero creer esto sería manifiesto engaño; porque, aunque muchas veces hace
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI

On Chickens

In some of the histories of the Indies that have come to light, I have read how in certain lands, among the various provisions [bastimentos] that the Indians offered to the Spaniards, they would come out to present chickens; from which one might infer that these birds were not brought from Spain, but must have already existed in this land. But to believe this would be manifest error; for although the histories of the Indies frequently mention gallinas [chickens], one should not understand them to be speaking of our own kind, but rather of native birds of the land. corpus_links.label: CS.Chik.7
corpus_links.title: Kushtha Chikitsa — skin disease treatment
corpus_links.original: खदिरः कुष्ठघ्नः श्रेष्ठः। तुम्बुरु शिरीषश्च।
corpus_links.translation: Khadira (Acacia catechu) is the foremost destroyer of skin diseases. Tumburu (Zanthoxylum) and shirisha (Albizia lebbeck) also [treat skin diseases]. The Charaka skin disease chapter is remarkable for its specificity — distinguishing 18 types of kushtha (skin conditions ranging from psoriasis to leprosy) and prescribing specific plants for each. Khadira's pharmacological content — catechin and epicatechin — has now been confirmed as anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial.
corpus_links.preparation: Khadira bark decoction; Panchatikta ghrita (five bitter plants in ghee)
corpus_links.condition: Psoriasis, leprosy, eczema, vitiligo, all skin conditions (18 types of kushtha)

corpus_links.label: CS.Chik.15
corpus_links.title: Unmada Chikitsa — psychiatric medicine
corpus_links.original: राजमाषादिं गणं जीवनीयम्। मनस्कान्तिकरं ब्राह्मी।
corpus_links.translation: The rajamasha group promotes life. Brahmi brings mental clarity and lustre to the mind. The Charaka psychiatric chapter documents a sophisticated understanding of mental illness — distinguishing endogenous (nija) from exogenous (agantuja) causes, roughly corresponding to endogenous psychiatric disorders vs. infectious/toxic conditions. Plants for psychiatric conditions: brahmi, shankhapushpi, jatamansi (Nardostachys). Jatamansi contains valerianol — related to the active compound in valerian, establishing a cross-tradition connection for the same neurological indication.
corpus_links.preparation: Multi-herb preparations with brahmi and shankhapushpi in ghee base
corpus_links.condition: Psychosis, mania, depression, anxiety, cognitive disorders

corpus_links.label: Canon.Book2.Senna
corpus_links.title: Sana (Senna) — the canonical laxative
corpus_links.original: السنا: حار يابس في الدرجة الثانية. ينقي الصفراء والسوداء.
corpus_links.translation: Senna: hot and dry in the second degree. It purges yellow bile and black bile. Ibn Sina documents senna as the primary oral laxative — distinguishing it from more violent purgatives by its moderate degree of action. The preparation: senna leaves steeped in hot water with violet and tamarind to moderate its griping action. This specific preparation — senna + tamarind to reduce cramping — is still the standard pharmaceutical formulation of senna today, 1,000 years later.
corpus_links.preparation: Senna leaves steeped in hot water with tamarind and violet; drunk fasting
corpus_links.condition: Constipation, melancholy (black bile excess), bilious conditions

corpus_links.label: DUB.Insamginseng
corpus_links.title: Korean Insam (Ginseng) — Heo Jun's detailed monograph
corpus_links.original: 인삼 — 원기를 보하고, 오장을 안정시키며, 정신을 맑게 한다
corpus_links.translation: Insam (Korean ginseng, Panax ginseng): supplements original qi, stabilizes the five organs, and clears the spirit. Heo Jun provides the most detailed pre-modern monograph on Korean ginseng — distinguishing wild mountain ginseng (sansam), cultivated ginseng (gaesam), and Chinese ginseng. He specifically notes that Korean-grown ginseng from specific mountain regions (Gaesong, Geumsan) is superior in effect to Chinese-grown — an observation validated by modern phytochemical analysis showing higher ginsenoside content in Korean varieties.
corpus_links.preparation: Root decoction; red ginseng (steamed and dried); white ginseng (dried); hwanggi-sam formula
corpus_links.condition: Fatigue, immune deficiency, cognitive decline, cardiovascular, general tonic

corpus_links.label: DUB.Hwanggi
corpus_links.title: Hwanggi (Astragalus) — the Korean surface guardian
corpus_links.original: 황기 — 피부를 단단하게 하고, 땀을 조절하며, 허약한 것을 보한다
corpus_links.translation: Hwanggi (Astragalus membranaceus): strengthens the skin surface, regulates sweating, and tonifies deficiency. Heo Jun's entry parallels the Bencao Gangmu and Shennong Bencaojing documentation of astragalus — confirming the same plant for the same indications across Chinese and Korean traditions. The Korean documentation adds clinical detail about the pattern of use: hwanggi is specifically for patients who sweat spontaneously (a deficiency pattern), distinguishing it from other tonics. This diagnostic specificity is a hallmark of the Dongui Bogam's clinical sophistication.
corpus_links.preparation: Decoction; Okhyeong-tang formula; Ssanghwa-tang formula
corpus_links.condition: Immune deficiency, spontaneous sweating, fatigue, wound healing, frequent colds

CAPITULO XXXII

De los tambos y chasquis, y el tributo que en servirlos daban los indios

Los dos caminos reales de Sierra y Llanos que habemos dicho pasaban por las poblaciones mayores del reino, que eran cabezas de provincias, como Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas y otros lugares de la Sierra, y de los Llanos Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha y otros pueblos grandes, estacionados dichos pueblos por el c
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXII

On the tambos [way-stations] and chasquis [relay runners], and the tribute that the Indians rendered in serving them

The two royal roads of the Sierra [highlands] and the Llanos [coastal plains] that we have described passed through the largest settlements of the kingdom, which were the principal towns of the provinces — such as Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas, and other places in the Sierra, and on the Llanos: Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha, and other large towns. These towns were spaced along the highland road at intervals of twenty to thirty leagues from one another, more or less depending on the stretch, and along the coastal road there was one in each of the principal valleys. corpus_links.label: CS.Kalpa.1
corpus_links.title: Kalpana — pharmaceutical preparation methods
corpus_links.original: स्वरसः कल्कश्च श्रितं हिमः फाण्टश्च। पञ्चविधः कषायः।
corpus_links.translation: Fresh juice (svarasa), paste (kalka), decoction (kwatha/shrita), cold infusion (hima), hot infusion (phanta) — these are the five types of kashayas (medicinal preparations). Charaka's pharmaceutical chapter defines the five primary methods of plant medicine preparation that form the basis of all Ayurvedic pharmacy. This classification is more systematic than any European pharmaceutical tradition before the 18th century — distinguishing preparations by extraction method, temperature, and concentration.

corpus_links.label: IBB.Cannabis
corpus_links.title: Al-Qinnab — the most detailed early cannabis pharmacology
corpus_links.original: القنب — الشراب المعمول منه يسكّر ويجنّن، والأكل منه بقدر الحاجة يُدرّ البول
corpus_links.translation: Cannabis — the drink made from it intoxicates and maddens; eating it in the required amount promotes urination. Ibn al-Baitar's cannabis entry is the most detailed pre-modern pharmacological documentation — distinguishing: the psychoactive dose (intoxicating, maddening) from the therapeutic dose (diuretic), the seed from the leaf and flower, and internal from external applications. He notes the difference between hemp seed (used nutritionally and medicinally) and the flowering tops (psychoactive). This precision of dose-effect documentation is unusual in medieval pharmacology.

corpus_links.title: Hammocks as Beds and Seating Customs in the Colonial Kingdom
corpus_links.original: Este reino como de otras partes, usan hamacas por cama. Es la hamaca dondequiera de una misma hechura, pero de diferente materia: las más hacen de una manta gruesa de algodón, larga como dos varas y media y ancha otro tanto; de sus extremos salen muchos hilos o cordones de lo mismo, que se van a recoger y rematar en sendas cuerdas gruesas. El armar y hacer esta cama no es más que atar estas cuerda
corpus_links.translation: In this kingdom, as in other regions, hammocks [hamacas] are used as beds. The hammock is everywhere of the same construction, though made of different materials: most are made of a thick cotton blanket, about two and a half varas [roughly 6–7 feet] long and equally wide; from its ends extend many threads or cords of the same material, which gather together and terminate in thick ropes on each side. Setting up and making this bed requires nothing more than tying these ropes, when sleeping indoors, to two posts or to opposite walls of the house, so that the bed is made once and for all, without any need to dress it anew each day as with our own beds. CAPITULO XLVI

De las corvinas, lizas, pescada, chita, vieja, curaca y coco

Corvinas se hallan en todas partes; son largas de dos o tres palmos y de buen mantenimiento. Las lizas son las que llaman albures en España; críanse muchas así en la mar como en muchos ríos, particularmente en las provincias del Paraguay y Tucumán, y la Nueva España en el río de Telmaii tejiec; es el pescado más sabroso q
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI

On the corvina, mullet, pescada, chita, vieja, curaca, and coco

Corvinas [drum fish] are found everywhere; they are two or three hand-spans in length and make good eating. The lizas [mullets] are what they call albures in Spain; great numbers are raised both in the sea and in many rivers, particularly in the provinces of Paraguay and Tucumán, and in New Spain in the river of Telmaii tejiec [ILLEGIBLE: likely a corrupted Nahuatl river name]; it is the most flavorful fish eaten in the Indies, though not the most wholesome. There are large and small mullets; the largest grow to two hand-spans in length. The pescada [whiting or hake] found here is small and scarce; the largest is no more than a third of a vara in length. De los dos últimos meses, y las fiestas que hacían en ellos

CHAPTER XXX

Concerning the last two months and the festivals celebrated in them

They called the eleventh month Tomaraymi piichayquiz [Tomaraymi piichayquiz], in which the ordinary sacrifice of one hundred llamas [carneros] was performed. If water [rain] was lacking during this month, they would tie a chosen llama belonging to the Sun—one that was entirely black—in an open plain, and they would pour around it a quantity of chicha [maize beer] with certain ceremonies. They gave it nothing to eat until it rained, saying that out of pity for seeing it suffer, the Sun would cause rain to fall. Los dos caminos reales de Sierra y Llanos que habemos dicho pasaban por las poblaciones mayores del reino, que eran cabezas de provincias, como Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas y otros lugares de la Sierra, y de los Llanos Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha y otros pueblos grandes, estacionados dichos pueblos por el c
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXII

On the tambos [way-stations] and chasquis [relay runners], and the tribute that the Indians rendered in serving them

The two royal roads of the Sierra [highlands] and the Llanos [coastal plains] that we have described passed through the largest settlements of the kingdom, which were the principal towns of the provinces — such as Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas, and other places in the Sierra, and on the Llanos: Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha, and other large towns. These towns were spaced along the highland road at intervals of twenty to thirty leagues from one another, more or less depending on the stretch, and along the coastal road there was one in each of the principal valleys. De la coginoa, ayangue, peje-chapín, pejesapo, peje-tamboril y peje-perro

La coginoa es un pescado muy parecido a la palometa. El ayanque es propio destas Indias, de dos palmos de largo, poco más o menos; tiene la boca grande y colorada y agudos dientes, y se cuenta entre los pescados regalados. El pece llamado de los pescadores chapín, por ser parecido en la figura a un chapín, t
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIV

On the coginoa, ayanque, peje-chapín, pejesapo, peje-tamboril, and peje-perro

The coginoa is a fish very similar to the palometa [pompano]. The ayanque is native to these Indies, roughly two hand-spans in length, more or less; it has a large, red mouth and sharp teeth, and is counted among the prized [regalados] fish. The fish called by fishermen the chapín [slipper-fish], because its shape resembles a chapín [a platform shoe or clog], is a palm and a half in length and more than six fingers in height; it has no scales, but rather a shell-like covering; its flesh is white, like chicken breast, and of good flavor. CAPITULO XI

De las gallinas

En algunas de las historias de Indias que han salido a luz, he leído cómo en algunas tierras, entre los demás bastimentos que los indios ofrecían a los españoles, salían a presentar gallinas; de donde podría inferir alguno que no se trujeron de España, sino que las debía de haber en esta tierra. Pero creer esto sería manifiesto engaño; porque, aunque muchas veces hace
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI

On Chickens

In some of the histories of the Indies that have come to light, I have read how in certain lands, among the various provisions [bastimentos] that the Indians offered to the Spaniards, they would come out to present chickens; from which one might infer that these birds were not brought from Spain, but must have already existed in this land. But to believe this would be manifest error; for although the histories of the Indies frequently mention gallinas [chickens], one should not understand them to be speaking of our own kind, but rather of native birds of the land. In New Spain, the native turkeys [pavas de la tierra] are commonly called by the name gallinas; and in the discovery and conquest of the provinces of Paraguay and Tucumán, chickens are likewise mentioned

Copal (pom) was both ritual and medicinal in Maya culture — a distinction the tradition did not draw as sharply as Western medicine. Medicinal uses documented: antimicrobial wound treatment
corpus_links.translation: Pom (Bursera copallifera / B. bipinnata) — Maya Copal Resin. From the Ritual of the Bacabs (translated by Roys): 'Ix-pom, ix-cacao, ix-ya-che — copal, cacao tree, sapodilla tree — these are the medicines of the great healers.' In Maya culture, copal (pom) served simultaneously as a ritual substance and a medicinal one — a distinction the tradition did not draw as sharply as Western medicine does. Documented medicinal uses include: antimicrobial wound treatment (resin applied directly to infected wounds); pain relief (smoke inhaled for headache); and treatment of respiratory conditions (resin burned in an enclosed space and the smoke inhaled). corpus_links.translation: Chapter VI. Since, from the time of the said two kings and by decree of both, Viracocha was held to be the universal god, at all solemn feasts in which the statues of the gods—those of the sun, moon, and stars—were brought out in public, reverence and homage were paid to the image of Viracocha; and from that time forward, the image of Viracocha that had been placed in the temple of the sun was set in a higher and more preeminent position, and particular sacrifices were offered to it. CHAPTER IX
On Dogs

There were only two breeds of dogs in this land at the time of the Spaniards' arrival, and they were very different from our own. Since then, all the varieties of dogs found in Spain have been brought over, and at present there are great numbers of them throughout all the Indies. The first Spaniards arrived in this kingdom of Peru in the year 1531. CHAPTER XLIX
On the Shark and the Mako

In all the seas of these Indies that fall within the torrid zone, there is a great abundance of sharks [tiburones]. This fish is very large, twelve feet or more in length, and six or seven handspans [palmos] in girth; its skin is hard and rough, its head large, and its mouth furnished with two or three rows of teeth exceedingly sharp, like a saw. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVIII
On the Sharks [cazones]

Along the entire coast of this kingdom of Peru there grows a great abundance of sharks [cazones] of all the species known in Spain, and also of others native to the Indies. They are known by the following names: cazón pique; another is called cazón negrito; others are canahotas, dentudo, guayas — which in Spain they call albariños. CHAPTER XXVIII

corpus_links.translation:

corpus_links.translation: Balché (Lonchocarpus violaceus / L. longistylus) — Sacred Maya Ritual Drink. From the Ritual of the Bacabs [a colonial-era Yucatec Maya manuscript of healing incantations], the text reads: 'U ts'o'ok u bin balché ti' noj nah... ka xoc-lah u k'ab u yich balché' — rendered as: 'The balché went to the great house... the hands and face of the balché were counted.' Balché is a ritual fermented beverage prepared from the bark of the Lonchocarpus tree, steeped in honey-water and allowed to ferment. It was employed in Maya healing ceremonies by the h-men [healer-priest] for purposes of purification, visionary experience, and the diagnosis of the cause of illness. According to Roys (1965) and Landa (1566, Relación de las Cosas de Yucatán): The term h-men (derived from h, meaning male, and men, meaning maker or one who does) designated the male Maya healer. Female counterparts bore the title ix-men. If the wound becomes infected [foul], chew strailwort [identity uncertain] and yarrow upon it. A wound salve: take yarrow and leechwort [identity uncertain], and boil in butter.

corpus_links.translation: 1. Against racking pain in the joints: pound lithwort [a plant remedy] with honey, or chew it and lay it on [the affected area]. Again, burn thoroughly the head-bone or skull of a wolf, pound it fine, sift it through a cloth, and apply it to the wound. Against pain in the joints: pound wormwood with tar and fen cress, wring out the juice, mix them together, press the residue upon the joint where the soreness is, and bind it on firmly. He who is wounded in the liver, if he be not sooner cured, then arriveth at the disorder in which a man speweth purulent matter. corpus_links.translation:
XIX.

Signs of a swollen and wounded liver; remedies for that; and concerning the hardening of the liver. He who has a wound in the liver, if he is not cured sooner, then arrives at the condition in which a man vomits purulent matter. If the man who is swollen in the liver, or the bloated one, remains so swollen until the twenty-fifth day without the swelling bursting, then the liver begins to harden; if it bursts, then there is a wound in the liver.

The signs of the wound are these: when the wound has burst outward, then the discharge through the belly runs like bloody water, and his face is red and swollen; and when you place your hand upon the liver then he feels very great pain, and the man is very tender, and from that disease very often come water-blisters. corpus_links.translation: XX. Remedies for abscess of the liver, when the purulent swelling bursts: take goat's milk still warm, freshly milked, and give the patient that to drink. When the sick person wishes to drink anything, let them drink nothing but water previously boiled with herbs — with wormwood and other such plants — and use such poultices [onlayings] as we described before. Chapter XXV.

Here are clear signs of disorders and sicknesses of the stomach [wamb], and how a man shall cure the evil humours of the stomach. When stomach disease is present, the signs are these: the stomach turns itself, is fevered, and feels sore when the man eats food; there are prickings [sharp pains] and loss of appetite. The knees are sluggish, the loins are heavy, there are spasms between the shoulders, and the whole body is gradually heavy; the feet are slow and the muscles of the loins are sore. When a man observes these signs, the first remedy [leechdom] is a day's fasting, so that by it he may cleanse the stomach and make it lighter. corpus_links.translation: Chapter XXX. If you wish that your belly [wamb] be always sound, you shall treat it thus, if you will. See to it every day that your fæcal discharge and your urine [mie] are of sound appearance, as is proper. If the urine be scanty, boil smallage [marche] and fennel, make a good broth, or boil the juice of [lacuna] and of other sweet herbs [worts]. corpus_links.original: 1. Drinks or potions and leechdoms against poison. Pound in ale betony, marche, wormwood, fennel, radish; administer this to drink. Against poison; put in holy water betony and the small atterlothe, drink the water and eat the worts. corpus_links.translation: 1. Drinks [potions] and leechdoms [medicinal remedies] against poison. Pound betony, marche [smallage/wild celery], wormwood, fennel, and radish in ale; administer this as a drink. Against poison: place betony and the small atterlothe [a plant identified as lesser burdock or possibly black hellebore] in holy water, drink the water and eat the plants. Against any poison: eat radish and clote [burdock] before the danger arrives; no man may then harm you with poison. Against any poison: boil the lower part of bishopwort [bishop's wort/wood betony] and lupin, and the lower part of springwort [dwarf spurge or caper spurge], everthroat [possibly vervain or a related plant], and clote [burdock] in ale; give to drink frequently. corpus_links.title: Remedies against accidental ingestion of a creeping thing and against being 'withheld' or 'restraine
corpus_links.original: 6. If one drink a creeping thing in water, let him cut into a sheep instantly, let him drink the sheep's blood hot. If a man be 'restrained' with worts, give him springwort for him to eat, and let him sup up holy water. In case that a man be 'withheld'; if he hath on him Scottish wax, and the small atterlothe; or let him drink it in boiled ale, he may not be 'restrained' by worts.
corpus_links.translation: 6. If someone accidentally swallows a creeping creature [insect, worm, or similar small animal] in water, let him immediately slaughter a sheep and drink the sheep's blood while it is still hot. If a man is 'restrained' [bewitched or physically bound/obstructed] by herbs [worts], give him springwort to eat, and let him drink holy water. In the case that a man is 'withheld' [similarly afflicted or magically bound]: if he carries upon him Scottish wax and the small atterlothe [a plant], or alternatively let him drink it in boiled ale — he cannot then be 'restrained' by herbs [worts].

corpus_links.title: Remedies against accidental ingestion of a creeping thing and against being 'withheld' or 'restraine
corpus_links.original: 6. If one drink a creeping thing in water, let him cut into a sheep instantly, let him drink the sheep's blood hot. If a man be 'restrained' with worts, give him springwort for him to eat, and let him sup up holy water. In case that a man be 'withheld'; if he hath on him Scottish wax, and the small atterlothe; or let him drink it in boiled ale, he may not be 'restrained' by worts.
corpus_links.translation: 6. If someone accidentally swallows a creeping creature [insect, worm, or similar small animal] in water, let him immediately slaughter a sheep and drink the sheep's blood while it is still hot. If a man is 'restrained' [bewitched or physically bound/obstructed] by herbs [worts], give him springwort to eat, and let him drink holy water. In the case that a man is 'withheld' [similarly afflicted or magically bound]: if he carries upon him Scottish wax and the small atterlothe [a plant], or alternatively let him drink it in boiled ale — he cannot then be 'restrained' by herbs [worts].

corpus_links.label: Canon.Book2.Cumin
corpus_links.title: Kammun (Cumin) — digestive and anti-flatulent
corpus_links.original: الكمون: حار يابس في الثانية. يطرد الرياح.
corpus_links.translation: Cumin: hot and dry in the second degree. It expels wind. Ibn Sina documents cumin as the primary carminative — for flatulence, digestive pain, and as a flavoring in medicinal preparations. The Canon distinguishes between Persian cumin (Bunium persicum) and common cumin (Cuminum cyminum), noting that Persian cumin is more effective medicinally. This botanical distinction — identifying a pharmacologically superior variety within the same species complex — demonstrates the empirical precision of the Canon's pharmacobotany.
corpus_links.preparation: Seed decoction; ground in preparations; added to food as medicinal spice
corpus_links.condition: Flatulence, digestive pain, colic, general digestive weakness

The Upaman [mourning period], and how long it lasts for different relatives.

§1. If one's father or mother dies, how long shall they [the survivors] remain [in mourning] — the son for his father, the daughter for her mother? How long [if the deceased was] righteous? How long [if the deceased was] a sinner?

Ahura Mazda answered: 'They shall remain thirty days for the righteous, and sixty days for the sinners.'

[Annotator's note 1: 'How long if the dead person died in a state of holiness (a dahma [state of ritual purity])? How long if in the state of a Peshotanu [one guilty of mortal sin]?']

corpus_links.translation:
Purity Laws Concerning Menstruation, Part I.

[Question] 1. O Maker of the material world, thou Holy One! If there be in the house of a worshipper of Mazda a woman who has the whites [leucorrhoea] or sees blood [menstrual bleeding], what shall the worshippers of Mazda do?

[Answer] 2. Ahura Mazda answered: 'They shall clear the way of the wood there — both plants and trees — they shall strew dry dust upon the ground, and they shall isolate a half, or a third, or a fourth, or a fifth part of the house, lest her gaze should fall upon the fire.'
[Note 1: 'The way of the Dashtanistan' — i.e., the prescribed path to the place of menstrual seclusion.]

corpus_links.translation:
The Upaman [mourning period], and how long it lasts for different relatives.

§1. If one's father or mother dies, how long shall they [the survivors] remain [in mourning] — the son for his father, the daughter for her mother? How long [if the deceased was] righteous? How long [if the deceased was] a sinner?

Ahura Mazda answered: 'They shall remain thirty days for the righteous, and sixty days for the sinners.'

[Annotator's note 1: 'How long if the dead person died in a state of holiness (a dahma [state of ritual purity])? How long if in the state of a Peshotanu [one guilty of mortal sin]?']

corpus_links.original: [Swahili] dawa ya asili — medicines of origin
corpus_links.translation: The Swahili coast (modern Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique coast) developed a hybrid medical tradition integrating Arabic Unani medicine with East African indigenous plant knowledge through centuries of Indian Ocean trade. Plants documented in Swahili coastal medicine include: mzeituni (olive, from Arabic), mnazi (coconut palm), mwembe (mango), and a range of endemic coastal forest plants. The Swahili medical tradition is documented in Arabic-script Swahili manuscripts held at the University of Dar es Salaam — largely unstudied by Western pharmacologists. The integration of Unani drug theory with African plant knowledge represents one of the most sophisticated medical synthesis traditions in the world.

Chapter 62. Piperitis, Libanotis, and Smyrnium.

[Continuation of the discussion of flavours in plants:] centaury [taury] is bitter; cucumbers, gourds, and lettuces are watery; parsley, anise, and fennel are pungent and odoriferous. The salt flavour is the only one not found in plants, with the sole exception of the chicheling vetch [Lathyrus sativus], and even there it is found only on the exterior surface of the plant, in the form of a kind of dust that settles upon it.

Wild cucumber, boiled in vinegar, is employed in fomentations [warm topical applications] for gout, and its juice is used as a remedy for toothache. The juice of the leaves, mixed with vinegar, is used as an ear injection in cases of deafness.

corpus_links.translation:
It is a distinct loss—especially when we observe that same scholar's translations of those fragments of medical papyri in the British Museum, dating back a thousand years earlier than the Papyrus Ebers. But he has not done it, neither he nor those others whose life-long studies and researches should have fitted them for the task. Until they do so, the English-speaking student is offered this little volume, a rendition into English of German and other translations of the Egyptian original.

One word more. 'Most Ancient of Books' is the claim made for the Papyrus Ebers; not, be it noted, 'Most Ancient of Papyri.' Not (by more than two thousand years) can it claim the latter distinction. corpus_links.translation:
The text describes a series of remedies drawn from the Papyrus Ebers, a collection of ancient Egyptian medical prescriptions, here presented with editorial commentary. The first remedy for blindness — a lotion made by crushing Dried Myrrh in Sour Milk — is judged by the modern commentator to have been entirely ineffective. The second remedy, a poultice of Powdered Onions applied to the eyes, would certainly have caused intense irritation ('made the blind man see stars'). The third remedy takes a different approach, treating the eye disease via the ear, presumably on the theory that this route would be less painful:

corpus_links.translation: Several remedies are given for 'Hotness in the Eyes' [ocular inflammation], a condition that must have been quite common among those who sought the care of an oculist during the Pharaonic period. As an eye-cooler, 'Baked Ox-liver, placed carefully thereon' does not sound very hopeful; and Soda-from-Upper-Egypt [natron], even when dissolved in spring-water, sounds positively alarming, despite the scribe's special marginal note appended to the prescription reading: 'It Heats It!' The third remedy, however, shows more promise and reveals once again the ancient physicians' belief in the homœopathic doctrine of like curing like: ANOTHER [REMEDY] TO DRIVE OUT HOTNESS IN THE EYES: Tallow from the jawbone of an ass. Take figs, a little sycamore-dough, or onions from the Oasis. Crush and grind these in sweet beer to which the potency of the required herbs has been added (also add wheat and barley beer). Bread of the Zizyphus-Lotus [jujube bread], cat's dung, red-lead [minium], watermelon, sweet beer, wine. Combine into one and apply as a plaster.

corpus_links.translation: Regarding the body, the Scribe set down several remedies. One internal remedy was compounded of Figs, Grapes, and Onions, Bread-of-the-Zizyphus-Lotus [bread made from the fruit of Ziziphus lotus], Blossoms-of-the-Cucumber, Incense, Wine, and Sweet Beer. It was to be taken over four days. Irregularities of the 'met' [the Egyptian concept of bodily channels or vessels] were treated by having the patient chew 'uwah-grain' while simultaneously applying a poultice of Goose's eggs to his buttocks — yet another illustration of the Scribe's adherence to the doctrine of like-curing-like [similia similibus curantur]. corpus_links.translation: The Egyptian word for this substance is d'd' (or didi), and it was originally translated as the Mandrake (or love-apple) owing to its resemblance to the Hebrew word dudaim in the Old Testament. For many years this identification was accepted without question, until in 'The Evolution of the Dragon' (1919) Professor G. Elliot Smith drew public attention to the error. Gauthier's researches, he pointed out, had led to the conclusion that didi was nothing other than red clay, while Griffith went further and correctly identified the substance as red ochre or hematite. In 1927, Dawson, writing in the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, provided a comprehensive summary of the occurrence of didi and the uses to which it was put throughout most of the Egyptian papyri. On the second day the head was anointed with Fish-oil. On the third day with Hippopotamus Oil. On the fourth day with abra-oil [an unidentified oil of Egyptian origin]. After this course of intensive treatment, if the Eczema still persisted, the affected scalp was smeared daily with Bread-meal and dressed with 'Rotted Cereals.'

Nine pages of the original papyrus are devoted to eye conditions, a fact which should surprise no one acquainted with that country, even across the thousands of years separating us from that remote period. In equal parts, [the preceding preparation] often sufficed to clear up bloodshot eyes [conjunctival hyperemia]. If it did not, a more complicated poultice composed of onions, verdigris [copper acetate], collyrium [kohl/antimony-based eye cosmetic], and Arabian-wood powder, crushed to a powder with ink and water, was recommended. There was then another prescription:

ANOTHER [REMEDY] TO DRIVE OUT BLOOD IN THE EYES
Two clay vessels: in one put powdered Fruit-of-the-Dompalm [doum palm fruit, Hyphaene thebaica] and Milk-of-a-Woman-who-has-borne-a-Son. In the other, Cow's Milk. Keep moist. In the morning bathe both eyes with the Fruit-of-the-Dompalm [preparation]. Next wash the eyes with the Cow's Milk four times [daily] for six days.

corpus_links.translation:
Those who complain of the slowness of medical progress should be thankful that in the extraction of splinters — to mention one department of minor surgery — we have advanced since the days of Tutankhamun. It does not seem much to boast of, and yet…

WHAT TO DO TO DRAW OUT SPLINTERS FROM THE FLESH
[Remedy 1:] The per-baibait bird [an unidentified Egyptian bird] with Honey. Apply thereto.

[Remedy 2:] Worms' blood, cooked and crushed in Oil; Mole, killed, cooked, and drained in Oil; Ass's dung, mixed in Fresh Milk. Apply to the opening.

[Remedy 3:] Male-and-Female-Semen [i.e., combined human semen]. Apply thereto.

[Remedy 4:] Skull of the Shadfish [a species of fish], cooked in Oil. Apply to the point of the splinter. Thereby it comes out.

[Remedy 5:] Incense, Dough, Sea-salt, Wasp's dung

The bite of a human — whether from the hands or, more precisely, the teeth of a lady or gentleman acquaintance — was considered to require more intensive treatment than even the bite of a crocodile.

REMEDY AGAINST THE BITE OR STING OF PEOPLE
Prepare for the patient a poultice of Raw Flesh on the first day. Afterwards, treat him with Oil and Honey to promote healing. Then apply Oil in Wax in order to effect a complete cure at once.

On Burns:
Burns are troublesome wounds under the best of circumstances, and much unnecessary suffering can be avoided if a quick and easy remedy is ready to hand. The ancients recognized this, though we may not readily appreciate the virtue of the preparations they employed:

TO PREVENT BURN WOUNDS
A Frog — warm in Oil and rub [the affected area] therewith.

corpus_links.title: Moerman's database — 4,029 uses across 291 nations
corpus_links.original: [Moerman, D.E. 1998. Native American Ethnobotany. Timber Press.]
corpus_links.translation: Daniel Moerman's Native American Ethnobotany database documents 4,029 medicinal plant uses across 291 indigenous North American nations — the most comprehensive documented indigenous pharmacopoeia in the world. Key statistical finding: plants used by more than five independent nations show significantly higher rates of confirmed pharmacological activity in modern research (Moerman, 1996) — validating the archive's convergence methodology. The most widely documented plants across the most nations: yarrow (46 nations), elderberry (27 nations), wild bergamot (21 nations), sage (19 nations), and echinacea (13 nations). These represent the highest-convergence indigenous North American plants.

corpus_links.translation:
The shad-fish and honey beaten together in yeast of sweet beer [were used as a salve ingredient]. Another salve, with surely more claim to colour than to cure, combined writing-fluid [ink], vermilion, and goat's fat with honey and several other ingredients that were certainly included only to add bulk. In yet another salve, ass's dung reappears; it is combined with yeast of the opium-drink, goat's fat, lettuce, onions, beans, and white oil. Sometimes it was a pathological cause such as 'Hardenings' [indurations or contractures] that prevented suppleness of the limbs. In such cases the 'Hardenings' had first to be removed:

SALVE TO MAKE SUPPLE THE HARDENINGS
Hog's fat
Oil of worms
Oil of the abxersu-animal [unidentified animal]
Mouse oil
Cat's oil
Gather all into one and anoint therewith.

corpus_links.translation: The Egyptian word for this substance is d'd' (or didi), and it was originally translated as the Mandrake (or love-apple) owing to its resemblance to the Hebrew word dudaim in the Old Testament. For many years this identification was accepted without question, until in 'The Evolution of the Dragon' (1919) Professor G. Elliot Smith drew public attention to the error. Gauthier's researches, he pointed out, had led to the conclusion that didi was nothing other than red clay, while Griffith went further and correctly identified the substance as red ochre or hematite. In 1927, Dawson, writing in the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, provided a comprehensive summary of the occurrence of didi and the uses to which it was put throughout most of the Egyptian papyri. On the second day the head was anointed with Fish-oil. On the third day with Hippopotamus Oil. On the fourth day with abra-oil [an unidentified oil of Egyptian origin]. After this course of intensive treatment, if the Eczema still persisted, the affected scalp was smeared daily with Bread-meal and dressed with 'Rotted Cereals.'

corpus_links.translation: Where prior treatment had failed, a douche [vaginal irrigation] composed of Fennel, Wonderfruit [unidentified Egyptian plant ingredient], Honey, and Sweet Beer was substituted and continued for four days. To protect a virgin from Leucorrhoea [vaginal discharge], it was necessary to anoint her breast, body, and all the limbs with a lotion prepared by crushing the dried liver of a Swallow in Sour Milk. To produce Milk in the breast of a woman about to nurse a child, Bones-of-the-Swordfish were warmed in Oil and her backbone smeared therewith. The same result could also be brought about by mixing Fragrant Bread (made from Soured Durra [sorghum]) with the Poppy-plant, and having her eat it while she sat cross-legged. On the second day the head was anointed with Fish-oil. On the third day with Hippopotamus Oil. On the fourth day with abra-oil [an unidentified oil of Egyptian origin]. corpus_links.translation: The ancient physician was at a loss when confronted with the so-called 'wood-like uha-disease' [Egyptian: uha, possibly a stiffening or sclerotic condition] occurring in isolation. An ointment compounded of hippopotamus fat and honey would have been more adhesive than picturesque. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVIII
On the Molle

The trees we find in these Indies that yield healthful gums and resins are beyond number; I shall treat here only of the best known, and the first shall be the one called molle [also molle] in this kingdom of Peru, a well-known tree that grows in temperate and warm lands. It is as large as an olive tree, and smaller below that size; it is pleasant to the eye, of a light green, and its leaf resembles that of the mastic tree [lentisco], though somewhat longer, narrower, and thinner.

The bite of a human — whether from the hands or, more precisely, the teeth of a lady or gentleman acquaintance — was considered to require more intensive treatment than even the bite of a crocodile.

REMEDY AGAINST THE BITE OR STING OF PEOPLE
Prepare for the patient a poultice of Raw Flesh on the first day. Afterwards, treat him with Oil and Honey to promote healing. Then apply Oil in Wax in order to effect a complete cure at once.

The text describes a series of remedies drawn from the Papyrus Ebers, a collection of ancient Egyptian medical prescriptions, here presented with editorial commentary. The first remedy for blindness — a lotion made by crushing Dried Myrrh in Sour Milk — is judged by the modern commentator to have been entirely ineffective. The second remedy, a poultice of Powdered Onions applied to the eyes, would certainly have caused intense irritation ('made the blind man see stars'). corpus_links.label: BGM.Danshen
corpus_links.title: Danshen (Salvia miltiorrhiza) — the heart blood mover
corpus_links.original: 丹參：苦，微寒，無毒。主心腹邪氣，腸鳴幽幽如走水，寒熱積聚，破癥除瘕，止煩滿，益氣。
corpus_links.translation: Danshen (red sage): bitter, slightly cold, non-toxic. Principal uses: pathogenic qi in the heart and abdomen, intestinal gurgling like running water, cold and heat accumulations, breaks up masses and concretions, stops vexation and fullness, benefits qi. Li Shizhen's documentation of danshen for cardiac conditions — 'one danshen equals four substances' (i.e., equals the blood-moving power of Si Wu Tang) — has been validated by modern research showing tanshinone IIA and salvianolic acid B are among the most potent natural cardiovascular compounds known. Danshen injection (Compound Danshen Dropping Pills) is an approved cardiovascular drug in China.
corpus_links.preparation: Compound Danshen Dropping Pills (approved drug China); decoction
corpus_links.condition: Angina, coronary artery disease, blood stasis conditions, liver fibrosis

corpus_links.label: Canon.Book2.Saffron
corpus_links.title: Zaafaran (Saffron) — heart and mood medicine
corpus_links.original: الزعفران: حار رطب في الدرجة الثانية. يفرّح النفس ويقوي القلب.
corpus_links.translation: Saffron: hot and moist in the second degree. It gladdens the soul and strengthens the heart. Ibn Sina's documentation of saffron for cardiac and mood conditions directly validates the existing archive entry (MMA-028). The Canon documents saffron as a primary cardiac tonic and antidepressant — 1,000 years before modern RCTs confirmed saffron's antidepressant activity comparable to fluoxetine (Prozac). The Canon also warns that excessive saffron produces 'immoderate laughter' — possibly the earliest documented description of saffron's psychoactive effects at high doses.

CHAPTER LXXV
On the Yoloxochitl

Yoloxochitl, in the Mexican tongue [Nahuatl], means 'heart-flower,' because it has the shape of a heart. Its form and appearance are such that, before it opens, it looks more like some kind of pointed fruit than a flower; for it is the size and figure of a bergamot pear [pera bergamota], and is composed of large, thick, and stiff leaves [petals], like the fleshy leaves of artichokes, pressed tightly one upon another. The opening of this flower consists in the outer leaves that encircle the whole bloom spreading apart slightly at their tips; these outer leaves are of a pale green that tends toward white. corpus_links.translation: Among the remedies placed into the mouths of ancient Egyptians by the physicians of the time, it is remarkable to note how little serious damage was done to the oral cavity and its contents. corpus_links.translation: The ancient physician was at a loss when confronted with the so-called 'wood-like uha-disease' [Egyptian: uha, possibly a stiffening or sclerotic condition] occurring in isolation. Principal uses: convulsions and epilepsy, alternating cold and heat, extreme heat with mania and tetany, eliminates pathogenic qi and expels demons. Li Shizhen documents cow gallstone (bezoar) for epilepsy and acute neurological conditions. This entry is significant because niuhuang contains bilirubin and bile salts — documented to have sedative and anticonvulsant activity in modern research. It connects to the Kyphi (Egyptian) documentation of the cow bile component in the Bald's Leechbook MRSA preparation, establishing a cross-tradition use of cattle bile products for specific conditions.

corpus_links.translation: Several remedies are given for 'Hotness in the Eyes' [ocular inflammation], a condition that must have been quite common among those who sought the care of an oculist during the Pharaonic period. As an eye-cooler, 'Baked Ox-liver, placed carefully thereon' does not sound very hopeful; and Soda-from-Upper-Egypt [natron], even when dissolved in spring-water, sounds positively alarming, despite the scribe's special marginal note appended to the prescription reading: 'It Heats It!' The third remedy, however, shows more promise and reveals once again the ancient physicians' belief in the homœopathic doctrine of like curing like: ANOTHER [REMEDY] TO DRIVE OUT HOTNESS IN THE EYES: Tallow from the jawbone of an ass. corpus_links.translation: Regarding the body, the Scribe set down several remedies. De la caparrosa y de las demás tierras de colores

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER X

On copperas [caparrosa] and the other colored earths

In many parts of these Indies there are mines of fine copperas [caparrosa], from which I have seen writing ink made with such ease that one need only cast the ground copperas together with a little ground tara [tannin-rich pod of Caesalpinia spinosa] into water just as it is cold naturally, stir it, and immediately upon finishing the mixing of the copperas, write with this ink, which turns out black with a slight tendency toward blue. From this I infer that it must differ from the copperas brought from Spain. All manner of good ashlar stone [piedra de cantería] suitable for working, the Indians of Peru call checorumi. They made use of it for the same purposes as we do, except for distilling water, which they did not know; and since they lacked iron tools, they worked the stone with other small, very hard and heavy stones, which in their language they call vini.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLI
On Mercury [azogue]

The mercury mines of this kingdom of Peru are considered of equal importance to those of silver, because the silver mines could not be worked without mercury, and even if some were worked, the great quantity of silver now extracted could not be obtained. In some parts of the Indies, mercury ores [metales de azogue] have been found, but none rich enough to be profitably processed. Only in the town of Huancavelica, in the diocese of Guamanga [Huamanga / Ayacucho], are there very abundant mines of this metal; and being so rich, they have been worked alone for many years and have yielded infinite wealth. On account of them that town was settled, and its inhabitants have no other trade or livelihood than the working of these mines. The hill from which the ores a

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXII
De la anchariipa

Esta es una yerba pequeña que produce unas varillas muy lisas y derechas; su temperamento es caliente y seco; aprovéchanse los indios destes varillas, metiéndolas por la vía de la orina cuando se sienten con alguna carnosidad, porque sin dolor la extirpan y gastan. El cocimiento desta yerba usado a menudo en las llagas muy maliciosas, las corrige, mundifica, deseca
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXII
On the anchariipa

This is a small herb that produces very smooth and straight little stalks [varillas]. Its temperament is hot and dry. The Indians make use of these stalks by inserting them through the urinary passage [vía de la orina] when they feel some fleshy growth [carnosidad] there, for they thereby extirpate and dissolve it without pain. A decoction [cocimiento] of this herb, used frequently on very malignant sores [llagas muy maliciosas], corrects, cleanses [mundifica], dries, and promotes the growth of new flesh [encarna]. And the herb pounded together with purslane [verdolagas], a little vinegar, and orpiment [oropimente], extirpates all warts [verrugas] and the films or membranes of scrofulous swellings [lamparones] or cysts [lobanillos].

De la caralahua

Esta es una mata delgada y pequeña; echa una vara tan alta como una pica, derecha y lisa, con algunos ramillos que nacen desde la mitad para arriba.

La hoja es del tamaño y talle de la del durazno, la cual y la corteza del árbol son de un verde muy blanquecino. Echa unas florecillas amarillas de la hechura y grandor de las del tabaco. Nace esta mata en las orillas de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LI

On the caralahua

This is a slender and small shrub; it sends up a stem as tall as a pike [i.e., roughly 12–18 feet], straight and smooth, with some small branches that grow from the middle upward.

The leaf is the size and shape of that of the peach tree, and both the leaf and the bark of the plant are of a very whitish green. It produces small yellow flowers similar in form and size to those of tobacco. This shrub grows on the banks of rivers in temperate lands [tierra templada]; its trunk and branches are of a spongy substance and of cold complexion [complexión fría, in the Galenic humoral sense]. Del Tacú

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX

On Tacú

The Indians of Peru, in the Aymara language, call tacú a substance that is properly Armenian Bole [Bolo Arménico] and is commonly administered as such; we may fittingly call it Indian Bole [Bolo Indico]. Tacú is found in the rich mountain of Potosí and in other metal mines, especially iron mines, and comes in three varieties: the first is a blood-red earth, used by painters and, principally, by gilders; the second is liver-colored; and the third, most common and most used by the Indians for curing certain ailments, is yellow. This last variety the Indians sell in the marketplaces in loaves and cakes, and they make use of it to treat bloody dysentery [cámaras de sangre], its powder being drunk dissolved in chicha, which is their wine. CAPITULO XIX

De las piedras de jaspe y pórfido

Así en este reino del Perú como en la Nueva España se halla toda suerte de jaspes y pórfidos. En la provincia de Atacama, diócesis de los Charcas, se dan unas piedras amarillas manchadas y muy vistosas, de rico jaspe, de que se hacen aras para los altares; y es útil este jaspe para mal de ijada y de orina, tomando sus polvos en vino en cantidad de m
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIX

On Jasper and Porphyry Stones

Both in this kingdom of Peru and in New Spain, every sort of jasper and porphyry is to be found. In the province of Atacama, in the diocese of Charcas, there occur certain yellow, spotted, and very striking stones of rich jasper, from which altar slabs [aras] are made. This jasper is useful for flank pain [mal de ijada] and afflictions of the urine, taken as a powder in wine in the quantity of half a dram or one dram [síc], and by applying the stone itself over the seat of pain.

In New Spain there is a certain species of jasper — a dark red stone with some green spots — that stanches the flow of blood, and it closely resembles chalcedony.

De la macay

Macay llaman los indios del Perú a unos panecillos pequeños como reales de a dos, aunque más gruesos, que ellos hacen de cierta piedra cama de cal. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVII
On Macay

The Indians of Peru call macay certain small loaves [panecillos] roughly the size of two-real coins, though thicker, which they make from a certain stone of the nature of lime [piedra cama de cal]. They are made by kneading the powders of the said stone with putrefied urine and baking them in an oven; once removed, the loaves are quenched [apagan] in urine mixed with powdered sulfur stone [piedra azufre], from which they acquire a very foul odor. This mixture is so potent that its powders readily cleanse [mundifican] any wound, however foul it may be. CAPÍTULO XXVI
De los tomates

La planta de los tomates es pequeña y se extiende sobre la tierra como la calabaza; mas no cunde tanto; echa un vástago más delgado que el dedo, del cual nacen otros muchos más delgados; la hoja es parecida en la hechura y tamaño a la de la yerba mora. La fruta que lleva se llama tomate; son unos granos muy parecidos al ají, redondos y colorados, y los menores, del ta
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVI
On Tomatoes

The tomato plant is small and spreads along the ground like a gourd, though it does not spread as far. It puts forth a stem thinner than a finger, from which many other, still thinner stems arise. The leaf resembles in shape and size that of black nightshade [yerba mora]. The fruit it bears is called the tomate; these are small round, red fruits very much resembling chili peppers [ají], and the smaller ones are the size of cherries. There are also yellow and green ones, some as large as plums and even as limes. Inside they contain a somewhat reddish watery substance and small seeds not much smaller than sesame [ajonjolí]; the skin is thin, almost like that of grapes. CAPITULO LXII
De la guaki

Llaman guahi los indios peruanos a una raíz muy conocida y estimada dellos; es muy amarga y de profundo olor no enfadoso; su temperamento es caliente y seco. Es tan parecida esta yerba a la que Dioscórides llama aristoquia luenga, que no parece distinguirse della. Usan los indios de su raíz para muchas enfermedades; con ella, mascada, se refriegan cualquiera parte del cu
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXII
On the Guaki

The Peruvian Indians call by the name guahi a root that is very well known and esteemed among them. It is very bitter and has a deep but not unpleasant smell; its temperament [complexion] is hot and dry. This herb so closely resembles what Dioscorides calls aristolochia longa [long birthwort] that it seems indistinguishable from it. The Indians use its root for many ailments; when chewed, they rub it on any painful part of the body. Its decoction [cocimiento] dispels all flatulence [ventosidad], cleanses the bowels, and warms cold parts of the body; drunk regularly, it cures jaundice [ictericia]. CAPITULO LXXV

De la hacagua guaní

Esta es una yerba de dos palmos en alto; tiene las hojas como las del lirio, algo más angostas, la flor purpúrea; las raíces son en gran cantidad y como los dedos de la mano y como zanahorias. Su temperamento es caliente y seco; el zumo de su raíz, echado en el oído, aprovecha para la sordera, y tomado en la boca, quita cualquiera dolor de muelas. El cocimiento
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXV

On the hacagua guaní

This is an herb reaching two palms [roughly 40 cm] in height; its leaves resemble those of the lily [lirio], though somewhat narrower, and its flower is purple. The roots are plentiful, shaped like the fingers of a hand and like carrots. Its temperament [complexion, in Galenic terms] is hot and dry. The juice of its root, dropped into the ear, is beneficial for deafness; and taken in the mouth, it relieves any toothache. A decoction [cocimiento] of these roots, taken on an empty stomach, counteracts urinary retention, provokes menstruation, and eases expectoration in pleuritic pains [dolores de costado]; and the roots, pounded and applied warm over the gout, relieve its pain.

CAPITULO LXXVII
De la anocara

Este nombre anocara, en la lengua aimará, significa el perro, y dando los indios a cierta yerba tan semejante a nuestro mastuerzo en la figura y en el gusto cálido y mordicante, que la llaman los españoles mastuerzo silvestre. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVII
On the Anocara

The name anocara, in the Aymara language, means 'the dog,' and the Indians give it to a certain herb so resembling our garden cress [mastuerzo] in form and in its hot, biting taste that the Spaniards call it wild cress [mastuerzo silvestre]. It grows in both cold and warm lands; in the former it does not grow as vigorously as in the latter. Its leaf is small, somewhat elongated, and deeply cut, with small points, like that of garden cress. It puts forth many stalks, all of them, along the upper portions, thickly covered with a very fine seed which, enclosed in its little husks [hollejuelos], has the shape of lentils, though it is much smaller.

CAPITULO XCIV
De la quinta-Laura

La quinta-Laura es una yerba muy parecida a la romaza; tiene las hojas largas de un palmo y anchas como dos dedos, y las raíces tan gruesas como un dedo. El cocimiento destas raíces y hojas, tomado en ayunas, ablanda el vientre del que está estreñido. CHAPTER XCIV
On the quinta-Laura

The quinta-Laura is an herb very similar to dock [romaza]; its leaves are a hand-span long and two fingers wide, and its roots are as thick as a finger. A decoction [cocimiento] of these roots and leaves, taken on an empty stomach, loosens the bowels of one who is constipated. The water of the leaves, extracted by alembic [alquitara], drunk on an empty stomach with a little cinnamon, is effective against stomach pains; and taken with sugar, it is used against bile disorders [cólera] and against jaundice [ictericia]. CAPITULO LXXIX
Del cauchuc

En este reino del Perú llaman cauchuc a un licor resinoso que en la Nueva España nombran ule, el cual es bien conocido en todas las Indias. El árbol es muy semejante a un nogal, si bien no es tan grande; echa las ramas muy largas, muy pobladas de hojas pareadas de dos en dos, como las del nogal, salvo que cada una destas hojas es larga dos palmos y ancha un jeme; es de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXIX
On the cauchuc

In this kingdom of Peru they call cauchuc a resinous liquid which in New Spain is called ule [hule], and which is well known throughout all the Indies. The tree is very similar to a walnut tree, though not as large; it puts forth very long branches, thickly set with leaves arranged in pairs, two by two, like those of the walnut, except that each of these leaves is two palms [roughly 16 inches] long and one hand-span [jeme, roughly 7 inches] wide; they are dark green, and both branches and leaves are covered with a short down. It produces a wild fruit, bitter and unpleasant in taste, resembling apples, which children are wont to eat as a treat. Such fine and well-glazed earthenware is produced here that there is no need for that of Talavera [de la Reina], for in recent years craftsmen have taken to imitating Chinese ware, and the result is very similar to it — particularly that made in the Puebla de los Ángeles in New Spain and in this city of Lima, which is of very good quality with beautiful glaze and colors. Del cuchuchu

Fuera de las muchas plantas que siembran y cultivan los indios para mantenerse de sus raíces, como son las que se contienen en los capítulos precedentes, hay otras muchas salvajes que nacen por los campos y tierras incultas las cuales no son de tan buen sustento ni tan estimadas como las hortenses y cultivadas. Destas raíces silvestres, la que en el Perú más se estima es
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXI
On the Cuchuchu

Beyond the many plants that the Indians sow and cultivate to sustain themselves from their roots, as described in the preceding chapters, there are many other wild plants that grow in the fields and uncultivated lands, which are not as nourishing nor as highly regarded as the garden-grown and cultivated ones. Of these wild roots, the one most esteemed in Peru is that which they call cuchuchu. This is a small root that grows in the high moorlands [páramos] and cold upland plains [punas] so severe that no other plant capable of sustaining man grows there. Many of these small roots grow together in the most humid parts of the moorlands; they are white, tender, very sweet and flavorsome, and the size of pine nuts. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LIV
De la ullaulla

La Ullaulla es una florecita llamada así en la lengua aimará, de color entre blanco y morado, del tamaño y talle de la del saúco, algún tanto mayor; compónese de cinco hojitas en rueda, las cuales tienen las puntas botas; nacen a manojitos de ocho a diez florecillas cada uno. Tienen un olor grato al olfato y vivo, y son de las de mayor fragancia que producen las sierra
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LIV
On the Ullaulla

The Ullaulla is a small flower called by this name in the Aymara language, of a color between white and purple, of the size and form of the elderflower [saúco], though somewhat larger; it is composed of five small petals arranged in a wheel [i.e., radially], whose tips are blunt [botas]. They grow in small clusters of eight to ten florets each. They have a fragrance that is pleasing and lively to the sense of smell, and they are among the most fragrant flowers produced by the mountain ranges [sierras] of Peru, where they grow in great abundance and greatly beautify the fields. De la yerba de la araña

Nace en lugares incultos, y en este valle de Lima se halla mucha junto al puerto del Callao; es muy parecida en el tamaño, ramos y hojas al tomillo, sólo que no tiene olor alguno. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CII

On the spider-herb [yerba de la araña]

The Spaniards gave this herb its name, derived from the effect it produces, which is to cure the bites of venomous spiders. It grows in uncultivated places, and in this valley of Lima it is found in great abundance near the port of Callao. It closely resembles thyme in size, branching, and leaves, except that it has no scent whatsoever. It is applied to a spider bite in the following manner: a decoction [cocimiento] is made from it, with which the affected area is washed very thoroughly, while pressing it so that the matter [venom/pus] is expelled; the powdered form of this same herb is then applied to the wound, and by this means one witnesses remarkable cures on a daily basis.

CAPITULO XXXVII

De la cantuta

La cantuta es una mata que echa muchas ramas alrededor, con que se viene a hacer copada; crece comúnmente dos estados; está muy poblada de hojas, la cual es como la del arrayán, algún tanto mayor y más delgada y tierna. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVII

On the Cantuta

The cantuta is a shrub that puts forth many branches all around, giving it a bushy, rounded crown. It commonly grows to about two fathoms [estados] in height and is thickly set with leaves resembling those of myrtle [arrayán], though somewhat larger, more slender, and more tender. This plant produces no other fruit than the flowers that share its name; some of these are purple of a vivid, glowing hue, and others are yellow—the purple ones being the finer and more pleasing in appearance. The stem or little neck [cuellecito] is hollow, about the thickness of a carnation's [clavellina's] stem and somewhat longer; both it and the petals of the flower are of the same substance, very fine, thin, and uniform in color. CAPITULO XLVII

De la ujuta

Los indios del Perú llaman ujuta al calzado que usan, y dan el mismo nombre a una flor, por tener, como tiene, la figura del dicho calzado. La mata que la produce crece dos o tres codos y echa muchas ramas o varas delgadas, pardas, redondas, lisas y correosas. Su hoja se parece a la del almendro, salvo que es un poco menor y más tierna. Es la flor amarilla de muy fino
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVII

Of the Ujuta

The Indians of Peru call ujuta the footwear [sandal] they use, and they give the same name to a flower because it has, as indeed it does, the shape of said footwear. The shrub that produces it grows two or three cubits tall and puts out many branches or thin stems, brownish, round, smooth, and tough [correosas]. Its leaf resembles that of the almond tree, except that it is somewhat smaller and more tender. The flower is yellow of a very fine color, of handsome appearance, though without fragrance; it has no more than a single petal [hoja] in the shape of a small gourd, a little shorter than a finger, thickest where it is about as wide as the ball of the thumb, tapering toward the stalk [pezón], and hollow within. CAPITULO XVII
De la usuma

También hallamos en esta tierra algunos géneros de frutas, que, por la similitud que tienen con nuestra ciruela, les damos este nombre. La primera de estas clases es la que los indios peruanos nombran usuma en la lengua aimará, y nosotros, ciruelas de la tierra. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVII
On the usuma

We also find in this land certain kinds of fruits which, by reason of their resemblance to our plum [ciruela], we give them that name. The first of these kinds is the one that the Peruvian Indians call usuma in the Aymara language, and which we call ciruelas de la tierra [plums of the land]. The tree is the size of a mulberry tree, very full-crowned, of good appearance and shade; its leaf resembles that of the orange tree, except that it is larger, smoother, stiffer, channeled [acanalada], and of a very dark green. The fruit is the size of a friar's plum [ciruela de fraile], red on the inside and on the outside; the skin is a thin little peel as delicate as a thin onion membrane; the flesh is very soft and sticky, but so choking [ahogadiza] that one cannot eat th

CAPITULO XCIX
Del sogue

Al árbol que los indios del Perú llaman sogue, los españoles le dan nombre de sauce, porque se le parece. Sus hojas, corteza y flores son estípticas; el cocimiento de las hojas con vino aprovecha para llagas de pierna, y cocido con leche y con ella dado baño, quita los dolores y los nudos de la gota. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCIX
On the Sogue

The tree that the Indians of Peru call sogue is given the name sauce [willow] by the Spaniards, because it resembles that tree. Its leaves, bark, and flowers are astringent [estípticas]; a decoction of the leaves with wine is beneficial for leg sores, and when boiled with milk and used as a bath, it relieves pains and the nodules of gout. A decoction of the said leaves, mixed with pomegranate juice and oil, relieves earache when a few warm drops are instilled into the ears. A decoction made with a little alum [alumbre] of the leaves, bark, and flowers strengthens the teeth and gums, and is used against chilblains [sabañones] when applied as a bath. De la religión falsa que tenían los del Perú, y cuán dados eran a ella

Eran los indios del Perú tan grandes idólatras que adoraban por dioses casi cuantas especies hay de criaturas. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER ONE

On the False Religion of the Peruvians and How Devoted They Were to It

The Indians of Peru were such great idolaters that they worshipped as gods nearly every species of creature in existence. For, lacking supernatural enlightenment, they fell into the same errors and follies as the other heathen nations, the same causes being at work in them as in those others that prevented them from finding the true God: namely, the great abyss of vices and sins in which they were submerged, which had rendered them incapable and unworthy of receiving the pure light of knowledge of their Creator; and the malice and cunning of the demon, enemy of the human race, who, out of his ancient pride and envy of our good, sought to usurp among these blind peoples the adoration owed to Him alone who c

Del hicho

Son también innumerables las diferencias que nacen por los campos de yerbas silvestres de grande utilidad para pasto y sustento de los ganados. Entre las demás crió Dios en esta América dos géneros de yerbas muy generales; en esta Meridional, el hicho, y en la Septentrional, el zacate. El hicho es la yerba más común que nace en las sierras del Perú y la más conocida de indi
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CVI
On the Hicho

The varieties of wild grasses that grow across the fields and are of great utility as pasture and sustenance for livestock are likewise innumerable. Among others, God created in this America two very widespread kinds of grass: in this Southern part, the hicho, and in the Northern part, the zacate [a general term for grasses in Mesoamerica and northern South America]. The hicho is the most common grass that grows in the highlands [sierras] of Peru, and the best known to both Indians and Spaniards. It is native to cold lands, and since the highlands of this realm are for the most part punas [high Andean plateaux] and barren páramos [high moorlands], they are all covered with this grass, which endures the cold and the frosts so well that where it does not grow, no ot

De los cazones

En toda la costa deste reino del Perú se cría gran copia de cazones de todas especies conocidas en España y aún de otras propias de las Indias, y son conocidos por los nombres siguientes: cazón pique; otro se llama cazón negrito; otros canahotas, dentudo, guayas, que llaman en España albariños. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVIII
On the Sharks [cazones]

Along the entire coast of this kingdom of Peru there grows a great abundance of sharks [cazones] of all the species known in Spain, and also of others native to the Indies. They are known by the following names: cazón pique; another is called cazón negrito; others are canahotas, dentudo, guayas — which in Spain they call albariños. Tenían estos indios del Perú el ejercicio de la milicia por el más grave y noble de todos; y así lo trataban con más primor, estudio y curiosidad que otro ninguno. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX

On the Military Art and How These Indians Practiced It, Their Weapons, and Their Manner of Fighting

The Indians of Peru regarded the exercise of arms as the most serious and noble of all pursuits, and they attended to it with greater refinement, study, and care than to any other. The Incas held military service and those who practiced it in the highest esteem, regarding it as the means by which they had risen to such great power and majesty and by which they maintained it. It was the sole title among their subjects by which one could advance to positions of honor, and there was scarcely any other path by which a man might rise and make himself of worth. CHAPTER XIII
On Common Stones

Turning now to the subject of mineral quarries [canteras minerales] and all manner of stones, I shall place first those most common, which are generally found everywhere, namely those we use in buildings and other domestic purposes. In this land one finds all the varieties of stone known in Europe, along with certain particular ones that are native to this region. All species of stone differ primarily in four respects: color, weight, hardness, and smoothness; for some are very solid and heavy while others are porous and light; some hard, others soft. They are found in every color—black, white, red, yellow, green, blue, mottled, and all intermediate shades. Some are sandy in texture, others earthy, others floury [harinosas], and others glassy [vedriosas].

CHAPTER XLIV
On Tin

Only a single tin mine is worked in Peru, and as far as I am informed, no other is known in this entire kingdom; yet this one is so rich that, although it has been in operation for many years now, it promises great longevity. It is located in the province of Caracollo, in the diocese of Charcas. De las costumbres más generales en que se conforman todos los indios

Gentes que tan sujetas y rendidas tenía el padre de la mentira y enemigo cruel del linaje humano, que hacía le diesen la honra y adoración debida a sólo el Criador, no es difícil de entender qué tal sería la enseñanza e institución en errores, crueldades y todo género de vicios, que de tan perverso maestro habrían

CHAPTER VII

On the most general customs shared by all Indians

Peoples so thoroughly subjected and surrendered to the father of lies and cruel enemy of the human race—who caused them to render the honor and worship due to the Creator alone to himself—it is not difficult to understand what manner of instruction in errors, cruelties, and every kind of vice they would have learned from so perverse a master. They were all idolaters, given over to endless superstitions and omens, with the exception here and there of some nation of men so coarse and savage that, being of a purely brutish nature, they recognized no deity in heaven or on earth, nor had any form of worship whatsoever. Del guayroro

El guayroro es un árbol muy grande, que se halla en las provincias de los Andes, en el Perú. CHAPTER XCI

On the Guayroro

The guayroro is a very large tree found in the provinces of the Andes, in Peru. It produces pods or tubes in the manner of those of the cassia fistula [amfistola], within whose cavity are found seeds that are rather round, though flat and smooth, of the color of fine coral; each one bears a black spot that lends it beauty. The Indians hold these seeds in great esteem, affirming that they are efficacious against ailments of the heart [mal de corazón] and melancholy, taken as a powder in wine or orange-blossom water [agua de azahar] at a dose of a little more than half a dram [drachm]. CHAPTER XXVII
On the Quenti

The quenti is the smallest of the birds found in these Indies, for it is so tiny that if one holds it in the hand and closes the fist around it, it makes no more bulk than an acorn of the oak [bellota de encina]; and plucked, it ends up scarcely larger than a horsefly [moscardón], since when plucked its head is no bigger than a chickpea [garbanzo]. Small as it is, it has a great deal of plumage, by means of which, from the tip of its beak to its tail, it measures in length the breadth of four fingers, and with its little wings spread, it measures six fingers from tip to tip. Cómo se hace el descubrimiento de minas

Respecto de haber en estas Indias tanto copia de minerales como queda dicho, y ocuparse en su labor y beneficio gran parte de la gente que las habita, hay en cada provincial establecidas leyes y ordenanzas que son obligados a guardar los mineros y por donde se dirimen los pleitos y diferencias que se levantan en los asientos y reales de minas

CHAPTER XXXV

How the Discovery of Mines is Conducted

Given that there exists in these Indies so great an abundance of mineral deposits as has already been described, and that a large portion of the population occupies itself in their working and processing [beneficio], each province has established laws and ordinances which miners are obliged to observe, and by which the lawsuits and disputes [pleitos y diferencias] that arise in mining camps and settlements [asientos y reales de minas] concerning these matters are adjudicated. CHAPTER XXXVI
On Gold

Gold has always held primacy among all metals, whose resplendent appearance so greatly gladdens men and draws them to it that scarcely any nation in the world has been found so rustic and barbarous as not to know it, seek it, and esteem it. It grows [is found] abundantly throughout all these Indies, whose native peoples worked it and made use of it for various purposes, though not for as many as we do. The caciques [chiefs] and nobles of Peru had many pieces of gold, some of which their descendants still possess today, while most have come into the hands of Spaniards. For this reason, at different times of year, the process takes more or fewer days to mature; and in order to gauge its progress, the refiner [beneficiador] assays it twice a day and adds whatever reagents [recaudo] he sees are needed. CAPITULO XLI
Del azogue

Por de igual importancia son tenidas en este reino del Perú las minas de azogue que las de plata, porque éstas, sin azogue, no se pudieran labrar, y si se labraran algunas, no se sacara tan grande cantidad de plata como ahora se saca. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLI
On Mercury [azogue]

The mercury mines of this kingdom of Peru are considered of equal importance to those of silver, because the silver mines could not be worked without mercury, and even if some were worked, the great quantity of silver now extracted could not be obtained. In some parts of the Indies, mercury ores [metales de azogue] have been found, but none rich enough to be profitably processed. Only in the town of Huancavelica, in the diocese of Guamanga [Huamanga / Ayacucho], are there very abundant mines of this metal; and being so rich, they have been worked alone for many years and have yielded infinite wealth. On account of them that town was settled, and its inhabitants have no other trade or livelihood than the working of these mines. The hill from which the ores a

corpus_links.title: Mercury Amalgamation Process for Silver Refining
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXIX
Del beneficio con azogue

El beneficio de azogue es de mucha más riqueza que el de fundición, porque es más copioso y general y se saca con él todo la plata de los metales, por bajos y pobres que sean. Cuando el metal acude de dos onzas para arriba por quintal, se puede beneficiar con ganancia, y de aquí para abajo, es con muy poca o ninguna, particularmente en los asientos de minas
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIX
On the Mercury Amalgamation Process

The mercury amalgamation process [beneficio de azogue] is far more productive than smelting [fundición], because it is more abundant in yield and more universally applicable, and by means of it all the silver is extracted from the ores, however low-grade and poor they may be. When the ore yields two ounces or more per hundredweight [quintal], it can be processed profitably; below this threshold, profit is very little or none at all, particularly in mining settlements that do not have Indians assigned by royal warrant and allotment [cédula y repartimiento], or by the mita, as it is called in Peru.

CHAPTER XL
On the Pigs and Bars of Silver

The ore having been washed and the mercury [azogue] that was bonded with the silver — which they call the pella [amalgam mass] — separated from the earth and slag, it is placed into coarse linen cloths, and by pressing and beating the pella, part of the mercury is expelled, since no further treatment remains to be done to the silver beyond separating it from its most intimate companion, the mercury.
