CAPITULO XVII
De la piedra de yeso

De piedra de yeso se hallan menos canteras que de cal, particularmente en tierras calientes; en las tierras frías hay grandes cerros della, y alguna muy fina, de espejuelo, como es en el distrito de Guamanga y del Cuzco. En los valles destos llanos se halla alguna, particularmente en los que son abundante de viñas, como son el de Vítor, en la diócesis de Arequip
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVII
On gypsum stone

Quarries of gypsum stone [piedra de yeso] are less common than those of lime, particularly in hot lands; in cold lands there are great hills of it, and some of very fine quality, of the selenite [espejuelo] variety, as is the case in the districts of Guamanga and Cuzco. In the coastal valleys some is found as well, particularly in those abounding in vineyards, such as the valley of Vítor, in the diocese of Arequipa, and that of Pisco, in this archbishopric of Lima: it would seem that God provided, so long in advance, for the need these valleys would have for gypsum in the treatment [beneficio] of the great quantity of wine that is presently harvested in them.

CAPITULO CXXVI
De la ceyba

En la lengua de la isla Española se llama ceyba un árbol de los mayores que se hallan en estas Indias. Es de buena sombra y echa muchas y muy extendidas ramas; su fruto son unas vainas como manzanas redondas llenas de cierta lana delgada y blanca como algodón, las cuales, después de secas, se abren y se lleva el aire la lana; entre la cual hay unos granillos o pepitas,
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXXVI
Of the Ceiba

In the language of the island of Hispaniola, a tree called the ceiba is one of the largest to be found in these Indies. It provides good shade and puts forth many widely spreading branches. Its fruit consists of pods like round apples, filled with a fine, white wool resembling cotton; once dried, these pods open and the wind carries off the wool, among which are small grains or seeds [pepitas], which constitute the seed proper. It puts forth its leaves on a stalk [pezón] like that of a grape-vine leaf, and the leaf itself resembles that of hemp [cáñamo], having six to seven points in the form of a star. Its wood is soft and not solid. These trees are commonly planted in the main squares [plazas] of Indian towns on account of their great beauty, and even in some

De los perros

Solas dos castas de perros, y muy diferentes de los nuestros, había en esta tierra a la entrada en ella de los españoles. Después acá se han traído de España todas las diferencias de perros que hay allá, de que al presente hay gran cantidad en todas las Indias. CHAPTER IX
On Dogs

There were only two breeds of dogs in this land at the time of the Spaniards' arrival, and they were very different from our own. Since then, all the varieties of dogs found in Spain have been brought over, and at present there are great numbers of them throughout all the Indies. The first Spaniards arrived in this kingdom of Peru in the year 1531. In the earliest conquests that the Spaniards carried out in the islands of the Windward [Barlovento] and in other provinces of Tierra Firme [the mainland], they made great use of dogs in the wars they waged against the Indians; for, once trained, these dogs were most useful, especially in rough and wooded terrain, where, the enemy being light on their feet, the Spaniards could not pursue them. CAPITULO XI

De las gallinas

En algunas de las historias de Indias que han salido a luz, he leído cómo en algunas tierras, entre los demás bastimentos que los indios ofrecían a los españoles, salían a presentar gallinas; de donde podría inferir alguno que no se trujeron de España, sino que las debía de haber en esta tierra. Pero creer esto sería manifiesto engaño; porque, aunque muchas veces hace
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI

On Chickens

In some of the histories of the Indies that have come to light, I have read how in certain lands, among the various provisions [bastimentos] that the Indians offered to the Spaniards, they would come out to present chickens; from which one might infer that these birds were not brought from Spain, but must have already existed in this land. But to believe this would be manifest error; for although the histories of the Indies frequently mention gallinas [chickens], one should not understand them to be speaking of our own kind, but rather of native birds of the land. CHAPTER III

On the Convent of Our Lady of the Rosary of the Order of Preachers

Although the fathers of Saint Dominic were not the first to have a house in this city, they were nonetheless the first friars of their order to enter it. The one who remained steadfast with the conquistadors was Father Friar Vicente de Valverde, who was present with the Marquis Don Francisco Pizarro through all the trials that occurred during the conquest of this kingdom. When the city of Cuzco had been settled, the said friar went to Spain, and upon returning he came back as bishop of that city, bringing with him friars of his order, who entered this city in the year fifteen hundred and thirty-eight. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVI
On Gold

Gold has always held primacy among all metals, whose resplendent appearance so greatly gladdens men and draws them to it that scarcely any nation in the world has been found so rustic and barbarous as not to know it, seek it, and esteem it. It grows [is found] abundantly throughout all these Indies, whose native peoples worked it and made use of it for various purposes, though not for as many as we do. The caciques [chiefs] and nobles of Peru had many pieces of gold, some of which their descendants still possess today, while most have come into the hands of Spaniards. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLI
On Mercury [azogue]

The mercury mines of this kingdom of Peru are considered of equal importance to those of silver, because the silver mines could not be worked without mercury, and even if some were worked, the great quantity of silver now extracted could not be obtained. Only in the town of Huancavelica, in the diocese of Guamanga [Huamanga / Ayacucho], are there very abundant mines of this metal; and being so rich, they have been worked alone for many years and have yielded infinite wealth. On Salt

CAPITULO XXXIX
Del beneficio con azogue

El beneficio de azogue es de mucha más riqueza que el de fundición, porque es más copioso y general y se saca con él todo la plata de los metales, por bajos y pobres que sean. Cuando el metal acude de dos onzas para arriba por quintal, se puede beneficiar con ganancia, y de aquí para abajo, es con muy poca o ninguna, particularmente en los asientos de minas
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIX
On the Mercury Amalgamation Process

The mercury amalgamation process [beneficio de azogue] is far more productive than smelting [fundición], because it is more abundant in yield and more universally applicable, and by means of it all the silver is extracted from the ores, however low-grade and poor they may be. When the ore yields two ounces or more per hundredweight [quintal], it can be processed profitably; below this threshold, profit is very little or none at all, particularly in mining settlements that do not have Indians assigned by royal warrant and allotment [cédula y repartimiento], or by the mita, as it is called in Peru.

corpus_links.translation: From De Materia Medica, Book V. On Quicksilver (Greek: ὑδράργυρος; Latin: Mercurius). Quicksilver is produced by pounding cinnabar [native mercuric sulfide] in iron mortars with vinegar. In its elemental qualities it is very cold and moist, and is deadly to living creatures, killing by its sheer weight when swallowed. It dissolves gold and silver, and for this reason it is stored in vessels of lead, glass, or silver. It is applied in ointments [as a topical treatment] against lice and against mange in animals. Those who work with it develop trembling of the hands. Preparation: topical application only. Conditions treated: lice [pediculosis], mange [in animals]. It dissolves gold and silver, and for this reason it is stored in vessels of lead, glass, or silver. It is applied in ointments [as a topical treatment] against lice and against mange in animals. Those who work with it develop trembling of the hands. Preparation: topical application only. Conditions treated: lice [pediculosis], mange [in animals]. CHAPTER XLI
On Mercury [azogue]

The mercury mines of this kingdom of Peru are considered of equal importance to those of silver, because the silver mines could not be worked without mercury, and even if some were worked, the great quantity of silver now extracted could not be obtained. In some parts of the Indies, mercury ores [metales de azogue] have been found, but none rich enough to be profitably processed. Only in the town of Huancavelica, in the diocese of Guamanga [Huamanga / Ayacucho], are there very abundant mines of this metal; and being so rich, they have been worked alone for many years and have yielded infinite wealth. De los volcanes que hay en el Perú y los grandes daños que suelen causar

CHAPTER XVIII

On the Volcanoes of Peru and the Great Destruction They Are Wont to Cause

The two richest and most important parts of Peru — namely the Lowlands [Llanos] and the Highlands [Sierra] — are subject to two plagues and calamities most burdensome, which are wont to bring notable harm to their inhabitants. Both arise from a single source: the fire-mouths or volcanoes found along the main cordillera [mountain range], which cause very frequent earthquakes, and whenever they erupt, hurling from their depths immense quantities of fire, ash, and pumice stone, they commonly lay waste and destroy the lands in their surroundings and even those far removed and distant. CHAPTER XXVII
On the Quenti

The quenti is the smallest of the birds found in these Indies, for it is so tiny that if one holds it in the hand and closes the fist around it, it makes no more bulk than an acorn of the oak [bellota de encina]; and plucked, it ends up scarcely larger than a horsefly [moscardón], since when plucked its head is no bigger than a chickpea [garbanzo]. De la piedra de yeso

De piedra de yeso se hallan menos canteras que de cal, particularmente en tierras calientes; en las tierras frías hay grandes cerros della, y alguna muy fina, de espejuelo, como es en el distrito de Guamanga y del Cuzco. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVII
On gypsum stone

Quarries of gypsum stone [piedra de yeso] are less common than those of lime, particularly in hot lands; in cold lands there are great hills of it, and some of very fine quality, of the selenite [espejuelo] variety, as is the case in the districts of Guamanga and Cuzco. In the coastal valleys some is found as well, particularly in those abounding in vineyards, such as the valley of Vítor, in the diocese of Arequipa, and that of Pisco, in this archbishopric of Lima: it would seem that God provided, so long in advance, for the need these valleys would have for gypsum in the treatment [beneficio] of the great quantity of wine that is presently harvested in them.

On Lead

Lead keeps such close company with silver that these two metals are commonly found mixed together, and for this reason we may say in truth that wherever there are silver mines, there are also lead mines. CAPITULO XI
De la suana

La suana es una mata de dos codos de alto, que echa muchos pimpollos o ramas muy derechas; la hoja es como la del As[phodelus], salvo que es dos tantos más ancha. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI
On the Suana

The suana is a shrub [mata] two cubits tall, which puts forth many shoots or very straight branches. The leaf resembles that of the asphodel, except that it is twice as wide. It produces a white flower in the shape of a little bell [campanilla], like a lily [azucena], and many thin roots whose bark [cortezas] dyes [things] the color of saffron. For this reason it is used and sold throughout Peru, and used in place of saffron in stews [guisados], although it is not known to produce any effect beyond imparting color. De los tambos y chasquis, y el tributo que en servirlos daban los indios

Los dos caminos reales de Sierra y Llanos que habemos dicho pasaban por las poblaciones mayores del reino, que eran cabezas de provincias, como Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas y otros lugares de la Sierra, y de los Llanos Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha y otros pueblos grandes, estacionados dichos pueblos por el c
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXII

On the tambos [way-stations] and chasquis [relay runners], and the tribute that the Indians rendered in serving them

The two royal roads of the Sierra [highlands] and the Llanos [coastal plains] that we have described passed through the largest settlements of the kingdom, which were the principal towns of the provinces — such as Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas, and other places in the Sierra, and on the Llanos: Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha, and other large towns. These towns were spaced along the highland road at intervals of twenty to thirty leagues from one another, more or less depending on the stretch, and along the coastal road there was one in each of the principal valleys. Del pica

Este es un árbol mediano, del grandor de un olivo; su hoja, redonda, y tan grande como la palma de la mano; echa una frutilla silvestre no comestible, colorada y redonda, del tamaño de pequeñas manzanas. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIII
On the Pica

This is a medium-sized tree, as large as an olive tree; its leaf is round and as large as the palm of the hand; it bears a small wild fruit that is not edible, red and round, the size of small apples. From this tree there distils a gum or resin of a golden colour and very lustrous, resembling incense in smell and colour, although its scent tends somewhat toward that of mastic [almáciga]. It is burned in place of incense in the provinces of the Collao, in Peru. The pica grows in the provinces of the Andes, and there is a great abundance of these trees throughout the Andean zone encompassing the provinces of Caraguaya and Larecaja—the first belonging to the diocese of Cuzco, the second to that of Chuquiabo [La Paz]. CAPITULO VI
Del chian

Es el chian natural de la Nueva España; la mata es muy parecida a la de la quínua y sus hojas se comen guisadas. Echa una espiga semejante a la de quínua, y en ella, la semilla, que es muy parecida en la hechura al ajonjolí, salvo que es menor y de color negro. Los indios de la Nueva España echan esta semilla molida en el atole o mazamorra, y le da buen sabor.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VI
On Chian

Chian is native to New Spain; the plant is very similar to that of quinoa, and its leaves are eaten cooked. It produces a spike resembling that of quinoa, and in it the seed, which is very similar in shape to sesame [ajonjolí], except that it is smaller and black in color. The Indians of New Spain add this seed, ground, to their atole or mazamorra [thin porridge or gruel], and it gives it a good flavor.

CAPITULO VIII
De la batata

La batata es raíz muy conocida no sólo en todas las Indias, sino también en España, y una de las más regaladas comidas que los indios tenían. La planta es pequeña, y sus ramas se extienden sobre el suelo sin levantarse mucho; produce cada mata muchos vástagos o tallos, los cuales son redondos, lisos y morados, y crecen como dos tercias tendidos sobre la tierra. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VIII
On the Batata

The batata [sweet potato] is a root well known not only throughout all the Indies, but also in Spain, and it was one of the most esteemed foods the Indians had. In the other things they use as much as in their own persons — which they ordinarily keep so filthy as to inspire disgust — and since they almost never change or wash their clothing, they give off a foul odor; yet they are not offended by this or by any other smell, nor do they prize good odor and fragrance, for they feel neither pleasure in the one nor discomfort in the other, being a people altogether unclean. They ordinarily eat little, which they do more out of wretchedness and poverty than from abstinence; for when the occasion presents itself they gorge themselves like wolves — as usually happens when they eat at the Spaniards' expense.

CAPITULO XLVI
Del hicaco

Este es un árbol que nace en las costas de la mar, tan pequeño, que no sube más que uno o dos estados de la tierra; de buen parecer; cuya hoja es semejante a la del madroño. La fruta que lleva es como un albaricoque, más agradable a la vista que al gusto, porque tiene color de manzana arrebolada; la cáscara es como de manzana y la carne blanca y esponjosa nada apetitosa,
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI
On the Hicaco

This is a tree that grows along the seacoasts, so small that it rises no more than one or two fathoms [estados] from the ground; it is of pleasing appearance, and its leaf resembles that of the strawberry tree [madroño, Arbutus unedo]. The fruit it bears is like an apricot [albaricoque], more pleasing to the eye than to the taste, for it has the color of a flushed apple; the skin is like that of an apple, and the flesh is white and spongy, not at all appetizing, for it is a wild and coarse fruit; it has a very large stone [pit] in proportion to its size.

corpus_links.translation:
The fruit [papaya] varies greatly according to the quality of the soil where it grows. The most common variety is the size of a large citron [cidra] or a medium melon; it has a spindle-like shape and is divided into five or seven segments, with as many lengthwise grooves, in the manner of a melon. The rind is yellow, thin, and tender, like that of a citron. The flesh is likewise yellow tending toward red, tender like melon, though not as watery. It is about two fingers thick, and the inner cavity is filled with small black, round, and soft seeds no larger than coriander [culantro], which are also eaten and have a flavor of cress [mastuerzo]. The papaya is a wild fruit, not very appetizing nor highly esteemed.

CAPITULO XXIV
De la copaquira

Copaquiri llaman los indios del Perú, en la lengua aimará, al cardenillo, y por la semejanza que con él tiene la piedra que aquí describo, le dan el mismo nombre, y los españoles, corrompiendo el vocablo, la llaman copaquira y piedra de los Lipes, por hallarse solamente en la provincia de los Lipes, que es del arzobispo de los Charcas. Es la copaquira una piedra azul
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIV
On Copaquira

The Indians of Peru, in the Aymara language, call verdigris [cardenillo] 'copaquiri,' and because of the resemblance that the stone I describe here bears to it, they give it the same name. The Spaniards, corrupting the word, call it copaquira and 'stone of the Lipes' [piedra de los Lipes], because it is found only in the province of the Lipes, which falls under the archbishopric of Charcas. Copaquira is a blue-green and transparent stone, which is extracted from a deposit found in the said province of the Lipes, whose veins are no thicker than a finger, although there are sometimes found pockets filled with medium-sized pieces weighing four or more pounds. Alum [piedra alumbre] is found in the same deposit, and the Indians who extract the copaquira affirm that, u

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XIII

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XIII
De las papas

En toda la Sierra y tierra fría del Perú donde no se coge maíz ni las demás semillas y legumbres que se dan en tierras templadas y calientes, son las sementeras ordinarias que hacen los indios de unas raíces llamadas papas, del tamaño y hechura de criadillas de tierra; las cuales, verdes y secas, son mantenimiento tan general en el Perú, que la mitad de los indios dél n
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIII
On Potatoes

Throughout the highland and cold lands of Peru, where neither maize nor the other seeds and legumes that grow in temperate and warm regions are harvested, the ordinary crops that the Indians cultivate are certain roots called papas [potatoes], of the size and shape of truffles [criadillas de tierra]. Both fresh and dried, these are so universally consumed in Peru that half the Indians there have nothing else to eat. The plant grows to a height of two hand-spans [palmos]; its leaves are so continuous and closely set along the stem that they appear to be a single leaf with many points, which points somewhat resemble the leaves of lemon balm [toronjil]. It produces a bell-shaped flower, slightly larger than a gillyflower [alhelí], with five or six small points; some

CAPITULO LI

De la caralahua

Esta es una mata delgada y pequeña; echa una vara tan alta como una pica, derecha y lisa, con algunos ramillos que nacen desde la mitad para arriba.

La hoja es del tamaño y talle de la del durazno, la cual y la corteza del árbol son de un verde muy blanquecino. Echa unas florecillas amarillas de la hechura y grandor de las del tabaco. Nace esta mata en las orillas de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LI

On the caralahua

This is a slender and small shrub; it sends up a stem as tall as a pike [i.e., roughly 12–18 feet], straight and smooth, with some small branches that grow from the middle upward.

The leaf is the size and shape of that of the peach tree, and both the leaf and the bark of the plant are of a very whitish green. It produces small yellow flowers similar in form and size to those of tobacco. This shrub grows on the banks of rivers in temperate lands [tierra templada]; its trunk and branches are of a spongy substance and of cold complexion [complexión fría, in the Galenic humoral sense]. CAPITULO XIV
De las ocas

Son las ocas unas raíces comestibles que se dan en las tierras frías donde las papas. La planta desta raíz se llama xibico; es del linaje de acederas, pequeña, de una tercia poco más o menos de alto; tiene las ramas recogidas, que la hacen copada; las hojas son muy pequeñas, de tres en tres, como las de las acederas. Las raíces desta planta son largüillas medio jeme, no l
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIV
On the Ocas

The ocas are edible roots that grow in the cold lands where the potatoes grow. The plant of this root is called xibico; it is of the sorrel family [linaje de acederas], small, about one third of a vara [roughly 11 inches] in height, more or less; its branches are gathered close together, giving it a bushy appearance; the leaves are very small, arranged in threes, like those of the sorrel. The roots of this plant are somewhat elongated, about half a jeme [roughly 3–4 inches] in length, not smooth but uneven and knotted; some are white, others purple, and of other colors, like the potatoes; they are very tender and floury. The Indians eat them green, roasted, and boiled; they also split them lengthwise and dry them in the sun for storage. Dried in this manner they ar

CAPITULO XVIII
De la isaña

La isaña es una raíz, que los indios comen, del tamaño y forma de la oca; unas, son amarillas exterior e interiormente, y otras, coloradas. La mata es muy parecida a la de los frísoles; cuando topa otras plantas donde asirse, trepa y se encarama sobre ellas; el vástago es redondo, verde y liso; la hoja es tan grande como la palma de la mano hendida en cinco puntas botas
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVIII
On the Isaña

The isaña is a root that the Indians eat, of the size and shape of the oca [Oxalis tuberosa]; some are yellow both on the outside and inside, and others are red. The plant is very similar to that of the bean [fríjol]; when it encounters other plants to cling to, it climbs and clambers over them. The stem is round, green, and smooth; the leaf is as large as the palm of the hand and is divided into five blunt points [lobes]; its petiole [pezón] is slender, round, and about one third of a vara in length. The flower is somewhat elongated, about half a finger long, in the shape of a small bell [campanilla]; it terminates in five small petals arranged around it, three of which are yellow and the other two, along with the rest of the flower, are red. When the isaña — w

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XIX

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XIX
De la ulluma

La ulluma es cierta raíz muy parecida a la oca; hállanse de tan diferentes colores como las ocas; son de temperamento frío y algo ventoso y muy mucilaginoso; bebiendo una buena porción del cocimiento destas raíces, junto con la muña, facilita el parto, y el mismo efecto dicen los indios que hacen ellas comidas solas en buena cantidad. Ultra desto, hecho lamedor del cocim
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIX
On the ulluma

The ulluma is a certain root very similar to the oca [Oxalis tuberosa]; roots of it are found in as many different colors as the oca. They are of a cold and somewhat flatulent [ventoso] temperament and highly mucilaginous [mucilaginoso]. Drinking a good portion of the decoction of these roots together with muña facilitates childbirth, and the Indians say that eating them alone in a sufficient quantity produces the same effect. Beyond this, a lincture [lamedor] made from the decoction of these roots with the requisite amount of sugar, and given frequently to those with penetrating wounds [heridos penetrantes], causes them to expectorate with ease the blood extravasated [extravenada] in the chest. CAPITULO XXXV
De la coaca

Usan los indios por mantenimiento muchos géneros de yerbas que, con nombre general, las llaman los del Perú, yayos, y los mexicanos, quilites, como si dijésemos hortaliza o verdura; de algunas queda ya hecha mención en los capítulos pasados; en lo que resta deste libro se irán tocando otras, de las cuales es una la coaca. Esta es una yerba parecida a la cerraja; crece do
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXV
On the Coaca

The Indians make use of many kinds of herbs for sustenance, which, by a general name, the people of Peru call yayos [yuyos], and the Mexicans call quilites — as if we were to say garden greens or vegetables. Some of these have already been mentioned in the preceding chapters; in what remains of this book, others will be touched upon, of which the coaca is one. This is a herb resembling the sow-thistle [cerraja]; it grows about two cubits in height, more or less. The stalk is as thick as the little finger, round, green, hairy, and sticky. Each plant produces many stalks, and at their tops a great quantity of flowers the size and form of those of chamomile, except that the small petals encircling the bud are yellow. These flowers are fragrant and pleasant in appear

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXXXVII
corpus_links.title: The Cacahuara Plant: Description and Use in Setting Fractures
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXVII
De la cacahuara

Esta es una yerba que produce desde el suelo sus hojas, que son poco más angostas que un dedo y largas dos palmos, por la haz lisas y verdes, y por el envés, blanquecinas y vellosas. Echa un tallo de un codo de alto, tan grueso como un dedo, cubierto de un vello blanco, con muchas flores amarillas en el remate, del tamaño y talle de las de la cerraja. Es yerba cal
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXVII
On the Cacahuara

This is an herb that produces its leaves from the ground; they are a little narrower than a finger and two spans [palmos] long, smooth and green on the upper face [haz], and whitish and hairy on the underside [envés]. It sends up a stalk one cubit [codo] high, as thick as a finger, covered in white down, with many yellow flowers at the tip, of the size and form of those of the sowthistle [cerraja]. It is a hot herb [yerba caliente] and very useful for knitting [soldar] any fractures [quebraduras]. In the Aymara language it is called racahuara.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXVIII
De la patacauri

La patacauri es una yerbecita pequeña que nace agarrada con el suelo; sus hojas parecen a las de las malvas cuando pequeñas; están hendidas en puntas botas y desiguales. El pecíolo de la hoja es largo un jeme, redondo, delgado, rojo y con un vellito blanco muy sutil. Echa esta yerba unas florecitas blancas de cinco hojas en ruedo, parecidas en el tamaño y talle a
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVIII
On the Patacauri

The patacauri is a small herb that grows close to the ground; its leaves resemble those of mallow [malvas] when young; they are divided into blunt and uneven points. The leaf stalk [pecíolo] is a handspan [jeme] in length, round, slender, red, and covered with a very fine white down. This herb bears small white flowers of five petals arranged in a whorl [en ruedo], similar in size and form to those of elderflower [saúco]. The Indians eat this herb among their greens [yuyos], and call it by this name in the Aymara language.

De la qixeaquea

La qixeaquea se llama así en la lengua aimará. Es una yerba pequeña; echa los ramillos largos un palmo, delgados, verdes y vellosos; sus hojas son como las del poleo, más puntiagudas, las cuales y los ramillos son pegajosos; produce unas florecicas blancas del tamaño y forma que las de la patacauri.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LV
On the qixeaquea

The qixeaquea is so called in the Aymara language. It is a small herb; it puts forth slender branches about a hand's span [palmo] in length, thin, green, and hairy; its leaves resemble those of pennyroyal [poleo], though more pointed, and both the leaves and the branches are sticky; it produces small white flowers of the same size and form as those of the patacauri.

CAPITULO XLV

De la hisachalahua

La hisachalahua es una mata que se levanta un codo en alto; echa muchas ramas delgadas y ñudosas; su hoja es pequeña como la del poleo, algún tanto más larga y puntiaguda, tan gruesa como la de la verdolaga, aunque no tan tierna y lisa. Así las hojas como los cogollos desta planta están cubiertos de un vello muy cortico, delgado y blanco, con que sus ramas tienen
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLV

On the Hisachalahua

The hisachalahua is a shrub that rises about one cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height; it puts forth many slender and knotty branches; its leaf is small like that of pennyroyal [poleo], somewhat longer and more pointed, as thick as that of purslane [verdolaga], though not as tender and smooth. Both the leaves and the young shoots [cogollos] of this plant are covered with a very short, fine, and white down, which gives its branches a whitish color, as though dusted with ash. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LIX

De la choclla

Dos especies se hallan en estas Indias de cierta yerba que los españoles llaman cebadilla, por la semejanza que tienen con la cebada: la una es natural de la Nueva España, y la otra, deste reino del Perú. La primera echa una espiga parecida a la del trigo, larga un palmo y más; su caña es asimismo como la del trigo, algo más gruesa, parda y maciza, de un estado de alto
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LIX

On the Choclla

Two species are found in these Indies of a certain herb that the Spaniards call cebadilla [little barley], on account of its resemblance to barley. One is native to New Spain and the other to this kingdom of Peru. The first puts forth a spike resembling that of wheat, a handspan or more in length; its stalk is likewise similar to that of wheat, somewhat thicker, brownish, and solid, about a man's height tall; it grows wild in the savannas without being sown. The grains are black, somewhat smaller than those of barley, and when ground they kill the worms [maggots] in the sores [saddle-galls] of beasts of burden, and likewise the chigoe fleas [niguas] that burrow into persons.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_XCVIII
corpus_links.title: On the Talquina plant: properties and medicinal uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCVIII
De la talquina

La talquina se levanta un codo de la tierra; tiene las hojas algo blanquecinas y mucilaginosas; echa flores amarillas y unas vainillas con la semilla, que es como garbancillos. Es caliente y húmeda esta yerba, y majada y aplicada en emplasto en las apostemas abiertas y heridas dolorosas, mitiga el dolor y dispone la parte a que críe buenas materias; y aplicada con m
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCVIII
On the Talquina

The talquina rises one cubit [approximately 18 inches] from the ground; its leaves are somewhat whitish and mucilaginous; it bears yellow flowers and small pods containing seeds that resemble small chickpeas. This herb is hot and moist in temperament [humoural classification], and when pounded and applied as a poultice [emplasto] to open abscesses [apostemas] and painful wounds, it relieves pain and prepares the affected part to generate healthy matter [buenas materias]. Applied with rose honey [miel rosada] to ulcers, it cleanses [mundifica] and promotes the growth of new flesh [encarna]. Pounded together with marshmallow and applied as a poultice, it resolves all swelling [tumor].

De la guaki

Llaman guahi los indios peruanos a una raíz muy conocida y estimada dellos; es muy amarga y de profundo olor no enfadoso; su temperamento es caliente y seco. Es tan parecida esta yerba a la que Dioscórides llama aristoquia luenga, que no parece distinguirse della. Usan los indios de su raíz para muchas enfermedades; con ella, mascada, se refriegan cualquiera parte del cu
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXII
On the Guaki

The Peruvian Indians call by the name guahi a root that is very well known and esteemed among them. It is very bitter and has a deep but not unpleasant smell; its temperament [complexion] is hot and dry. This herb so closely resembles what Dioscorides calls aristolochia longa [long birthwort] that it seems indistinguishable from it. The Indians use its root for many ailments; when chewed, they rub it on any painful part of the body. Its decoction [cocimiento] dispels all flatulence [ventosidad], cleanses the bowels, and warms cold parts of the body; drunk regularly, it cures jaundice [ictericia]. De la quina-quina

Llaman en el Perú a un árbol grande y hermoso como un melo o olivo; la hoja, del tamaño y talle que la del limón ceutí; el tronco es algo colorado, resinoso y aromático. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXI
On the Quina-Quina

In Peru they give this name to a large and handsome tree resembling a quince or olive; the leaf is the size and shape of that of the Ceuti lemon [a variety of citron]; the trunk is somewhat reddish, resinous, and aromatic. The tree is hot in the second degree [of the Galenic humoral scale], astringent [estíptico], dry, and of a pleasant odor. It produces seeds the size of almonds, yellow in color and of an oily substance, which smell agreeably with a fine fragrance; these too are hot and astringent in the second degree, and dry in more than the first. CAPITULO LXV
De la pupusa

Esta es una yerba pequeña de tallos lisos algo colorados, cuyas hojas, que algunos tallos suelen tener, son como agraz que sale de la cierne, algo prolongadas, a manera de arroz; acaba el tallo en una roseta de muchas hojillas agregadas, las cuales, llegando a maduración, paran en una flocadura que salta y se pega fácilmente a la ropa. Tiene un profundo olor que a veces
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXV
On the Pupusa

This is a small herb with smooth, somewhat reddish stems, whose leaves—which some stems tend to bear—resemble unripe grape clusters emerging from the blossom, somewhat elongated, in the manner of rice. The stem ends in a rosette of many small clustered leaflets, which, upon reaching maturity, turn into a flocculent [feathery, burr-like] mass that leaps off and clings easily to clothing. It has a penetrating odor that is at times disagreeable, and more so when the herb is greener. Its [humoral] temperament is hot in the third degree and dry in the second. It is a powerful caustic [agent] for wounds [llagas], and when applied over any pain arising from a cold cause, it relieves it and disperses any swelling.

CAPITULO IX
De los demás cardones

De las muchas diferencias de cardones que yo he visto, no deben de quedar más que tres o cuatro, mas no dudo sino que habrá otros de que yo no tenga noticias. Uno de los más pequeños es el que se dice pullapulla, el cual no se levanta de la tierra más que, cuando mucho, un jeme. Hácese una mata redonda algo ahusada, que no parece sino un montoncillo de peras o de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX
On the Other Cardones [cacti]

Of the many varieties of cardones [columnar or globose cacti] that I have seen, there remain no more than three or four to describe, though I do not doubt that there are others of which I have no knowledge. One of the smallest is the one called pullapulla, which rises from the ground no more than, at most, one span [jeme: the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the index finger, roughly 7–8 cm]. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XI
De la racacha

En la lengua quichua deste reino se llama racacha una planta cuya raíz es comestible y muy parecida a la achira; la mata es de tres palmos de alto, muy copada y poblada de hojas, las cuales son de un verde oscuro y todas inmediatamente de la raíz. El pezón dellas o tallo es de un codo de largo, tan grueso como un mediano junco, liso y con unas pequeñas rayas o venas colo
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI
Of the Racacha

In the Quechua language of this kingdom, the name racacha is given to a plant whose root is edible and very similar to the achira [Canna edulis]. The bush stands three hand-spans [palmos] tall, very full-crowned and densely leafed, the leaves being dark green and all springing directly from the root. Their petiole or stalk is one cubit [codo] in length, as thick as a medium-sized rush [junco], smooth, and marked along its length with small reddish streaks or veins; it is entirely hollow like a tube, and at its tip grow three leaves, each with three or four deeply cut points longer than those of nettles. The plant sends up a flowering stalk four cubits tall, as thick as a finger of the hand, round, smooth, tough [correoso], and dark green shading toward purple, at

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXVII
corpus_links.title: The herb perebecenu
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXVII

De la yerba perebecenu

Llaman así en la lengua de la isla Española a una yerba medicinal. Es tan alta como un hombre, sus tallos son morados o rojos, y las hojas, con las puntas del mismo color, siendo verdes en lo restante; son puntiagudas, de hechura de hierro de lanza. Echa unas flores coloradas, luengas y a manojos como el hinojo y el flueco, pero apartadas unas de otras. El c
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXVII

On the herb perebecenu

This is the name given in the language of the island of Hispaniola to a medicinal herb. It stands as tall as a man; its stems are purple or red, and the leaves are tipped with the same color while remaining green over the rest of their surface. They are pointed, shaped like the head of a lance. It produces red flowers, elongated and borne in small clusters [manojos] like those of fennel and tassel-like plants, but set apart from one another. A decoction [cocimiento] of the young shoots [cogollos] of this herb is good for healing wounds [llagas].

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::CUARTO::cap_LXXXIV
corpus_links.title: On the Herb of Santa María
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXIV
De la yerba de Santa María

Nace esta yerba en la costa de la mar del Sur de la Nueva España y allí le dan este nombre; crece un estado en alto; su hoja es de forma de corazón y mayor que la palma de la mano; echa unos botoncillos largos y delgados, muy semejantes a los canelones de disciplina. Tiene su hoja olor y sabor de hinojo, y puesta en la cabeza, es buena para el dolor dell
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIV
On the Herb of Santa María

This herb grows on the coast of the South Sea [Pacific coast] of New Spain, where it is given this name. It grows to the height of one estado [approximately one fathom, or the height of a man]; its leaf is heart-shaped and larger than the palm of the hand. It puts forth long, slender little buds very similar to the lashes [tails] of a discipline whip [flagellant's scourge]. Its leaf has the smell and taste of fennel, and when placed on the head it is good for headache caused by the sun.

corpus_links.title: Herbs Brought from Spain: Fennel, Aloe, Dill, Viznaga, Rue, Poppies, Sage, Tarragon, and Teasel
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLII

De todas las demás hierbas que se han traído de España hasta ahora

En este capítulo se comprenden todas las hierbas y plantas que restan de las traídas de España; las cuales sirven más al uso de la medicina que para otros menesteres, como son el hinojo, la zabila, eneldo, viznaga, ruda, adormideras, salvia y taragontia; las cuales todas nacen copiosamente en este reino del Perú, ad
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII

On all the other herbs that have been brought from Spain up to the present

This chapter covers all the remaining herbs and plants that have been brought from Spain, which serve more for medicinal use than for other purposes, such as fennel [hinojo], aloe [zabila], dill [eneldo], viznaga [toothpick-weed], rue [ruda], poppies [adormideras], sage [salvia], and tarragon [taragontia]. All of these grow in great abundance in this kingdom of Peru, where, owing to the fertility of the soil, some have gone wild, now sprouting without being sown in uncultivated places. corpus_links.translation:
However, it should be noted that within these same coastal valleys [valles de los Llanos] there is some difference in the time at which fruits begin to ripen, which consists in the fact that the farther a valley is removed from the seacoast, the less humid its climate becomes and, consequently, the earlier its fruits ripen. Thus we observe that in Sisicaya, which lies nine leagues from this city [Lima] toward the Sierra, both native and Castilian fruits begin to ripen one to two months earlier than in this city.

CAPITULO LXVIII
De la camina

La camina es una yerba de un codo en alto, cuyas hojas son muy parecidas a las del apio. Echa unas flores como las del eneldo; huele esta planta con fragancia como la del apio. Su temperamento es caliente y seco. Mascada esta yerba, tiene partes sutiles, pica la lengua y la deja áspera por un buen rato. Tiene virtud de resolver, y su zumo mundifica las llagas. Su coci
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXVIII
On the camina

The camina is an herb about one cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height, whose leaves closely resemble those of celery [apio]. It produces flowers like those of dill [eneldo]; the plant smells fragrant, much like celery. Its temperament [complexion, in Galenic humoral terms] is hot and dry. When this herb is chewed, it has subtle [penetrating] properties, stings the tongue, and leaves it rough for a good while. It has the virtue of resolving [dispersing humors], and its juice cleanses [mundifies] wounds. De todas las demás hierbas que se han traído de España hasta ahora

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII

On all the other herbs that have been brought from Spain up to the present

This chapter covers all the remaining herbs and plants that have been brought from Spain, which serve more for medicinal use than for other purposes, such as fennel [hinojo], aloe [zabila], dill [eneldo], viznaga [toothpick-weed], rue [ruda], poppies [adormideras], sage [salvia], and tarragon [taragontia]. All of these grow in great abundance in this kingdom of Peru, where, owing to the fertility of the soil, some have gone wild, now sprouting without being sown in uncultivated places. corpus_links.title: On the Anchariipa herb: urological and dermatological uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXII
De la anchariipa

Esta es una yerba pequeña que produce unas varillas muy lisas y derechas; su temperamento es caliente y seco; aprovéchanse los indios destes varillas, metiéndolas por la vía de la orina cuando se sienten con alguna carnosidad, porque sin dolor la extirpan y gastan. El cocimiento desta yerba usado a menudo en las llagas muy maliciosas, las corrige, mundifica, deseca
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXII
On the anchariipa

This is a small herb that produces very smooth and straight little stalks [varillas]. Its temperament is hot and dry. The Indians make use of these stalks by inserting them through the urinary passage [vía de la orina] when they feel some fleshy growth [carnosidad] there, for they thereby extirpate and dissolve it without pain. A decoction [cocimiento] of this herb, used frequently on very malignant sores [llagas muy maliciosas], corrects, cleanses [mundifica], dries, and promotes the growth of new flesh [encarna]. And the herb pounded together with purslane [verdolagas], a little vinegar, and orpiment [oropimente], extirpates all warts [verrugas] and the films or membranes of scrofulous swellings [lamparones] or cysts [lobanillos].

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LII
On the Pupa

The pupa, also known by another name as hamillo, is a shrub about one estado [roughly one fathom, approximately six feet] in height; it has green branches and leaves like those of purslane [verdolagas], only somewhat narrower and more elongated; both leaf and shoot are very tender. It produces a small, slender reddish flower shaped like that of the cantuta [cantuta flower], and tiny berries exactly like those of nightshade [yerba-mora], except that it does not bear them in clusters but each one separately, attached to the small branches. From this plant the Indians extract birdlime for catching birds, and it is as good as that of Spain. CAPITULO XLII
De la parca

En este reino del Perú llaman parca a un árbol no muy grande, cuyas ramas y raíces son de color amarillo debajo de corteza parda que tira a blanca. Su cocimiento sirve para enrubiar los cabellos. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII
Of the Parca

In this kingdom of Peru they call 'parca' a tree of no great size, whose branches and roots are yellow in color beneath a bark that is brownish tending toward white. A decoction [cocimiento] of it serves to lighten [enrubiar, lit. 'to make reddish-blond'] the hair. It produces sizeable pods, and within them a certain fruit resembling broad beans [habas], which the Indians eat roasted and which is somewhat tasty. Its temperament [in the Galenic humoral sense] is hot and dry. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXVIII
Del haratuc

Esta es una yerba áspera, algo olorosa y aparrada en la tierra; echa unas flores blancas que, secas, parecen flocaduras y saltan en tocándolas; es de virtud caliente y húmeda, y yerba pectoral. Usan della los indios para muchas enfermedades, en particular en los dolores de costado, dando en ayunas y de parte de noche una buena porción de su cocimiento con miel de abej
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVIII
On the haratuc

This is a rough herb [yerba], somewhat fragrant and spreading low upon the ground; it bears white flowers which, when dry, resemble tassels [flocaduras] and spring apart when touched. It is of hot and moist virtue [virtud caliente y húmeda] and is a pectoral herb [yerba pectoral]. The Indians use it for many ailments, particularly for pains in the side [dolores de costado], administering a generous portion of its decoction [cocimiento] with honey on an empty stomach and at night, while also applying the herb itself, warmed and sprinkled with wine, directly over the area of pain. Its decoction is likewise effective against stomach pains, against all manner of obstruction [opilación], and against retention of urine.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXI
De la hopahopa.

Llaman hopahopa los indios a ciertas lentejuelas que se dan encima del agua encharcada y en los totorales o juncales; son algo coloradas y de complexión templada, con muy poca estipticidad; majada esta yerba y puesta en la muela que duele, quita el dolor; y asimismo, puesta sobre las quebraduras o fracturas de huesos con un poco de sal y polvos de muña, las restaura
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXI
On the hopahopa.

The Indians call hopahopa certain small lentil-like [plants] that grow on the surface of stagnant water and in reed beds or rush beds [totorales o juncales]. They are somewhat reddish and of a temperate complexion [temperament], with very little astringency [estipticidad]. This herb, ground [majada] and applied to the aching molar, relieves the pain; and likewise, applied over fractures or broken bones together with a little salt and powdered muña, it restores them. Its decoction taken with wine and alum [alumbre], drunk frequently, heals mouth sores [llagas de la boca] and firms the teeth.

CAPITULO LXXXV
De la congona

La congona es una yerba muy parecida a la siempreviva; crece media vara en alto, poco más o menos; hace sus ramas tan gruesas como un junco mediano, son verdes, tiernas y pobladas de hojas, que es lo que en esta planta se estima; es esta hoja semejante a la de la verdolaga, un poco mayor y dos veces más gruesa que ella, verde, lisa, tierna y muy aguanosa. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXV
On the Congona

The congona is an herb very similar to the houseleek [siempreviva]; it grows to about half a vara [approximately 16–17 inches] in height, more or less. Its branches are as thick as a medium-sized rush [junco], and are green, tender, and densely covered with leaves, which are the most prized part of the plant. The leaf resembles that of purslane [verdolaga], being somewhat larger and twice as thick, green, smooth, tender, and very succulent. The qualities for which it is esteemed are its fragrance and the fact that, when chewed, it has a sharp and pungent flavor similar to that of nutmeg or cloves, and it leaves the mouth fragrant for a while, as if one had held some of the aforementioned spices in it. CAPITULO XLV

De la hisachalahua

La hisachalahua es una mata que se levanta un codo en alto; echa muchas ramas delgadas y ñudosas; su hoja es pequeña como la del poleo, algún tanto más larga y puntiaguda, tan gruesa como la de la verdolaga, aunque no tan tierna y lisa. Así las hojas como los cogollos desta planta están cubiertos de un vello muy cortico, delgado y blanco, con que sus ramas tienen
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLV

On the Hisachalahua

The hisachalahua is a shrub that rises about one cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height; it puts forth many slender and knotty branches; its leaf is small like that of pennyroyal [poleo], somewhat longer and more pointed, as thick as that of purslane [verdolaga], though not as tender and smooth. Both the leaves and the young shoots [cogollos] of this plant are covered with a very short, fine, and white down, which gives its branches a whitish color, as though dusted with ash. De la acana

La acana crece un codo de alto; en las ramas y hojas es muy parecida a la alfalfa; tiene flor amarilla del talle de la de la manzanilla; nace entre peñas y es yerba pectoral, más amarga al gusto que la acíbar; es caliente y seca en el segundo grado. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIX

On the Acana

The acana grows to a cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height; in its branches and leaves it closely resembles alfalfa; it bears a yellow flower of the shape of that of camomile; it grows among rocks and is a pectoral herb [i.e., beneficial to the chest and lungs], more bitter to the taste than aloes [acíbar]; it is hot and dry in the second degree [following Galenic humoral classification]. The Indians eat coca with it. A decoction of it with a little alum is good for sores of the mouth; and taken warm on an empty stomach with sugar candy [alfeñique], it is beneficial against cough and asthma, and softens and cleanses the chest and stomach. CAPITULO IX
De los demás cardones

De las muchas diferencias de cardones que yo he visto, no deben de quedar más que tres o cuatro, mas no dudo sino que habrá otros de que yo no tenga noticias. Uno de los más pequeños es el que se dice pullapulla, el cual no se levanta de la tierra más que, cuando mucho, un jeme. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX
On the Other Cardones [cacti]

Of the many varieties of cardones [columnar or globose cacti] that I have seen, there remain no more than three or four to describe, though I do not doubt that there are others of which I have no knowledge. The acana grows to a cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height; in its branches and leaves it closely resembles alfalfa; it bears a yellow flower of the shape of that of camomile; it grows among rocks and is a pectoral herb [i.e., beneficial to the chest and lungs], more bitter to the taste than aloes [acíbar]; it is hot and dry in the second degree [following Galenic humoral classification]. The Indians eat coca with it. A decoction of it with a little alum is good for sores of the mouth; and taken warm on an empty stomach with sugar candy [alfeñique], it is beneficial against cough and asthma, and softens and cleanses the chest and stomach. De la quinta-Laura

La quinta-Laura es una yerba muy parecida a la romaza; tiene las hojas largas de un palmo y anchas como dos dedos, y las raíces tan gruesas como un dedo. El cocimiento destas raíces y hojas, tomado en ayunas, ablanda el vientre del que está estreñido. On the quinta-Laura

The quinta-Laura is an herb very similar to dock [romaza]; its leaves are a hand-span long and two fingers wide, and its roots are as thick as a finger. CAPITULO XLVI
Del hicaco

Este es un árbol que nace en las costas de la mar, tan pequeño, que no sube más que uno o dos estados de la tierra; de buen parecer; cuya hoja es semejante a la del madroño. La fruta que lleva es como un albaricoque, más agradable a la vista que al gusto, porque tiene color de manzana arrebolada; la cáscara es como de manzana y la carne blanca y esponjosa nada apetitosa,
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI
On the Hicaco

This is a tree that grows along the seacoasts, so small that it rises no more than one or two fathoms [estados] from the ground; it is of pleasing appearance, and its leaf resembles that of the strawberry tree [madroño, Arbutus unedo]. The fruit it bears is like an apricot [albaricoque], more pleasing to the eye than to the taste, for it has the color of a flushed apple; the skin is like that of an apple, and the flesh is white and spongy, not at all appetizing, for it is a wild and coarse fruit; it has a very large stone [pit] in proportion to its size.

CAPITULO C

Del chamico

La yerba que los indios llaman chamico crece un codo, poco más o menos; tiene las hojas mayores algo que los dedos, con unas puntas a los lados; echa una flor blanca de hechura de campanilla, pequeña, que se convierte en unas cabezuelas del tamaño de las adormideras, cubiertas de agudas espinas, en cuya cavidad se encierra la semilla, que es como de rábano, la cual dicen q
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER C

On the Chamico

The herb that the Indians call chamico grows to about one cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height, more or less. Its leaves are somewhat larger than one's fingers, with pointed tips along the sides. It produces a small white flower in the shape of a little bell, which turns into small heads the size of poppy capsules, covered with sharp spines, within whose cavity the seed is enclosed; the seed resembles that of the radish, and is said to be as cooling [in humoral temperament] as celery. A decoction of it taken internally dulls the senses. The Indians use it to intoxicate themselves, and if a large quantity is consumed, it deprives a person of their senses in such a way that, though their eyes remain open, they neither see nor recognize anything. CAPITULO XLII

De todas las demás hierbas que se han traído de España hasta ahora

En este capítulo se comprenden todas las hierbas y plantas que restan de las traídas de España; las cuales sirven más al uso de la medicina que para otros menesteres, como son el hinojo, la zabila, eneldo, viznaga, ruda, adormideras, salvia y taragontia; las cuales todas nacen copiosamente en este reino del Perú, ad
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII

On all the other herbs that have been brought from Spain up to the present

This chapter covers all the remaining herbs and plants that have been brought from Spain, which serve more for medicinal use than for other purposes, such as fennel [hinojo], aloe [zabila], dill [eneldo], viznaga [toothpick-weed], rue [ruda], poppies [adormideras], sage [salvia], and tarragon [taragontia]. All of these grow in great abundance in this kingdom of Peru, where, owing to the fertility of the soil, some have gone wild, now sprouting without being sown in uncultivated places. CAPITULO CII

De la yerba de la araña

Han puesto a esta yerba los españoles este nombre, tomado del efecto que hace, que es curar las picaduras de arañas ponzoñosas. Nace en lugares incultos, y en este valle de Lima se halla mucha junto al puerto del Callao; es muy parecida en el tamaño, ramos y hojas al tomillo, sólo que no tiene olor alguno. Aplícase a la picadura de araña desta manera: hácese
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CII

On the spider-herb [yerba de la araña]

The Spaniards gave this herb its name, derived from the effect it produces, which is to cure the bites of venomous spiders. It grows in uncultivated places, and in this valley of Lima it is found in great abundance near the port of Callao. It closely resembles thyme in size, branching, and leaves, except that it has no scent whatsoever. It is applied to a spider bite in the following manner: a decoction [cocimiento] is made from it, with which the affected area is washed very thoroughly, while pressing it so that the matter [venom/pus] is expelled; the powdered form of this same herb is then applied to the wound, and by this means one witnesses remarkable cures on a daily basis.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXI

De la Cunturire

Los indios del Perú llaman cunturire a la raíz nombrada de los españoles contrayerba. Nace esta yerba en las provincias de Tomina y Mizque; echa un ramillo pequeño con cuatro o cinco hojas cada uno, las cuales son tan largas como las del naranjo, pero más angostas y de más escuro verde. Sus raíces son pequeñas, menores que un dedo de la mano, ñudosas y muy semejantes
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXI

On the Cunturire

The Indians of Peru call cunturire the root known among the Spaniards as contrayerba [counterherb / antidote herb]. This plant grows in the provinces of Tomina and Mizque; it puts forth small branches bearing four or five leaves each, which are as long as those of the orange tree, but narrower and of a darker green. Its roots are small, no larger than a finger of the hand, knotted, and very similar to ginger; they are of a hot and dry temperament in the second degree [humoral classification], of aromatic scent, somewhat bitter and mordant [biting to the taste]; they are effective against all poisons, for which reason both the Indians and the Spaniards regard them as the theriac [universal antidote] of Peru. corpus_links.title: The Herb of the Knuckle (Yerba del Ñudillo)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CV
De la yerba del ñudillo

La yerba del ñudillo se llama así porque todo el tallo es muy ñudoso; crece un estado y echa muchos tallos no más gruesos que la caña del trigo. Su hoja es del talle y grandeza de la del alhelí y con ella curan las heridas. Nace esta yerba en lugares húmedos, y tallos, y hojas es muy tierna y pasto del ganado.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CV
On the herb of the knuckle [yerba del ñudillo]

The herb of the knuckle [yerba del ñudillo] is so called because the entire stem is very knotty [jointed]; it grows to the height of a man and puts out many stalks no thicker than the stem of a wheat plant. Its leaf is of the shape and size of that of the wallflower [alhelí], and with it they treat wounds. This herb grows in moist places; its stalks and leaves are very tender and serve as fodder for livestock.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_XXXV
corpus_links.title: The Stinking Herb (Yerba Hedionda)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXV
De la yerba hedionda

Este nombre damos en este reino del Perú, y con el mismo la vi nombrar en la isla Española, a cierta planta que da de sí mal olor en tanto grado, que llegándose cerca della la persona, aunque no la vea, conocerá por el hedor haberla allí. Esta es una mata que crece dos estados y echa muchas ramas, cuya hoja es parecida a la del durazno, salvo que es de un verde
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXV
Of the Stinking Herb

This is the name we give in this kingdom of Peru — and I saw it called by the same name on the island of Hispaniola — to a certain plant that gives off such a foul odor that a person coming near it, even without seeing it, will know it is there by the stench. It is a shrub [mata] that grows to the height of two fathoms [estados] and puts out many branches, whose leaf resembles that of the peach tree, except that it is of a lighter green. There is no need to describe its properties further, since its foul smell makes it readily identifiable, and I know of no other plant that resembles it in this respect. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XCII

Del árbol llamado caá

En la provincia del Paraguay se llama caá un árbol grande que echa la hoja parecida a la del zumaque. Hállase este árbol solamente en la tierra de los indios gentiles y de guerra, y ellos salen a vender la hoja seca a los españoles, los cuales, como no han visto el árbol sino la hoja, la llaman comúnmente hierba del Paraguay, siendo, como es, hoja de árbol. To
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCII

Of the tree called caá

In the province of Paraguay, a large tree that puts forth leaves resembling those of the sumac [zumaque] is called caá. This tree is found only in the lands of the pagan and warring Indians, who go out to sell its dried leaves to the Spaniards. The Spaniards, having seen only the leaf and not the tree itself, commonly call it 'herb of Paraguay' [hierba del Paraguay], though it is, properly speaking, a tree leaf. The Paraguayan Indians take this herb, and after their example so do the Spaniards of that province, and even of others quite distant — for I myself saw it taken in Mexico. CAPITULO CVII

Del zacate

La yerba que en la Nueva España corresponde al hicho es el zacate, que si bien es nombre genérico para toda suerte de yerba silvestre, con todo eso, se aplica a cierta especie della, que es más general en aquel reino, de que están cubiertos los campos y sabanas, particularmente de la Tierra caliente, y se sustentan los ganados y bestias de carga. Crece el zacate dos o tr
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CVII

On Zacate

The grass that in New Spain corresponds to the hicho [of Peru] is the zacate. Although this is a generic name for all manner of wild grass, it is nonetheless applied to a particular species thereof, which is the most widespread in that kingdom, covering the fields and savannas—particularly in the Tierra Caliente [hot lowlands]—and upon which livestock and pack animals are sustained. Zacate grows two or three cubits [roughly three to four feet] in height, such that it reaches the stirrups of travelers; and so that the moisture it carries from the dew does not wet the feet of those who pass through it, they use wooden stirrups closed at the front, and boots greased with ule [natural rubber]. This grass grows very densely, and its leaf resembles that of the sugarcane

corpus_links.title: On the Hicho Grass: Varieties and Uses in the Peruvian Highlands
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CVI
Del hicho

Son también innumerables las diferencias que nacen por los campos de yerbas silvestres de grande utilidad para pasto y sustento de los ganados. Entre las demás crió Dios en esta América dos géneros de yerbas muy generales; en esta Meridional, el hicho, y en la Septentrional, el zacate. El hicho es la yerba más común que nace en las sierras del Perú y la más conocida de indi
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CVI
On the Hicho

The varieties of wild grasses that grow across the fields and are of great utility as pasture and sustenance for livestock are likewise innumerable. Among others, God created in this America two very widespread kinds of grass: in this Southern part, the hicho, and in the Northern part, the zacate [a general term for grasses in Mesoamerica and northern South America]. The hicho is the most common grass that grows in the highlands [sierras] of Peru, and the best known to both Indians and Spaniards. It is native to cold lands, and since the highlands of this realm are for the most part punas [high Andean plateaux] and barren páramos [high moorlands], they are all covered with this grass, which endures the cold and the frosts so well that where it does not grow, no ot

De las matas que se hallaron en estas Indias de una misma especie con las de España

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER ONE

On the shrubs found in these Indies of the same species as those of Spain

The second rank of plants comprises all those which the Latins call frutex and which Calepino's dictionary renders in the vernacular as mata [shrub]; for although this term is common to all sorts of plants, it has by now been appropriated to signify solely those which have a greater kinship with trees than with herbs — both by virtue of their long life, like trees, and because they consist of a more solid, tough, and woody substance than all annual herbs [yerbas cadañales], which, once they have borne their fruit, die. CAPITULO X
De la achira

En la lengua quichua o general del Perú se llama achira una planta cuya raíz sirve de mantenimiento a los indios, la cual crece cuatro codos en alto; echa unas varas tan gruesas como un dedo de la mano, derechas, sin que de ellas brote rama, algo parecidas a las cañas, por tener a trechos nudos y estar envueltas en la hoja antes que ella se extienda y aparte del vástago, c
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER X
On the Achira

In the Quechua language, the general tongue of Peru, a plant is called achira whose root serves as sustenance for the Indians. It grows four cubits [roughly six feet] in height; it sends up stalks as thick as a finger of the hand, straight, without any branches sprouting from them, somewhat resembling canes [reeds], as they have nodes at intervals and are sheathed within the leaf before it spreads and separates from the stalk, as canes are; they are solid and tough. The leaf is so large that it measures more than two spans [palmos] in length and, at its widest, one span across; it is stiff, smooth, and entirely covered with veins or somewhat raised ridges running from the midrib out to the edges. At the top it produces small red flowers, pleasant to the eye but ent

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER ONE

On the shrubs found in these Indies of the same species as those of Spain

The second rank of plants comprises all those which the Latins call frutex and which Calepino's dictionary renders in the vernacular as mata [shrub]; for although this term is common to all sorts of plants, it has by now been appropriated to signify solely those which have a greater kinship with trees than with herbs — both by virtue of their long life, like trees, and because they consist of a more solid, tough, and woody substance than all annual herbs [yerbas cadañales], which, once they have borne their fruit, die. CAPITULO XLVII

De la ujuta

Los indios del Perú llaman ujuta al calzado que usan, y dan el mismo nombre a una flor, por tener, como tiene, la figura del dicho calzado. La mata que la produce crece dos o tres codos y echa muchas ramas o varas delgadas, pardas, redondas, lisas y correosas. Su hoja se parece a la del almendro, salvo que es un poco menor y más tierna. Es la flor amarilla de muy fino
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVII

Of the Ujuta

The Indians of Peru call ujuta the footwear [sandal] they use, and they give the same name to a flower because it has, as indeed it does, the shape of said footwear. The shrub that produces it grows two or three cubits tall and puts out many branches or thin stems, brownish, round, smooth, and tough [correosas]. Its leaf resembles that of the almond tree, except that it is somewhat smaller and more tender. The flower is yellow of a very fine color, of handsome appearance, though without fragrance; it has no more than a single petal [hoja] in the shape of a small gourd, a little shorter than a finger, thickest where it is about as wide as the ball of the thumb, tapering toward the stalk [pezón], and hollow within. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLVI
Del hicaco

Este es un árbol que nace en las costas de la mar, tan pequeño, que no sube más que uno o dos estados de la tierra; de buen parecer; cuya hoja es semejante a la del madroño. La fruta que lleva es como un albaricoque, más agradable a la vista que al gusto, porque tiene color de manzana arrebolada; la cáscara es como de manzana y la carne blanca y esponjosa nada apetitosa,
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI
On the Hicaco

This is a tree that grows along the seacoasts, so small that it rises no more than one or two fathoms [estados] from the ground; it is of pleasing appearance, and its leaf resembles that of the strawberry tree [madroño, Arbutus unedo]. The fruit it bears is like an apricot [albaricoque], more pleasing to the eye than to the taste, for it has the color of a flushed apple; the skin is like that of an apple, and the flesh is white and spongy, not at all appetizing, for it is a wild and coarse fruit; it has a very large stone [pit] in proportion to its size.

De los cardones

Al otro genero de matas espinosas que no echan hojas anchas llamamos, generalmente, cardones, en que se comprehenden mucha mayor multiplicidad y variedad de especies que en el linaje de las tunas. Difieren primeramente los cardones en el tamaño, porque los más crecidos son tan altos como cipreses, y los menores no se levantan del suelo. Destos pequeñuelos hay unos del
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IV

On the Cardones [Columnar Cacti]

The other genus of thorny shrubs that do not put forth broad leaves we call, generally, cardones [columnar or tree cacti], which encompass a far greater multiplicity and variety of species than does the lineage of the tunas [prickly pears]. The cardones differ first of all in size, because the tallest among them are as high as cypress trees, while the smallest do not rise from the ground. Among these small ones, some are as slender as the thumb and spread across the earth; others, the very smallest of all, grow in the shape of a star, have no spines, and are eaten by livestock; and because they are very watery, the animals that eat them have no need to drink. Between these two extremes there are specimens of varying height.

CAPITULO IX
De los demás cardones

De las muchas diferencias de cardones que yo he visto, no deben de quedar más que tres o cuatro, mas no dudo sino que habrá otros de que yo no tenga noticias. Uno de los más pequeños es el que se dice pullapulla, el cual no se levanta de la tierra más que, cuando mucho, un jeme. CHAPTER IX
On the Other Cardones [cacti]

Of the many varieties of cardones [columnar or globose cacti] that I have seen, there remain no more than three or four to describe, though I do not doubt that there are others of which I have no knowledge. One of the smallest is the one called pullapulla, which rises from the ground no more than, at most, one span [jeme: the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the index finger, roughly 7–8 cm]. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVIII
On the Piñuelas

The plant that bears the piñuelas belongs to the genus of the maguey [agave], under which genus there are comprehended as many species as there are in that of the cardones [columnar cacti], all of them agreeing in having leaves like those of the zabila [aloe], some larger and thicker than others, of different colors, with a stalk in the middle more or less thick and tall according to the variety of maguey. This shrub of the piñuelas rises three or four cubits from the ground; its leaves [pencas] are of a whitish green, armed along the edges with sharp spines, on account of which they are used in some places to enclose [fence] gardens. Del avacollay y otros cardones

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VI
On the Avacollay and Other Columnar Cacti [cardones]

The columnar cactus [cardón] called avacollay is the largest of the second class, which includes all those that are green, spiny, ribbed, and that yield no serviceable timber; there must be more than ten or twelve varieties of them. The avacollay sometimes grows upright and erect, and at other times sprawls along the ground, looking for all the world like a green serpent. It has four to six ridges [esquinas]; in its shape it resembles a large candle with many wicks [pábulos]. It is as thick as an arm and between one and two fathoms [estados] in length. CHAPTER V
On the Queylla

The queylla is the genus of cardones [columnar cacti] that grows largest of all, encompassing five or six distinct varieties, all of which, when dried, are so tough and strong that their wood serves for construction and other uses. All of those in this class are green or brownish, and removing the core—which is hard wood—the remainder is tender and watery like a green gourd, consisting of the rind and outer bark, which is three to four finger-widths thick. They are ribbed, with a deep and narrow channel between one rib and the next. Some have more ribs and ridges than others; some reach as many as twenty, and from there the number decreases. De la vadea

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XV
On the vadea

In the city and province of Guayaquil, in the diocese of Quito, the Spaniards call vadea a species of passionflower vine [apincolia, sic] that grows there, very similar in its leaves, flower, and fruit to the tumbo. CAPITULO XIX
De los piros

En la provincia de Tierra Firme llaman piros a una frutilla silvestre cuya mata es semejante a la de las piñuelas, salvo que no hace sus pencas tan gruesas y espinosas. No produce tallo, sino, en medio de las pencas, a raíz de la tierra, una cabeza llana en que nacen los piros muy apretados unos con otros; los cuales son de hechura de cermeñas, algo larguillos un poco qu
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIX
On the Piros

In the province of Tierra Firme [the Spanish Main], they call piros a small wild fruit whose plant is similar to that of the piñuelas [wild bromeliads], except that it does not produce leaves [pencas] as thick and spiny. It produces no stalk, but rather, in the midst of the leaves, at ground level, a flat head from which the piros grow very closely packed together. These are shaped like cermeñas [small pears or wardens], somewhat more elongated than the piñuelas; red on the outside, with white flesh, of better flavor than the piñuelas, and of a pleasant and so powerful a fragrance that, when they are ripe, one can tell they are there by their scent alone.

En la provincia de Tierra Firme llaman piros a una frutilla silvestre cuya mata es semejante a la de las piñuelas, salvo que no hace sus pencas tan gruesas y espinosas. No produce tallo, sino, en medio de las pencas, a raíz de la tierra, una cabeza llana en que nacen los piros muy apretados unos con otros; los cuales son de hechura de cermeñas, algo larguillos un poco qu
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIX
On the Piros

In the province of Tierra Firme [the Spanish Main], they call piros a small wild fruit whose plant is similar to that of the piñuelas [wild bromeliads], except that it does not produce leaves [pencas] as thick and spiny. It produces no stalk, but rather, in the midst of the leaves, at ground level, a flat head from which the piros grow very closely packed together. These are shaped like cermeñas [small pears or wardens], somewhat more elongated than the piñuelas; red on the outside, with white flesh, of better flavor than the piñuelas, and of a pleasant and so powerful a fragrance that, when they are ripe, one can tell they are there by their scent alone.

corpus_links.title: The Añaguaya shrub of the Collao region
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXI
De la añaguaya

La añaguaya es una mata espinosa a la canilla; levántase de la tierra de uno a dos codos; la hoja es de la forma que la de la sabina y algo más menuda; las espinas son menores que las del naranjo, derechas, agudas y blanquiscas. Da una florecita amarilla de ningún olor, del talle que la de la retama, un poquito menor. Nace esta planta en las provincias del Collao, en t
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXI
On the añaguaya

The añaguaya is a thorny shrub of slender [cane-like] form; it rises from the ground one to two cubits [roughly 18 to 36 inches]; the leaf is shaped like that of the savin [juniper] and somewhat smaller; the thorns are smaller than those of the orange tree, straight, sharp, and whitish. It produces a small yellow flower of no scent, in shape like that of the broom plant [retama], though a little smaller. This plant grows in the provinces of the Collao [the altiplano region around Lake Titicaca], in very cold country, and serves only as firewood.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_L
corpus_links.title: The Guarango Tree (Chapter 50)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO L

Del guarango

En el Perú tienen nombre de guarango cinco o seis especies de árboles muy parecidos entre sí, que casi todos echan unas vainas como algarrobas. Al que produce las mejores llaman los españoles algarrobo de las Indias, el es de diferente casta que el algarrobo de España. Es árbol mediano, del grandor de un olivo; la hoja es muy menuda, la cual en tamaño y hechura es parecid
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER 50

On the Guarango

In Peru, the name guarango is given to five or six species of trees that closely resemble one another, nearly all of which produce pods similar to carob [algarrobas]. The one that bears the finest pods the Spaniards call the 'algarrobo of the Indies' [carob of the Indies]; it is of a different kind from the algarrobo of Spain. It is a medium-sized tree, about the size of an olive tree; its leaf is very small, and in size and shape closely resembles the leaf of a fern or of a savin [juniper]. The fruit of the guarango consists of pods like carobs, though not as wide and long, whose seeds, in color and smoothness, resemble those of our carobs, except that they have many spines. This fruit is good to eat, and the Indians in some places make flour and bread from it

CAPITULO LXV
Del pinco-pinco

Esta es una mata de tres o cuatro codos en alto; echa muchas varillas juntas delgadas y parejas como las de la retama; son macizas, leñosas y desnudas de hojas, y aunque lisas, de trecho a trecho ñudosas. Nace por los suelos una frutilla colorada del tamaño de garbanzos, con dos granitos negros dentro poco menores que los de la linaza. Es muy estimada esta planta en e
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXV
On the Pinco-Pinco

This is a shrub three or four cubits [codos] in height; it puts forth many slender and even stems together, like those of the broom plant [retama]; they are solid, woody, and bare of leaves, and although smooth, knotted at intervals. At ground level it produces a small red fruit the size of chickpeas, containing two small black seeds inside, somewhat smaller than those of flaxseed. This plant is highly esteemed in Peru for its many and marvelous effects. It is hot and dry with a manifest astringency [estipticidad]. Its leaves or branches, pounded and applied to fresh wounds, draw them together, dry them, and heal them. Its powders, mixed with those of alum, have the power to dry out any sore or ulcer.
