CAPITULO CII

De la tipa

Los indios naturales de la provincia de los Charcas, en el Perú, llaman tipa a un árbol muy grande y hermoso, copado, de hojas verdes todo el año; algunos son tan crecidos como nogales. La hoja es del tamaño y hechura que la del lentisco, algún tanto mayor y blanquecina. Echa unas vainillas del largor de un dedo, delgadas y enjutas, salvo que junto al pezón son gruesecill
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CII

On the Tipa

The native Indians of the province of Charcas, in Peru, call tipa a very large and beautiful tree, broad-crowned, with green leaves throughout the year; some specimens grow as large as walnut trees. The leaf is similar in size and shape to that of the mastic tree [lentisco], somewhat larger and whitish. It produces small pods about a finger's length, slender and dry, except that near the stem they are somewhat thicker, as if they contained a chickpea inside. Each of these little pods resembles in shape and form the wing of a butterfly. corpus_links.title: The Mamón: Description of the Tree and Fruit
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO VI

Del mamón

En la isla Española llaman mamón a otro árbol y fruta parecida a la anona. Es el mamón árbol mediano, del grandor de un durazno, de muy buen parecer; su hoja es semejante a la del aliso, algo mayor y más acanalada y de un verde muy claro, que hermosea mucho el árbol; la fruta tiene el mismo nombre, la cual, cuando está pequeña y verde, parece alcachofa, por la cáscara muy d
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VI

On the Mamón

On the island of Hispaniola they call mamón another tree and fruit resembling the anona [custard apple]. The mamón is a medium-sized tree, about the size of a peach tree [durazno], and of very pleasing appearance; its leaf resembles that of the alder [aliso], being somewhat larger and more channeled, and of a very light green that greatly beautifies the tree. The fruit bears the same name; when it is small and unripe, it resembles an artichoke [alcachofa] on account of its very uneven surface, as though composed of green scales layered one upon another.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO X

Del mamey de Cartagena

El mamey de Cartagena, que dondequiera que se da conserva este nombre, por haberse llevado de aquella provincia, aunque es muy parecido al mamey del capítulo pasado, se distingue de él en especie. Es este árbol el más hermoso y de mejor parecer de cuantos yo he visto propios de las Indias. Es de la grandeza de un nogal, muy poblado de hoja, bien hecho y copado.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER X

On the Mamey of Cartagena

The mamey of Cartagena [Mammea americana or Pouteria sapota, var.], which wherever it grows retains this name on account of having been brought from that province, although it greatly resembles the mamey of the preceding chapter, is nonetheless a distinct species. This tree is the most beautiful and handsome of all those I have seen native to the Indies. It is the size of a walnut tree [nogal], very full of leaves, well-formed and spreading. The leaf is also very beautiful, somewhat resembling that of the citron [cidra], but better proportioned; it measures a span in length and five fingers in width, flat, with very little channeling, stiff and very smooth, thick, covered with small white dots that run from the midrib to the margins; the upper surface

Del yoloxochitl

Yoloxochitl, en lengua mexicana, quiere decir flor de corazón, porque tiene hechura de corazón; y es de tal disposición y forma, que más parece, antes de abrirse, algún género de fruta puntiaguda, que flor; porque es del tamaño y talle de una pera bergamota y se compone de unas hojas grandes, gruesas y tiesas, como pencas de alcachofas, que unas están apretadas sobre
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXV
On the Yoloxochitl

Yoloxochitl, in the Mexican tongue [Nahuatl], means 'heart-flower,' because it has the shape of a heart. Its form and appearance are such that, before it opens, it looks more like some kind of pointed fruit than a flower; for it is the size and figure of a bergamot pear [pera bergamota], and is composed of large, thick, and stiff leaves [petals], like the fleshy leaves of artichokes, pressed tightly one upon another. The opening of this flower consists in the outer leaves that encircle the whole bloom spreading apart slightly at their tips; these outer leaves are of a pale green that tends toward white. CAPITULO X

Del mamey de Cartagena

El mamey de Cartagena, que dondequiera que se da conserva este nombre, por haberse llevado de aquella provincia, aunque es muy parecido al mamey del capítulo pasado, se distingue de él en especie. Es este árbol el más hermoso y de mejor parecer de cuantos yo he visto propios de las Indias. Es de la grandeza de un nogal, muy poblado de hoja, bien hecho y copado.

On the Mamey of Cartagena

corpus_links.title: The Land Apple (Manzano de la Tierra) of New Spain
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXIV
De las manzanas de la tierra

El árbol que llamamos manzano de la tierra sólo se halla en la Nueva España. Es pequeño y muy parecido en todo al manzano de Castilla, salvo que es mucho mayor y de hojas más pequeñas, aunque de la misma hechura. El fruto que produce son unas manzanillas pequeñas, redondas y amarillas, de tamaño y hechura de níspero. Es fruta silvestre y desabrida; tiene
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIV
On the Land Apples

The tree we call the land apple [manzano de la tierra] is found only in New Spain. It is small and very similar in every respect to the apple tree of Castile [manzano de Castilla], except that it is much larger and has smaller leaves, though of the same shape. The fruit it produces consists of small, round, yellow little apples [manzanillas], of the size and shape of a medlar [níspero]. It is a wild and insipid fruit; each one contains three seeds inside shaped like pine nuts [piñones], and so hard that they cannot be broken with the teeth. The Spaniards use these apples to make preserves [conservas]; and Castilian apples graft well onto this tree.

CAPITULO IX
Del mamey

El nombre de mamey es tomado de la isla Española, y comprende al árbol y a la fruta. Hállanse cuatro diferencias de mameyes: el uno es general, y los otros particulares de varias provincias donde se hallaron. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX
On the Mamey

The name mamey is taken from the island of Hispaniola and refers to both the tree and its fruit. Four varieties of mamey are found: one is common and widespread, and the others are particular to the various provinces where they were discovered. The common and ordinary mamey is a large tree, comparable in size to a medium walnut tree, very well formed, full-crowned, green, and of very pleasant appearance. Its leaf resembles that of the orange tree, but is smoother and stiffer, and of a lighter green on the outside than on the inside. The fruit is round and about the size of a medium pomegranate; the rind is a dark amber tending toward brown [pardo], somewhat thinner and stiffer than that of a pomegranate. corpus_links.title: The Chicozapote Fruit
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XV

Del chicozapote

El chicozapote es fruta de la Nueva España, y de las más regaladas que se hallan en aquel reino; el árbol es de la grandeza del mamey y de menor hoja; la fruta es redonda, del tamaño de una lima, de un color leonado que tira a rojo, y el mismo color tiene la carne, la cual es blanda, muy jugosa y dulce; las pepitas, pequeñas y lisas, de tamaño de piñones. Es fruta de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XV

On the Chicozapote

The chicozapote is a fruit of New Spain [Nueva España], and among the most prized [regaladas] to be found in that kingdom. The tree is of the same size as the mamey and has smaller leaves. The fruit is round, the size of a lime, of a tawny [leonado] color tending toward red, and the flesh [carne] is the same color; it is soft, very juicy, and sweet. The seeds [pepitas] are small and smooth, the size of pine nuts [piñones]. It is a fruit of fine flavor and nourishment, and as such is highly esteemed. The best chicozapotes I have seen are those grown in Tehuantepec, in the diocese of Oaxaca [Guajaca].

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XII_part1
corpus_links.title: On Zapotes: Varieties, Tree, and Fruit Description
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XII
De los zapotes.

Los zapotes son propios de la Nueva España, adonde se hallan cinco diferencias dellos; los mejores son los colorados. El árbol que los lleva es grande y copado como el mamey, con los cogollos muy poblados de hoja; ésta es larga un palmo, lisa, tiesa, de un verde oscuro y más ancha al cabo que en medio. La fruta es del tamaño de un membrillo y aun como una grande cidra
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XII
On Zapotes.

The zapotes are native to New Spain, where five varieties of them are found; the best are the red ones [colorados]. The tree that bears them is large and spreading [copado], like the mamey, with the young shoots [cogollos] very densely leafed; the leaf is a palm's length [approx. 8 inches] long, smooth, stiff, of a dark green, and wider at the tip than in the middle. The fruit is the size of a quince and even as large as a big citron [cidra], spindle-shaped [ahusada], with a thin and tender skin; the flesh is very red and soft [text breaks off].

Del pacay

CHAPTER XXXV
Of the Pacay

The pacay is a tree of the size of a mulberry [moral], of handsome appearance and very full of leaves; the leaf is shaped like that of the lemon tree [limo], somewhat larger, of a darker green, very smooth and shiny. This tree produces its leaves in the manner of the walnut [nogal], on slender little branches, paired two by two with four or five pairs on each branchlet. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XLI
corpus_links.title: The Olozapote Tree
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLI
Del olozapote

Es el olozapote un árbol de la grandeza de un crecido naranjo, muy copado y de buena sombra; tiene la hoja grande y tiesa, de la forma y tamaño de la del limo; echa la flor en racimos; y su fruta es colorada, semejante en la hechura y color al dátil; tiénenla los indios por sabrosa y plantan este árbol en sus casas.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLI
Of the Olozapote

The olozapote is a tree of the size of a large orange tree, very broad-crowned and of good shade; it has a large and stiff leaf, of the shape and size of that of the lime [limo]; it bears its flowers in clusters [racimos]; and its fruit is red, resembling a date [dátil] in shape and color; the Indians consider it tasty and plant this tree near their houses.

Del tilxochil

Llámase así en la Nueva España la planta que produce las vainillas que se echan en el chocolate y le dan muy agradable olor. Es una mata de género de bejuco; su tallo voluble y verde; las hojas, grandes, largas un palmo y dos o tres dedos de ancho, y por todas partes es igual su ancho, con que hace figura de lengua; es gruesa y muy lisa. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVII
On the Tilxochil

This is the name given in New Spain to the plant that produces the vanilla pods [vainillas] that are added to chocolate and impart to it a very pleasant aroma. It is a climbing shrub [mata de género de bejuco]; its stem is twining and green; the leaves are large, a span [palmo] long and two or three fingers wide, of equal width throughout, giving them the shape of a tongue; they are thick and very smooth. The flower is whitish, and the fruit consists of pods a span in length, more slender than carob pods [algarrobas], and when ripe they turn yellow. Once harvested from the plant, they are cured in the sun with great care, and after curing they become the color of raisins, tough and juicy, like them. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO L

Del guarango

En el Perú tienen nombre de guarango cinco o seis especies de árboles muy parecidos entre sí, que casi todos echan unas vainas como algarrobas. Al que produce las mejores llaman los españoles algarrobo de las Indias, el es de diferente casta que el algarrobo de España. Es árbol mediano, del grandor de un olivo; la hoja es muy menuda, la cual en tamaño y hechura es parecid
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER 50

On the Guarango

In Peru, the name guarango is given to five or six species of trees that closely resemble one another, nearly all of which produce pods similar to carob [algarrobas]. The one that bears the finest pods the Spaniards call the 'algarrobo of the Indies' [carob of the Indies]; it is of a different kind from the algarrobo of Spain. It is a medium-sized tree, about the size of an olive tree; its leaf is very small, and in size and shape closely resembles the leaf of a fern or of a savin [juniper]. The fruit of the guarango consists of pods like carobs, though not as wide and long, whose seeds, in color and smoothness, resemble those of our carobs, except that they have many spines. This fruit is good to eat, and the Indians in some places make flour and bread from it

corpus_links.title: The Spiny Guarango (Yara) and Related Species
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LI
Del guarango-espino

Por tener este guarango muchas espinas le llamamos espino, a diferencia del primero, que no las tiene; pero los indios de este reino lo llaman yara. En esta especie de guarango se halla macho y hembra: el macho da fruto, y a la hembra se le cae en flor; una casta de la yara crece alta, y ora se extiende y arrastra por la tierra como zarza. CHAPTER LI
On the Spiny Guarango [guarango-espino]

Because this guarango has many thorns we call it the spiny [guarango], to distinguish it from the first kind, which has none; but the Indians of this kingdom call it yara. In this species of guarango there are male and female: the male bears fruit, and on the female the fruit drops off in flower. One variety of the yara grows tall, while another spreads out and trails along the ground like a bramble. The tree that grows upright is the size of a tall, spreading mulberry tree with a thick trunk, though smaller specimens also exist. Its leaf is very small, in every respect resembling that of the guarango; all its branches are covered with thorns like those of the orange tree, but harder and sharper. corpus_links.title: On the espingo plant and its medicinal pods
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XC

Del espingo

Los indios gentiles de las provincias de los Andes, en el Perú, suelen sacar a los pueblos de su frontera unas vainillas como algarrobas, de color leonado oscuro, cuya sustancia, cuajada, es como sangre de drago, aunque reluciente y tirante a negra, y de suave y profundo olor. Produce estas vainas un árbol que nace en aquella tierra, llamado espingo. Sacan los indios bárb
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XC

On the Espingo

The pagan Indians of the Andean provinces of Peru are accustomed to bringing out to the frontier towns certain small pods resembling carob [algarroba], of a dark tawny color, whose coagulated substance is like dragon's blood [sangre de drago], though lustrous and tending toward black, with a gentle and deep fragrance. These pods are produced by a tree that grows in that land, called the espingo. These barbarous Indians bring out the pods as a precious commodity, trading them for knives, scissors, and other small items that they value greatly; this they easily obtain from the Spaniards, for these pods are held to be highly medicinal. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_CXV
corpus_links.title: Four Timber Trees of Warm and Andean Regions: Guachapelí, Harca, Cacha Cacha, and Soto
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CXV

Del guachapelí

El guachapelí es un árbol que sólo nace en tierras calientes; no crece muy alto, porque no sube derecho, sino que echa el tronco torcido y encorvado y muchas y muy gruesas ramas. Su hoja es pequeña como la de la alfalfa. Es árbol silvestre infructífero, pero de muy buena madera para labrar, de la cual se hacen comúnmente los corvatones y costillas de los navíos; y par
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXV

On the Guachapelí

The guachapelí is a tree that grows only in warm lowland regions [tierras calientes]. It does not grow very tall, because it does not rise straight up; rather, it sends out its trunk twisted and curved, with many very thick branches. Its leaf is small, like that of alfalfa. It is a wild tree that bears no fruit, but yields very good timber for working. From this timber, the knees [corvatones] and ribs of ships are commonly made. In order to obtain pieces suitable for this purpose, the trunk is cut one or two varas [a vara being roughly 33 inches] above the ground, and from that junction together with an equal length of the root, a ship's knee is fashioned. corpus_links.title: On Goats in the New World (Peru and Chile)
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO VII
Del ganado cabrío

Es el ganado cabrío tan general en toda la América como el que más, porque se cría en tierras frías y calientes, si bien no con igual abundancia en todas partes, que también quiere, como todas las cosas, que el clima le sea favorable. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VII
On Goats [ganado cabrío]

Goats are as widespread throughout all of America as any livestock, for they are raised in both cold and warm lands, though not with equal abundance everywhere, since they too, like all things, require a favorable climate. Throughout this kingdom of Peru they have multiplied greatly, both in the highlands and in the lowlands, and most abundantly in the provinces of the Llanos, owing to the great quantity of wild algarroba or guarango, as it is called here, which is excellent pasture for goats. CAPITULO LV
De las almendras de los Andes

Los indios gentiles de las provincias de los Andes que confinan por la parte oriental con la diócesis del Cuzco, sacan a vender a tierra de cristianos ciertas almendras que se dan en las suyas, a las cuales los españoles, por no saber su propio nombre, llamamos almendras de los Andes. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LV
On the Almonds of the Andes

The pagan Indians [indios gentiles] of the Andean provinces that border on the eastern side of the diocese of Cuzco bring to the Christian settlements certain almonds that grow in their lands, which the Spaniards, not knowing their proper name, call almendras de los Andes [almonds of the Andes]. The tree that produces them is larger than a great walnut tree, and in the Andean provinces there is such a vast quantity of them that forests of these almond trees stretch over fifty leagues and more. They produce their fruit inside husks [cocos] about the size of a quince, somewhat elongated, with a hard, brownish, cracked shell half a finger's breadth thick, which must generally be sawed open; inside are more than a dozen slightly curved almonds arranged a

De las palmas de cocos grandes

Innumerables son las diferencias de palmas que se hallan en estas Indias, así en tierras calientes como en las templadas y frías, como no lleguen a tener temple de páramo, y mucho más las que nacen en las islas Filipinas, porque me han certificado personas prácticas de aquella tierra, que se cuentan más de cincuenta géneros dellas. CHAPTER LX

On the Large Coconut Palms

Innumerable are the varieties of palms to be found in these Indies, both in hot lands and in temperate and cold ones, so long as they do not reach the climate of the high moorland [páramo], and still more so among those that grow in the Philippine Islands, for persons of practical experience in that land have assured me that more than fifty kinds of them are counted. I shall describe here only those we find in this America of which I have knowledge, and indeed personal acquaintance by sight with the greater part of them. It must be noted above all that not all of them grow everywhere, because, being of different natures and qualities, they require different climates [temples]. CAPITULO LXI
De los cocos de Chachapoyas

Todas las especies de palmas que nacen en estas Indias me parece que se pueden reducir a tres géneros, y cada género se puede subdividir después por sus especies. CHAPTER LXI
On the Cocos of Chachapoyas

All the species of palms that grow in these Indies seem to me reducible to three genera [géneros], each of which may afterwards be subdivided into its species. They are first to be divided into two members: in the first we shall include all those whose branches and leaves resemble our date palms [palmas de dátiles], and in the second, those whose branches grow in a different form—not long and straight, but rounded, after the manner of rays, very much resembling the open hand of a man and the dwarf palms [palmillas] from which brooms are made in Spain. The first member of this division encompasses two of the three genera we have described, and the third genus falls under the second member. CAPITULO IX
Del mamey

El nombre de mamey es tomado de la isla Española, y comprende al árbol y a la fruta. Hállanse cuatro diferencias de mameyes: el uno es general, y los otros particulares de varias provincias donde se hallaron. El mamey común y ordinario es árbol grande como un mediano nogal, muy bien hecho, copado, verde y de muy agradable parecer; la hoja se parece a la del naranjo, pero es
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX
On the Mamey

The name mamey is taken from the island of Hispaniola and refers to both the tree and its fruit. Four varieties of mamey are found: one is common and widespread, and the others are particular to the various provinces where they were discovered. The common and ordinary mamey is a large tree, comparable in size to a medium walnut tree, very well formed, full-crowned, green, and of very pleasant appearance. Its leaf resembles that of the orange tree, but is smoother and stiffer, and of a lighter green on the outside than on the inside. The fruit is round and about the size of a medium pomegranate; the rind is a dark amber tending toward brown [pardo], somewhat thinner and stiffer than that of a pomegranate. Inside it contains one or two seeds [huesos, lit. 'stones'] s

CAPITULO LII
Del nogal del Perú

El nogal que se halla en este reino parece en todo ser del mismo género que los de España; si bien la gran diferencia que vemos entre estas nueces y otras es argumento de haber entre ellas diferencia específica. El árbol es grande y la hoja de la misma forma que la del nogal de Europa, y también el olor es el mismo, salvo que la madera de éste no es tan buena como
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LII
On the Walnut of Peru

The walnut tree found in this kingdom appears in all respects to belong to the same genus [género] as those of Spain; although the great difference we observe between these nuts and the others is an argument for there being a specific difference [diferencia específica] between them. The tree is large and its leaf is of the same shape as that of the European walnut, and the smell is likewise the same, except that the wood of this one is not as good as that of the other. Nevertheless, some articles are made from it, and in particular the stocks [cajas] of arquebuses [arcabuces]. CAPITULO LXXIV
Del ocot

El ocot es un árbol grande y grueso; la hoja, del tamaño de la del nogal, es un poco más ancha. Nace en tierras yuncas y su fruto son solas flores. Produce antes de la flor un botón como una avellana, y déste nace una punta larga medio jeme, de hechura y grosor de la bellota; la cual se abre en cinco hojas delgadas y correosas y dentro dellas nace un plumaje hermosísimo qu
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXIV
Of the Ocot

The ocot is a large and stout tree; its leaf, roughly the size of a walnut leaf, is somewhat broader. It grows in the lowland [yunca] regions, and its fruit consists solely of flowers. Before the flower appears, it produces a bud the size of a hazelnut, from which grows a spike about half a [jeme, a hand's-breadth measure] in length, in shape and thickness resembling an acorn. This spike opens into five thin, leathery leaflets, and from within them emerges a most beautiful plumage: a little bundle of slender filaments about half a jeme in length. These filaments are, from the base [pezón] to the midpoint, a fine crimson color, and from there to the tip they are white, with each filament terminating in a tiny knob like a grain of anise. corpus_links.title: Various Flowering Trees of the Americas

CAPITULO LXXVII

De los demás árboles de flores

Entre las muchas especies de árboles que llevan flores, una es la de cierto árbol llamado sicahani, el cual es pequeño, copado y que produce la hoja poco más larga que la de arrayán, muy fina y áspera, y una florecita colorada, de color de azafrán, que huele bien; y tiene una frutilla del mismo color y del tamaño de ciruelas pequeñas en que nace la
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXVII

On the Remaining Flowering Trees

Among the many species of trees that bear flowers, one is a certain tree called sicahani, which is small, bushy, and produces a leaf slightly longer than that of the myrtle [arrayán], very fine and rough, and a small reddish flower, saffron-colored, that smells pleasant; it also bears a small fruit of the same color and of the size of small plums, at the point where the flower emerges.

In New Spain, a certain flower is called the 'ear flower' [flor de la oreja] because it is shaped like a human ear; this flower is added to chocolate. The tree that produces it is of medium size, with long, narrow leaves of a dark green color, hanging from a withered little stem. The flower smells pleasant, and its leaves are purple on the inner side and gre

corpus_links.title: Four Timber Trees of Warm and Andean Regions: Guachapelí, Harca, Cacha Cacha, and Soto

CAPITULO CXV

Del guachapelí

El guachapelí es un árbol que sólo nace en tierras calientes; no crece muy alto, porque no sube derecho, sino que echa el tronco torcido y encorvado y muchas y muy gruesas ramas. Su hoja es pequeña como la de la alfalfa. Es árbol silvestre infructífero, pero de muy buena madera para labrar, de la cual se hacen comúnmente los corvatones y costillas de los navíos; y par
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXV

On the Guachapelí

The guachapelí is a tree that grows only in warm lowland regions [tierras calientes]. It does not grow very tall, because it does not rise straight up; rather, it sends out its trunk twisted and curved, with many very thick branches. Its leaf is small, like that of alfalfa. It is a wild tree that bears no fruit, but yields very good timber for working. From this timber, the knees [corvatones] and ribs of ships are commonly made. In order to obtain pieces suitable for this purpose, the trunk is cut one or two varas [a vara being roughly 33 inches] above the ground, and from that junction together with an equal length of the root, a ship's knee is fashioned. corpus_links.title: On the Palo Santo: Two Trees of That Name, and Conclusion of the Trees Treatise

CAPITULO CXXIX

Del palo santo

Los españoles habitadores de la provincia de Santa Cruz de la Sierra han puesto este nombre a cierto árbol que nace en aquella tierra no porque sea santo, sino en sentido contrario, huyen todos de llegarse a él, por el daño que han experimentado los que incautamente se le han arrimado. Es del tamaño de un manzano pequeño, tiene las hojas grandes como cidro, pocas ra
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXXIX

On the Palo Santo [Holy Wood]

The Spanish inhabitants of the province of Santa Cruz de la Sierra have given this name to a certain tree that grows in that land, not because it is holy [santo], but rather in the opposite sense: everyone avoids approaching it, on account of the harm experienced by those who have incautiously drawn near to it. It is the size of a small apple tree, has large leaves like those of the citron [cidro], few branches, and a trunk no thicker than a man's thigh. The entire tree is hollow from the trunk to its thinnest branches, and filled with certain reddish, elongated ants so venomous that their sting commonly brings on fevers and always causes very great pain (18). Because the ants are hidden inside the tree they cannot be seen, which is the reason

corpus_links.title: On the Trees of the Indies in General
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO PRIMERO

De los árboles de las Indias en común

Son tantos los géneros y especies de árboles, así frutales como infructíferos y silvestres que se hallan en este Nuevo Mundo, que faltan nombres con que significarlos; porque, demás de muchos que son generales y nacen en todas partes, en cada provincia se hallan nuevas plantas no vistas ni sabidas antes; y lo que pone gran admiración, es ver
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER THE FIRST

On the Trees of the Indies in General

So numerous are the genera and species of trees — both fruit-bearing and unfruitful [infructíferos] or wild — found in this New World, that names are wanting to signify them all; for, beyond the many that are widespread and grow in every region, in each province new plants are encountered that were never before seen or known. De los árboles que se hallaron en estas Indias de los mismos géneros que los de España

Muy pocos son los árboles que cuando vinieron a esta tierra los españoles hallaron en ella semejantes en especie a los de España; y ésos los más son infructíferos y silvestres. El árbol más general deste género que se halla en todas las provincias del Perú es el aliso, el cual nace en los valles te

CHAPTER II

On the trees found in these Indies of the same genera as those of Spain

Very few are the trees that, when the Spaniards came to this land, they found to be similar in species to those of Spain; and most of those are unfruitful [infructíferos] and wild [silvestres]. Del Hoque

El Hoque es un árbol que nace en la [sierra] del Perú, de madera recia y [dura]. Echa sus ramas largas y derechas, de las cuales se hacen bordones, que salen muy pesados, nudosos y recios, y varas para otros usos para que se requiere madera fuerte.

Del canacaspi

El canacaspi nace en tierras yuncas. Es árbol muy grande; produce las ramas y hojas muy semejan
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXX

On the Hoque

The Hoque is a tree that grows in the [sierra, i.e., highlands] of Peru, with hard and [tough] wood. It puts forth long, straight branches, from which walking staffs [bordones] are made, which turn out very heavy, knotted, and strong, as well as rods for other uses that require strong timber.

CHAPTER CXXI

On the Canacaspi

The canacaspi grows in the yunca [lowland/coastal valley] lands. It is a very large tree; it produces branches and leaves very similar to those of the guarango-espino [thorny guarango], except that it has no thorns. From this kind of tree [the text is cut off here...]

CAPITULO XVI
Del gaguey

Algunas frutas lleva esta tierra que corresponden a nuestros higos de Europa, sin embargo que son de muy distinto género, de los cuales hallamos cinco o seis especies diferentes: la primera es la del gaguey, que es un árbol así llamado en la lengua de la isla Española, y nómbranlo los españoles higuera de las Indias, por la semejanza que tiene su fruta con los higos verdad
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVI
On the Gaguey

This land bears certain fruits that correspond to our European figs, though they are of a very different genus, of which we find five or six distinct species. The first is that of the gaguey, a tree known by that name in the language of the island of Hispaniola, and called by the Spaniards higuera de las Indias [Indian fig-tree] on account of the resemblance its fruit bears to true figs. It is a large tree like a mulberry, very tall, abundantly leafed, and very spreading because it produces its branches in a very even manner. Its leaf is like that of the walnut, except that it is smoother, flatter, and stiffer, and broader toward the tip than in the middle. This tree has one property in which it closely resembles the fig tree: namely, that upon breaking off a bra

corpus_links.title: On Balsam: Three or Four Species of Balsam-Yielding Trees in the Indies
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXXXII
Del bálsamo

El árbol que destila el bálsamo en estas Indias no de sola una especie, sino de tres o cuatro. Es este licor muy semejante al bálsamo de Siria, y no inferior a él en olor y facultades. La una especie de árboles que lo dan y de mayor grandeza, nace en la diócesis de Guatemala, donde yo lo vi, y en otras tierras calientes; crece más que un moral, y hace un tronco grueso
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXII
On Balsam

The tree that yields balsam in these Indies is not of a single species, but of three or four. This liquor is very similar to the balsam of Syria, and in no way inferior to it in fragrance or properties. One species—the largest of those that produce it—grows in the diocese of Guatemala, where I myself saw it, and in other warm lands. It grows taller than a mulberry tree and forms a thick trunk of fragrant and very hard wood, so strong that it serves for purposes requiring very sturdy timber, such as axles for sugar mills and similar uses. De la vicura espinosa

En la Nueva España nombran los indios a este animalillo huitztlacuatzin, que es tanto como hahuatzin espinoso, porque es del tamaño y forma que la vicura; tiene el color negro, y está cubierto de unas púas huecas y agudas, que tienen casi un jeme de largo, muy parecidas a las del puerco espín; tiene mezclados algunos pelos blancos a modo de vello, salvo en la
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXIII
On the Spiny Vicura

In New Spain the Indians call this little animal huitztlacuatzin, which is much the same as saying 'spiny hahuatzin,' because it is the size and shape of the vicura [a small rodent]. It is black in color and is covered with hollow, sharp quills nearly a hand-span [jeme] in length, very similar to those of the porcupine. It has some white hairs mixed in, resembling fine fur, except on the head, where they end in black. When this animal finds itself cornered, it hurls its quills at those who pursue it, embedding them in the flesh, where they work their way in little by little and cannot be removed by any means. CAPITULO LXVI
De la onza

Llaman los Españoles onza a cierto animal que nace en estas Indias, que no sé si le dan este nombre porque sea de la misma especie que la de Europa, o por alguna semejanza que con ella tenga. Es del tamaño y hechura de galgo, ceñido de cintura y muy ligero, el color es ceniciento como de ratón, las uñas agudas, la cabeza no tan ahusada como de galgo, y las orejas caídas.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXVI
On the Onza

The Spaniards call by the name 'onza' [ounce] a certain animal found in these Indies; I do not know whether they give it this name because it belongs to the same species as the onza of Europe, or merely on account of some resemblance it bears to that creature. It is the size and shape of a greyhound, slender at the waist and very swift; its color is ashen, like that of a mouse; its claws are sharp; its head is not so tapered as a greyhound's, and its ears hang down. It fights with tigers [jaguars] and lions [pumas], and commonly overcomes and kills them, more through its swiftness and cunning than through brute strength. CHAPTER XLIV

On the Chilca

This is a shrub very well known to the Indians and Spaniards alike for its beneficial effects. It grows in great abundance in the coastal plains [Llanos] of Peru, on the banks of rivers, and serves as firewood. It grows to about one estado [roughly six feet] in height, more or less; it puts forth many thin, straight branches; its leaves are longish, tender, and slender, very similar to those of the willow, and are somewhat resinous. The chilca is of a hot and moist temperament [in the humoral sense]; the Indians use it, applying it warm against all pain caused by cold, and for this purpose they toast it with cinnamon and sprinkle it with wine or brandy [aguardiente]. CAPITULO LXXXIV
De la tecoma haca

Es planta mordaz y odorífera, cortando este árbol mana dél una goma como la del copal, muy provechosa, que la suelen usar en lugar de la mirra y en la cura de muchas enfermedades, y principalmente corrige las
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIV
Of the Tecoma Haca

This is a tree with round, serrated leaves; it bears a small, round, red fruit full of seeds resembling the pits of the peach [durazno]. It is a pungent and fragrant plant; when this tree is cut, a gum [resin] flows from it similar to that of copal, which is very beneficial and is commonly used in place of myrrh in the treatment of many ailments. It principally corrects cold imbalances [destemplanzas frías] and fortifies the stomach. This tree grows in the hot lands [tierra caliente] of New Spain.

Del copal

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CV
On Copal

The copal tree is large; its leaves resemble those of the holm oak [encina], except that they are longer; its fruit is round and tends toward red; it has the same flavor as the gum that flows from the tree, which sometimes exudes spontaneously and at other times by making incisions [sajando] in the tree. This congealed resin [licor cuajado] is white and transparent, good for fumigations [sahumerios], by means of which headache is relieved, and it is a remedy for all ailments arising from a cold cause [causa fría]; and all the various kinds of copal, of which there are many, do the same. corpus_links.translation: Pom (Bursera copallifera / B. bipinnata) — Maya Copal Resin. From the Ritual of the Bacabs (translated by Roys): 'Ix-pom, ix-cacao, ix-ya-che — copal, cacao tree, sapodilla tree — these are the medicines of the great healers.' In Maya culture, copal (pom) served simultaneously as a ritual substance and a medicinal one — a distinction the tradition did not draw as sharply as Western medicine does. Documented medicinal uses include: antimicrobial wound treatment (resin applied directly to infected wounds); pain relief (smoke inhaled for headache); and treatment of respiratory conditions (resin burned in an enclosed space and the smoke inhaled). De la sangre de drago

El árbol que mana la sangre de drago se dice en la lengua mexicana ezpuahuilt, que es tanto como decir árbol que mana sangre, por ser de ese color el licor que produce. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXVII
Of Dragon's Blood

The tree that yields dragon's blood is called in the Mexican tongue ezpuahuilt, which is to say 'tree that flows blood,' because the liquor it produces is of that color. It is a large tree with broad, angular leaves. It grows in many parts of the Indies and its liquor is very well known; this liquor strengthens the teeth and produces the same effects as the dragon's blood [sangre de drago] used in Spain. Painters also make use of it. The finest quality obtained in the Indies comes from the province of Cartagena.

CHAPTER CII

On the Tipa

The native Indians of the province of Charcas, in Peru, call tipa a very large and beautiful tree, broad-crowned, with green leaves throughout the year; some specimens grow as large as walnut trees. The leaf is similar in size and shape to that of the mastic tree [lentisco], somewhat larger and whitish. It produces small pods about a finger's length, slender and dry, except that near the stem they are somewhat thicker, as if they contained a chickpea inside. Each of these little pods resembles in shape and form the wing of a butterfly. Del guayroro

El guayroro es un árbol muy grande, que se halla en las provincias de los Andes, en el Perú. Echa unas vainas o canutos al modo de los de la cañafístola, en cuya cavidad se hallan unas pepitas más redondas, aunque llanas y lisas, de color de un fino coral; tiene cada una, una mancha negra que la hermosea. Estiman mucho estas pepitas los indios, afirmando valer contra el
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCI

On the Guayroro

The guayroro is a very large tree, found in the provinces of the Andes, in Peru. It produces pods or tubes in the manner of those of the cassia fistula [cañafístola], in whose cavity are found seeds that are rather round, though flat and smooth, the color of fine coral; each one bears a black spot that adorns it. The Indians hold these seeds in high esteem, asserting that they are effective against heart ailments and melancholy, the powder being taken in wine or orange-blossom water in a dose of just over half a dram [sic]. Beyond this, they say that wearing a string of them around the neck so that it rests upon the chest is beneficial against sorrows of the heart, and that they strengthen the sight and the brain.

CHAPTER XCIX
On the Sogue

The tree that the Indians of Peru call sogue is given the name sauce [willow] by the Spaniards, because it resembles that tree. Its leaves, bark, and flowers are astringent [estípticas]; a decoction of the leaves with wine is beneficial for leg sores, and when boiled with milk and used as a bath, it relieves pains and the nodules of gout. A decoction of the said leaves, mixed with pomegranate juice and oil, relieves earache when a few warm drops are instilled into the ears. A decoction made with a little alum [alumbre] of the leaves, bark, and flowers strengthens the teeth and gums, and is used against chilblains [sabañones] when applied as a bath. De las granadas

Y la razón es porque las más vinieron juntamente con los primeros

On Pomegranates

On the Tipa

The native Indians of the province of Charcas, in Peru, call tipa a very large and beautiful tree, broad-crowned, with green leaves throughout the year; some specimens grow as large as walnut trees. The leaf is similar in size and shape to that of the mastic tree [lentisco], somewhat larger and whitish. It produces small pods about a finger's length, slender and dry, except that near the stem they are somewhat thicker, as if they contained a chickpea inside. Each of these little pods resembles in shape and form the wing of a butterfly. De los salmonados, guavinas, dihachu, vermejuelos, barbos, bacallao, corvinas, peje-ángelo y jibia

Estas nueve especies de pescados se crían en esta mar del Sur, aunque no son tan comunes como otros. El bacallao es menor que el de España, porque no se halla mayor que de una tercia y es raro el que se mata. El peje-ángelo tiene el cuero muy duro y áspero, del cual usan los carpint
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVII

On the salmonados [salmon-trout], guavinas, dihachu, vermejuelos [small red fish], barbels, bacallao [cod], corvinas, angel-fish, and cuttlefish

These nine species of fish are found in this South Sea, although they are not as common as others. The bacallao [cod] is smaller than that of Spain, for none is found larger than a third of a vara [approximately 28 cm], and it is rarely caught. The peje-ángelo [angel-fish] has a very tough and rough skin, which carpenters and sculptors use for scraping wood. The cuttlefish here does not have the shell [cuttlebone] that the Spanish one has; it is half a braza [approximately 84 cm] in length.

CAPITULO XV
De varios pedernales

En todas partes, señaladamente en las sierras y tierras frías, se hallan muchas diferencias de pedernales finos, los cuales conocían muy bien y estimaban los indios, aunque no para sacar fuego: pero usaban dellos en lugar de cuchillos y otras herramientas. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XV
On Various Flints

Everywhere, and especially in the mountain ranges and cold lands, one finds many varieties of fine flints [pedernales], which the Indians knew well and held in high esteem — not, however, for striking fire, but rather for use in place of knives and other tools. Flints of every color are found, and there is one kind of stone that resembles flint, as red as coral, much prized by the Indians, which they call mulk; from it they make strings of beads, which the Indian women wear around their necks as adornment. Among the river pebbles and those along the sea-coast, many are found that are perfect flints; among these are certain very hard pebbles brought from the Guayaquil River, of a dark yellow color. De la vadea

En la ciudad y provincia de Guayaquil, diócesis de Quito, llaman los españoles vadea a una especie de apincolia [sic] que allí nace, muy parecida en sus hojas, flor y fruto al tumbo. CHAPTER XV
On the vadea

In the city and province of Guayaquil, in the diocese of Quito, the Spaniards call vadea a species of passionflower vine [apincolia, sic] that grows there, very similar in its leaves, flower, and fruit to the tumbo. It is as large as a medium-sized gourd, about one-third of a vara [roughly 11 inches] in length, and some are larger; it is oval in shape, yellow on the exterior, with a tender rind like that of a citron [cidra], two fingers thick, in the manner of a melon, with white and tender flesh, containing many seeds inside like those of a granadilla [passionfruit], but somewhat larger, and a watery, sweet juice with a hint of a pleasant tartness [agrete sabroso], amounting to about a quartillo [roughly a quarter pint]. CAPITULO LIX
De los piñones de purgar

El árbol que lleva los piñones de purgar es pequeño, de hasta dos estados de alto; tiene todo el tronco nudoso, las ramas recogidas y muy copado; la hoja, en la hechura, tira algo a la de la higuera, pero es mucho más pequeña y poco mayor que la del manzano; no tiene las puntas hendidas como la de la higuera, ni es áspera, sino lisa, blanda y las orillas reto
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LIX
On the Purging Nuts

The tree that bears the purging nuts [piñones de purgar] is small, reaching up to two fathoms [estados] in height; its trunk is entirely knotted, its branches gathered inward, and it is very bushy. The leaf in its shape resembles somewhat that of the fig tree, but it is much smaller—only slightly larger than that of the apple tree; it does not have the notched points of the fig leaf, nor is it rough, but rather smooth and soft, with curled edges. This tree produces a fruit the size of an apricot, which, when ripe, resembles it in both color and shape. It has a tender, leathery rind that is yellow on the outside and gradually turns black as it dries. CAPITULO LXXXIX

De la vilca

En el Perú llaman vilca a un árbol de la grandeza de un olivo, de hoja menuda, muy parecida a la del guarango, de verde más oscuro. Es árbol copado y de buen parecer. Produce unas vainas enjutas, como algarrobas, de una tercia de largo y dos dedos de ancho, y en ellas una pepita del tamaño y delgadeza de medio real, la cáscara lisa, de un color leonado oscuro y muy de
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXIX

On the Vilca

In Peru, the name vilca is given to a tree of the size of an olive tree, with small leaves very similar to those of the guarango [Caesalpinia spinosa], but of a darker green. It is a broad-crowned, handsome tree. It produces dry pods, like carob pods, one third of a vara in length and two fingers in width, and within them a seed [pepita] the size and thinness of half a real [a small silver coin], with a smooth husk of a dark tawny color and very thin. The substance inside these seeds is yellow and bitter like aloe [acíbar]. The Indians hold them in great esteem on account of their medicinal properties. CAPITULO CXV

Del guachapelí

El guachapelí es un árbol que sólo nace en tierras calientes; no crece muy alto, porque no sube derecho, sino que echa el tronco torcido y encorvado y muchas y muy gruesas ramas. Su hoja es pequeña como la de la alfalfa. Es árbol silvestre infructífero, pero de muy buena madera para labrar, de la cual se hacen comúnmente los corvatones y costillas de los navíos; y par
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXV

On the Guachapelí

The guachapelí is a tree that grows only in warm lowland regions [tierras calientes]. It does not grow very tall, because it does not rise straight up; rather, it sends out its trunk twisted and curved, with many very thick branches. Its leaf is small, like that of alfalfa. It is a wild tree that bears no fruit, but yields very good timber for working. From this timber, the knees [corvatones] and ribs of ships are commonly made. In order to obtain pieces suitable for this purpose, the trunk is cut one or two varas [a vara being roughly 33 inches] above the ground, and from that junction together with an equal length of the root, a ship's knee is fashioned. CAPITULO LXXXII
De la zarzaparrilla

A la yerba llamada zarzaparrilla pusieron este nombre los españoles, porque sale de su nacimiento como zarza. Echa por los pimpollos y más partes de sus ramos unas pequeñas hojas. Nace en muchas partes de las Indias y háyla de diferentes especies; pero la mejor de todas y donde nace gran cantidad es en el Perú, en los términos de la ciudad de Guayaquil y en la
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXII
On Sarsaparilla

The Spaniards gave the herb called sarsaparilla [zarzaparrilla] this name because it emerges from the ground like a bramble [zarza]. From its shoots and along most parts of its branches it puts forth small leaves. It grows in many parts of the Indies and is found in different species; but the best of all, and where it grows in great abundance, is in Peru, in the territory of the city of Guayaquil and on the island of Puná, which falls within its jurisdiction. It also grows abundantly in the province of Honduras, from where a great deal is sent to Spain. The root of this plant is already well known throughout the world for the admirable benefits found in it for curing various diseases.

CAPITULO LXXXII
De la guadgua

Las diferencias de cañas que nacen en este Nuevo Mundo no conocidas en España son muchas, entre las cuales no se halló la caña común de Europa, hasta que la trajeron los españoles; solamente haré aquí mención de las que yo he visto y que sirven a los moradores destas tierras en varios usos. Déstas es la guadgua, la mayor, a la cual llaman en este reino los españoles
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXII
On the Guadua

The varieties of canes [cañas] that grow in this New World and are unknown in Spain are many; among them, the common cane of Europe was not found until the Spaniards brought it over. I shall here mention only those that I myself have seen and that serve the inhabitants of these lands in various ways. Of these, the guadua is the largest, and the Spaniards of this kingdom call it the cane of Guayaquil, because all those consumed in this city of Lima and in many other parts of this kingdom are brought from that province. The guadua resembles the common cane in color and form, but differs greatly in its leaf and size, for it is so thick that in some parts its circumference [ruedo] measures three handspans [palmos], and at its mid-section more than two. CAPITULO XIV
Del palo

La fruta que llaman palo en el Perú no he visto en otra parte fuera deste reino. El árbol es de la grandeza de un mediano olivo, aunque los hay, de aquí para abajo, de diferente grandor, y los menores serán de poco más de un estado en alto. La hoja es como la del guayabo y muy parecida a la del manzano, salvo que es más ancha y retorcida o encorvada hacia el pezón. La fruta
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIV
Of the Palo

The fruit they call palo [literally 'stick' or 'tree'] in Peru I have not seen anywhere outside this kingdom. The tree is the size of a medium olive tree, though they vary somewhat in stature, and the smallest will be little more than a man's height [un estado, approx. 1.7 m] tall. The leaf resembles that of the guava tree and is very similar to that of the apple tree, except that it is broader and twisted or curved toward the stem. The fruit is small and round, very similar in size and shape to small pears; on the outside it is yellow, and on the inside, white. It has a somewhat sharp but not unpleasant smell; the skin is very thin and tender and does not separate from the flesh. corpus_links.title: The Balsa Tree and Its Uses
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXXIV
Of the Balsa Tree [palo de balsa]

If some timbers are prized for being rare and heavy, the soft and lightweight ones are not on that account to be rejected, since different uses require contrary qualities. Such is the wood we call in these Indies the balsa tree [palo de balsa], because good rafts [balsas] are made from it. The tree is large, and in some places grows taller than the biggest walnut trees; its leaf resembles that of the laurel; it bears no fruit, but only galls or little buds like those of the wand [vara]. Its timber is so soft and spongy that when this tree is cut, with every stroke the axe sinks entirely into the trunk. From its timbers, once dried, rafts are made in many parts of this realm for sailing the sea and navigating the rivers; which, being of so li

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_CXXV
corpus_links.title: The Chahuar Tree and Its Bark Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CXXV
Del chahuar

El chahuar parece tener algún parentesco con el palo de balsa. Es un árbol derecho, muy copado, no más grueso que el muslo, de madera muy liviana, la hoja poco mayor que la del naranjo y más delgada. Tiene la corteza gruesa y correosa, de la cual se hacen las sogas para encestar la coca, alpargatas y cuerdas de arcabuz.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXXV
On the chahuar

The chahuar appears to bear some kinship to the balsa tree [palo de balsa]. It is an upright tree, very full-crowned, no thicker than a thigh, with very lightweight wood; its leaf is somewhat larger than that of the orange tree and thinner. It has a thick and leathery bark, from which are made the ropes used for basketing [encesting] coca, sandals [alpargatas], and musket [arcabuz] cords.

corpus_links.title: Cañahuasopo — a rosemary-like shrub of the Collao region
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLII

Del cañahuasopo

El cañahuasopo es una mata tan parecida al romero en sus ramas y hojas, que fácilmente se engañara cualquiera teniéndolo por tal; sólo se diferencia en que sus hojas son un poco más cortas que las del romero y de un verde más blanquecino. Produce una flor pequeña y amarilla como la de la ruda; levántase de la tierra esta planta dos o tres codos; mascadas sus hojas s
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII

On the Cañahuasopo

The cañahuasopo is a shrub so closely resembling rosemary in its branches and leaves that anyone might easily mistake it for such; it differs only in that its leaves are somewhat shorter than those of rosemary and of a more whitish green. It produces a small yellow flower like that of rue [ruda]; the plant rises two or three cubits [codos] from the ground; when its leaves are chewed they are as bitter and pungent as those of rosemary; its branches, near the base, are of a black colour, so that they appear scorched. This plant grows in great abundance in the lands of the Collao [the Altiplano region around Lake Titicaca], where it is most commonly used as firewood, and it is called by this name in the Aymara language.

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_LXI
corpus_links.title: The Añaguaya shrub of the Collao region
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXI
De la añaguaya

La añaguaya es una mata espinosa a la canilla; levántase de la tierra de uno a dos codos; la hoja es de la forma que la de la sabina y algo más menuda; las espinas son menores que las del naranjo, derechas, agudas y blanquiscas. Da una florecita amarilla de ningún olor, del talle que la de la retama, un poquito menor. Nace esta planta en las provincias del Collao, en t
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXI
On the añaguaya

The añaguaya is a thorny shrub of slender [cane-like] form; it rises from the ground one to two cubits [roughly 18 to 36 inches]; the leaf is shaped like that of the savin [juniper] and somewhat smaller; the thorns are smaller than those of the orange tree, straight, sharp, and whitish. It produces a small yellow flower of no scent, in shape like that of the broom plant [retama], though a little smaller. This plant grows in the provinces of the Collao [the altiplano region around Lake Titicaca], in very cold country, and serves only as firewood.

CAPITULO CXXVIII
De la quínua

La quínua es un árbol del tamaño de un olivo y de ahí para abajo hasta no crecer más de un estado; tiene las ramas y tronco rojos, con la corteza muy delgada, que con facilidad se despide; echa las hojas de tres en tres, las cuales son poco más cortas que las del olivo, por dentro verdes y por fuera blanquecinas, las puntas botas y aserradas sutilmente por toda su re
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXXVIII
Of the Quínua

The quínua is a tree of the size of an olive tree, ranging downward to no more than one [estado, roughly one man's height] in growth. Its branches and trunk are red, with a very thin bark that peels away easily. It puts forth its leaves in groups of three; these leaves are somewhat shorter than those of the olive tree, green on the inner [upper] surface and whitish on the outer [lower] surface, with blunt tips and finely serrated all around their edges. It produces small flowers without scent or notable appearance; they are green and no larger than those of the olive tree. This tree is as hardy in withstanding the rigors of cold and frost as the quishuar [Buddleja incana], and thus these two kinds of trees alone grow in the harsh high moorlands [páramos] of P

De los tambos y chasquis, y el tributo que en servirlos daban los indios

On the tambos [way-stations] and chasquis [relay runners], and the tribute that the Indians rendered in serving them

The two royal roads of the Sierra [highlands] and the Llanos [coastal plains] that we have described passed through the largest settlements of the kingdom, which were the principal towns of the provinces — such as Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas, and other places in the Sierra, and on the Llanos: Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha, and other large towns. These towns were spaced along the highland road at intervals of twenty to thirty leagues from one another, more or less depending on the stretch, and along the coastal road there was one in each of the principal valleys. CHAPTER XXXIX

On Radishes, Turnips, and Other Vegetables of This Kind

All the herbs and plants that remain among those brought from Spain can be reduced to two categories, as follows: the first encompasses every sort of kitchen garden produce and greens (taking that term in its fullest extent), and the second comprises all other plants whose principal use is in medicine. Todo el imperio de los Incas, aunque tan extendido y compuesto de tantas y tan diversas naciones, era una sola república, regida por unas mismas leyes, fueros y costumbres, y observantes de una misma religión, ritos y ceremonias

CHAPTER XXIII

How the Incas Organized Newly Acquired Lands by Settling Them with Foreign Indians Called Mitimaes, and the Distinctions Among Them

The entire Inca empire, extensive as it was and composed of so many diverse nations, constituted a single commonwealth [república], governed by the same laws, statutes [fueros], and customs, and observing the same religion, rites, and ceremonies — notwithstanding that each of its provinces, before being brought under Inca obedience, had its own statutes and its own distinct manner of living and governing itself. CAPITULO V

Del segundo Inca, llamado Cinchi-Roca

Muerto Manco-Cápac, fue obedecido en rey su hijo mayor Cinchi-Roca, el cual era ya hombre de más de veinte años. Quedó tan bien industriado por su padre en las cosas del gobierno y república, y procedía con tan gran prudencia, que alcanzó ser amado de todos no menos que su padre, por el buen tratamiento que les hacía. Por principio de su reinado v

CHAPTER V

On the Second Inca, Called Cinchi-Roca

Upon the death of Manco-Cápac, his eldest son Cinchi-Roca was obeyed as king; he was already a man of more than twenty years of age. He had been so well instructed by his father in matters of government and statecraft [república], and conducted himself with such great prudence, that he came to be loved by all no less than his father had been, on account of the good treatment he showed them. At the outset of his reign he visited the settlements and villages of the valley of Cuzco, which were by then greatly enlarged and grown in buildings and people; and in the course of this visit he commanded that all should cultivate whatever lands they might need for sowing their potatoes [papas]; and thus cultivation spread as far as Cinga, which is a

De Viracocha-Inca, octavo rey

El Inca Viracocha, octavo rey del Cuzco, en poniéndose la borla, que era lo mismo que coronarse por rey, dio grandes muestras de valeroso príncipe, así en la paz como en la guerra; por lo cual fué muy amado y respetado de sus vasallos y temido de sus enemigos; porque la fama de su saber y valor llegó en breve a las provincias más apartadas. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI
Of Viracocha-Inca, Eighth King

The Inca Viracocha, eighth king of Cuzco, upon taking the [borla]—the royal fringe, equivalent to being crowned king—gave great demonstrations of a valiant prince, both in peace and in war; for which reason he was greatly loved and respected by his subjects and feared by his enemies, as the fame of his wisdom and valor quickly reached the most distant provinces. Since his father had not been a warrior, nor had he sought to conquer new lands, Viracocha found the military arts in a greatly diminished and disregarded state; and thus the first thing he set about doing was to restore them, offering great honors and rewards to those who wished to follow that calling. De Manco-Cápac, primer rey de los Incas

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XV
De la maca

En la sola provincia de Chinchaycocha, diócesis de Lima, se halla la raíz llamada maca en la lengua de los naturales de aquella tierra. Nace esta planta en lo más áspero y frío de la Sierra, donde no se da otra planta alguna de las que se cultivan para sustento de los hombres; que parece proveyó Dios a los indios de aquella provincia desta raíz, para que no quedasen sin ten
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XV
On Maca

Only in the province of Chinchaycocha [Chinchay cocha], diocese of Lima, is found the root called maca in the language of the native people of that land. This plant grows in the harshest and coldest parts of the Sierra [highland range], where no other plant cultivated for the sustenance of men can survive; it would seem that God provided the Indians of that province with this root so that they would not be left without some natural foodstuff of their own land. Maca serves them as bread, both fresh and dried—as they store it—throughout the entire year. De los tambos y chasquis, y el tributo que en servirlos daban los indios

Los dos caminos reales de Sierra y Llanos que habemos dicho pasaban por las poblaciones mayores del reino, que eran cabezas de provincias, como Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas y otros lugares de la Sierra, y de los Llanos Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha y otros pueblos grandes, estacionados dichos pueblos por el c
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXII

On the tambos [way-stations] and chasquis [relay runners], and the tribute that the Indians rendered in serving them

The two royal roads of the Sierra [highlands] and the Llanos [coastal plains] that we have described passed through the largest settlements of the kingdom, which were the principal towns of the provinces — such as Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas, and other places in the Sierra, and on the Llanos: Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha, and other large towns. These towns were spaced along the highland road at intervals of twenty to thirty leagues from one another, more or less depending on the stretch, and along the coastal road there was one in each of the principal valleys. CHAPTER VIII
On the Pururáuca Gods

CAPITULO XI
De Viracocha-Inca, octavo rey

El Inca Viracocha, octavo rey del Cuzco, en poniéndose la borla, que era lo mismo que coronarse por rey, dio grandes muestras de valeroso príncipe, así en la paz como en la guerra; por lo cual fué muy amado y respetado de sus vasallos y temido de sus enemigos; porque la fama de su saber y valor llegó en breve a las provincias más apartadas. Como su padre
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI
Of Viracocha-Inca, Eighth King

The Inca Viracocha, eighth king of Cuzco, upon taking the [borla]—the royal fringe, equivalent to being crowned king—gave great demonstrations of a valiant prince, both in peace and in war; for which reason he was greatly loved and respected by his subjects and feared by his enemies, as the fame of his wisdom and valor quickly reached the most distant provinces. Since his father had not been a warrior, nor had he sought to conquer new lands, Viracocha found the military arts in a greatly diminished and disregarded state; and thus the first thing he set about doing was to restore them, offering great honors and rewards to those who wished to follow that calling. corpus_links.label: NAM.WildBergamot
corpus_links.title: Wild Bergamot (Monarda) — 21 nations
corpus_links.original: [Monarda fistulosa — documented across 21 nations by Moerman]
corpus_links.translation: Wild bergamot (Monarda fistulosa) is documented across 21 North American nations including Blackfoot, Cheyenne, Cherokee, Iroquois, Ojibwe, and Potawatomi. Applications: respiratory infections, fever, digestive complaints, and topical antiseptic. The Blackfoot used it for respiratory infections; the Iroquois for fever; multiple nations used it as a wound antiseptic. Modern research: thymol and carvacrol — the same compounds that validate oregano and thyme in the Mediterranean and Andean traditions — are the primary active compounds. This is the North American parallel to Mediterranean oregano, an independent pharmacological discovery of the same thymol/carvacrol antimicrobial class.
corpus_links.preparation: Fresh or dried leaves decocted for internal use; leaves applied topically for antiseptic; steam inhalation
corpus_links.condition: Respiratory infections, fever, digestive complaints, wound antiseptic

corpus_links.label: EA.Gesho
corpus_links.title: Gesho (Rhamnus) — the Ethiopian hop
corpus_links.original: [Amharic] gesho — ye tej tera, ye tela tera
corpus_links.translation: Gesho (Rhamnus prinoides) — used both as the bittering agent in Ethiopian tej (honey wine) and tella (beer) and as a medicine for digestive complaints, liver conditions, and hypertension. The dual use as food flavoring and medicine is characteristic of Ethiopian plant knowledge. Gesho contains glycosides with documented anti-inflammatory and hepatoprotective activity. Its use as a traditional beer bitter predates European hops in this role by unknown centuries — establishing an independent discovery of bittering agent use in fermented beverages.
corpus_links.preparation: Leaves and stems dried and added to fermenting beverages; decoction for medicinal use
corpus_links.condition: Digestive complaints, liver conditions, hypertension, malaria

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXV

Cómo se hace el descubrimiento de minas

Respecto de haber en estas Indias tanto copia de minerales como queda dicho, y ocuparse en su labor y beneficio gran parte de la gente que las habita, hay en cada provincial establecidas leyes y ordenanzas que son obligados a guardar los mineros y por donde se dirimen los pleitos y diferencias que se levantan en los asientos y reales de minas
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXV

How the Discovery of Mines is Conducted

Given that there exists in these Indies so great an abundance of mineral deposits as has already been described, and that a large portion of the population occupies itself in their working and processing [beneficio], each province has established laws and ordinances which miners are obliged to observe, and by which the lawsuits and disputes [pleitos y diferencias] that arise in mining camps and settlements [asientos y reales de minas] concerning these matters are adjudicated. In accordance with these ordinances, in this kingdom of Peru it is lawful for all residents—whether native-born or foreign—to discover mines; and provided they pay the royal fifth [quinto] to the king, the mine they discover remains their own property. Del sogue

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCIX
On the Sogue

The tree that the Indians of Peru call sogue is given the name sauce [willow] by the Spaniards, because it resembles that tree. Its leaves, bark, and flowers are astringent [estípticas]; a decoction of the leaves with wine is beneficial for leg sores, and when boiled with milk and used as a bath, it relieves pains and the nodules of gout. A decoction of the said leaves, mixed with pomegranate juice and oil, relieves earache when a few warm drops are instilled into the ears. A decoction made with a little alum [alumbre] of the leaves, bark, and flowers strengthens the teeth and gums, and is used against chilblains [sabañones] when applied as a bath. Del achiote

En la Nueva España llaman achime a una pasta o panecillos colorados que hacen de las pepitas de cierto árbol y sirve para dar color al chocolate y a los guisados. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVIII
On Achiote

In New Spain they call achime [achiote] a paste or small reddish cakes made from the seeds of a certain tree, which serves to give color to chocolate and to stews. The tree is of the size of a medium orange tree, wide-crowned and of pleasant appearance; the leaf is like that of a walnut tree, except that it is narrow and long; the fruit it bears is a burr the size of a walnut, very similar to a mussel shell, rough on the outside from being covered with soft little spines that do not prick, brownish in color once dry, with a small point at the tip like that of a walnut; the husk is softer than that of the poppy; inside it has very red seeds the size of small grape pips, quite round. corpus_links.title: On the Names of the West Indies and the New World

CAPITULO PRIMERO

De los nombres destas Indias Occidentales y Nuevo Mundo

A las dos últimas partes de la tierra, que llamamos América y Tierra Austral (y son el sujeto propio de esta historia), doy principio desde este segundo libro; y porque habernos de tratar en él de la grandeza, sitio y naturaleza desde Nuevo Mundo, que comprehende las susodichas dos partes de la tierra y el gran archipiélago

CHAPTER ONE

On the Names of These West Indies and the New World

I begin this second book with the two last parts of the earth, which we call América and the Austral Land [Tierra Austral] (and which are the proper subject of this history). De las gallinas

En algunas de las historias de Indias que han salido a luz, he leído cómo en algunas tierras, entre los demás bastimentos que los indios ofrecían a los españoles, salían a presentar gallinas; de donde podría inferir alguno que no se trujeron de España, sino que las debía de haber en esta tierra. Pero creer esto sería manifiesto engaño; porque, aunque muchas veces hace
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI

On Chickens

In some of the histories of the Indies that have come to light, I have read how in certain lands, among the various provisions [bastimentos] that the Indians offered to the Spaniards, they would come out to present chickens; from which one might infer that these birds were not brought from Spain, but must have already existed in this land. But to believe this would be manifest error; for although the histories of the Indies frequently mention gallinas [chickens], one should not understand them to be speaking of our own kind, but rather of native birds of the land. Used as ordeal poison in judicial trials and by healers for eye conditions ('clouding of vision' = glaucoma). Daniel (1846) documented; Christison (1855) pharmacological study; Fraser (1863) isolated physostigmine (eserine). First glaucoma treatment: Laqueur (1876). Active compound: physostigmine — reversible acety
corpus_links.translation: Physostigma venenosum — the Calabar Bean, known in the Efik language as 'Esère', from Calabar, Nigeria. As recorded by Dalziel (1937), this plant was employed both as an ordeal poison administered during judicial trials and by traditional healers for eye conditions described as 'clouding of vision' — now identified as glaucoma. The plant was first formally documented by Daniel (1846); a pharmacological study was conducted by Christison (1855); and Fraser (1863) isolated the active alkaloid physostigmine (also called eserine). The first documented therapeutic use of physostigmine for glaucoma treatment was by Laqueur (1876). Active constituents: ginsenosides [steroidal saponins], with a distinct phytochemical profile compared to Asian P. ginseng — American ginseng exhibits a higher ratio of ginsenoside Rb1 relative to Rg1, which predominates in the Asian species. Multiple clinical trials have demonstrated: positive results for blood sugar regulation in Type 2 diabetes; modest positive results for cognitive function; and immune modulation. corpus_links.translation: Nicotiana rustica / N. tabacum — Tobacco (medicinal applications, treated here as distinct from ritual use). corpus_links.original: [Hierochloe odorata — Blackfoot, Ojibwe, Lakota documentation]
corpus_links.translation: Sweetgrass (Hierochloe odorata) — documented across Plains and Eastern Woodland nations for both ceremonial and medicinal use. The Blackfoot used it for colds and coughs; the Ojibwe for ceremonial smudging and respiratory conditions; the Lakota for wound healing. Sweetgrass smoke was documented as an antimicrobial fumigation — consistent with the documented antimicrobial activity of coumarin (the compound responsible for sweetgrass's distinctive vanilla-hay scent). This connects to the archive's documentation of Tonka bean (coumarin source) in South American traditions — an independent discovery of the same antimicrobial compound from a different plant.

corpus_links.translation: Niyog-niyogan (Quisqualis indica Linn.) — Family: Combretaceae. Source: Quisumbing (1951), pp. 267–269. corpus_links.translation: Pom (Bursera copallifera / B. bipinnata) — Maya Copal Resin. From the Ritual of the Bacabs (translated by Roys): 'Ix-pom, ix-cacao, ix-ya-che — copal, cacao tree, sapodilla tree — these are the medicines of the great healers.' In Maya culture, copal (pom) served simultaneously as a ritual substance and a medicinal one — a distinction the tradition did not draw as sharply as Western medicine does. Documented medicinal uses include: antimicrobial wound treatment (resin applied directly to infected wounds); pain relief (smoke inhaled for headache); and treatment of respiratory conditions (resin burned in an enclosed space and the smoke inhaled). Of Manco Cápac, First King of the Incas

De los perros

Solas dos castas de perros, y muy diferentes de los nuestros, había en esta tierra a la entrada en ella de los españoles. Después acá se han traído de España todas las diferencias de perros que hay allá, de que al presente hay gran cantidad en todas las Indias. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX
On Dogs

There were only two breeds of dogs in this land at the time of the Spaniards' arrival, and they were very different from our own. Since then, all the varieties of dogs found in Spain have been brought over, and at present there are great numbers of them throughout all the Indies. The first Spaniards arrived in this kingdom of Peru in the year 1531. In the earliest conquests that the Spaniards carried out in the islands of the Windward [Barlovento] and in other provinces of Tierra Firme [the mainland], they made great use of dogs in the wars they waged against the Indians; for, once trained, these dogs were most useful, especially in rough and wooded terrain, where, the enemy being light on their feet, the Spaniards could not pursue them. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LVIII

De la vicuña

La vicuña es un animal silvestre menor que la llama, y muy parecido a ella en su disposición y hechura; es del tamaño de una cabra, más delgada y crecida de piernas, pati-hendida, de pescuezo largo y delgado, y la parte alta del cuerpo y mayor parte dél de un color rubio que tira a leonado claro, con el vientre blanco y parte inferior del pecho. Son todas las vicuñas
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LVIII

On the Vicuña

The vicuña is a wild animal smaller than the llama, and very similar to it in its constitution and form. It is the size of a goat [cabra], slender and long-legged, cloven-hoofed, with a long, thin neck, and the upper part of the body—and the greater part of it—is a tawny color tending toward a light leonine hue, with a white belly and lower chest. All vicuñas are this color. They travel in herds, though they are often seen grazing singly. They are found only in the mountain ranges of Peru, in the coldest high plateaus [páramos], among the snow-covered cordilleras. They are the swiftest and most agile animals known; and although they are hunted with dogs, they are not caught in the first run—rather, the dogs watch which way the vicuña runs and either head it of

CHAPTER XXXV

On the Great Subjection and Dominion the Incas Had Acquired Over Their Vassals, and the Fear and Reverence with Which the Latter Obeyed and Served Them

Although the government of the Incas, considered in light of the condition and capacity of the Indians (who are all a servile people, obeying and attending to their obligations more out of fear and severity than out of love and gentleness), appeared sound and good, yet when examined on its own merits and measured against free peoples possessed of reason and civil order [policía], it was the most unjust and tyrannical that can be imagined—in which the Incas, for all that they were men of great judgment, did not fail to reveal themselves as barbarians toward their subjects. CAPITULO XXXII

De los tambos y chasquis, y el tributo que en servirlos daban los indios

Los dos caminos reales de Sierra y Llanos que habemos dicho pasaban por las poblaciones mayores del reino, que eran cabezas de provincias, como Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas y otros lugares de la Sierra, y de los Llanos Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha y otros pueblos grandes, estacionados dichos pueblos por el c
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXII

On the tambos [way-stations] and chasquis [relay runners], and the tribute that the Indians rendered in serving them

The two royal roads of the Sierra [highlands] and the Llanos [coastal plains] that we have described passed through the largest settlements of the kingdom, which were the principal towns of the provinces — such as Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas, and other places in the Sierra, and on the Llanos: Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha, and other large towns. These towns were spaced along the highland road at intervals of twenty to thirty leagues from one another, more or less depending on the stretch, and along the coastal road there was one in each of the principal valleys. In these towns there were royal lodgings [aposentos reales], tambos, and storehouses [depósitos]

CAPITULO IV

Del dios Viracocha, que era tenido de los indios por supremo señor y hacedor de todo

En medio de las tinieblas espesas de la ignorancia, no dejó la luz de la razón de obrar algo en estos indios; porque, alumbrados della, vinieron a alcanzar y creer que había un Dios Criador universal de todas las cosas y Soberano Señor, y gobernador dellas; aunque fue tan corta y oscura esta noticia,
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IV

On the god Viracocha, who was regarded by the Indians as supreme lord and maker of all things

Amidst the thick darkness of ignorance, the light of reason did not cease to produce some effect in these Indians; for, illumined by it, they came to grasp and believe that there was a universal God, Creator of all things, Sovereign Lord and Governor thereof; though this knowledge was so limited and obscure that they did not even possess a proper word with which to name him. All the names they gave him were metaphorical [translaticios], as I shall presently explain. De Tupac-Inca-Yupanqui, décimo rey

corpus_links.translation:
