CAPITULO LX

De la guachanca

Por parecerse las raíces desta yerba a las papas, las llaman los españoles popillas de purga. Crece la guachanca un palmo; hace los ramos tan delgados y más que el pezón de la hoja de la vid, redondos, lisos y tiernos, con pocas hojas hasta la cumbre, en que echa tres o cuatro juntas, las cuales, en el tamaño y talle, son semejantes a las del trébol. Su flor es tan pe
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LX

On the Guachanca

Because the roots of this herb resemble potatoes [papas], the Spaniards call it 'purgative little potato' [popillas de purga]. The guachanca grows to a hand's breadth [palmo] in height; it produces branches as slender as, or more so than, the stalk of a grape leaf, round, smooth, and tender, with few leaves up to the top, where it puts forth three or four together, which in size and shape resemble those of clover. Its flower is as small as that of clover or mustard, followed by seeds that are small triangular granules, about the size of coriander seeds. The roots are like truffles [criadillas de tierra], white, with a thin, brownish skin. Both from the root of this plant and from its broken branches there flows a white milky sap, similar to that of the spurge

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XII
De los zapotes.

Los zapotes son propios de la Nueva España, adonde se hallan cinco diferencias dellos; los mejores son los colorados. El árbol que los lleva es grande y copado como el mamey, con los cogollos muy poblados de hoja; ésta es larga un palmo, lisa, tiesa, de un verde oscuro y más ancha al cabo que en medio. La fruta es del tamaño de un membrillo y aun como una grande cidra
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XII
On Zapotes.

The zapotes are native to New Spain, where five varieties of them are found; the best are the red ones [colorados]. The tree that bears them is large and spreading [copado], like the mamey, with the young shoots [cogollos] very densely leafed; the leaf is a palm's length [approx. 8 inches] long, smooth, stiff, of a dark green, and wider at the tip than in the middle. The fruit is the size of a quince and even as large as a big citron [cidra], spindle-shaped [ahusada], with a thin and tender skin; the flesh is very red and soft [text breaks off].

Such fine and well-glazed pottery is produced here that the wares of Talavera are not missed, for in recent years craftsmen have taken to imitating Chinese porcelain, and the result is very similar to it — particularly that which is made in the Puebla de los Ángeles in New Spain and in this city of Lima, which is of very fine glaze and colors. Likewise, very handsome glazed tiles [azulejos] are made here, which formerly used to be brought from Spain; though it is true that those made here do not achieve quite so fine a range of colors.

CAPITULO XVIII

De los membrillos

La fruta que con verdad se puede decir que es mejor en esta tierra que en España son los membrillos, porque todos, generalmente, son buenos, muy olorosos, tiernos, jugosos, sin nudos y muy livianos. Y la causa de ser tan buenos, debe de ser la humedad de la tierra que remite la aspereza y acedía que suelen tener los que nacen en España. Los hay de todas las difer
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVIII

On Quinces

The fruit that can truly be said to be better in this land than in Spain is the quince [membrillo], for all of them, generally speaking, are good — very fragrant, tender, juicy, free of knots, and very light. The reason they are so fine must be the moisture of the soil, which softens the harshness and sourness that quinces grown in Spain usually have. Every variety found there is represented here, and one more besides: a graft that has been made in this kingdom of quince onto lúcuma, a fruit native to these parts; of the lúcuma's traits, what these grafted quinces took most is its very deep yellow color. corpus_links.original: Capítulo IX — conviene a saber, que todas estas gentes descienden de un linaje, queda deshecha la opinión que llevaba proceder de muchas naciones del viejo mundo. Ni obsta alegar en contrario la dificultad, que a prima faz se ofrece, de haberse poblado tantas y tan extendidas tierras de un solo linaje de hombres, pues de no más de uno solo se ha venido a henchir todo el mundo de las innumerables g
corpus_links.translation: Chapter IX — that is to say, that all these peoples descend from a single lineage, which disposes of the opinion holding that they derived from many nations of the Old World. Nor does it constitute a valid objection to cite, as an apparent difficulty, the fact that such vast and extensive lands were populated by a single lineage of men; for from no more than one single stock has the entire world come to be filled with the innumerable peoples who inhabit it today. And very readily, and without any difficulty whatsoever, the first men to set foot in this land—however few in number they may have been—could, together with their descendants, have spread out and occupied it all in the course of time. Del hospital de San Diego de los hermanos de San Juan de Dios

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXX

On the Hospital of San Diego of the Brothers of Saint John of God

In the year fifteen hundred and ninety-four, this hospital was founded under the dedication of Saint Diego [San Diego de Alcalá], and two wealthy persons, husband and wife, named Don Cristóbal Sánchez Bilbao and Doña María de Esquivel, residents of this city, endowed it with their estate. Having had no children, they appointed the poor of Christ as their heirs. In the year sixteen hundred and six, the Brothers of Saint John of God entered this kingdom and city to establish their order, and they took charge of the hospital in order to cure and serve the poor sick, as their rule professes. CAPITULO XXXI
Del hospital de San Pedro

En el hospital de San Pedro no se curan más pobres que clérigos de orden sacro, el cual tuvo este principio: saliéndose un día a pasear tres o cuatro clérigos juntos por el barrio de San Lázaro, hallaron un sacerdote enfermo en un rancho de un indio, tan desamparado, que no tenía más cama que una barbacoa o zarzo de cañas, ni otro regalo que un poco de maíz
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXI
On the Hospital of San Pedro

At the Hospital of San Pedro, none but poor clergymen of holy orders [clérigos de orden sacro] are treated. Its origin was as follows: one day, three or four clergymen went out together for a walk through the neighborhood [barrio] of San Lázaro, where they found a sick priest in the hut of an Indian, in so wretched a condition that he had no bed other than a barbacoa or zarzo [a raised platform or frame of canes], nor any other comfort than a little maize that the Indian gave him. Moved to compassion, they took him to be treated at the Hospital of San Andrés, where they cared for him throughout his illness. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIV

That the Incas resettled into towns the peoples they subjected, and the order they imposed upon them

It has already been stated above how the Peruvian Indians, before being governed by the Inca kings, did not have organized towns laid out [trazados] in the form and manner of our own towns, but rather lived in small hamlets [caseríos] of sparse population, most of them situated on hills and ridges [cerros y collados] in order to defend themselves from the raids that they carried out upon one another. I say now that upon the Inca placing [a people] under his domin[ion —]

CAPITULO LXXXI
De la quina-quina

Llaman en el Perú a un árbol grande y hermoso como un melo o olivo; la hoja, del tamaño y talle que la del limón ceutí; el tronco es algo colorado, resinoso y aromático. Es árbol caliente en el segundo grado, estíptico y seco y de suave olor. Echa unas pepitas por semilla del tamaño de almendras, de color amarillo y de sustancia oleaginosa, que con fragancia huele
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXXI
On the Quina-Quina

In Peru they give this name to a large and handsome tree resembling a quince or olive; the leaf is the size and shape of that of the Ceuti lemon [a variety of citron]; the trunk is somewhat reddish, resinous, and aromatic. The tree is hot in the second degree [of the Galenic humoral scale], astringent [estíptico], dry, and of a pleasant odor. It produces seeds the size of almonds, yellow in color and of an oily substance, which smell agreeably with a fine fragrance; these too are hot and astringent in the second degree, and dry in more than the first. corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::SEXTO::cap_XXIII
corpus_links.title: The Mamón of Cartagena
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXIII
Del mamón de Cartagena

En la provincia de Cartagena se da una fruta que allí nombran mamón; es del tamaño de un limón ceutí, redonda, verde por de fuera; la cáscara, delgada y correosa como de limón; en el interior, está llena de una sustancia muy aguanosa, como la de las uvas, de sabor apetitoso, agridulce, que se come chupándola. Los huesecillos son unas pepitas blancas y redonda
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIII
Of the Mamón of Cartagena

In the province of Cartagena there grows a fruit that is locally called mamón. It is the size of a Ceuta lemon [a small variety of lemon], round, and green on the outside; the rind is thin and leathery like that of a lemon. Inside, it is filled with a very watery pulp, similar to that of grapes, with an appealing bittersweet flavor, which is eaten by sucking it. The small seeds [huesecillos] are little white, round kernels the size of hazelnuts, which are eaten toasted and have the flavor of acorns.

CAPITULO XVII
De la jiquima

La jiquima es una raíz tan gruesa por la cabeza como la pierna, de hechura de nabo, muy corta en proporción de su grosor, porque no tiene de largo más de un palmo, y se remata en punta; por de fuera, es parda, y por de dentro, blanca, con unas pintas rojas como jaspeado, muy aguanosa y dulce. Las ramas desta planta se extienden por la tierra; echa unos vastaguillos com
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVII
On the Jiquima

The jiquima is a root as thick at the crown as a man's leg, shaped like a turnip, very short in proportion to its girth, for it is no longer than a hand-span [palmo], tapering to a point at the end. On the outside it is brownish, and on the inside white, with reddish specks like jasper [jaspeado], very watery and sweet. The branches of this plant spread along the ground; it sends out small shoots like rushes; the leaves are the size of mallow leaves, with three lobed [hendidas] points; the seeds it produces are grains like kidney beans [frisoles] enclosed in small pods like those of broad beans. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XX

Del maguey

El nombre genérico de maguey se atribuye a cierta especie dél, que es el más común y de que se hace el cáñamo de la tierra. Es una mata del talle de la zabila, que echa muchas hojas o pencas a la redonda, todas nacidas del tronco junto a la tierra; las cuales son delgadas, enjutas, correosas, acanaladas, de un verde escuro, con unas pequeñas espinas en las orillas, de cuat
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XX

On the Maguey

The generic name maguey is applied to a certain species of this plant, which is the most common and from which the hemp [cáñamo] of this land is made. It is a shrub of the form of the aloe [zabila], which puts forth many leaves or fronds [pencas] all around, all growing from the base near the ground. These leaves are thin, dry, tough, channeled, of a dark green color, with small spines along the edges, more than four fingers wide, and from one to four feet tall. A great many leaves grow from each plant, and as they grow and rise upward they spread outward, so that the plant with its fronds takes on the shape of a large bell with its mouth turned upward. CAPITULO IV
Del guanábano

La fruta llamada guanábana en lengua de la isla Española da el nombre de guanábano al árbol que la produce; el cual es mediano, de la grandeza de un durazno, copado y de mejor parecer que su fruta merece. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IV
On the Guanábano

The fruit called guanábana in the language of the island of Hispaniola [Isla Española] gives its name to the tree that produces it. The tree is of medium size, roughly as large as a peach tree [durazno], with a spreading crown and of finer appearance than its fruit deserves. Its leaf is slightly larger than that of the orange tree, smooth and stiff, not as sharply pointed, and of a darker green. The fruit is as large as a pineapple [piña], and some are as large as medium-sized melons, with a thin and tender skin of a green color tending toward yellow, with small protruding points in the manner of scales, yet flat and smooth like those of the pineapple. CAPITULO XXX

De la guazuma

Dan este nombre en la isla Española a un árbol llamado de los españoles moral de las Indias, porque se parece al moral de España; el cual es grande y tiene la hoja muy semejante a la del moral, un poco mayor y muy verde, como la del saúco. La madera de este árbol es fofa, tierna y tan vedriosa que subiendo en él con poco peso, se desgajan las ramas. Las moras son redon
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXX

On the guazuma

This name is given in Hispaniola [isla Española] to a tree called by the Spaniards the 'moral de las Indias' [mulberry of the Indies], because it resembles the mulberry [moral] of Spain. It is a large tree, with a leaf very similar to that of the mulberry, somewhat larger and very green, like that of the elder [saúco]. The wood of this tree is spongy, soft, and so brittle that when one climbs it with even a small load, the branches snap off. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LIX
De los piñones de purgar

El árbol que lleva los piñones de purgar es pequeño, de hasta dos estados de alto; tiene todo el tronco nudoso, las ramas recogidas y muy copado; la hoja, en la hechura, tira algo a la de la higuera, pero es mucho más pequeña y poco mayor que la del manzano; no tiene las puntas hendidas como la de la higuera, ni es áspera, sino lisa, blanda y las orillas reto
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LIX
On the Purging Nuts

The tree that bears the purging nuts [piñones de purgar] is small, reaching up to two fathoms [estados] in height; its trunk is entirely knotted, its branches gathered inward, and it is very bushy. The leaf in its shape resembles somewhat that of the fig tree, but it is much smaller—only slightly larger than that of the apple tree; it does not have the notched points of the fig leaf, nor is it rough, but rather smooth and soft, with curled edges. This tree produces a fruit the size of an apricot, which, when ripe, resembles it in both color and shape. It has a tender, leathery rind that is yellow on the outside and gradually turns black as it dries. corpus_links.title: The Higüero Tree (Calabash Tree)
corpus_links.original:
CAPÍTULO CXI
Del higüero

Higüero se llama en la lengua que tenían los indios de la isla Española un árbol mediano como un granado. Es de mucha hoja, la cual se parece a la del granado, salvo que es más ancha y luenga y lo ancho lo tiene en el remate, de donde va ensangostando hasta el pezón; es lisa, tiesa y retorcida o crespa. La madera de este árbol es recia y correosa, parecida a la del granad
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXI
On the Higüero

"Higüero" is the name given in the language of the Indians of Hispaniola [isla Española] to a medium-sized tree resembling a pomegranate tree. It has abundant foliage, which resembles that of the pomegranate, except that the leaves are wider and longer, with their greatest width at the tip, from which they taper down to the stalk [pezón]; they are smooth, stiff, and twisted or curly. The wood of this tree is hard and tough, similar to that of the pomegranate; from it many things are made, particularly saddle-frames [fustes de sillas]. Its fruit consists of small gourds [calabazas] with very thin shells, some round and others elongated. The largest are commonly about the size of a man's head, and from there downward to no larger than a hen's egg. Many things are

corpus_links.title: Viracocha-Inca, Eighth King of Cuzco: Early Reign, Conquests, and Marriage
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XI
De Viracocha-Inca, octavo rey

El Inca Viracocha, octavo rey del Cuzco, en poniéndose la borla, que era lo mismo que coronarse por rey, dio grandes muestras de valeroso príncipe, así en la paz como en la guerra; por lo cual fué muy amado y respetado de sus vasallos y temido de sus enemigos; porque la fama de su saber y valor llegó en breve a las provincias más apartadas. Como su padre
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI
Of Viracocha-Inca, Eighth King

The Inca Viracocha, eighth king of Cuzco, upon taking the [borla]—the royal fringe, equivalent to being crowned king—gave great demonstrations of a valiant prince, both in peace and in war; for which reason he was greatly loved and respected by his subjects and feared by his enemies, as the fame of his wisdom and valor quickly reached the most distant provinces. Since his father had not been a warrior, nor had he sought to conquer new lands, Viracocha found the military arts in a greatly diminished and disregarded state; and thus the first thing he set about doing was to restore them, offering great honors and rewards to those who wished to follow that calling. As it is common in all nations that subjects embrace whatever they see their prince inc

CAPITULO XXXVI
Del oro

El oro ha tenido siempre el primado entre todos los metales, cuya resplandeciente vista de tal manera alegra y aficiona a sí a los hombres, que casi no se ha hallado nación en el mundo tan rústica y bárbara que no lo conozca, busque y estime. Críase copiosamente en todas estas Indias, cuyos naturales lo labraban y se servían de él en varios usos, aunque no en tantos como no
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVI
On Gold

Gold has always held primacy among all metals; its brilliant appearance so gladdens men and draws them to it that scarcely any nation in the world has been found so rustic and barbarous as not to know it, seek it, and prize it. It is produced in abundance throughout all these Indies, whose native peoples worked it and made use of it for various purposes, though not for as many as we do. The chieftains [caciques] and nobles of Peru possessed many pieces of gold, some of which their descendants still own today, while most have come into the hands of Spaniards. CAPÍTULO XXVI
De las pulgas y niguas

Todas las tierras yuncas y medianamente calientes deste Nuevo Mundo son muy infestadas de pulgas, de las cuales se hallan dos diferencias: las unas son las comunes, que aunque son molestas, no tan ofensivas como las segundas. Engéndrase a tiempos tanta copia dellas, aun en tierras templadas, que dan mucha molestia así a los hombres como a los animales caseros,
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVI
On Fleas and Chigoe Fleas [niguas]

All the lowland [yunca] and moderately warm regions of this New World are greatly infested with fleas, of which two varieties are found: the first are the common kind, which, though troublesome, are not as harmful as the second. At times such a multitude of them breeds, even in temperate lands, that they cause great annoyance to men as well as to domestic and even wild animals. For they are harbored not only by cats, dogs, mice, and domesticated guanacos, but also by wild rats and field mice; and the abundance produced by these wild hosts further swells the populations born in settled areas.

The other sort of flea we call niguas [chigoe fleas], giving them the common name that the Indians of Hispaniola used for fleas in general. The niguas,

corpus_links.title: Priests and Their Offices Among the Inca

CAPITULO XXXIII
De los sacerdotes y oficios que tenían

Debajo del nombre de sacerdotes se han de entender todos los hombres que estaban dedicados al culto de sus falsos dioses y entendían en ofrecerles sacrificios y hacer cuantas supersticiones entre ellos se usaban; y como éstas eran muchas, así también lo eran las suertes que había de sacerdotes. Porque, primeramente, unos entendían en la guard
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIII
Of the Priests and the Offices They Held

Under the name of priests are to be understood all men who were devoted to the worship of their false gods and were occupied in offering sacrifices to them and performing whatever superstitions were practiced among them. And since these were many, so too were the various kinds of priests. First, some were engaged in the guardianship and ministry of the huacas [sacred shrines or idols], offering the sacrifices ordained by their rite—both ordinary and extraordinary—and these were sustained by the revenues of religion. corpus_links.title: Chapter LVIII: On the Vicuña
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LVIII

De la vicuña

La vicuña es un animal silvestre menor que la llama, y muy parecido a ella en su disposición y hechura; es del tamaño de una cabra, más delgada y crecida de piernas, pati-hendida, de pescuezo largo y delgado, y la parte alta del cuerpo y mayor parte dél de un color rubio que tira a leonado claro, con el vientre blanco y parte inferior del pecho. Son todas las vicuñas
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LVIII

On the Vicuña

The vicuña is a wild animal smaller than the llama, and very similar to it in its constitution and form. It is the size of a goat [cabra], slender and long-legged, cloven-hoofed, with a long, thin neck, and the upper part of the body—and the greater part of it—is a tawny color tending toward a light leonine hue, with a white belly and lower chest. All vicuñas are this color. They travel in herds, though they are often seen grazing singly. They are found only in the mountain ranges of Peru, in the coldest high plateaus [páramos], among the snow-covered cordilleras. They are the swiftest and most agile animals known; and although they are hunted with dogs, they are not caught in the first run—rather, the dogs watch which way the vicuña runs and either head it of

Del soycosoyco

CHAPTER XXXVI
On the Soycosoyco

The soycosoyco is a small herb that appears to be a species of the roses or carnations [davdlinas, i.e., davelinas/clavellinas] of the Indies. It rises about one cubit [roughly half a meter] above the ground, putting forth many thin, round, smooth, tough, and somewhat reddish stems, and few leaves; these leaves are so small and fine that they resemble little cut threads of silk. It produces small yellow flowers, each having four petals no larger than those of the flower of rue [Ruta graveolens], which emerge from small, elongated buds resembling pine nuts; and after these flowers dry, they end in a tuft of fibers issuing from the same bud. De la hacagua guaní

Esta es una yerba de dos palmos en alto; tiene las hojas como las del lirio, algo más angostas, la flor purpúrea; las raíces son en gran cantidad y como los dedos de la mano y como zanahorias. Su temperamento es caliente y seco; el zumo de su raíz, echado en el oído, aprovecha para la sordera, y tomado en la boca, quita cualquiera dolor de muelas. El cocimiento
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXV

On the hacagua guaní

This is an herb reaching two palms [roughly 40 cm] in height; its leaves resemble those of the lily [lirio], though somewhat narrower, and its flower is purple. The roots are plentiful, shaped like the fingers of a hand and like carrots. Its temperament [complexion, in Galenic terms] is hot and dry. The juice of its root, dropped into the ear, is beneficial for deafness; and taken in the mouth, it relieves any toothache. A decoction [cocimiento] of these roots, taken on an empty stomach, counteracts urinary retention, provokes menstruation, and eases expectoration in pleuritic pains [dolores de costado]; and the roots, pounded and applied warm over the gout, relieve its pain.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CII

On the spider-herb [yerba de la araña]

The Spaniards gave this herb its name, derived from the effect it produces, which is the curing of bites from venomous spiders. It grows in uncultivated places, and in the valley of Lima a great deal of it is found near the port of Callao. It closely resembles thyme [tomillo] in size, branches, and leaves, except that it has no scent whatsoever. It is applied to a spider bite in the following manner: a decoction [cocimiento] is made from it, with which the site of the bite is washed very thoroughly, pressing it so that the matter [venom/fluid] is drawn out; the powdered form of this same herb is then applied to the wound, by which means marvellous cures are witnessed daily.

Del vihao

El vihao es una planta salvaje parecida a la taragontia, cuyas hojas son mayores, más delgadas y correosas que las de taragontia. Nace en tierras calientes, y en la provincia de Panamá y Nicaragua se hacen espesos bosques dellas. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXII
On the Vihao

The vihao is a wild plant resembling the taragontia [dragon arum or similar aroid], whose leaves are larger, thinner, and more leathery than those of the taragontia. It grows in hot lowland regions, and in the provinces of Panama and Nicaragua it forms dense thickets. It grows to a height of one or two estados [roughly six to twelve feet]; at the top of the stem, over a span of about one third of a vara [approximately eleven inches], its flower appears — consisting of small, stiff, reddish spathes [penquillas coloradas y tiesas], each one shaped like the large beak of a bird. CHAPTER XLII

On all the other herbs that have been brought from Spain up to the present

This chapter covers all the remaining herbs and plants that have been brought from Spain, which serve more for medicinal use than for other purposes, such as fennel [hinojo], aloe [zabila], dill [eneldo], viznaga [toothpick-weed], rue [ruda], poppies [adormideras], sage [salvia], and tarragon [taragontia]. corpus_links.label: EA.Teff
corpus_links.title: Teff — the ancient Ethiopian grain-medicine
corpus_links.original: [Amharic] teff — ye rist tera, ye lijoch tera
corpus_links.translation: Teff (Eragrostis tef) — indigenous Ethiopian grain documented as a therapeutic food for digestive weakness, diarrhea in children, and as a nutritive medicine during illness. The injera (fermented teff flatbread) is simultaneously the primary Ethiopian food and a fermented probiotic medicine. Teff is naturally gluten-free and has a low glycaemic index — now understood to explain traditional observations about its gentle digestive properties. The grain is endemic to Ethiopia, making this documentation culturally specific to East African traditional medicine.
corpus_links.preparation: Fermented as injera; grain porridge for illness; dried and ground for digestive preparations
corpus_links.condition: Digestive weakness, diarrhea (children), malnutrition, celiac-friendly nutrition

corpus_links.label: SA.Hoodia
corpus_links.title: Hoodia — the San hunger suppressant
corpus_links.original: [!Kung San oral tradition — documented by van der Post and Gericke]
corpus_links.translation: Hoodia gordonii — used by the San (Bushmen) to suppress hunger and thirst during long hunting expeditions across the Kalahari Desert. The San would cut a piece of the stem and chew it to eliminate hunger and thirst for extended periods. This practice was documented by anthropologists studying the San from the 1930s onwards. In the 1990s, the South African Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) identified P57 — the active compound — and licensed it to Unilever for development as a weight-loss drug. The subsequent dispute over benefit-sharing with the San community became one of the landmark cases in indigenous intellectual property rights under the Nagoya Protocol.
corpus_links.preparation: Fresh stem chewed directly during hunting expeditions
corpus_links.condition: Hunger suppression, thirst suppression, endurance during physical exertion

corpus_links.label: SA.Buchu
corpus_links.title: Buchu — the urinary medicine of the Cape
corpus_links.original: [Khoikhoi / Cape Malay oral tradition — documented from 1650s Dutch colonial records]
corpus_links.translation: Buchu (Agathosma betulina / A. crenulata) — used by the Khoikhoi people of the Cape for urinary tract conditions, digestive complaints, and as an antiseptic. The distinctive anise-blackcurrant smell of buchu made it recognizable to Dutch colonists who adopted it and exported it to Europe in the 17th century. Buchu became a listed medicine in the British Pharmacopoeia (1821) and was prescribed specifically for urinary tract infections — making it one of the few indigenous African plants that entered the European pharmacopoeia. Modern research confirms diosphenol (buchu camphor) has significant antimicrobial activity against urinary tract pathogens.
corpus_links.preparation: Leaves infused in brandy (buchu brandy) — both medicinal and commercial; leaves decocted in water
corpus_links.condition: Urinary tract infections, digestive complaints, antiseptic wound treatment

De la arena

CHAPTER XII
On Sand

There are various kinds of sand to be found in this land, both on the shores of the sea and of rivers, and in many other places on the surface and in the bowels of the earth. This variety is chiefly manifested in two respects: one is in color, and the other is in some sand being finer or coarser than another. From the grinding and washing of silver ores there results a great quantity of sand. On the seacoast of Pisco and Callao one finds much sand made of crushed and ground shells: it is white, and they mix it with lime for building construction. Beyond common sand, in many places one finds a fine, black sand [arenilla], which is customarily sprinkled over freshly written documents in place of bran [salvado], and there is so great a quantity of it in this kingdom that

CAPITULO XIII
De las papas

En toda la Sierra y tierra fría del Perú donde no se coge maíz ni las demás semillas y legumbres que se dan en tierras templadas y calientes, son las sementeras ordinarias que hacen los indios de unas raíces llamadas papas, del tamaño y hechura de criadillas de tierra; las cuales, verdes y secas, son mantenimiento tan general en el Perú, que la mitad de los indios dél n
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIII
On Potatoes

Throughout the highland and cold lands of Peru, where neither maize nor the other seeds and legumes that grow in temperate and warm regions are harvested, the ordinary crops that the Indians cultivate are certain roots called papas [potatoes], of the size and shape of truffles [criadillas de tierra]. Both fresh and dried, these are so universally consumed in Peru that half the Indians there have nothing else to eat. The plant grows to a height of two hand-spans [palmos]; its leaves are so continuous and closely set along the stem that they appear to be a single leaf with many points, which points somewhat resemble the leaves of lemon balm [toronjil]. It produces a bell-shaped flower, slightly larger than a gillyflower [alhelí], with five or six small points; some

Es tanta la cantidad de tabaco que se gasta en las Indias y se lleva a España, que hay provincias que todo el trato y granjerías de sus habitantes es cultivarlo y beneficiarlo; y tienen más precio los de unas partes que los de otras. corpus_links.translation:
...the herbalists [herbolarios].

So great is the quantity of tobacco [tabaco] consumed in the Indies and carried to Spain that there are provinces whose entire trade and livelihood [granjerías] of their inhabitants consists in cultivating and curing [beneficiarlo] it; and tobacco from some regions commands a higher price than that from others. In New Spain the tobacco of Papantla is the most renowned, and in this kingdom of Peru that of Jaén de Pacamoros. The instrument with which the Indians of Hispaniola inhaled tobacco smoke was called tabaco, which name the Spaniards gave to this herb and by which it has been known ever since. In the general language [lengua general] of Peru it is called sayri, and in the Mexican tongue, picietl.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CVII

On Zacate

The grass that in New Spain corresponds to the hicho [of Peru] is the zacate. Although this is a generic name for all manner of wild grass, it is nonetheless applied to a particular species thereof, which is the most widespread in that kingdom, covering the fields and savannas—particularly in the Tierra Caliente [hot lowlands]—and upon which livestock and pack animals are sustained. Zacate grows two or three cubits [roughly three to four feet] in height, such that it reaches the stirrups of travelers; and so that the moisture it carries from the dew does not wet the feet of those who pass through it, they use wooden stirrups closed at the front, and boots greased with ule [natural rubber]. The leaf is half a third [approximately 5–6 inches] long and slightly less in width, of equal breadth on all sides, giving it an oval and somewhat channeled form. Its flower is of the same form as that described in the preceding chapter, a little larger, of more vivid colors, and more fragrant. The fruit in appearance resembles the ordinary granadilla [passion fruit], somewhat more elongated, but differs in other respects: it is most fragrant, the rind thick and tender like that of an orange, from which a choice preserve [conserva] is made; the interior is like that of the other granadilla, bu

CAPITULO XXVII
Del cayú

El cayú es árbol natural de tierra caliente, como lo son casi todas las frutas naturales de Indias; es de la grandeza de un crecido naranjo; la hoja, de buen parecer, algo mayor que la del naranjo; la fruta que lleva es muy parecida en lo exterior a un pero grande, muy tierna, dulce, aguanosa y de muy buen sabor. Su pezón es otra fruta distinta, y media entre árbol y la fr
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVII
On the Cayú

The cayú is a tree native to warm lands, as are nearly all the fruits indigenous to the Indies. It is as large as a well-grown orange tree; its leaf is of handsome appearance, somewhat larger than that of the orange tree. The fruit it bears closely resembles in outward appearance a large pear [pero]; it is very tender, sweet, watery, and of excellent flavor. Its stem [pezón] is another distinct fruit, intermediate between the tree and the cayú fruit itself; it is the size and shape of a chestnut. This stem is eaten roasted, and its inner flesh [meollo] is like that of a chestnut.

CHAPTER XXVIII
On the Guiávara

The Indians of the province of Anemarca, in the district of Cuzco, held the following legend: They relate that one month before the Flood came, the llamas or sheep of the land [carneros de la tierra, i.e., llamas] displayed such great sadness that during the day they would not eat, and their nights were spent gazing at the stars. A shepherd, taking notice of this, asked them the cause of their sorrow. They replied that he should look upon a certain grouping of stars they pointed out to him, which were in assembly and deliberation over the fact that the world was to be destroyed by water. Las navajas, cuchillas, lancetas y todo género de herramientas que nosotros hacemos de hierro, solían hacer los indios, así del Perú como de la Nueva España, de cierta piedra que los mexicanos llaman itzli, y los del Perú, chillca lisa; la cual es transparente, como vidrio y se halla de tres co

The razors, blades, lancets, and all manner of tools that we make of iron, the Indians—both of Peru and of New Spain—were accustomed to make from a certain stone which the Mexicans call itzli [obsidian], and those of Peru call chillca lisa; this stone is transparent, like glass, and is found in three colors: white, black, and blue. There are many quarries of it, both in Peru and in New Spain.

CAPITULO XLII
Del cobre

Hallase mayor copia de minas de cobre en este reino y en otras muchas partes de Indias, que de plata ni de otros metales. Sacábanlo antiguamente los indios en mucha cantidad, a cuya causa se ven hoy muchas minas labradas de tiempo antiguo. Porque, como carecían de hierro, forjaban deste metal las armas, herramientas e instrumentos para la agricultura y algunos otros oficio
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII
On Copper

Greater quantities of copper mines are found in this kingdom and in many other parts of the Indies than of silver or any other metals. The Indians formerly extracted it in great amounts, on account of which many mines worked in ancient times are still visible today. Because they lacked iron, they forged from this metal their weapons, tools, and instruments for agriculture and various other trades; however, they made no use of it in any application of medicine. CAPITULO IV
De la chicha del maíz

Debajo de este nombre de chicha se comprehenden todas las bebidas que usaban los naturales de este Nuevo Mundo en lugar de vino, y con que frecuentemente se embriagan; al cual vicio son tan inclinados, que ni ha aprovechado haberse convertido a nuestra Santa Fe, ni el trato y comunicación con los españoles, ni los castigos hacen en ellos sus curas y las [ordenanz
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IV
On the chicha of maize

Under this name of chicha are comprehended all the beverages that the natives of this New World used in place of wine, and with which they frequently make themselves drunk; to which vice they are so inclined that neither their conversion to our Holy Faith has availed, nor their dealings and intercourse with the Spaniards, nor do the punishments [administered by] their curates and [the ordinances enacted] to turn them from it have effect upon them—though in some provinces a degree of improvement is seen, and in general [the text continues].

CAPITULO PRIMERO

De las matas que se hallaron en estas Indias de una misma especie con las de España

En el segundo grado de plantas se comprehenden todas aquellas los latinos llaman frutex y el Calepino romancea mata; porque, aunque este nombre es común para toda suerte de plantas, ya está apropiado para significar solas aquéllas que tienen mayor parentesco con los árboles que con las yerbas, as
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER ONE

On the shrubs found in these Indies of the same species as those of Spain

The second rank of plants comprises all those which the Latins call frutex and which Calepino's dictionary renders in the vernacular as mata [shrub]; for although this term is common to all sorts of plants, it has by now been appropriated to signify solely those which have a greater kinship with trees than with herbs — both by virtue of their long life, like trees, and because they consist of a more solid, tough, and woody substance than all annual herbs [yerbas cadañales], which, once they have borne their fruit, die. Having, then, to treat in this book of all plants of this second class native to this New World, I begin in this chapter with those found here to be of the same species as the plants nati

corpus_links.title: On the Puscolulo fruit of Popayán
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XVI
Del puscolulo

En la provincia de Popayán nace una mata llamada puscolulo, que es semejante a la higuerilla de infierno en la grandeza, hoja y hechura. Lleva una fruta muy parecida a una manzana en el tamaño, color y cáscara; mas está toda ella cubierta de unas espinillas que fácilmente se quitan. La carne es entre verde y amarilla, aguanosa y llena de unas pepitas como de ají, que se
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVI
On the Puscolulo

In the province of Popayán there grows a shrub called puscolulo, which resembles the higuerilla de infierno [castor-oil plant / Ricinus communis] in size, leaf, and form. It bears a fruit very similar to an apple in size, color, and rind; but it is entirely covered with small spines that come off easily. The flesh is between green and yellow, watery, and full of small seeds like those of chile pepper [ají], which are eaten together with the flesh. The flavor tends more toward sour than sweet, and if many are eaten, they set the teeth on edge [lit. give tooth-sensitivity / dentera].

corpus_links.label: cobo_vol1::QUINTO::cap_XXIII
corpus_links.title: On the Naranjilla Plant of Quito
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXIII
De la naranjillas

En la provincia de Quito nace una mata de un estado, poco más o menos; su hoja es del talle de la higuerilla de infierno, un poco mayor, y espinosa por las venas. A la fruta que lleva dan nombre de naranjillas, por tener alguna semejanza con las naranjas. Es del tamaño de un mediano durazno, redonda, de color naranjado; en la cáscara y sustancia se parece a los to
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIII
On the Naranjillas

In the province of Quito there grows a shrub of about one estado [approximately six feet] in height, more or less. Its leaf is shaped like that of the castor-oil plant [higuerilla de infierno], somewhat larger, and spiny along the veins. The fruit it bears is called naranjillas [little oranges] on account of its resemblance to oranges. It is the size of a medium peach, round, and orange in color; in its rind and substance it resembles tomatoes. The interior is a watery substance with a bittersweet flavor; it contains many seeds inside, as the tomato does, and has a pleasant taste.

CAPITULO XIV
Del manatí

Manatí, en lengua de la isla Española, es un pescado propio de las Indias; hay muchos en las islas de Barlovento y en otras costas de la Tierra Firme. Es mucho mayor que un tiburón; tienen de longitud, los mayores, catorce o quince pies, y de grueso, ocho palmos; y hay manatí que pesa cuarenta arrobas. Es animal de apariencia fea; tiene la cabeza tan grande como la de un b
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XIV
On the Manatee

'Manatí,' in the language of the island of Hispaniola, is a fish [pescado] native to the Indies. There are many of them in the Windward Islands and along other coasts of the Tierra Firme [mainland]. It is much larger than a shark; the largest measure fourteen or fifteen feet in length and eight handspans [palmos] in girth; and there are manatees that weigh forty arrobas [approximately 1,000 lbs / 460 kg]. It is an ugly-looking animal; its head is as large as that of an ox and somewhat resembles one; its eyes are small relative to its size; close to the head it has two large flippers or stumps with which it swims; in place of ears it has two very small holes; it is a hide-covered animal, brownish in color, with scattered sparse hairs. Its hide is as thick as a fi

corpus_links.title: On the Cuy (Guinea Pig) and the Chinchilla: Natural History, Food Uses, and Medicinal Properties
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLVI
Del cuy

El cuy es el menor de los animales mansos y domésticos que tenían los naturales destas Indias, el cual criaban dentro de sus casas y en sus mismos aposentos, como lo hacen hoy día. Es poco mayor que una rata, en la figura muy semejante al conejo; el pelo blando y corto; carece de cola; en cada uno de los pies tiene tres uñas pequeñuelas y cuatro en cada una de sus manecillas
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI
On the Cuy

The cuy [guinea pig] is the smallest of the tame and domestic animals kept by the native peoples of these Indies; they raised it inside their houses and in their very own rooms, as they still do today. It is slightly larger than a rat, and in form very similar to a rabbit; its fur is soft and short; it lacks a tail; on each of its hind feet it has three small claws, and four on each of its forepaws. It has no more than two teeth in the upper part of its mouth and another two in the lower, very long and slender. They come in many colors: white, black, brownish-gray [pardo], ash-gray [ceniciento], reddish [bermejo], and some mottled with various colors. corpus_links.label: Canon.Book2.Cannabis
corpus_links.title: Qinnab (Cannabis) — pain, appetite, and the mind
corpus_links.original: القنب: حار يابس في الدرجة الثالثة. يجفف رطوبات الدماغ.
corpus_links.translation: Cannabis: hot and dry in the third degree. It dries out the moisture of the brain. Ibn Sina documents cannabis for: ear pain (oil dropped into the ear), wound cleaning, and brain conditions. He is the first physician to document cannabis-induced tachycardia ('it quickens the heart') — an observation that precedes modern understanding of cannabis's cardiovascular effects by nearly a thousand years. His warning that excess cannabis 'corrupts the mind' and produces 'flatulent colic' is among the earliest documented descriptions of adverse cannabis effects.
corpus_links.preparation: Seed oil dropped into ear for pain; seeds applied to wounds; smoke inhaled (with warnings)
corpus_links.condition: Ear pain, wound cleaning, brain moisture excess, pain

CAPITULO XCVI

De la tinyatinja

Esta es una yerba de un codo en alto, la cual está verde todo el año; pica la lengua, si la gustan, y su temperamento es caliente. Vale su cocimiento contra el dolor de ijada, y particularmente si sobre el dolor se aplican las hojas calientes rociadas con vino; y asimismo aplicadas por esta orden, quitan todo dolor de causa fría.

CAPITULO XCVII

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XCVI

On the Tinyatinja

This is an herb about one cubit [approximately 18 inches] in height, which remains green throughout the year; it stings the tongue if tasted, and its temperament [complexion, in humoral terms] is hot. Its decoction is effective against pain of the flank [dolor de ijada: pain in the side or kidney/flank region], and particularly if the warm leaves, sprinkled with wine, are applied directly over the site of the pain; applied in this manner, they likewise relieve all pain arising from a cold cause [i.e., pain of cold humoral origin].

On the Tulma

corpus_links.title: Mamey de Cartagena, Níspero, and Lúcuma: Descriptions and Uses
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO X

Del mamey de Cartagena

El mamey de Cartagena, que dondequiera que se da conserva este nombre, por haberse llevado de aquella provincia, aunque es muy parecido al mamey del capítulo pasado, se distingue de él en especie. Es este árbol el más hermoso y de mejor parecer de cuantos yo he visto propios de las Indias. Es de la grandeza de un nogal, muy poblado de hoja, bien hecho y copado.
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER X

On the Mamey of Cartagena

The mamey of Cartagena [Mammea americana or Pouteria sapota, var.], which wherever it grows retains this name on account of having been brought from that province, although it greatly resembles the mamey of the preceding chapter, is nonetheless a distinct species. This tree is the most beautiful and handsome of all those I have seen native to the Indies. It is the size of a walnut tree [nogal], very full of leaves, well-formed and spreading. The leaf is also very beautiful, somewhat resembling that of the citron [cidra], but better proportioned; it measures a span in length and five fingers in width, flat, with very little channeling, stiff and very smooth, thick, covered with small white dots that run from the midrib to the margins; the upper surface

CAPITULO CIX
De la madre de coco

El árbol que en el Perú llaman madre de coco es pequeño, alto de dos estados, de hechura de ciprés y de agradable parecer, muy copado y poblado de hoja; la copa es abusada; comienza a menos de un estado del suelo, y como se va levantando, se va adelgazando a modo de ciprés. La hoja es muy parecida a la del sauce. Echa por fruto unos racimillos de unas hojitas muy
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CIX
Of the Madre de Coco

The tree that in Peru is called madre de coco [mother of coco] is small, standing two estados [roughly 11–12 feet] tall, shaped like a cypress and of pleasant appearance, very bushy and densely leafed; the crown [copa] is wide at the base; it begins less than one estado from the ground, and as it rises it tapers in the manner of a cypress. The leaf closely resembles that of the willow. It bears as fruit small clusters of very thin little leaves, white tending toward red, joined three by three and rounded so as to form a triangular figure, each one the size of a thumbnail; at their juncture lies the seed, which consists of three small grains in each cluster, black and smooth, the size of a radish seed. When these little clusters of leaves are dry and the br

CAPITULO XXXIV

De la coginoa, ayangue, peje-chapín, pejesapo, peje-tamboril y peje-perro

La coginoa es un pescado muy parecido a la palometa. El ayanque es propio destas Indias, de dos palmos de largo, poco más o menos; tiene la boca grande y colorada y agudos dientes, y se cuenta entre los pescados regalados. El pece llamado de los pescadores chapín, por ser parecido en la figura a un chapín, t
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIV

On the coginoa, ayanque, peje-chapín, pejesapo, peje-tamboril, and peje-perro

The coginoa is a fish very similar to the palometa [pompano]. The ayanque is native to these Indies, roughly two hand-spans in length, more or less; it has a large, red mouth and sharp teeth, and is counted among the prized [regalados] fish. The fish called by fishermen the chapín [slipper-fish], because its shape resembles a chapín [a platform shoe or clog], is a palm and a half in length and more than six fingers in height; it has no scales, but rather a shell-like covering; its flesh is white, like chicken breast, and of good flavor. De las corvinas, lizas, pescada, chita, vieja, curaca y coco

Corvinas se hallan en todas partes; son largas de dos o tres palmos y de buen mantenimiento. Las lizas son las que llaman albures en España; críanse muchas así en la mar como en muchos ríos, particularmente en las provincias del Paraguay y Tucumán, y la Nueva España en el río de Telmaii tejiec; es el pescado más sabroso q
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVI

On the corvina, mullet, pescada, chita, vieja, curaca, and coco

Corvinas [drum fish] are found everywhere; they are two or three hand-spans in length and make good eating. There are large and small mullets; the largest grow to two hand-spans in length. The pescada [whiting or hake] found here is small and scarce; the largest is no more than a third of a vara in length. CAPÍTULO XXVIII

Del hospital del Espíritu Santo

En este hospital se curan solos marineros y gente de la mar. Fundóse en esta ciudad por estar sólo dos leguas de distancia del puerto del Callao, que es el más principal y frecuentado de esta costa del Perú, de donde se trae aquí a curar la gente pobre de la mar: y la razón de no haberse fundado en el mismo puerto, que sin duda fuera de más comodid
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVIII

On the Hospital of the Holy Spirit

In this hospital only sailors and seafaring people are treated. It was founded in this city [Lima] because it lies only two leagues from the port of Callao, which is the most important and frequented port on this coast of Peru, from which the poor seafaring people are brought here to be treated. The reason it was not founded at the port itself — which would undoubtedly have been more convenient for the purpose it was intended to serve — was that at the time there was almost no Spanish settlement there, nor any provision of a physician, apothecary [botica], or the other necessities for the care of the sick, as there is today. CAPITULO CIV
De la yerba dicha Y

En muchas partes de las Indias, especialmente en las islas de Barlovento, nace una yerba que los indios de la isla Española llamaban Y. Hace una rama luenga, y levántase como la correhuela o la yedra, y tiene la hoja casi de aquella hechura; la cual es gran pasto para el ganado de cerda y lo engorda mucho, y le es tan provechosa como la bellota en España. También
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CIV
On the herb called Y

In many parts of the Indies, especially in the Windward Islands [islas de Barlovento], there grows a herb which the Indians of Hispaniola called Y. It sends out a long branch and climbs like bindweed [correhuela] or ivy [yedra], and its leaf is nearly the same shape as theirs. This plant is excellent fodder for swine and fattens them greatly, being as beneficial to them as acorns are in Spain. It is also a medicinal herb, and in some places it is used as a purgative.

De las matas que se hallaron en estas Indias de una misma especie con las de España

En el segundo grado de plantas se comprehenden todas aquellas los latinos llaman frutex y el Calepino romancea mata; porque, aunque este nombre es común para toda suerte de plantas, ya está apropiado para significar solas aquéllas que tienen mayor parentesco con los árboles que con las yerbas, as
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER ONE

On the shrubs found in these Indies of the same species as those of Spain

The second rank of plants comprises all those which the Latins call frutex and which Calepino's dictionary renders in the vernacular as mata [shrub]; for although this term is common to all sorts of plants, it has by now been appropriated to signify solely those which have a greater kinship with trees than with herbs — both by virtue of their long life, like trees, and because they consist of a more solid, tough, and woody substance than all annual herbs [yerbas cadañales], which, once they have borne their fruit, die. The fruit [papaya] varies greatly according to the quality of the soil where it grows. The most common variety is the size of a large citron [cidra] or a medium melon; it has a spindle-like shape and is divided into five or seven segments, with as many lengthwise grooves, in the manner of a melon. The rind is yellow, thin, and tender, like that of a citron. The flesh is likewise yellow tending toward red, tender like melon, though not as watery. It is about two fingers thick, and the inner cavity is filled with small black, round, and soft seeds no larger than coriander [culantro], which are also eaten and have a flavor of cress [mastuerzo]. The papaya is a wild fruit, not very appetizing nor highly esteemed.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO CXIV
De la caobana

En la lengua de la isla Española se llama caobana un árbol que parece de género de cedro, pero de más fina madera. Es tan grande que se sacan de él vigas de a setenta y a ochenta pies de largo, y tan grueso, que se asierran tablones de dos varas de ancho, que son ocho palmos. Su madera es muy preciosa, recia, más densa y de mejor tez que el cedro, de buen olor y colora
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXIV
On the Caobana

In the language of the island of Hispaniola, a tree is called caobana that appears to be of the cedar family [género de cedro], but with finer timber. It is so large that beams of seventy and eighty feet in length are obtained from it, and so thick that planks two varas wide—that is, eight palms [roughly 66 inches]—can be sawn from it. Its timber is very precious, strong, denser and of finer grain [mejor tez] than cedar, of good fragrance, and reddish in color, more vivid [más encendida] than cedar. From this wood we have had crafted the sacristy cabinets [cajones de la sacristía] of our professed house [casa profesa] in Mexico City, and they are very handsome. CAPITULO XXXVIII

De las demás especies de culebras

En las islas de Barlovento se halla un género de culebras que son pequeñas y verdes, de las cuales, colgadas vivas de un árbol, sale y destila un agua venenosa de que los indios flecheros de aquellas islas hacían hierba mortífera, y no son ofensivas en otra cosa.

En el reino de Tierra Firme y en otras provincias se cría una especie de culebras
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVIII

On the Other Species of Snakes [culebras]

In the Windward Islands [islas de Barlovento] there is found a kind of snake that is small and green, from which, when hung alive from a tree, a venomous water drips and distills, from which the Indian archers [indios flecheros] of those islands made a deadly arrow-poison [hierba mortífera]; in all other respects they are not harmful.

In the territory of Tierra Firme and in other provinces there lives a species of snake bearing a small horn [cornezuelo] on its forehead, which is of such a nature that if it is steeped in a little wine for a quarter of an hour and the wine is drunk, it provokes lust so powerfully that those who take it sometimes die as punishment for their unbridled appetite.

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO PRIMERO

De los nombres destas Indias Occidentales y Nuevo Mundo

A las dos últimas partes de la tierra, que llamamos América y Tierra Austral (y son el sujeto propio de esta historia), doy principio desde este segundo libro; y porque habernos de tratar en él de la grandeza, sitio y naturaleza desde Nuevo Mundo, que comprehende las susodichas dos partes de la tierra y el gran archipiélago
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER ONE

On the Names of These West Indies and the New World

I begin this second book with the two last parts of the earth, which we call América and the Austral Land [Tierra Austral] (and which are the proper subject of this history). Because we are to treat in it of the greatness, situation, and nature of this New World—which encompasses the aforementioned two parts of the earth and the great archipelago of San Lázaro [the Philippines], adjacent to Asia—it is fitting first to explain the various names that the Spaniards have given it since they discovered it in the year 1492, together with those by which it is most commonly called at present, and in what sense each name is taken, whether broadening or restricting its meaning, along with the causes and motives that its discoverers ha

CHAPTER XLIX
On the Shark and the Mako

In all the seas of these Indies that fall within the torrid zone, there is a great abundance of sharks [tiburones]. This fish is very large, twelve feet or more in length, and six or seven handspans [palmos] in girth; its skin is hard and rough, its head large, and its mouth furnished with two or three rows of teeth exceedingly sharp, like a saw. De los cazones

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLVIII
On the Sharks [cazones]

Along the entire coast of this kingdom of Peru there grows a great abundance of sharks [cazones] of all the species known in Spain, and also of others native to the Indies. They are known by the following names: cazón pique; another is called cazón negrito; others are canahotas, dentudo, guayas — which in Spain they call albariños. To these, which are true sharks [cazones], are also reckoned other fish by virtue of some resemblance and kinship they share with them, and they partake of the name of sharks chiefly because they have no scales, but rather a hide [cuero], such as the mielga [spiny dogfish], which is a fish that has spines on its back; the pintarroja [spotted dogfish/rockfish], which is like a medium-sized shark, somewhat dark in color; the

CAPITULO IV

De las moscas

Acerca destos animalejos y sabandijas que se contienen en este libro, se debe notar que los que en unas tierras son ponzoñosos y mortíferos, en otras no lo son tanto, y en algunas carecen totalmente de ponzoña, de tal manera, que sirven de mantenimiento a los indios. Porque se hallan entre ellos naciones tan bárbaras y salvajes, que no perdonan ninguna destas sabandijas
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IV

On Flies

Concerning these small creatures and vermin treated in this book, it should be noted that those which are venomous and deadly in some lands are not so in others, and in some places are entirely without venom, to such a degree that they serve as food for the Indians. For among them are found nations so barbarous and savage that they spare none of these vermin, but eat with greater relish and without harm snakes, vipers, toads, lizards, and the rest, just as we eat our ordinary food. All the varieties of flies and horseflies found in Europe are bred in these Indies, and some additional ones besides. They breed in far greater numbers in the hot lands than in the cold, and they are not as troublesome to livestock as they are in Spain.

CAPITULO LXXX

De la higuana

La higuana es una planta muy pareja a la yerba de la estrella; son sus hojas como las del apio: echa una flor marina en forma de estrella; sus raíces son largas y delgadas. Es yerba de temperamento caliente, a cuya causa, el zumo della es un cáustico fuerte que abrasa las partes do llega y puesto en moderada cantidad mundifica las llagas viejas con presteza, aunque es
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXX

On the Higuana

The higuana is a plant very similar to the herb of the star [yerba de la estrella]; its leaves resemble those of celery [apio]; it puts forth a sea-like [marina] flower in the shape of a star; its roots are long and slender. It is an herb of hot temperament [temperamento caliente], by reason of which its juice [zumo] is a powerful caustic [cáustico fuerte] that burns the parts it touches; yet applied in moderate quantity it cleanses [mundifica] old wounds [llagas viejas] with speed, even when they are very foul and fetid. The Indians were accustomed to use the powders of this herb mixed into drink in order to poison their enemies.

CAPITULO XXXI
Del escorpión

En la Nueva España se halla cierto género de lagarto, que los indios llaman caltetepon, y los españoles, escorpión; es muy parecido a la iguana; tiene de largo dos o tres palmos, la cola luenga, las piernas cortas, la cabeza chata, la lengua bermeja, ancha y partida en dos partes, el cuero duro y variado de pintas pequeñas leonadas y blancas, y desde los pies a la cabe
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXI
On the Scorpion [Lizard]

In New Spain there is found a certain kind of lizard which the Indians call caltetepon, and the Spaniards call escorpión [scorpion lizard]. It closely resembles the iguana. It measures two or three handspans [palmos] in length, has a long tail, short legs, a flat head, a crimson tongue that is broad and forked in two parts, a tough hide variegated with small tawny and white spots, and from the feet to the head, and from there to the tail, certain lines that encircle the body like rings. It is a fearsome animal to behold, slow in running, and one that does not usually bite unless first provoked. Its bite is lethal in some regions and not in others, though it is always harmful. De la iguana

En la apariencia exterior es el
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI

Of the Iguana

The word iguana, in the language of the island of Hispaniola, names an animal of very strange nature that is bred in the warm lands of the Indies, found both on land and in water, and for this reason it is classified as a fish [pescado]; although there are places that lack rivers and yet iguanas are raised in the mountains, as in the province of Yucatán in New Spain. In outward appearance, this is the most fearsome animal that men eat, and to such a degree that if painters wished to depict a fierce and frightful demon, they could find no more fitting model to imitate than this creature. CAPITULO LV
Del zahino

El zahino es cierta casta de puerco distinto de los de Europa; de pequeño cuerpo, no mayor que un gran lechón, algo bermejo y de pocas carnes. Tiene en mitad del lomo un lobanillo que parece el ombligo, donde se recoge un humor tan hediondo, que si en matando el animal no se lo quitan, lo inficiona y corrompe muy en breve. Dicen algunos que el zahino tiene el ombligo en las
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LV
On the Peccary [zahino]

The peccary [zahino] is a particular breed of pig distinct from those of Europe; small in body, no larger than a great suckling pig, somewhat reddish and with little flesh. It has in the middle of its back a cyst [lobanillo] that resembles a navel, in which gathers a humor so foul-smelling that if it is not removed immediately upon killing the animal, it infects and corrupts the meat very quickly. Some people say that the peccary has its navel on its back, believing the said cyst to be such; but this is not so, for it has its navel in the same place as other animals. CHAPTER XXVI

On the Laws and Punishments by which the Incas
Governed their Kingdom

Because the Indians lacked letters [i.e., a writing system], they had no written laws; rather, they preserved those which their kings had established through tradition and through the use and observance in which they were maintained. The most important of these, and those best remembered among them, I shall set down here.

CHAPTER XXXIII
Of the Priests and the Offices They Held

Under the name of priests are to be understood all men who were devoted to the worship of their false gods and were occupied in offering sacrifices to them and performing whatever superstitions were practiced among them. And since these were many, so too were the various kinds of priests. First, some were engaged in the guardianship and ministry of the huacas [sacred shrines or idols], offering the sacrifices ordained by their rite—both ordinary and extraordinary—and these were sustained by the revenues of religion. CAPITULO IV
De la chicha del maíz

Debajo de este nombre de chicha se comprehenden todas las bebidas que usaban los naturales de este Nuevo Mundo en lugar de vino, y con que frecuentemente se embriagan; al cual vicio son tan inclinados, que ni ha aprovechado haberse convertido a nuestra Santa Fe, ni el trato y comunicación con los españoles, ni los castigos hacen en ellos sus curas y las [ordenanz
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IV
On the chicha of maize

Under this name of chicha are comprehended all the beverages that the natives of this New World used in place of wine, and with which they frequently make themselves drunk; to which vice they are so inclined that neither their conversion to our Holy Faith has availed, nor their dealings and intercourse with the Spaniards, nor do the punishments [administered by] their curates and [the ordinances enacted] to turn them from it have effect upon them—though in some provinces a degree of improvement is seen, and in general [the text continues].

CAPITULO XXV
Del ají

Entre las legumbres que producen el fruto en sus ramas, tiene el ají, después del maíz, el primer lugar, como la planta más general y de mayor estima entre los indios de cuantas se hallaron en esta tierra; porque entre las especias que dió Dios a los naturales de ella, es tan recibida de todas las naciones deste Nuevo Mundo, que no se ha hallado ninguna que no tuviese el uso
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXV
On Ají

Among the vegetables that bear their fruit on their branches, ají holds, after maize, the foremost place, as the most widespread and highly esteemed plant among the Indians of all those found in this land; for among the spices that God gave to its native peoples, it is so universally received by all the nations of this New World that none has been found that did not make use of it and hold it in great esteem; and not only

CAPÍTULO VIII
En que prosigue lo mismo

Todavía resta por decir de las costumbres y vicios que los indios tienen contra la virtud de la justicia, de que tratará este capítulo. Caciques y señores de los pueblos eran aquellos que no con otro derecho que el de la fuerza y poder los sojuzgaban; y como la adquisición era tiránica y cruel, lo era también su gobierno. Porque no ponían la mira en el bien
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VIII
Which continues the same subject

There still remains to be said concerning the customs and vices that the Indians exhibit contrary to the virtue of justice, which this chapter will treat. The caciques [chiefs] and lords of the villages were those who subjugated the people by no other right than that of force and power; and as their acquisition of rule was tyrannical and cruel, so too was their governance. For they did not aim at the welfare and benefit of their vassals, but rather at satisfying their own ambition and greed, reducing the people to so heavy a servitude that there was no difference between it and outright slavery. The poor subjects lived so oppressed, cowed and terrified by the tremendous spectacles they witnessed carried out before their eyes upon those who com

CAPITULO IX

Del Tacú

Tacú llaman los indios del Perú, en la lengua aimará, a la tierra que propiamente es Bolo Arménico y por tal se suele administrar, a la cual podemos llamar con propiedad Bolo Indico. Hállase el tacú en el cerro rico de Potosí y en otras minas de metales, en especial de hierro, en tres diferencias: la primera, es una tierra colorada como sangre, de que usan los pintores y, pr
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER IX

On Tacú

The Indians of Peru, in the Aymara language, call tacú a substance that is properly Armenian Bole [Bolo Arménico] and is commonly administered as such; we may fittingly call it Indian Bole [Bolo Indico]. Tacú is found in the rich mountain of Potosí and in other metal mines, especially iron mines, and comes in three varieties: the first is a blood-red earth, used by painters and, principally, by gilders; the second is liver-colored; and the third, most common and most used by the Indians for curing certain ailments, is yellow. This last variety the Indians sell in the marketplaces in loaves and cakes, and they make use of it to treat bloody dysentery [cámaras de sangre], its powder being drunk dissolved in chicha, which is their wine. This earth is also useful, especial

CAPITULO XXXVI
Del soycosoyco

El soycosoyco es una yerba menuda que parece especie de las rosas o davdlinas de las Indias; levántase un codo de la tierra; echa muchos tallos delgados, redondos, lisos, correosos y algún tanto rojos, y pocas hojas; las cuales son tan pequeñas y menudas, que parecen hebrillas de seda cortadas. Produce unas florecitas amarillas que cada una tiene cuatro hojuelas no m
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVI
On the Soycosoyco

The soycosoyco is a small herb that appears to be a species of the roses or carnations [davdlinas, i.e., davelinas/clavellinas] of the Indies. It rises about one cubit [roughly half a meter] above the ground, putting forth many thin, round, smooth, tough, and somewhat reddish stems, and few leaves; these leaves are so small and fine that they resemble little cut threads of silk. It produces small yellow flowers, each having four petals no larger than those of the flower of rue [Ruta graveolens], which emerge from small, elongated buds resembling pine nuts; and after these flowers dry, they end in a tuft of fibers issuing from the same bud. This herb gives off a somewhat aromatic odor. It is hot in the second degree and moist in the first [according to Galen

corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XI
De la suana

La suana es una mata de dos codos de alto, que echa muchos pimpollos o ramas muy derechas; la hoja es como la del As[phodelus], salvo que es dos tantos más ancha. Produce una flor blanca de forma de campanilla, como azucena, y muchas raíces delgadas, cuyas cortezas tiñen de [color] como azafrán, por lo cual la [usan] y venden por todo el Perú, y [usan] de azafrán en los gu
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XI
On the Suana

The suana is a shrub [mata] two cubits tall, which puts forth many shoots or very straight branches. The leaf resembles that of the asphodel, except that it is twice as wide. It produces a white flower in the shape of a little bell [campanilla], like a lily [azucena], and many thin roots whose bark [cortezas] dyes [things] the color of saffron. For this reason it is used and sold throughout Peru, and used in place of saffron in stews [guisados], although it is not known to produce any effect beyond imparting color. Because this plant grows in the Andean provinces, the Spaniards call it 'saffron of the Andes' [azafrán de los Andes]; but the Indians of the province of Larecaja, in the diocese of Chuquiabo [La Paz], who inhabit the lowland [tierra yanca] of that distr

CAPITULO LVI

De la casigua

Esta es una mata pequeña semejante al romero así en las ramillas delgadas como en el tamaño de las hojas, son algo puntiagudas, espinosas y más gruesas; si se tratan entre las manos, son algo pegajosas y dulces al principio, pero al fin de mascarlas, dejan algún género de amargo. Es caliente y seca; su cocimiento con culantrillo y anís es contra la tos; y con mayor fue
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LVI

On the casigua

This is a small shrub resembling rosemary both in its slender little branches and in the size of its leaves; the leaves are somewhat pointed, thorny, and rather thick. If handled between the fingers, they are somewhat sticky and sweet at first, but after chewing them they leave a certain bitterness in the mouth. It is hot and dry in temperament [in the Galenic sense]. A decoction of it made with maidenhair fern [culantrillo] and anise is used against cough; and it takes effect with greater force if a syrup [lamedor, a lick-medicine] is prepared from the decoction and taken frequently.

On the cilla-cilla

CAPITULO LXVI
Del mío

En las provincias de Tucumán y Paraguay nace una mata que los indios llaman mío, que es como decir yerba ponzoñosa, la cual se parece mucho en las hojas y altor al romero; es de tal calidad, que si los caballos la comen, al punto se comienzan a hinchar y dentro de un cuarto de hora mueren sin remedio. A cuya causa, los que caminan por donde hay esta planta, el remedio que ha
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXVI
Of the Mío

In the provinces of Tucumán and Paraguay there grows a shrub that the Indians call mío, which is as much as to say 'poisonous herb' [yerba ponzoñosa]. It closely resembles rosemary in its leaves and height. It is of such a nature that if horses eat it, they immediately begin to swell and within a quarter of an hour they die without remedy. For this reason, those who travel through areas where this plant grows resort to rubbing it on the muzzles of their horses, which prevents the animals from eating it.

CHAPTER LXVII
Of the Flor de la Trinidad [Flower of the Trinity]

Among the natural flowers of the Indies, the most spectacular, in the judgment of many, is the one we call the Flor de la Trinidad. The shrub from which it grows stands two or three palms [spans] tal

CAPITULO CXV

Del guachapelí

El guachapelí es un árbol que sólo nace en tierras calientes; no crece muy alto, porque no sube derecho, sino que echa el tronco torcido y encorvado y muchas y muy gruesas ramas. Su hoja es pequeña como la de la alfalfa. Es árbol silvestre infructífero, pero de muy buena madera para labrar, de la cual se hacen comúnmente los corvatones y costillas de los navíos; y par
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXV

On the Guachapelí

The guachapelí is a tree that grows only in warm lowland regions [tierras calientes]. It does not grow very tall, because it does not rise straight up; rather, it sends out its trunk twisted and curved, with many very thick branches. Its leaf is small, like that of alfalfa. It is a wild tree that bears no fruit, but yields very good timber for working. From this timber, the knees [corvatones] and ribs of ships are commonly made. In order to obtain pieces suitable for this purpose, the trunk is cut one or two varas [a vara being roughly 33 inches] above the ground, and from that junction together with an equal length of the root, a ship's knee is fashioned. The wood of this tree is very hard, tough, and does not split, which is why blocks [motones] and pulley

The men and women of each nation and province had their own marks and [divisas] [insignia] by which they were known, and they were not permitted to go about without them nor to exchange them for those of another nation, under severe penalties. Del dios Viracocha, que era tenido de los indios por supremo señor y hacedor de todo

CHAPTER IV

On the god Viracocha, who was regarded by the Indians as supreme lord and maker of all things

Amidst the thick darkness of ignorance, the light of reason did not cease to produce some effect in these Indians; for, illumined by it, they came to grasp and believe that there was a universal God, Creator of all things, Sovereign Lord and Governor thereof; though this knowledge was so limited and obscure that they did not even possess a proper word with which to name him. All the names they gave him were metaphorical [translaticios], as I shall presently explain. CAPITULO XC

Del espingo

Los indios gentiles de las provincias de los Andes, en el Perú, suelen sacar a los pueblos de su frontera unas vainillas como algarrobas, de color leonado oscuro, cuya sustancia, cuajada, es como sangre de drago, aunque reluciente y tirante a negra, y de suave y profundo olor. Produce estas vainas un árbol que nace en aquella tierra, llamado espingo. Sacan los indios bárb
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XC

On Espingo

The pagan Indians [indios gentiles] of the Andean provinces of Peru customarily bring out to the frontier settlements certain small pods resembling carob beans [algarrobas], dark tawny in color, whose congealed substance resembles dragon's blood [sangre de drago], though more lustrous and tending toward black, with a gentle and deep fragrance. These pods are produced by a tree native to that land, called espingo. The barbarous Indians bring these pods out as something precious, to barter for knives, scissors, and other small goods that they value greatly; this they obtain with ease from the Spaniards, since these pods are held to be highly medicinal. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXIV
De las manzanas de la tierra

El árbol que llamamos manzano de la tierra sólo se halla en la Nueva España. Es pequeño y muy parecido en todo al manzano de Castilla, salvo que es mucho mayor y de hojas más pequeñas, aunque de la misma hechura. El fruto que produce son unas manzanillas pequeñas, redondas y amarillas, de tamaño y hechura de níspero. Es fruta silvestre y desabrida; tiene
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIV
On the Land Apples

The tree we call the land apple [manzano de la tierra] is found only in New Spain. It is small and very similar in every respect to the apple tree of Castile [manzano de Castilla], except that it is much larger and has smaller leaves, though of the same shape. The fruit it produces consists of small, round, yellow little apples [manzanillas], of the size and shape of a medlar [níspero]. It is a wild and insipid fruit; each one contains three seeds inside shaped like pine nuts [piñones], and so hard that they cannot be broken with the teeth. The Spaniards use these apples to make preserves [conservas]; and Castilian apples graft well onto this tree.

De las palmas de dátiles

CHAPTER XV
On Date Palms

Date palms must have been planted in this city of Lima at the very beginning of its founding, as is evident from the large and ancient palms that I found here fifty-three years ago. These undoubtedly grew from date stones [huesos de dátiles] brought from Spain, for I have seen many planted from such stones and sprouting in very short order. From longtime residents of this city I heard, many years ago, that there was for a long while a single palm tree here — which must have been the first — that never bore fruit until another grew up in a different courtyard and reached such a height as to overtop the buildings of the houses that stood between them, so that the two trees could see one another; and that it was only then that the first began to bear fruit.
