CAPITULO XVIII

De los membrillos

La fruta que con verdad se puede decir que es mejor en esta tierra que en España son los membrillos, porque todos, generalmente, son buenos, muy olorosos, tiernos, jugosos, sin nudos y muy livianos. Y la causa de ser tan buenos, debe de ser la humedad de la tierra que remite la aspereza y acedía que suelen tener los que nacen en España. Los hay de todas las difer
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVIII

On Quinces

The fruit that can truly be said to be better in this land than in Spain is the quince [membrillo], for all of them, generally speaking, are good — very fragrant, tender, juicy, free of knots, and very light. The reason they are so fine must be the moisture of the soil, which softens the harshness and sourness that quinces grown in Spain usually have. Every variety found there is represented here, and one more besides: a graft that has been made in this kingdom of quince onto lúcuma, a fruit native to these parts; of the lúcuma's traits, what these grafted quinces took most is its very deep yellow color. Del hospital de Nuestra Señora de Atocha de los niños huérfanos

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXII

On the Hospital of Our Lady of Atocha for Orphaned Children

So that no class of poor persons of either sex or any age should fail to partake of the great charity of this city—after so many hospitals for men and women had already been founded here, as we have seen—a house and shelter was established where abandoned orphaned children [niños expuestos, i.e., foundlings] could be gathered and raised. This is one of the most beneficial pious works [obras pías] that this commonwealth possesses, and its origin was as follows. In the year fifteen hundred and ninety-six, there came to this city in the company of the Viceroy Don Luis de Velasco a servant of God who, out of humility, called himself Luis Pecador [Luis the Sinner]. CHAPTER XXVIII
On the Indian Court of Justice

In order that the good governance and order of this commonwealth [república] might extend to all its members, the Indians were granted a separate court [juzgado aparte], whose judge is the corregidor of the Cercado [the Indian parish district of Lima]. He has jurisdiction over the cases of all of them—both those resident in this city and its surrounding area, and those outsiders who come here from all parts. This tribunal was instituted by Viceroy Don Luis de Velasco on the fifth day of the month of June in the year sixteen hundred and three, and a little more than one month later he issued the founding provision [provisión de su fundación], the text of which is as follows:

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER L
On the Sunchu

The sunchu is a genus of yellow-flowered plants, encompassing several varieties that are all very similar to one another in appearance: the shape of the flower resembles that of chamomile [manzanilla], and the plant itself is a shrub about one fathom [estado] in height, aromatic and resinous, which puts forth slender, round, and somewhat reddish stems. Its leaves are similar to those of nightshade [yerba-mora], and when touched to the tongue they prove abstersive [cleansing] or astringent [estípticas]. Both the leaves and the stems are covered with a short, rough down. The various sunchos differ from one another in height and in the shape of their leaves, for some have leaves larger than those of nightshade and bearing small points like those of the mallow. corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XVIII

On the Volcanoes of Peru and the Great Destruction They Are Wont to Cause

The two richest and most important parts of Peru — namely the Lowlands [Llanos] and the Highlands [Sierra] — are subject to two plagues and calamities most burdensome, which are wont to bring notable harm to their inhabitants. Both arise from a single source: the fire-mouths or volcanoes found along the main cordillera [mountain range], which cause very frequent earthquakes, and whenever they erupt, hurling from their depths immense quantities of fire, ash, and pumice stone, they commonly lay waste and destroy the lands in their surroundings and even those far removed and distant. Those who suffer most from these afflictions are the inhabitants of the Lowlands, though the people of the Highlands also

De las costumbres más generales en que se conforman todos los indios

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER VII

On the most general customs shared by all Indians

Peoples so thoroughly subjected and surrendered to the father of lies and cruel enemy of the human race—who caused them to render the honor and worship due to the Creator alone to himself—it is not difficult to understand what manner of instruction in errors, cruelties, and every kind of vice they would have learned from so perverse a master. They were all idolaters, given over to endless superstitions and omens, with the exception here and there of some nation of men so coarse and savage that, being of a purely brutish nature, they recognized no deity in heaven or on earth, nor had any form of worship whatsoever. And although many peoples of this New World have already received holy baptism, there are still far more who remai

corpus_links.original: 大黃：苦，寒，無毒。下瘀血⋯蕩滌腸胃，推陳致新，有將軍之號。
corpus_links.translation: Dahuang (rhubarb): bitter, cold, non-toxic. Drives out static blood... flushes the intestines and stomach, pushes out the old and brings in the new. It has the name 'General.' Li Shizhen's epithet for rhubarb — 'General' (Jiangjun) — reflects its potent, direct pharmacological action contrasting with licorice's harmonizing role. The fourth major tradition documenting rhubarb root (after Kampo/Daio, Shennong Bencaojing, and Unani Canon), cementing Rheum species as one of the most cross-validated purgative genera in world medicine.

corpus_links.translation: Xiu (Plants in general) — The Maya concept of plant medicine. According to Roys (1965), in his introduction to the Ritual of the Bacabs: 'The Maya h-men [healer-priest] was simultaneously a botanist, pharmacologist, priest, and diviner. The separation of these roles is a European imposition upon a system that understood them as unified.' Maya disease classification distinguished between diseases sent by supernatural forces (u kinil ik — diseases from the winds or spirits) and diseases arising from natural causes (u kinil tan — diseases from the body itself). Plant medicines were employed for both categories; however, ritual observance and spoken incantation accompanied the treatment of supernaturally caused diseases. CHAPTER IV

Of Manco Cápac, First King of the Incas

Having taken command of that small community and republic of barbarous men, the Inca Manco Cápac conducted himself among them with more humanity and the familiarity of a brother than with the authority of a superior. He devoted all his industry to seeking the welfare and advancement of his people.

CHAPTER VII

Concerning Mayta Cápac, Fourth King of the Incas

The governors raised the prince with more indulgence and freedom than the other sons of kings before him had customarily been raised; on account of which Mayta Cápac grew into a mischievous and bold youth, beyond the fact that by his natural disposition he was brave and spirited. De los dos últimos meses, y las fiestas que hacían en ellos

Llamaban al undécimo mes Tomaraymi piichayquiz, en el cual se hacía el sacrificio ordinario de los cien carneros; y si faltaba el agua en este mes, ponían atado en un llano un carnero escogido de los del sol, que fuese todo negro, y derramaban alrededor dél cantidad de chicha con ciertas ceremonias. No le daban de comer cos
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXX

Concerning the last two months and the festivals celebrated in them

They called the eleventh month Tomaraymi piichayquiz [Tomaraymi piichayquiz], in which the ordinary sacrifice of one hundred llamas [carneros] was performed. If water [rain] was lacking during this month, they would tie a chosen llama belonging to the Sun—one that was entirely black—in an open plain, and they would pour around it a quantity of chicha [maize beer] with certain ceremonies. They gave it nothing to eat until it rained, saying that out of pity for seeing it suffer, the Sun would cause rain to fall. CHAPTER XXIV
On the College of Santo Toribio

The College of Santo Toribio was founded by the second archbishop of this city, Don Toribio Alfonso Mogrovejo, in the year fifteen ninety-four. Its foundation gave rise to certain disputes with the viceroy, who had forbidden the archbishop to place his coat of arms above the door of the college. On this account the archbishop had the college vacated shortly after its founding, and it remained deserted for nearly two years. In order that the circumstances of its foundation be better understood, I set down here the royal cedula [royal decree] that follows, in which the whole matter is laid out at length, and which reads as follows:

CAPITULO XXXI
Del hospital de San Pedro

En el hospital de San Pedro no se curan más pobres que clérigos de orden sacro, el cual tuvo este principio: saliéndose un día a pasear tres o cuatro clérigos juntos por el barrio de San Lázaro, hallaron un sacerdote enfermo en un rancho de un indio, tan desamparado, que no tenía más cama que una barbacoa o zarzo de cañas, ni otro regalo que un poco de maíz
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXI
On the Hospital of San Pedro

At the Hospital of San Pedro, none but poor clergymen of holy orders [clérigos de orden sacro] are treated. Its origin was as follows: one day, three or four clergymen went out together for a walk through the neighborhood [barrio] of San Lázaro, where they found a sick priest in the hut of an Indian, in so wretched a condition that he had no bed other than a barbacoa or zarzo [a raised platform or frame of canes], nor any other comfort than a little maize that the Indian gave him. Moved to compassion, they took him to be treated at the Hospital of San Andrés, where they cared for him throughout his illness. corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO LXIII
De la palma real

El primer lugar de las palmas de este primer género se debe a la que los españoles llaman palma real, y los indios de la provincia de Santa Cruz de la Sierra, cuci; cuyo fruto excede en bondad al de todas las otras. No tiene tronco grueso esta palma, sino que las ramas nacen de junto a la tierra, y son tan largas, que se levantan tres o cuatro estados; su hoja se p
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXIII
On the Royal Palm

The first place among the palms of this primary genus belongs to that which the Spaniards call the royal palm [palma real], and which the Indians of the province of Santa Cruz de la Sierra call cuci; whose fruit surpasses in quality that of all the others. This palm does not have a thick trunk; rather, its fronds spring up from near the ground and are so long that they rise three or four fathoms [estados]; its leaf resembles that of other palms. It bears its fruit in large clusters [racimos], which, on account of their weight, fall to the ground. The fruit is like a large pear, and when ripe it turns yellow; the rind is stiff, though not hard; when broken open, it contains three or four flat kernels [almendras chatas], each slightly smaller than half a hand

corpus_links.original: coicas, en todas las provincias del Perú, en que se encerraban y guardaban los tributos y hacienda del rey, y de la religión. En tres partes señaladamente había estos depósitos reales y sagrados: primeramente, en las tierras realengas y de la religión de cada provincia, donde se encerraban inmediatamente los frutos y tributos como se iban recogiendo; los segundos estaban en las cabeceras de las go
corpus_links.translation: …[qollqas], throughout all the provinces of Peru, in which the tributes and property of the king and of the [state] religion were stored and kept. There were three notable locations for these royal and sacred storehouses: first, on the royal lands and the religious lands of each province, where the produce and tributes were deposited directly as they were collected; the second were in the capital towns of the governorships where the viceroys resided; and the third were in the city of Cuzco; for the same produce and provisions were distributed from all of them. The royal storehouses and those of the religion were distinct from one another, though they were always situated together, just as the owners of what was stored within them were distinct, as were the purposes to which it was applied.

De los tambos y chasquis, y el tributo que en servirlos daban los indios

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXII

On the tambos [way-stations] and chasquis [relay runners], and the tribute that the Indians rendered in serving them

The two royal roads of the Sierra [highlands] and the Llanos [coastal plains] that we have described passed through the largest settlements of the kingdom, which were the principal towns of the provinces — such as Cajamarca, Jauja, Vilcas, and other places in the Sierra, and on the Llanos: Túmbez, Chimo, Pachacama, Chincha, and other large towns. These towns were spaced along the highland road at intervals of twenty to thirty leagues from one another, more or less depending on the stretch, and along the coastal road there was one in each of the principal valleys. Del orden cómo se repartía el ganado manso, y la renta que en él y en la ropa de sus lanas tenían el Inca y la religión; y cómo los cazaderos y montes eran realengos

corpus_links.title: The Royal Roads Built by the Incas Across Their Kingdom
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXXI

De los caminos que hicieron los Incas por todo su reino, y la contribución de gente que para aderezarlos daban las provincias

Tenían hechos los Incas dos caminos reales que tomaban todo el largo de su reino desde la provincia de Quito hasta el reino de Chile, que son novecientas leguas, el uno por los Llanos y costa de la mar, y el otro la tierra adentro por las provincias de la Si
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXI

Concerning the roads that the Incas built throughout their kingdom, and the contribution of labor that the provinces provided for their upkeep

The Incas had constructed two royal roads [caminos reales] that ran the entire length of their kingdom, from the province of Quito to the kingdom of Chile—a distance of nine hundred leagues [leguas]. One road ran along the lowlands [los Llanos] and the sea coast, and the other ran inland through the provinces of the highlands [la Sierra], set back from the coast by as much as thirty leagues in some places and five in others.

Del juzgado de los indios

Para que el buen gobierno y concierto de esta república se extendiese a todos sus miembros se les dió a los indios juzgado aparte, cuyo juez es el corregidor del Cercado; él conoce de las causas de todos ellos, así de los habitantes en esta ciudad y su comarca como de los forasteros que aquí ocurren de todas partes. Instituyó este tribunal el virrey don L
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVIII
On the Indian Court of Justice

In order that the good governance and order of this commonwealth [república] might extend to all its members, the Indians were granted a separate court [juzgado aparte], whose judge is the corregidor of the Cercado [the Indian parish district of Lima]. He has jurisdiction over the cases of all of them—both those resident in this city and its surrounding area, and those outsiders who come here from all parts. This tribunal was instituted by Viceroy Don Luis de Velasco on the fifth day of the month of June in the year sixteen hundred and three, and a little more than one month later he issued the founding provision [provisión de su fundación], the text of which is as follows:

In the cemetery of the time of the ancient Empire excavated by the Hearst Expedition at the Giza Pyramids, more than five hundred skeletons of aristocrats of the time of the pyramid-builders (circa 2800 BC.) were brought to light, and in these bodies it was found that tartar-formation, dental caries, and alveolar abscesses were at least as common as they are in modern Europe to-day
corpus_links.translation: learned luxury. In the cemetery of the ancient Empire period excavated by the Hearst Expedition at the Giza Pyramids, more than five hundred skeletons of aristocrats from the era of the pyramid-builders (circa 2800 BC) were brought to light. In these bodies it was found that tartar formation, dental caries, and alveolar abscesses were at least as common as they are in modern Europe today. At every subsequent period of Egyptian history one finds the same thing—a wide prevalence of every form of dental disease among wealthy people who indulged in a luxurious diet, and relative immunity from such ailments among poorer people who lived mainly on a coarse, uncooked vegetable diet. CAPITULO CXV

Del guachapelí

El guachapelí es un árbol que sólo nace en tierras calientes; no crece muy alto, porque no sube derecho, sino que echa el tronco torcido y encorvado y muchas y muy gruesas ramas. Su hoja es pequeña como la de la alfalfa. Es árbol silvestre infructífero, pero de muy buena madera para labrar, de la cual se hacen comúnmente los corvatones y costillas de los navíos; y par
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER CXV

On the Guachapelí

The guachapelí is a tree that grows only in warm lowland regions [tierras calientes]. It does not grow very tall, because it does not rise straight up; rather, it sends out its trunk twisted and curved, with many very thick branches. Its leaf is small, like that of alfalfa. It is a wild tree that bears no fruit, but yields very good timber for working. From this timber, the knees [corvatones] and ribs of ships are commonly made. In order to obtain pieces suitable for this purpose, the trunk is cut one or two varas [a vara being roughly 33 inches] above the ground, and from that junction together with an equal length of the root, a ship's knee is fashioned. corpus_links.translation: Keishi [桂枝, also romanized from Chinese as Gui Zhi] — the young twigs of Cinnamomum cassia. According to the Honzō Wamyō [本草和名, a classical Japanese materia medica]: 'Keishi; Japanese name, Kani. [Flavor:] pungent; [nature:] warm. Indicated for wind-cold with headache, warm malaria, promotes sweating to dispel exterior pathogens, clears fever-heat, stops coughing and rebellious qi, dispels alternating cold and heat, breaks up hard accumulations. Kampo clinical refineme
corpus_links.translation: Ma Huang [麻黄] — Japanese name: Umanokusa [宇末乃久佐]. Flavor: bitter; Temperament: warm. Principal indications: wind-cold [中風傷寒] with headache; warm malaria [温瘧]; promotion of sweating to expel exterior pathogens [發表出汗]; clearing of febrile heat [邪熱気]; arrest of coughing and rebellious rising qi [咳逆上気]; dispelling of alternating cold and heat [寒熱]; and breaking up of hard masses and accumulations [癥堅積聚]. Kampo clinical refinement: The physician Yoshimasu Todo observed that Japanese patients required lower doses than those prescribed in Chinese classical medical texts, and dosing was adjusted empirically over many generations of practice. The alkaloid ephedrine was first isolated from ma huang by the Japanese chemist Nagai Nagayoshi in 1885.

Traditional indications: muscle spasms, cramping, abdominal pain, leg cramps. Modern
corpus_links.translation: Shakuyaku-kanzo-to [芍薬甘草湯], known in English as 'Peony and Licorice Decoction,' is among the most frequently prescribed Kampo [traditional Japanese herbal medicine] formulas in contemporary Japan. It is a two-ingredient preparation composed of Shakuyaku [芍薬; Paeonia lactiflora, white peony root] at 20g and Kanzo [甘草; Glycyrrhiza uralensis or G. glabra, licorice root] at 20g. The formula is documented in the Jinkikyo [仁機経; the Japanese reading of the classical Chinese text Jin Gui Yao Lue, 'Essential Prescriptions of the Golden Cabinet'], and has been adapted within the Japanese Kampo tradition at notably higher dosages than those employed in Chinese herbal practice. corpus_links.translation: Kakkonto [葛根湯, 'Kudzu Combination Decoction']: The most widely recognised formula [処方, shohō] in the Japanese Kampo [漢方] tradition. Composition: Kakkon [葛根, Pueraria lobata root] 8g; Mao [麻黄, Ephedra herb] 4g; Keishi [桂枝, Cinnamomum cassia twig] 3g; Shakuyaku [芍薬, Paeonia lactiflora root] 3g; Taiso [大棗, Ziziphus jujuba fruit] 4g; Shokyo [生姜, fresh Zingiber officinale rhizome] 4g; Kanzo [甘草, Glycyrrhiza uralensis root] 2g. Traditional indications [適応症]: early-stage cold or influenza presenting with rigidity of the nape of the neck and upper back, fever without perspiration, and aversion to cold [悪寒, okan]. corpus_links.original: 四物湯 (Shimotsu-to / Si Wu Tang) — Four Substance Decoction. One of the foundational blood-tonifying formulas in Kampo. Components: 当帰 (Toki/Dang Gui, Angelica sinensis) 12g + 芍薬 (Shakuyaku/Shao Yao, Paeonia lactiflora) 12g + 川芎 (Senkyu/Chuan Xiong, Ligusticum chuanxiong) 8g + 地黄 (Jio/Di Huang, Rehmannia glutinosa) 16g. Yoshimasu Todo on Shimotsu-to: This formula addresses blood deficiency patterns
corpus_links.translation: Four Substance Decoction [四物湯, Japanese: Shimotsu-to; Chinese: Si Wu Tang] — One of the foundational formulas for tonifying the blood [補血] in the Kampo [Japanese traditional medicine] tradition. Formula components: Toki [当帰, Dang Gui; Angelica sinensis] 12g + Shakuyaku [芍薬, Shao Yao; Paeonia lactiflora] 12g + Senkyu [川芎, Chuan Xiong; Ligusticum chuanxiong] 8g + Jio [地黄, Di Huang; Rehmannia glutinosa] 16g. Commentary of Yoshimasu Todo on Shimotsu-to: This formula is indicated for patterns of blood deficiency [血虚], presenting clinically as pallor of the complexion, dizziness, palpitations, menstrual irregularity, and dryness of the skin. corpus_links.original: 当帰 (Toki / Dang Gui) — Angelica acutiloba (Japanese species distinct from Chinese A. sinensis). Honzo Wamyo: 当帰、和名 也末止己呂。甘辛、温。主咳逆上気、温瘧寒熱洒洒在皮膚中、婦人漏下絶子、諸悪瘡瘍、金創。
corpus_links.translation: Toki [当帰, also known by the Chinese name Dang Gui]. Japanese name: Yamatorokoro [也末止己呂]. Flavor: sweet-pungent; thermal quality: warm. Principal indications: cough with rebellious qi [counterflow ascent of breath]; warm malaria [温瘧] with alternating cold and heat pervading the skin; women's uterine spotting [漏下, lit. 'dripping downward'] accompanied by infertility; all malign sores and ulcers [諸悪瘡瘍]; and wounds from metal implements [金創, i.e., cuts or punctures from bladed or metal weapons/tools]. corpus_links.translation: Arura (ཨ་རུ་ར།) — Terminalia chebula (Chebulic myrobalan). Regarded as the king of all medicines within the Tibetan medical tradition. From the Gyushi [rGyud bzhi, the Four Tantras, the foundational Tibetan medical canon]: 'Arura is the king of medicines. It is beneficial for all diseases. It is called the medicine of gods and demons [lha bdud kyi sman].' Properties: all five tastes [ro lnga] are present — sour [skyur], sweet [mngar], bitter [kha ba], pungent [tsha ba], and astringent [bska ba] — with only salt [lan tshwa] absent. On account of possessing these five tastes, arura may be employed in the treatment of all three humors [nyes pa gsum]: Wind [rlung], Bile [mkhris pa], and Phlegm [bad kan]. corpus_links.original: སྐྱུ་རུ་ར། (Kyuru / Baru) — Terminalia bellirica / T. belerica (Belleric myrobalan) and Phyllanthus emblica (Amla / Amalaki). Two of the Three Fruits combination. corpus_links.translation: 1. For a horse's leprosy [scabrous or mange-like skin condition], take harewort, pound it well, then mix with fresh butter, boil thoroughly in butter, apply it to the horse as hot as possible, smear every day, and always keep the salve on. If the leprosy be severe [mickle = great], take urine, heat it with hot stones, wash the horse with the urine while it is hot; when it is dry, smear with the salve, and also apply remedies [leechdoms] internally. Again, take brine [runnings of salt], heat it, wash the horse with that, and when it is dry, smear with fish grease. If a horse be galled [has a sore or abrasion], take stichwort, and goutweed, and maythe [mayweed/chamomile], pound well, add butter, wring the mixture through a cloth, add white salt, shake thoroughly, and treat the gall with it.

corpus_links.translation: 1. Drinks [potions] and leechdoms [medicinal remedies] against poison. Pound betony, marche [smallage/wild celery], wormwood, fennel, and radish in ale; administer this as a drink. Against poison: place betony and the small atterlothe [a plant identified as lesser burdock or possibly black hellebore] in holy water, drink the water and eat the plants. Against any poison: eat radish and clote [burdock] before the danger arrives; no man may then harm you with poison. Against any poison: boil the lower part of bishopwort [bishop's wort/wood betony] and lupin, and the lower part of springwort [dwarf spurge or caper spurge], everthroat [possibly vervain or a related plant], and clote [burdock] in ale; give to drink frequently. corpus_links.title: Kurkum (Turmeric) — liver and wound medicine
corpus_links.original: الكركم: حار يابس في الدرجة الثانية. ينفع الكبد والمرارة.
corpus_links.translation: Turmeric: hot and dry in the second degree. It benefits the liver and gallbladder. Ibn Sina documents turmeric for liver conditions, wound healing, and as a blood purifier — connecting the Canon documentation to the existing archive entry for turmeric (MMA-012) which includes Ayurvedic and other tradition entries. The Canon's documentation of turmeric for liver conditions is consistent with curcumin's documented hepatoprotective activity. Ibn Sina also recommends turmeric applied topically for wounds — consistent with curcumin's antimicrobial and wound-healing properties.

Ibn Sina's documentation of frankincense (Boswellia) for wound healing and inflammatory conditions extends the convergence signal for MMA-075 (Frankincense/Boswellia) to include Unani as a fifth tradition. The Canon specifically recommends burning frankincense for respiratory conditions — consistent with the Kyphi (Egyptian) documentation and modern research on incensole acetate's psychoactive and anti-inflammatory effects.

corpus_links.translation: Henna: cold and dry in the second degree. It consolidates wounds and prevents inflammation. Ibn Sina documents henna (Lawsonia inermis) for wound healing, inflammatory skin conditions, and headache (applied to the forehead). De la higuana

La higuana es una planta muy pareja a la yerba de la estrella; son sus hojas como las del apio: echa una flor marina en forma de estrella; sus raíces son largas y delgadas. Es yerba de temperamento caliente, a cuya causa, el zumo della es un cáustico fuerte que abrasa las partes do llega y puesto en moderada cantidad mundifica las llagas viejas con presteza, aunque es
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LXXX

On the Higuana

The higuana is a plant very similar to the herb of the star [yerba de la estrella]; its leaves resemble those of celery [apio]; it puts forth a sea-like [marina] flower in the shape of a star; its roots are long and slender. It is an herb of hot temperament [temperamento caliente], by reason of which its juice [zumo] is a powerful caustic [cáustico fuerte] that burns the parts it touches; yet applied in moderate quantity it cleanses [mundifica] old wounds [llagas viejas] with speed, even when they are very foul and fetid. The Indians were accustomed to use the powders of this herb mixed into drink in order to poison their enemies.

De la chacalia

La chacalia es una mata pequeña, cuyas hojas son como las del lentisco, pegajosas y de temperamento caliente. Usan dellas los indios aplicándolas majadas y tostadas en cazuela y rociadas con vino, en cualquiera quebradura de hueso; y las mismas hojas majadas o su zumo, sueldan las heridas frescas. Dando baño en la cabeza con su cocimiento, le quita el dolor, y tiene vir
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER LV
On the Chacalia

The chacalia is a small shrub whose leaves resemble those of the mastic tree [lentisco], being sticky and of a hot temperament [caliente]. The Indians use them by applying the leaves pounded and toasted in an earthenware pan [cazuela] and sprinkled with wine to any fracture of the bone [quebradura de hueso]; and the same leaves when pounded, or their juice, knit together [sueldan] fresh wounds. Applied as a wash to the head in the form of a decoction [cocimiento], it relieves pain, and it has the virtue of fixing [afijar] hair that is falling out due to some poor quality or weakness of the scalp.

corpus_links.original: Ἴρις — ἐμετικόν, κοιλιακόν, ῥυπτικόν
corpus_links.translation: Iris root — emetic, loosens the bowels, cleansing. Dioscorides documents iris root for digestive complaints and wound cleaning — a use consistent with the documented antibacterial activity of iridals (iris triterpenoids). The Florentine iris (Iris florentina) whose root was the basis of orris powder (used in perfumery) has documented antimicrobial properties that validate its traditional wound-cleaning application.

corpus_links.translation: Usnea species — commonly known as Old Man's Beard Lichen, documented in the Moerman ethnobotanical database. XIX.

Signs of a swollen and wounded liver; remedies for that; and concerning the hardening of the liver. He who has a wound in the liver, if he is not cured sooner, then arrives at the condition in which a man vomits purulent matter. If the man who is swollen in the liver, or the bloated one, remains so swollen until the twenty-fifth day without the swelling bursting, then the liver begins to harden; if it bursts, then there is a wound in the liver.

corpus_links.title: Chikichi / Artemisia afra — the African wormwood
corpus_links.original: [Amharic] chikichi — ye wagagen tera; [Swahili] mchichiri
corpus_links.translation: Artemisia afra (African wormwood) — the most widely used plant medicine across Eastern and Southern Africa. Documented across Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, and southern Africa for: respiratory infections, fever, malaria, digestive complaints, and wound healing. The same genus as artemisinin (Artemisia annua) — Nobel Prize 2015. Artemisia afra does not contain artemisinin but contains other artemisia sesquiterpenes with documented antimalarial and antimicrobial activity. The extraordinary geographic range of Artemisia afra medicinal use across independent African communities mirrors the multi-tradition convergence signal for Artemisia absinthium (wormwood) in European, Egyptian, and Celtic traditions.
corpus_links.preparation: Leaves decocted; steam inhalation; fresh leaves applied topically

corpus_links.title: Book V — Wines, vinegar, and minerals
corpus_links.original: Περὶ οἴνων καὶ μεταλλικῶν — οἶνοι ἐπὶ ζωμοὺς τιθέμενοι
corpus_links.translation: On wines and minerals — wines prepared by infusing plants. Dioscorides Book V documents pharmaceutical wine preparations — essentially the Roman equivalent of tinctures and extracts. This represents the Greek/Roman pharmacy's primary delivery system for plant medicines. Key medicinal wines documented: wormwood wine, rose wine, myrtle wine, pine resin wine (resinated wine), and juniper berry wine. Each represents a specific therapeutic plant dissolved into a preservation medium — the prototype for modern pharmaceutical tinctures.

corpus_links.label: DMM.Book1.Intro
corpus_links.title: Book I — Aromatics, oils, salves, trees, and shrubs
corpus_links.original: Περὶ ὕλης ἰατρικῆς βιβλίον πρῶτον — ἀρώματα, ἔλαια, βάλσαμα, ῥητίναι
corpus_links.translation: De Materia Medica Book I — On aromatics, oils, balsams, and resins. Book I covers approximately 130 aromatic plants, oils, and resins — the pharmacological preparation foundation. This book contains the most complete ancient documentation of: olive oil preparations, wine-based medicines, aromatics including iris root, spikenard, cinnamon, cassia, and the Balsam of Judea. Book I was omitted from the initial corpus but contains critical documentation for several plants already in the archive, adding Greek/Roman primary source confirmation to aromatic plants previously documented only through secondary sources.

In another salve Ass's dung reappears; it is combined with Yeast-of-the-Opium-drink, Goat's Fat, Lettuce, Onions, Beans, and White Oil. Someti
corpus_links.translation:
The shad-fish and honey beaten together in yeast of sweet beer [were used as a salve ingredient]. Another salve, with surely more claim to colour than to cure, combined writing-fluid [ink], vermilion, and goat's fat with honey and several other ingredients that were certainly included only to add bulk. In yet another salve, ass's dung reappears; it is combined with yeast of the opium-drink, goat's fat, lettuce, onions, beans, and white oil. Sometimes it was a pathological cause such as 'Hardenings' [indurations or contractures] that prevented suppleness of the limbs. In such cases the 'Hardenings' had first to be removed:

SALVE TO MAKE SUPPLE THE HARDENINGS
Hog's fat
Oil of worms
Oil of the abxersu-animal [unidentified animal]
Mouse oil
Cat's oil
Gather all into one and anoint therewith.

corpus_links.translation: The ancient physician was at a loss when confronted with the so-called 'wood-like uha-disease' [Egyptian: uha, possibly a stiffening or sclerotic condition] occurring in isolation. corpus_links.original: 1. For a sore and swollen maw; take oil, and put mastic, and dill, and southern wormwood into the oil, let it stand three nights, and arrange that the worts be sodden in the oil, then put that upon raw fresh wool, smear the maw therewith. corpus_links.translation:
1. For a sore and swollen maw [stomach]: take oil, and put mastic, and dill, and southern wormwood into the oil; let it stand three nights, and arrange that the herbs be steeped [sodden] in the oil; then apply that upon raw fresh wool and smear the maw therewith. Again, for the same ailment: take old lard, triturate it in a wooden mortar, mix therewith the white of an egg, put it on a cloth and lay it on. For a sore maw, again: put into warm oil the herb called fenugreek, and bunches of laurel flowers, and dill; smear the maw with that.

If the leprosy be mickle, take piss, heat it with stones, wash the horse with the piss so hot; when it is dry, smear with the salve, apply also leechdoms inwardly. Again, take runnings of salt, heat the
corpus_links.translation: 1. For a horse's leprosy [scabrous or mange-like skin condition], take harewort, pound it well, then mix with fresh butter, boil thoroughly in butter, apply it to the horse as hot as possible, smear every day, and always keep the salve on. If the leprosy be severe [mickle = great], take urine, heat it with hot stones, wash the horse with the urine while it is hot; when it is dry, smear with the salve, and also apply remedies [leechdoms] internally. Again, take brine [runnings of salt], heat it, wash the horse with that, and when it is dry, smear with fish grease. If a horse be galled [has a sore or abrasion], take stichwort, and goutweed, and maythe [mayweed/chamomile], pound well, add butter, wring the mixture through a cloth, add white salt, shake thoroughly, and treat the gall with it.

corpus_links.title: Cañahuasopo — a rosemary-like shrub of the Collao region
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XLII

Del cañahuasopo

El cañahuasopo es una mata tan parecida al romero en sus ramas y hojas, que fácilmente se engañara cualquiera teniéndolo por tal; sólo se diferencia en que sus hojas son un poco más cortas que las del romero y de un verde más blanquecino. Produce una flor pequeña y amarilla como la de la ruda; levántase de la tierra esta planta dos o tres codos; mascadas sus hojas s
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII

On the Cañahuasopo

The cañahuasopo is a shrub so closely resembling rosemary in its branches and leaves that anyone might easily mistake it for such; it differs only in that its leaves are somewhat shorter than those of rosemary and of a more whitish green. It produces a small yellow flower like that of rue [ruda]; the plant rises two or three cubits [codos] from the ground; when its leaves are chewed they are as bitter and pungent as those of rosemary; its branches, near the base, are of a black colour, so that they appear scorched. This plant grows in great abundance in the lands of the Collao [the Altiplano region around Lake Titicaca], where it is most commonly used as firewood, and it is called by this name in the Aymara language.

If a mans hair fall off, work him a salve, take the mickle wolfs bane, and vipers bugloss, and the netherward part of burdock, and ferdwort, work the salve out of that wort, and out of all these, and out of that butter on which no water hath come. corpus_links.translation:
1. If a man's hair falls off, work him a salve: take the great wolf's bane [aconite], and viper's bugloss, and the lower/root part of burdock, and ferdwort [herb uncertain]; work the salve from that plant and from all these, and from butter upon which no water has come [i.e., clarified/unsalted butter]. If hair falls off, boil the polypody fern and foment [bathe] the head with that, warm. In case a man be bald, Pliny, the great physician [leech], gives this remedy: take dead bees, burn them to ashes, and linseed likewise; add oil to that, and boil very long over coals [gledes]; then strain and wring out; then take willow leaves, pound them, and pour the juice into the oil; boil again for a while on the coals; strain; smear therewith after the bath.

CAPÍTULO XXVI
De las pulgas y niguas

Todas las tierras yuncas y medianamente calientes deste Nuevo Mundo son muy infestadas de pulgas, de las cuales se hallan dos diferencias: las unas son las comunes, que aunque son molestas, no tan ofensivas como las segundas. Engéndrase a tiempos tanta copia dellas, aun en tierras templadas, que dan mucha molestia así a los hombres como a los animales caseros,
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXVI
On Fleas and Chigoe Fleas [niguas]

All the lowland [yunca] and moderately warm regions of this New World are greatly infested with fleas, of which two varieties are found: the first are the common kind, which, though troublesome, are not as harmful as the second. At times such a multitude of them breeds, even in temperate lands, that they cause great annoyance to men as well as to domestic and even wild animals. For they are harbored not only by cats, dogs, mice, and domesticated guanacos, but also by wild rats and field mice; and the abundance produced by these wild hosts further swells the populations born in settled areas.

CHAPTER XXXIX

On Radishes, Turnips, and Other Vegetables of This Kind

All the herbs and plants that remain among those brought from Spain can be reduced to two categories, as follows: the first encompasses every sort of kitchen garden produce and greens (taking that term in its fullest extent), and the second comprises all other plants whose principal use is in medicine. De las diligencias que hizo el gobernador Pizarro en buscar sitio conveniente donde asentar esta población

Signs of a swollen and wounded liver; remedies for that; and concerning the hardening of the liver. He who has a wound in the liver, if he is not cured sooner, then arrives at the condition in which a man vomits purulent matter. If the man who is swollen in the liver, or the bloated one, remains so swollen until the twenty-fifth day without the swelling bursting, then the liver begins to harden; if it bursts, then there is a wound in the liver.

corpus_links.translation: Chapter XXX. If you wish that your belly [wamb] be always sound, you shall treat it thus, if you will. Ahura Mazda answered: 'Directly after death, as soon as the soul has left the body, O Spitama Zarathushtra! the Druj Nasu comes and rushes upon him from the regions of the north — for Hell lies in the north [cf. CAPITULO V

Del segundo Inca, llamado Cinchi-Roca

Muerto Manco-Cápac, fue obedecido en rey su hijo mayor Cinchi-Roca, el cual era ya hombre de más de veinte años. Quedó tan bien industriado por su padre en las cosas del gobierno y república, y procedía con tan gran prudencia, que alcanzó ser amado de todos no menos que su padre, por el buen tratamiento que les hacía. Por principio de su reinado v
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER V

On the Second Inca, Called Cinchi-Roca

Upon the death of Manco-Cápac, his eldest son Cinchi-Roca was obeyed as king; he was already a man of more than twenty years of age. He had been so well instructed by his father in matters of government and statecraft [república], and conducted himself with such great prudence, that he came to be loved by all no less than his father had been, on account of the good treatment he showed them. At the outset of his reign he visited the settlements and villages of the valley of Cuzco, which were by then greatly enlarged and grown in buildings and people; and in the course of this visit he commanded that all should cultivate whatever lands they might need for sowing their potatoes [papas]; and thus cultivation spread as far as Cinga, which is a

The Earth

I. 1. O Maker of the material world, thou Holy one! Which is the first place where the Earth feels most happy?

Part I.

Purity Laws, Part I.

§1. Zarathushtra asked Ahura Mazda: 'O Ahura Mazda, most beneficent Spirit, Maker of the material world, thou Holy One! When a man dies, at what moment does the Druj Nasu [the Corpse Demoness] rush upon him?'

Ahura Mazda answered: 'They shall stay thirty days for the righteous, sixty days for the sinners.' Notes: 1. How long if the dead person died in a state of holines
corpus_links.translation:
The Upaman [mourning period], and how long it lasts for different relatives.

§1. If one's father or mother dies, how long shall they [the survivors] remain [in mourning] — the son for his father, the daughter for her mother? How long [if the deceased was] righteous? How long [if the deceased was] a sinner?

Ahura Mazda answered: 'They shall remain thirty days for the righteous, and sixty days for the sinners.'

[Annotator's note 1: 'How long if the dead person died in a state of holiness (a dahma [state of ritual purity])? How long if in the state of a Peshotanu [one guilty of mortal sin]?']

§2. O Maker of the material world, thou Holy One! How shall I cleanse the house? How shall it be made clean again?

corpus_links.translation:
Purity Laws, Part I.

Section 1. A man dies in the depths of a valley. A bird descends from the top of a mountain into the valley and feeds upon the corpse of the dead man there. It then flies back up from the valley to the mountaintop and alights upon one of the trees there, whether hardwood or softwood, and upon that tree it vomits and deposits its dung.

Section 2. Now, a man comes up from the valley to the mountaintop. He approaches the tree upon which the bird had perched; from that tree he intends to take wood for the sacred fire. He fells the tree, hews it, splits it into logs, and kindles the fire — that fire which is the son of Ahura Mazda. What penalty shall he incur?

corpus_links.original: Atoning for the murder of a water-dog. 1. Zarathushtra asked Ahura Mazda: 'O Ahura Mazda, most beneficent Spirit, Maker of the material world, thou Holy One! He who smites one of those water-dogs that are born one from a thousand dogs and a thousand she-dogs, so that he gives up the ghost and the soul parts from the body, what is the penalty that he shall pay?' Notes: 1. See preceding Fargard § 51
corpus_links.translation: Atonement for the killing of a water-dog [otter]. 1. Zarathushtra asked Ahura Mazda: 'O Ahura Mazda, most beneficent Spirit, Maker of the material world, thou Holy One! He who strikes and kills one of those water-dogs that are born but one in a thousand [ordinary] dogs and a thousand she-dogs, so that it gives up the ghost and the soul departs from the body — what penalty shall he pay?' [Note 1: See the preceding Fargard, §51.] 2. corpus_links.translation:
Purity Laws Concerning Menstruation, Part I.

[Question] 1. O Maker of the material world, thou Holy One! If there be in the house of a worshipper of Mazda a woman who has the whites [leucorrhoea] or sees blood [menstrual bleeding], what shall the worshippers of Mazda do?

[Answer] 2. Ahura Mazda answered: 'They shall clear the way of the wood there — both plants and trees — they shall strew dry dust upon the ground, and they shall isolate a half, or a third, or a fourth, or a fifth part of the house, lest her gaze should fall upon the fire.'
[Note 1: 'The way of the Dashtanistan' — i.e., the prescribed path to the place of menstrual seclusion.]
[Note 2: Lest the wood be touched and defiled by the woman on her way to the Dashtanistan.]
[Note 3: Lest the earth be touched and defiled by her.

He is a thief when he takes a view not to restore; he is a robber when, being asked to restore, he answers, 'I will not' (Comm.) 2. Every moment th
corpus_links.translation:
Contracts and Offenses — Part I.

Note 1: He who does not restore a loan to the man who lent it steals the thing and robs the man. He does this every day and every night, for as long as he keeps his neighbour's property in his house as though it were his own.

[Commentator's gloss:] He is a thief at the moment he decides not to restore it; he becomes a robber when, being asked to restore it, he answers, 'I will not.'

Note 2: Every moment he holds the property unlawfully, he steals it anew. 'The basest thing among Persians is to lie; the next basest is to be in debt, for this reason among many others: that one who is in debt must in the end resort to lying' (Herodotus I, 139). corpus_links.translation:
Purity Laws, Part I.

Section 1. A man dies in the depths of a valley. A bird descends from the top of a mountain into the valley and feeds upon the corpse of the dead man there. It then flies back up from the valley to the mountaintop and alights upon one of the trees there, whether hardwood or softwood, and upon that tree it vomits and deposits its dung.

Section 2. Now, a man comes up from the valley to the mountaintop. He approaches the tree upon which the bird had perched; from that tree he intends to take wood for the sacred fire. He fells the tree, hews it, splits it into logs, and kindles the fire — that fire which is the son of Ahura Mazda. What penalty shall he incur?

corpus_links.translation:
Purity Laws, Section I.

1. [Zarathustra asks:] How long shall a piece of ground remain fallow upon which dogs or men have died? Ahura Mazda answered: 'O holy Zarathustra, a piece of ground upon which dogs or men have died shall remain fallow for a full year.

2. 'For a full year, no worshipper of Mazda shall sow or irrigate that piece of ground upon which dogs or men have died; the remainder of the ground he may sow and irrigate as he pleases.' [Cross-reference: Vd7.45 seq.]

3. 'If within that year they shall sow or irrigate the piece of ground upon which dogs or men have died, they are guilty of the sin of "burying the dead" against the water, against the earth, and against the plants.' corpus_links.translation:
The Upaman [mourning period], and how long it lasts for different relatives.

§1. If one's father or mother dies, how long shall they [the survivors] remain [in mourning] — the son for his father, the daughter for her mother? How long [if the deceased was] righteous? How long [if the deceased was] a sinner?

Ahura Mazda answered: 'They shall remain thirty days for the righteous, and sixty days for the sinners.'

[Annotator's note 1: 'How long if the dead person died in a state of holiness (a dahma [state of ritual purity])? How long if in the state of a Peshotanu [one guilty of mortal sin]?']

Concerning Nature, for which we shall cite the very words of Cicero himself: "The lentisk, ever green and ever bowed beneath its fruit, yields a threefold harvest: thrice ripening, thrice it signals when to plough." One of the periods referred to here is the same as that now under discussion, being likewise the proper time for sowing flax and the poppy. Regarding the latter, Cato offers the following advice: "On land where grain has been grown, burn the twigs and branches that are of no use to you, and when that is done, sow the poppy there." The wild poppy, which is of truly marvellous usefulness, is boiled in honey as a remedy for diseases of the throat, while the cultivated variety is a powerful narcotic. So much concerning winter sowing.

CHAPTER 44. (17.) — THE DISEASES OF GRAIN: THE OAT.

The principal form of disease in wheat is the oat. Barley, too, will degenerate into the oat; so much so, indeed, that the oat has come to serve as an equivalent for grain [corn]; for the people of Germany are accustomed to sowing it, and make their porridge [puls] of nothing else. This degeneration arises most particularly from humidity of soil and climate; a second cause is a weakness in the seed, resulting from its being retained too long in the ground before it emerges above the surface. Over-luxuriance in grain [corn] is checked by the grazing of cattle, but only while the crop is still in the blade [i.e., before the ear has formed]; if grazed upon as many times as one likes at that stage, no harm to the ear will result. If the ear itself is once cut off, however, the grain will, as is well known, assume a larger form, but will be hollow within and worthless, and if sown will come to nothing. At Babylon, however, they cut the blade twice and then allow the cattle to graze upon it a third time, for otherwise the crop would run entirely to leaf. Even so, the soil is so fertile that it yields fifty-fold, and indeed, with careful management, as much as a hundred-fold. It is a well-known fact that some lands require more seed than others, from which circumstance first arose a superstition common among the peasantry: they believe that when the ground demands seed with greater avidity than usual, it is famished and is devouring the grain. It is reasonable to sow seed in humid soil sooner than elsewhere, to prevent the grain from rotting in the rain; on dry spots it should be sown later, and just before a shower falls, so that it may not lie long without germinating and thus come to nothing. When seed is put in early it should be sown thickly, as it takes a considerable time to germinate; but when put in later, it should be sown thinly, lest it be suffocated. Over-luxuriance in grain [corn] is checked by the grazing of cattle, but only while the crop is still in the blade [i.e., before the ear has formed]; if grazed upon as many times as one likes at that stage, no harm to the ear will result. If the ear itself is once cut off, however, the grain will, as is well known, assume a larger form, but will be hollow within and worthless, and if sown will come to nothing. At Babylon, however, they cut the blade twice and then allow the cattle to graze upon it a third time, for otherwise the crop would run entirely to leaf. corpus_links.translation: Ramon (Brosimum alicastrum) — Breadnut Tree / Maya Nut. According to Landa (1566) and archaeological evidence, ramon seeds constituted a major caloric staple of Classic Maya civilization (250–900 CE); indeed, some Maya sites preserve ramon seed caches larger than those of maize. The Maya name for this plant is 'ox' in certain regional dialects. Medicinal uses recorded include: the leaves, employed both as cattle fodder and in traditional human medicine as an astringent [styptic/drying] poultice; a decoction [boiled extract] of the bark administered for asthma; and the seeds used as an anti-galactagogue [a substance that reduces or suppresses milk flow in lactating women]. CHAPTER 44. (17.) — THE DISEASES OF GRAIN: THE OAT.

The principal form of disease in wheat is the oat. This degeneration arises most particularly from humidity of soil and climate; a second cause is a weakness in the seed, resulting from its being retained too long in the ground before it emerges above the surface. This passage, from Pliny's Natural History Book XIX, Chapter 32, concerns the varieties of the onion and related bulbous plants, as well as observations on flowering and leaf-fall in various herbs.

On the subject of flowering: in some plants, flowering begins at the lower parts and proceeds upward, which is why it lasts so long — as is also the case with the plant called heliotropium [Heliotropium Europaeum]. In some plants the flower is white, in others yellow, in others purple. In wild-marjoram and elecampane, the leaves fall first from the upper part, and sometimes in rue as well, when it has been accidentally damaged. CHAPTER 59. WHAT PLANTS ARE BENEFITTED BY SALT WATER. A particular remedy for the diseases to which radishes, beet, rue, and cunila [savory] are prone is salt water, which also has the additional benefit of greatly contributing to their sweetness and fertility. Other plants are equally benefitted by being watered with fresh water, the most desirable of which is the coldest and sweetest to drink; pond water and drain water, on the other hand, are less suitable, as they tend to carry the seeds of weeds with them. It is rainwater, however, that constitutes the principal nourishment of plants; it also has the effect of killing insects as they develop upon the plants.

On Radishes, Turnips, and Other Vegetables of This Kind

This variety [of turnip] withstands extreme cold best of all. CHAPTER 59. WHAT PLANTS ARE BENEFITTED BY SALT WATER. A particular remedy for the diseases to which radishes, beet, rue, and cunila [savory] are prone is salt water, which also has the additional benefit of greatly contributing to their sweetness and fertility. Other plants are equally benefitted by being watered with fresh water, the most desirable of which is the coldest and sweetest to drink; pond water and drain water, on the other hand, are less suitable, as they tend to carry the seeds of weeds with them. It is rainwater, however, that constitutes the principal nourishment of plants; it also has the effect of killing insects as they develop upon the plants.

Concerning Nature, for which we shall cite the very words of Cicero himself: "The lentisk, ever green and ever bowed beneath its fruit, yields a threefold harvest: thrice ripening, thrice it signals when to plough." One of the periods referred to here is the same as that now under discussion, being likewise the proper time for sowing flax and the poppy. Regarding the latter, Cato offers the following advice: "On land where grain has been grown, burn the twigs and branches that are of no use to you, and when that is done, sow the poppy there." The wild poppy, which is of truly marvellous usefulness, is boiled in honey as a remedy for diseases of the throat, while the cultivated variety is a powerful narcotic. So much concerning winter sowing.

They also use it [spartum] to kindle fires and make torches; shoes and garments for shepherds are likewise made from it. As fodder for animals it is highly harmful, with the sole exception of the tender growing tips of the shoots. When it is needed for other purposes, it is pulled up by the roots with considerable effort; the legs of those doing this work are protected by boots and their hands by gloves, and the plant is twisted around levers made of bone or holm-oak to lift it out more easily. In the present day it is even gathered during winter, but the work is most easily done between the Ides of May [15th of May] and the Ides of June [13th of June], that being the season when the plant is fully ripe.

corpus_links.translation:
Wild cucumber, boiled in vinegar, is employed in fomentations [warm topical applications] for gout, and its juice is used as a remedy for toothache. When dried and mixed with resin, the root is a cure for impetigo [a contagious skin infection] and the skin diseases known as 'psora' [itch-scab] and 'lichen' [a scabrous skin condition resembling moss or lichen in appearance]. It is also beneficial for abscesses [imposthumes] of the parotid glands and inflammatory tumours [pani], and it restores the natural colour of the skin after a scar [cicatrix] has formed. The juice of the leaves, mixed with vinegar, is used as an ear injection in cases of deafness.

On the Anocarazapallo

CHAPTER XXXIX

On Radishes, Turnips, and Other Vegetables of This Kind

CHAPTER 59. WHAT PLANTS ARE BENEFITTED BY SALT WATER. A particular remedy for the diseases to which radishes, beet, rue, and cunila [savory] are prone is salt water, which also has the additional benefit of greatly contributing to their sweetness and fertility. Other plants are equally benefitted by being watered with fresh water, the most desirable of which is the coldest and sweetest to drink; pond water and drain water, on the other hand, are less suitable, as they tend to carry the seeds of weeds with them. It is rainwater, however, that constitutes the principal nourishment of plants; it also has the effect of killing insects as they develop upon the plants.

This passage, from Pliny's Natural History Book XIX, Chapter 32, concerns the varieties of the onion and related bulbous plants, as well as observations on flowering and leaf-fall in various herbs.

On the subject of flowering: in some plants, flowering begins at the lower parts and proceeds upward, which is why it lasts so long — as is also the case with the plant called heliotropium [Heliotropium Europaeum]. In some plants the flower is white, in others yellow, in others purple. In wild-marjoram and elecampane, the leaves fall first from the upper part, and sometimes in rue as well, when it has been accidentally damaged. In some plants the leaves are hollow, most notably the onion and the scallion [Allium schoenoprasum].

CHAPTER 59. WHAT PLANTS ARE BENEFITTED BY SALT WATER. A particular remedy for the diseases to which radishes, beet, rue, and cunila [savory] are prone is salt water, which also has the additional benefit of greatly contributing to their sweetness and fertility. Other plants are equally benefitted by being watered with fresh water, the most desirable of which is the coldest and sweetest to drink; pond water and drain water, on the other hand, are less suitable, as they tend to carry the seeds of weeds with them. It is rainwater, however, that constitutes the principal nourishment of plants; it also has the effect of killing insects as they develop upon the plants.

corpus_links.translation: Fever is in itself a disease or the symptom of a disease, and everything that is a fever has a cycle. Ibn Sina's fever classification is the most sophisticated in any pre-modern medical tradition: he distinguishes ephemeral fever (from fatigue, emotion), humoral fevers (corresponding to each of the four humours), and putrid fevers (from rotting matter in the organs). The recognition that malarial fevers follow a three-day cycle (Plasmodium vivax) or four-day cycle (P. malariae) — documented in detail in the Canon — is a genuine epidemiological observation that predates germ theory by 850 years.

CHAPTER 40. BEET: FOUR VARIETIES OF IT.

Beet is the smoothest of all garden plants. The Greeks distinguish two kinds of beet by colour: the black and the white. The latter, which is the variety generally preferred, produces very little seed and is commonly known as the Sicilian beet — just as it is the white lettuce that is held in the highest esteem. Chapter 62. Piperitis, Libanotis, and Smyrnium.

[Continuation of the discussion of flavours in plants:] centaury [taury] is bitter; cucumbers, gourds, and lettuces are watery; parsley, anise, and fennel are pungent and odoriferous. The salt flavour is the only one not found in plants, with the sole exception of the chicheling vetch [Lathyrus sativus], and even there it is found only on the exterior surface of the plant, in the form of a kind of dust that settles upon it.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XLII

On all the other herbs that have been brought from Spain up to the present

This chapter covers all the remaining herbs and plants that have been brought from Spain, which serve more for medicinal use than for other purposes, such as fennel [hinojo], aloe [zabila], dill [eneldo], viznaga [toothpick-weed], rue [ruda], poppies [adormideras], sage [salvia], and tarragon [taragontia]. All of these grow in great abundance in this kingdom of Peru, where, owing to the fertility of the soil, some have gone wild, now sprouting without being sown in uncultivated places. CHAPTER 56. (9.) FOUR KINDS OF FERULACEOUS [fennel-stalked] PLANTS. HEMP.

There is also hemp [Cannabis sativa], a plant of remarkable utility for the making of ropes, and ordinarily sown after the west winds have begun to blow. CHAPTER 59. WHAT PLANTS ARE BENEFITTED BY SALT WATER. A particular remedy for the diseases to which radishes, beet, rue, and cunila [savory] are prone is salt water, which also has the additional benefit of greatly contributing to their sweetness and fertility. Other plants are equally benefitted by being watered with fresh water, the most desirable of which is the coldest and sweetest to drink; pond water and drain water, on the other hand, are less suitable, as they tend to carry the seeds of weeds with them. It is rainwater, however, that constitutes the principal nourishment of plants; it also has the effect of killing insects as they develop upon the plants.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER 59. WHAT PLANTS ARE BENEFITTED BY SALT WATER. A particular remedy for the diseases to which radishes, beet, rue, and cunila [savory] are prone is salt water, which also has the additional benefit of greatly contributing to their sweetness and fertility. Other plants are equally benefitted by being watered with fresh water, the most desirable of which is the coldest and sweetest to drink; pond water and drain water, on the other hand, are less suitable, as they tend to carry the seeds of weeds with them. It is rainwater, however, that constitutes the principal nourishment of plants; it also has the effect of killing insects as they develop upon the plants.

Compound fracture of both bones of the left forearm in a patient who died fifty centuries ago within a few hours of the injury. Palm fibre had been pushed through the skin wound into the broken ulna (see the left-hand fragment) in order to stop the hemorrhage. This may have been the source of the infection that proved fatal. The broken bones were set in bark splints which formed a tube tied up with linen. This is one of a pair of the earliest splints discovered; the other set was used for setting the broken thigh of a boy buried in the same cemetery.

Two of them are of particular interest. At Shellal (First Cataract), a trench outside a Roman fort was found to contain 104 bodies of Nubians, all of whom had been executed. Most of them had been hanged, and it is interesting to note that the noose of the rope did not catch the neck as it usually does in modern hanging, but rather the head, the bones of which were forced apart by the shock. corpus_links.translation: Kosso (Hagenia abyssinica) — the female flowers used universally across Ethiopia for tapeworm (Taenia species). The preparation: dried female flowers mixed with tej (honey wine) and drunk fasting. Ethiopia has historically had among the highest rates of Taenia tapeworm infection globally, and kosso was the standard treatment across virtually all Ethiopian communities for centuries. European physicians who encountered Ethiopian medicine in the 19th century introduced kosso to Western pharmacy — it appeared in the London Pharmacopoeia (1867) and was used in Europe until anthelmintic drugs replaced it in the 1950s.

corpus_links.translation: The Great Theriac: a grand compound of sixty drugs or more. Ibn Sina documents the Theriac — the legendary universal antidote inherited from the Greek tradition (Mithridates VI, Galen) — with 60+ ingredients including opium, viper flesh, and dozens of plant medicines. The Canon's documentation of theriac is historically significant because Ibn Sina attempts to rationalize it pharmacologically — explaining each ingredient by its humoral action — rather than simply transmitting it as magical tradition. Theriac remained in use as a pharmaceutical preparation in European and Islamic medicine until the 18th century.

CHAPTER XXVI
On the Coravari

The Indians of Peru call 'coravari' a green stone that the Indians of the province of Lipes bring from their ancient copper mines to sell in Potosí and elsewhere. This stone appears to be nothing other than what Dioscorides calls 'chrysocolla' [crisolita]. Beyond its use by painters on account of its pleasing green color, the coravari is beneficial for many things, its primary virtue being to dissolve [resolver] and dry [desecar]. A preparation of it in moderate quantity, made with water of fennel or of celandine, removes and disperses cloudiness [nubes], clarifies the vision, and checks watering of the eyes [lágrimas]. CHAPTER XXVII
On Macay

The Indians of Peru call macay certain small loaves [panecillos] roughly the size of two-real coins, though thicker, which they make from a certain stone of the nature of lime [piedra cama de cal]. Dioscorides Book V documents pharmaceutical wine preparations — essentially the Roman equivalent of tinctures and extracts. corpus_links.title: Mangalya — the auspicious opening and purpose of medicine
corpus_links.original: प्रयोजनं चास्य स्वस्थस्य स्वास्थ्यरक्षणमातुरस्य विकारप्रशमनं च।
corpus_links.translation: The purpose of this [Ayurveda] is the maintenance of health in the healthy and the alleviation of disease in the diseased. Charaka opens with this foundational statement establishing Ayurveda's dual mission: preventive and curative medicine. The text positions itself as a complete system — not merely a collection of remedies but a science of life (Ayur = life, Veda = knowledge/science).

corpus_links.translation: Where prior treatment had failed, a douche [vaginal irrigation] composed of Fennel, Wonderfruit [unidentified Egyptian plant ingredient], Honey, and Sweet Beer was substituted and continued for four days. To protect a virgin from Leucorrhoea [vaginal discharge], it was necessary to anoint her breast, body, and all the limbs with a lotion prepared by crushing the dried liver of a Swallow in Sour Milk. The same result could also be brought about by mixing Fragrant Bread (made from Soured Durra [sorghum]) with the Poppy-plant, and having her eat it while she sat cross-legged. corpus_links.title: Phala Varga — therapeutic fruits
corpus_links.original: आमलकानां श्रेष्ठतमं। दाडिमं हृद्यं पाचनं रोचनं।
corpus_links.translation: Among fruits, amalaki is the foremost. Pomegranate (dadima) is cardiotonic, digestive, and appetizing. Charaka's fruit chapter documents the therapeutic properties of the major fruits used in Ayurvedic medicine. Amalaki is ranked supreme among all fruits — later research has confirmed it has one of the highest Vitamin C concentrations of any food. Pomegranate for cardiac conditions connects to the Greek/Roman, Persian, and Tibetan documentation of pomegranate for the same indication.

corpus_links.translation: A mixture composed of onion crushed in honey and taken in beer was prescribed [for itch]. If the itch was confined to the neck, a chopped-up bat applied as a poultice was said to heal it 'at once.' For the thigh, the prescribed remedy consisted of onions, dried beans, red natron [sodium carbonate/bicarbonate], sea-salt, and sour milk, made into a poultice — declared to heal at once. If the itching spread to all the limbs and became generalized, several remedies were available, among them a poultice of corn, natron, clay-from-the-gate [a locally sourced clay], onions, incense, and refuse-of-dates [date-palm waste]. corpus_links.translation:
In equal parts, [the preceding preparation] often sufficed to clear up bloodshot eyes [conjunctival hyperemia]. If it did not, a more complicated poultice composed of onions, verdigris [copper acetate], collyrium [kohl/antimony-based eye cosmetic], and Arabian-wood powder, crushed to a powder with ink and water, was recommended. There was then another prescription:

ANOTHER [REMEDY] TO DRIVE OUT BLOOD IN THE EYES
Two clay vessels: in one put powdered Fruit-of-the-Dompalm [doum palm fruit, Hyphaene thebaica] and Milk-of-a-Woman-who-has-borne-a-Son. In the other, Cow's Milk. Keep moist. In the morning bathe both eyes with the Fruit-of-the-Dompalm [preparation]. Next wash the eyes with the Cow's Milk four times [daily] for six days.

The bite of a human — whether from the hands or, more precisely, the teeth of a lady or gentleman acquaintance — was considered to require more intensive treatment than even the bite of a crocodile.

REMEDY AGAINST THE BITE OR STING OF PEOPLE
Prepare for the patient a poultice of Raw Flesh on the first day. Afterwards, treat him with Oil and Honey to promote healing. Then apply Oil in Wax in order to effect a complete cure at once.

On Burns:
Burns are troublesome wounds under the best of circumstances, and much unnecessary suffering can be avoided if a quick and easy remedy is ready to hand. The ancients recognized this, though we may not readily appreciate the virtue of the preparations they employed:

TO PREVENT BURN WOUNDS
A Frog — warm in Oil and rub [the affected area] therewith.

INTRODUCTION

It is often assumed, even by the most learned historians, that the history of medicine began with the Greeks, and that before the time of Hippocrates there was little or nothing that could be called a science of medicine. Yet for more than thirty centuries before the emancipation of human reason in Ionia, numerous practitioners had been attempting to diagnose and treat disease in Egypt, Mesopotamia, and elsewhere. The Papyrus Ebers is the longest and most famous of the documents relating to this more ancient practice of medicine. The Papyrus, although written around 1500 B.C., is in reality a collection of fragments of folk-lore, much of it five centuries older and some of it probably twenty centuries older still. The Ebers Papyrus is a miscellaneous collection of extracts and jottings gathered from at least forty different sources. It consists mainly of a large collection of prescriptions for a number of named ailments, specifying the names of the drugs, the quantities of each, and the method of administration. A few sections deal with diagnosis and symptoms; another passage is physiological in character and describes the action of the heart and its vessels; and the concluding portion is surgical, being concerned with the treatment of wounds and suppurating sores. CHAPTER 59. WHAT PLANTS ARE BENEFITTED BY SALT WATER. A particular remedy for the diseases to which radishes, beet, rue, and cunila [savory] are prone is salt water, which also has the additional benefit of greatly contributing to their sweetness and fertility. Other plants are equally benefitted by being watered with fresh water, the most desirable of which is the coldest and sweetest to drink; pond water and drain water, on the other hand, are less suitable, as they tend to carry the seeds of weeds with them. It is rainwater, however, that constitutes the principal nourishment of plants; it also has the effect of killing insects as they develop upon the plants.

CHAPTER VIII
On the Batata

The batata [sweet potato] is a root well known not only throughout all the Indies, but also in Spain, and it was one of the most esteemed foods the Indians had. corpus_links.label: NAM.Sweetgrass
corpus_links.title: Sweetgrass — the ceremonial medicine of the Plains
corpus_links.original: [Hierochloe odorata — Blackfoot, Ojibwe, Lakota documentation]
corpus_links.translation: Sweetgrass (Hierochloe odorata) — documented across Plains and Eastern Woodland nations for both ceremonial and medicinal use. The Blackfoot used it for colds and coughs; the Ojibwe for ceremonial smudging and respiratory conditions; the Lakota for wound healing. Sweetgrass smoke was documented as an antimicrobial fumigation — consistent with the documented antimicrobial activity of coumarin (the compound responsible for sweetgrass's distinctive vanilla-hay scent). This connects to the archive's documentation of Tonka bean (coumarin source) in South American traditions — an independent discovery of the same antimicrobial compound from a different plant.

corpus_links.translation:
The shad-fish and honey beaten together in yeast of sweet beer [were used as a salve ingredient]. Another salve, with surely more claim to colour than to cure, combined writing-fluid [ink], vermilion, and goat's fat with honey and several other ingredients that were certainly included only to add bulk. In yet another salve, ass's dung reappears; it is combined with yeast of the opium-drink, goat's fat, lettuce, onions, beans, and white oil. Sometimes it was a pathological cause such as 'Hardenings' [indurations or contractures] that prevented suppleness of the limbs. In such cases the 'Hardenings' had first to be removed:

SALVE TO MAKE SUPPLE THE HARDENINGS
Hog's fat
Oil of worms
Oil of the abxersu-animal [unidentified animal]
Mouse oil
Cat's oil
Gather all into one and anoint therewith.

corpus_links.translation:
Those who complain of the slowness of medical progress should be thankful that in the extraction of splinters — to mention one department of minor surgery — we have advanced since the days of Tutankhamun. It does not seem much to boast of, and yet…

WHAT TO DO TO DRAW OUT SPLINTERS FROM THE FLESH
[Remedy 1:] The per-baibait bird [an unidentified Egyptian bird] with Honey. Apply thereto.

[Remedy 2:] Worms' blood, cooked and crushed in Oil; Mole, killed, cooked, and drained in Oil; Ass's dung, mixed in Fresh Milk. Apply to the opening.

[Remedy 3:] Male-and-Female-Semen [i.e., combined human semen]. Apply thereto.

[Remedy 4:] Skull of the Shadfish [a species of fish], cooked in Oil. Apply to the point of the splinter. Thereby it comes out.

[Remedy 5:] Incense, Dough, Sea-salt, Wasp's dung

corpus_links.translation: Where prior treatment had failed, a douche [vaginal irrigation] composed of Fennel, Wonderfruit [unidentified Egyptian plant ingredient], Honey, and Sweet Beer was substituted and continued for four days. To protect a virgin from Leucorrhoea [vaginal discharge], it was necessary to anoint her breast, body, and all the limbs with a lotion prepared by crushing the dried liver of a Swallow in Sour Milk. To produce Milk in the breast of a woman about to nurse a child, Bones-of-the-Swordfish were warmed in Oil and her backbone smeared therewith. The same result could also be brought about by mixing Fragrant Bread (made from Soured Durra [sorghum]) with the Poppy-plant, and having her eat it while she sat cross-legged. corpus_links.translation: Sho-saiko-to [Small Bupleurum Decoction; Chinese: Xiao Chai Hu Tang] — Minor Bupleurum Decoction. corpus_links.translation: A mixture composed of onion crushed in honey and taken in beer was prescribed [for itch]. If the itch was confined to the neck, a chopped-up bat applied as a poultice was said to heal it 'at once.' For the thigh, the prescribed remedy consisted of onions, dried beans, red natron [sodium carbonate/bicarbonate], sea-salt, and sour milk, made into a poultice — declared to heal at once. If the itching spread to all the limbs and became generalized, several remedies were available, among them a poultice of corn, natron, clay-from-the-gate [a locally sourced clay], onions, incense, and refuse-of-dates [date-palm waste]. corpus_links.title: Jvarachikitsa — fever treatment
corpus_links.original: सर्वरोगाणाम् अग्रणी ज्वरः। गुडूची ज्वरघ्नी।
corpus_links.translation: Fever is foremost among all diseases. Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia) destroys fever. The Charaka fever chapter documents a hierarchy of fever treatment — from simple fasting and rest to complex multi-herb decoctions. Guduchi is the primary anti-fever plant. The pippali (long pepper) + ginger + black pepper combination (Trikatu) is documented for digestive fever. Neem (nimba) is documented for malarial fever types — one of the earliest documented antimalarial treatments.
corpus_links.preparation: Guduchi decoction; Trikatu (long pepper + ginger + black pepper) for digestive fever
corpus_links.condition: Fever (all types), malarial fever, digestive fever, fever with ama (toxins)

corpus_links.title: Gouqi (Goji Berry) — vision and longevity
corpus_links.original: 枸杞子：味苦，寒。主五內邪氣，熱中消渴，周痹。久服堅筋骨，輕身不老。
corpus_links.translation: Goji berry: flavor bitter, cold. Principally treats pathogenic qi in the five organs, internal heat and wasting thirst (diabetes), and painful obstruction throughout the body. Long-term use strengthens tendons and bones, lightens the body, and prevents aging. The 'wasting thirst' (xiaoke) documented here corresponds to diabetes — one of the earliest documented plant treatments for what we now call diabetes. Modern research: betaine and polysaccharides show blood glucose lowering activity.
corpus_links.preparation: Berries eaten; decoction; infusion in rice wine
corpus_links.condition: Diabetes (wasting thirst), eye conditions, longevity, fatigue, bone weakness

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XX

On the Stone That Congeals from Water

In the town of Huancavelica, in the diocese of Guamanga [Huamanga], there issues a hot spring [fuente de agua caliente] of a volume roughly equivalent to the bulk of a man's body, more or less. This water runs toward the river, and along its course a great part of it converts into stone. Other springs of this same character are also found in various parts of this kingdom and of New Spain. The stone engendered by this water is whitish and porous [cavernosa], and very well suited for construction; there are many buildings in the aforementioned town of Huancavelica made of it. The bite of a human — whether from the hands or, more precisely, the teeth of a lady or gentleman acquaintance — was considered to require more intensive treatment than even the bite of a crocodile.

REMEDY AGAINST THE BITE OR STING OF PEOPLE
Prepare for the patient a poultice of Raw Flesh on the first day. Afterwards, treat him with Oil and Honey to promote healing. Then apply Oil in Wax in order to effect a complete cure at once.

corpus_links.translation:
The text describes a series of remedies drawn from the Papyrus Ebers, a collection of ancient Egyptian medical prescriptions, here presented with editorial commentary. The first remedy for blindness — a lotion made by crushing Dried Myrrh in Sour Milk — is judged by the modern commentator to have been entirely ineffective. The second remedy, a poultice of Powdered Onions applied to the eyes, would certainly have caused intense irritation ('made the blind man see stars'). The third remedy takes a different approach, treating the eye disease via the ear, presumably on the theory that this route would be less painful:

corpus_links.translation: Niyog-niyogan (Quisqualis indica Linn.) — Family: Combretaceae. Source: Quisumbing (1951), pp. 267–269. Filipino vernacular names: Niyog-niyogan (Tagalog; the name translates literally as 'Chinese lantern'); Tartarau (Ilocano); Kasumpangi (Bisaya/Visayan). corpus_links.translation: Ashwagandha and bala and other rasayanas [are used] in tuberculosis/wasting disease. Long pepper destroys wasting cough. Rajayakshma — the 'King of Diseases' — corresponds primarily to tuberculosis and other wasting conditions. The treatment strategy is remarkable: Charaka prescribes nutritive rasayana plants (ashwagandha, bala, shatavari) to rebuild the patient while using antimicrobial plants (long pepper, giloy) to fight the infection. This dual strategy — nutritive support + antimicrobial — anticipates modern TB treatment principles.
