shrubs. It now remains for us to complete our account of all the cereals, and we shall here devote a portion of that account to the diseases to which they are subject.

CHAPTER 44. (17.) — THE DISEASES OF GRAIN: THE OAT.

The principal form of disease in wheat is the oat. Barley, too, will degenerate into the oat; so much so, indeed, that the oat has come to serve as an equivalent for grain [corn]; for the people of Germany are accustomed to sowing it, and make their porridge [puls] of nothing else. This degeneration arises most particularly from humidity of soil and climate; a second cause is a weakness in the seed, resulting from its being retained too long in the ground before it emerges above the surface. corpus_links.translation: Among the maladies that attack cereal crops—regarded rather as plagues visited upon the earth—mildew [rubigo], a malady arising from inclement weather, attacks both the vine and corn equally and is no less harmful. It strikes corn most frequently in localities exposed to dew and in valleys where there is no thorough draft of wind; windy, elevated sites, on the other hand, are entirely exempt. Another ill afflicting corn is over-luxuriance, when the stalk falls to the ground under the weight of the grain itself. One evil to which all crops alike are subject—even the chick-pea—is the assault of caterpillars: rain washes away the natural saltiness of the plants and renders them all the more palatable by their sweetness. A thousand years later, an example of the splints used for treating fractures of the forearm (Plate VI). Altogether a great variety of injuries was found, which, however, I shall not attempt to enumerate.

INTRODUCTION (XXVI)

Two of them are of particular interest. At Shellal (First Cataract), a trench outside a Roman fort was found to contain 104 bodies of Nubians, all of whom had been executed. Most of them had been hanged, and it is interesting to note that the noose of the rope did not catch the neck as it usually does in modern hanging, but rather the head, the bones of which were forced apart by the shock. One of these Nubians had had his head severed with a sword.

On the second day the head was anointed with Fish-oil. On the third day with Hippopotamus Oil. On the fourth day with abra-oil [an unidentified oil of Egyptian origin]. After this course of intensive treatment, if the Eczema still persisted, the affected scalp was smeared daily with Bread-meal and dressed with 'Rotted Cereals.'

CHAPTER XVI: DISEASES OF THE EYES

Nine pages of the original papyrus are devoted to eye conditions, a fact which should surprise no one acquainted with that country, even across the thousands of years separating us from that remote period. In a separate volume published in 1889, Ebers provided a detailed translation of this interesting chapter, distinguishing the following conditions: Blepharitis [inflammation of the eyelids], Blindness, Carcinoma, Cataract, Chala

In equal parts, [the preceding preparation] often sufficed to clear up bloodshot eyes [conjunctival hyperemia]. If it did not, a more complicated poultice composed of onions, verdigris [copper acetate], collyrium [kohl/antimony-based eye cosmetic], and Arabian-wood powder, crushed to a powder with ink and water, was recommended. There was then another prescription:

ANOTHER [REMEDY] TO DRIVE OUT BLOOD IN THE EYES
Two clay vessels: in one put powdered Fruit-of-the-Dompalm [doum palm fruit, Hyphaene thebaica] and Milk-of-a-Woman-who-has-borne-a-Son. In the other, Cow's Milk. Keep moist. In the morning bathe both eyes with the Fruit-of-the-Dompalm [preparation]. Next wash the eyes with the Cow's Milk four times [daily] for six days.

corpus_links.translation: Several remedies are given for 'Hotness in the Eyes' [ocular inflammation], a condition that must have been quite common among those who sought the care of an oculist during the Pharaonic period. As an eye-cooler, 'Baked Ox-liver, placed carefully thereon' does not sound very hopeful; and Soda-from-Upper-Egypt [natron], even when dissolved in spring-water, sounds positively alarming, despite the scribe's special marginal note appended to the prescription reading: 'It Heats It!' The third remedy, however, shows more promise and reveals once again the ancient physicians' belief in the homœopathic doctrine of like curing like: ANOTHER [REMEDY] TO DRIVE OUT HOTNESS IN THE EYES: Tallow from the jawbone of an ass. corpus_links.translation: Among the remedies placed into the mouths of ancient Egyptians by the physicians of the time, it is remarkable to note how little serious damage was done to the oral cavity and its contents. Diseases of the tongue are addressed with only a few simple remedies. At first, a milk gargle was deemed sufficient — the heading reads: BEGINNING OF THE REMEDIES TO DRIVE OUT DISEASES OF THE TONGUE: Milk. Gargle and spit out onto the ground. If the disease persisted, the milk was reinforced with goose-grease and the gargle transformed into a chewing-remedy: ANOTHER [amaa-erain, Egyptian term untranslated]: Goose-grease, Milk. Chew. corpus_links.translation: Yimucao (motherwort): acrid and bitter, slightly cold, non-toxic. Principal uses: static blood, menstrual obstruction, postpartum blood dizziness. The name 'Benefit Mother Herb' comes from its function. Leonurus japonicus (Chinese motherwort) is the primary gynecological herb in classical Chinese medicine — documented by Li Shizhen specifically for menstrual regulation and postpartum conditions. Modern research has confirmed uterotonic activity from leonurine — directly validating the traditional 'moves the uterus' mechanism. This connects to the archive's documentation of rue (MMA-046) for the same gynecological application via a different but parallel uterotonic mechanism.

corpus_links.translation: Chuanxiong (Ligusticum): acrid, warm, non-toxic. Principal uses: wind entering the brain, headache, cold-type painful obstruction, tendon cramping, metal wounds, blood obstruction in women. Li Shizhen documents Ligusticum chuanxiong as the primary blood-moving herb for headache — its combination with Angelica (Dang Gui) in Si Wu Tang (Four Substances Decoction) is the most prescribed formula for gynecological blood deficiency globally. Modern research: ligustilide — the primary phthalide — shows significant vasodilatory and neuroprotective activity.

corpus_links.translation: Panax quinquefolius — American Ginseng. Cherokee uses: general tonic [restorative], aphrodisiac, and treatment of headache. Iroquois uses: fever reduction, digestive complaints, and female [gynecological] disorders. Ojibwe uses: tonic for the weak and elderly. Meskwaki uses: menstrual cramps. Multiple clinical trials have demonstrated: positive results for blood sugar regulation in Type 2 diabetes; modest positive results for cognitive function; and immune modulation. corpus_links.title: Teff — the ancient Ethiopian grain-medicine
corpus_links.original: [Amharic] teff — ye rist tera, ye lijoch tera
corpus_links.translation: Teff (Eragrostis tef) — indigenous Ethiopian grain documented as a therapeutic food for digestive weakness, diarrhea in children, and as a nutritive medicine during illness. The injera (fermented teff flatbread) is simultaneously the primary Ethiopian food and a fermented probiotic medicine. Teff is naturally gluten-free and has a low glycaemic index — now understood to explain traditional observations about its gentle digestive properties. The grain is endemic to Ethiopia, making this documentation culturally specific to East African traditional medicine.
corpus_links.preparation: Fermented as injera; grain porridge for illness; dried and ground for digestive preparations
corpus_links.condition: Digestive weakness, diarrhea (children), malnutrition, celiac-friendly nutrition

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER ONE

On the ancient inhabitants of Peru before the Incas came to reign

Because the Indians lacked a system of writing, the knowledge of their antiquities that we find among them is very scant. And although the Peruvians made use of certain threads and cords [quipus] to preserve the memory of their deeds (as we shall see further on), these records contained nothing beyond what had occurred from the time the empire of the Incas began—with the conquests they undertook and the provinces they subjugated during their rule—and even that with so little distinction and clarity that not even the number of years each king held the scepter could be calculated from their accounts.

corpus_links.translation: Chapter IX — that is to say, that all these peoples descend from a single lineage, which disposes of the opinion holding that they derived from many nations of the Old World. Nor does it constitute a valid objection to cite, as an apparent difficulty, the fact that such vast and extensive lands were populated by a single lineage of men; for from no more than one single stock has the entire world come to be filled with the innumerable peoples who inhabit it today. And very readily, and without any difficulty whatsoever, the first men to set foot in this land—however few in number they may have been—could, together with their descendants, have spread out and occupied it all in the course of time. corpus_links.original: ¿Qué pudo ser la causa de extinguirse con tan universal olvido, que ni por historias ni tradición de gente alguna llegó a nosotros? Pues no creo eran entonces los hombres más descuidados que agora ni menos ambiciosos de honra, para no publicar sus hechos y procurar por ellos se perpetuase su memoria. What could have been the cause of its falling into oblivion so complete that neither through written histories nor through the oral tradition of any people did it reach us? For I do not believe that men in those days were more careless than they are now, nor less ambitious for honor, that they would have failed to publish their deeds and to seek thereby to perpetuate their memory. The plain truth is that we find no mention whatsoever in ancient histories of such lands, nor of any voyage made to them.

INTRODUCTION

It is often assumed, even by the most learned historians, that the history of medicine began with the Greeks, and that before the time of Hippocrates there was little or nothing that could be called a science of medicine. Yet for more than thirty centuries before the emancipation of human reason in Ionia, numerous practitioners had been attempting to diagnose and treat disease in Egypt, Mesopotamia, and elsewhere. The Papyrus Ebers is the longest and most famous of the documents relating to this more ancient practice of medicine. The Papyrus, although written around 1500 B.C., is in reality a collection of fragments of folk-lore, much of it five centuries older and some of it probably twenty centuries older still. corpus_links.translation: Licorice root: moderate in heat and cold, moist in the first degree. It benefits the chest and lungs. Ibn Sina's documentation of licorice adds the sixth independent tradition to this plant's convergence record — Egyptian, Greek/Roman, Persian/Zoroastrian, Ayurvedic, Chinese, and now Unani. The Canon specifically recommends licorice for respiratory conditions, cough, and as a demulcent — consistent with glycyrrhizin's documented anti-inflammatory and soothing properties. Ibn Sina also documents licorice as an antidote to bitter medicines, explaining its near-universal use as a flavoring agent in compound preparations.

corpus_links.original: 大黄 (Daio / Da Huang) — Rheum palmatum / R. officinale. Honzo Wamyo entry: 大黄、和名 加波良久佐。性寒、味苦。主下瘀血、血閉、寒熱、破癥瘕積聚、留飲宿食、蕩滌腸胃、推陳致新、通利水穀、調中化食、安和五臓。Daio, Japanese name Kawarakusa. Nature: cold. Taste: bitter. Primary uses: dispels static blood, opens blocked blood, treats alternating cold and heat, breaks up accumulations and masses, dissolves retained fluids and old food, flushes and purges the intestines
corpus_links.translation: Rhubarb [大黄, Daio / Da Huang] — Japanese vernacular name: Kawarakusa [加波良久佐]. Thermal nature: cold. Flavour: bitter. Primary therapeutic actions: dispels static [stagnant] blood [瘀血, oketsu], opens blockage of blood, treats patterns of alternating cold and heat [寒熱, kannetsu], breaks up accumulations and masses [癥瘕積聚, chōka-shakkyo], dissolves retained fluids and old undigested food [留飲宿食], flushes and purges [蕩滌, tōteki] the intestines and stomach, eliminates the old and generates the new [推陳致新], facilitates the passage of water and grain [water metabolism and digestion], regulates the middle [burner] and transforms food, and calms and harmonises the five viscera [五臓, gozō]. corpus_links.label: honzo_wamyo::kanzo_licorice
corpus_links.title: Kanzo (Licorice Root) — Glycyrrhiza uralensis in Honzō Wamyō
corpus_links.original: 甘草 (Kanzo / Gan Cao) — Glycyrrhiza uralensis. 甘草、和名 阿末加都良。甘、平。主五臓六腑寒熱邪気、堅筋骨、長肌肉、倍力、金創腫、解毒。久服輕身延年。
corpus_links.translation: Kanzo [甘草, 'sweet herb'], Japanese name Amakatsura [阿末加都良]. Flavour: sweet; temperament [qi]: neutral [平]. Indicated for cold and heat pathogenic factors [寒熱邪気] in the five viscera [五臓] and six bowels [六腑]; strengthens sinews and bones [筋骨]; builds flesh and muscle [肌肉]; multiplies strength [倍力]; treats swelling from metal wounds [金創腫, i.e. lacerations from bladed implements]; antidotes poisons [解毒]. Long-term use lightens the body [輕身] and extends the years of life [延年]. Kanzo is the most frequently employed herb across all of Kampo [Japanese classical medicine], appearing in approximately 70% of compound formulae in the role of harmoniser [調和] and moderator of the actions of other constituent herbs.

corpus_links.title: Shakuyaku (Peony Root) — Paeonia lactiflora in Honzō Wamyō
corpus_links.original: 芍薬 (Shakuyaku / Shao Yao) — Paeonia lactiflora. Honzo Wamyo: 芍薬、和名 恵比須久佐。苦、平。主邪気腹痛、除血痺、破堅積、寒熱疝瘕、止痛、利小便、益気。Shakuyaku, Japanese name Ebisukusa. Bitter, neutral. Main uses: pathogenic factor causing abdominal pain, dispels blood obstruction, breaks up hard accumulations, alternating cold and heat with shan conglomeration, stops pain, promotes urination, benefits qi. Active compound: paeoniflorin — mu
corpus_links.translation: Shakuyaku [芍薬], Japanese vernacular name Ebisukusa [恵比須久佐]. Taste: bitter; temperament [qi nature]: neutral [平, ping]. Principal indications: pathogenic qi [邪気] causing abdominal pain; dispels blood obstruction [血痺, blood impediment/stasis]; breaks up hard accumulations [堅積]; alternating cold and heat associated with shan [疝] conglomeration [瘕, mobile or fixed abdominal masses]; stops pain; promotes urination; augments qi [益気]. — The active constituent paeoniflorin acts as a muscle relaxant, anti-spasmodic, and anti-inflammatory agent. The compound Kampo formula Shakuyaku-kanzō-tō (peony root combined with licorice root) is a well-regarded anti-spasmodic preparation, supported by randomized controlled trial [RCT] evidence for the treatment of muscle cramps and dysmenorrhea, and is among th

corpus_links.label: honzo_wamyo::boiogito_formula
corpus_links.title: Boi-ogi-to (Stephania and Astragalus Decoction): Formula Composition, Indications, and Clinical Evid
corpus_links.original: 防已黄耆湯 (Boi-ogi-to) — Stephania and Astragalus Decoction. Documented in Ishinho (984 CE) and standard Kampo formulary. Components: 防已 (Boii/Stephania tetrandra) 5g + 黄耆 (Ougi/Astragalus) 5g + 白术 (Byakujutsu/Atractylodes) 3g + 甘草 (Kanzo/Glycyrrhiza) 1.5g + 生姜 (Shokyo/Zingiber) 1g + 大棗 (Taiso/Jujube) 3g. Traditional indications: sweating, heaviness, joint swelling particularly in the knees, knee oste
corpus_links.translation: Boi-ogi-to [防已黄耆湯, 'Stephania and Astragalus Decoction']: A compound decoction [tō] recorded in the Ishinhō [医心方, compiled 984 CE] and included in the standard Kampo [Japanese classical herbal medicine] formulary. Composition: Bōi [防已, Stephania tetrandra root] 5 g; Ōgi [黄耆, Astragalus membranaceus root] 5 g; Byakujutsu [白术, Atractylodes macrocephala or A. japonica rhizome] 3 g; Kanzō [甘草, Glycyrrhiza uralensis root, liquorice] 1.5 g; Shōkyō [生姜, Zingiber officinale, fresh ginger] 1 g; Taisō [大棗, Ziziphus jujuba fruit, jujube] 3 g. Traditional indications: spontaneous sweating [jishukan], sensation of bodily heaviness, articular swelling with particular involvement of the knees, and knee osteoarthritis. corpus_links.title: Shakuyaku-kanzo-to (Peony and Licorice Decoction): Formula, Historical Basis, and Clinical Evidence
corpus_links.original: 芍薬甘草湯 (Shakuyaku-kanzo-to) — Peony and Licorice Decoction. One of the most prescribed Kampo formulas in modern Japan. Components: 芍薬 (Shakuyaku/Paeonia) 20g + 甘草 (Kanzo/Glycyrrhiza) 20g. Documented in Jinkikyo (Jin Gui Yao Lue, classical Chinese), adapted in Japanese Kampo with higher doses than Chinese tradition. Traditional indications: muscle spasms, cramping, abdominal pain, leg cramps. Modern
corpus_links.translation: Shakuyaku-kanzo-to [芍薬甘草湯], known in English as 'Peony and Licorice Decoction,' is among the most frequently prescribed Kampo [traditional Japanese herbal medicine] formulas in contemporary Japan. It is a two-ingredient preparation composed of Shakuyaku [芍薬; Paeonia lactiflora, white peony root] at 20g and Kanzo [甘草; Glycyrrhiza uralensis or G. glabra, licorice root] at 20g. The formula is documented in the Jinkikyo [仁機経; the Japanese reading of the classical Chinese text Jin Gui Yao Lue, 'Essential Prescriptions of the Golden Cabinet'], and has been adapted within the Japanese Kampo tradition at notably higher dosages than those employed in Chinese herbal practice. corpus_links.label: honzo_wamyo::shosaikoto_formula
corpus_links.title: Sho-saiko-to (Minor Bupleurum Decoction): Classical Kampo Formula — Composition, Indications, and Ph
corpus_links.original: 小柴胡湯 (Sho-saiko-to) — Minor Bupleurum Decoction. Classical Kampo formula documented from earliest Japanese adaptation of Chinese medicine. Components: 柴胡 (Saikou/Bupleurum) 7g + 半夏 (Hange/Pinellia) 5g + 生姜 (Shokyo/Ginger) 4g + 黄芩 (Ogon/Scutellaria) 3g + 人参 (Ninjin/Ginseng) 3g + 甘草 (Kanzo/Licorice) 2g + 大棗 (Taiso/Jujube) 3g. Traditional indications: alternating fever and chills, bitter taste in mou
corpus_links.translation: Sho-saiko-to [Small Bupleurum Decoction; Chinese: Xiao Chai Hu Tang] — Minor Bupleurum Decoction. This is a classical Kampo [Japanese traditional medicine] compound formula, documented from the earliest period of Japanese adaptation of Chinese medical tradition. Constituent ingredients and standard dosages: Saikou [柴胡, Bupleurum root] 7 g; Hange [半夏, Pinellia rhizome] 5 g; Shokyo [生姜, fresh Ginger rhizome] 4 g; Ogon [黄芩, Scutellaria root] 3 g; Ninjin [人参, Ginseng root] 3 g; Kanzo [甘草, Licorice root] 2 g; Taiso [大棗, Jujube fruit] 3 g. Traditional indications [as recognised in classical Kampo nosology]: alternating fever and chills [a 'Shao-yang stage' [少陽病] presentation], bitter taste in the mouth, dry throat, nausea, and a sensation of fullness in the chest and hypochondriac [subcostal] re

corpus_links.title: Kakkonto (Kudzu Combination Decoction): Formula Composition, Traditional Indications, and Modern App
corpus_links.original: 葛根湯 (Kakkon-to) — Kudzu Combination Decoction. Most widely recognised Kampo formula in Japan. Components: 葛根 (Kakkon/Pueraria lobata root) 8g + 麻黄 (Mao/Ephedra) 4g + 桂枝 (Keishi/Cinnamon) 3g + 芍薬 (Shakuyaku/Peony) 3g + 大棗 (Taiso/Jujube) 4g + 生姜 (Shokyo/Ginger) 4g + 甘草 (Kanzo/Licorice) 2g. corpus_links.translation: Kakkonto [葛根湯, 'Kudzu Combination Decoction']: The most widely recognised formula [処方, shohō] in the Japanese Kampo [漢方] tradition. Composition: Kakkon [葛根, Pueraria lobata root] 8g; Mao [麻黄, Ephedra herb] 4g; Keishi [桂枝, Cinnamomum cassia twig] 3g; Shakuyaku [芍薬, Paeonia lactiflora root] 3g; Taiso [大棗, Ziziphus jujuba fruit] 4g; Shokyo [生姜, fresh Zingiber officinale rhizome] 4g; Kanzo [甘草, Glycyrrhiza uralensis root] 2g. Traditional indications [適応症]: early-stage cold or influenza presenting with rigidity of the nape of the neck and upper back, fever without perspiration, and aversion to cold [悪寒, okan]. corpus_links.label: CS.Kalpa.1.2
corpus_links.title: Vamana Dravya — emetic plants for panchakarma
corpus_links.original: मदनफलं वमनोत्तमम्। इक्ष्वाकु च यष्टीमधुकं च।
corpus_links.translation: Madana fruit (Randia dumetorum) is the foremost emetic. Ikshvaku (bottle gourd) and licorice root (yashtimadhu) also [serve as emetics]. The Vamana chapter documents the emetic plants used in panchakarma — the Ayurvedic therapeutic purification system. Licorice root (yashtimadhu / Glycyrrhiza glabra) appears here as an emetic adjuvant — the same plant documented in Persian, Greek/Roman, and Egyptian traditions for respiratory and digestive conditions. This represents convergence for licorice across five independent traditions.

corpus_links.label: SBC.Convergence.Licorice
corpus_links.title: Convergence note — Licorice across five traditions
corpus_links.original: [Cross-archive analysis]
corpus_links.translation: Licorice root (Glycyrrhiza species) is documented in: Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (c.1550 BCE), Greek/Roman (Dioscorides, 77 CE and Pliny), Persian/Zoroastrian (Avestan texts), Ayurvedic Charaka Samhita (yashtimadhu), and now the Shennong Bencaojing (gancao, c.200 CE). Five independent medical traditions across four continents documented the same plant genus for overlapping indications: respiratory complaints, wound healing, digestive conditions, and as a harmonizing/sweetening agent in compound preparations. This is the strongest multi-tradition convergence signal for any single plant genus in the entire archive.

corpus_links.label: BGM.Gancao
corpus_links.title: Gancao (Licorice) — the national elder of herbs
corpus_links.original: 甘草：甘，平，無毒。主五臟六腑寒熱邪氣⋯調和諸藥，故有國老之名。
corpus_links.translation: Gancao (licorice): sweet, neutral, non-toxic. Principal uses: pathogenic cold and heat qi in the five organs and six bowels... It harmonizes all medicines, hence it has the name 'National Elder.' Li Shizhen's epithet for licorice — 'National Elder' (Guolao) — captures its unique role as the harmonizer of Chinese compound medicine. Appears in approximately 70% of all classical Chinese formulas. Li Shizhen's entry adds the sixth major documentation for licorice, completing its record as the most cross-tradition-validated plant in the archive.

corpus_links.label: BGM.Convergence
corpus_links.title: Cross-archive synthesis — Bencao Gangmu's new convergence signals
corpus_links.original: [Cross-archive analysis]
corpus_links.translation: The Bencao Gangmu adds several significant convergence upgrades to the existing archive: (1) Licorice (gancao) — now six traditions confirmed with the Unani addition; Li Shizhen's epithet 'National Elder' acknowledges its harmonizing role that explains its universal appearance across traditions. (2) Rhubarb (dahuang) — now four traditions: Kampo (MMA-030), Shennong, Unani (Canon), and Bencao Gangmu; the purgative anthraquinone mechanism is the most cross-tradition validated pharmacological mechanism in the archive. (3) Ephedrine/Mahuang — the most famous single traditional-to-pharmaceutical compound discovery, with the Bencao Gangmu providing the definitive traditional documentation. (4) Danshen — approved cardiovascular drug in China from a plant documented for cardiac conditions 1,000 ye

corpus_links.label: Canon.Book5.Antidotes
corpus_links.title: Tiyaqat — theriac and compound antidotes
corpus_links.original: الترياق الكبير: مركب عظيم من ستين دواءً أو أكثر.
corpus_links.translation: The Great Theriac: a grand compound of sixty drugs or more. Ibn Sina documents the Theriac — the legendary universal antidote inherited from the Greek tradition (Mithridates VI, Galen) — with 60+ ingredients including opium, viper flesh, and dozens of plant medicines. The Canon's documentation of theriac is historically significant because Ibn Sina attempts to rationalize it pharmacologically — explaining each ingredient by its humoral action — rather than simply transmitting it as magical tradition. Theriac remained in use as a pharmaceutical preparation in European and Islamic medicine until the 18th century.

corpus_links.label: Canon.Convergence.Licorice
corpus_links.title: Convergence note — Licorice: six traditions confirmed
corpus_links.original: [Cross-archive analysis]
corpus_links.translation: With Ibn Sina's Canon documentation, licorice root (Glycyrrhiza species) is now confirmed in six independent medical traditions: Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (c.1550 BCE), Greek/Roman Dioscorides (77 CE), Persian/Zoroastrian texts, Ayurvedic Charaka Samhita (yashtimadhu), Chinese Shennong Bencaojing (gancao), and now Unani Canon of Medicine (irsa). Six independent civilizations across four continents documented the same plant genus for overlapping indications across 2,600 years. This is the single strongest convergence signal in the entire archive — and glycyrrhizin's documented anti-inflammatory and antiviral activity (used in Japan as an approved anti-hepatitis drug) provides the pharmacological validation.

corpus_links.label: DUB.Ssanghwa
corpus_links.title: Ssanghwa-tang — Korea's most famous medicinal beverage
corpus_links.original: 쌍화탕 — 기력 회복, 피로 해소에 효과가 있다
corpus_links.translation: Ssanghwa-tang (Double Harmony Decoction) — Korea's most famous medicinal compound preparation, documented by Heo Jun and still sold in Korean convenience stores today as a commercial health drink. Ingredients include: rehmannia, white peony, cnidium, angelica, astragalus, licorice, ginger, jujube, and cinnamon. Prescribed for: fatigue recovery, sexual exhaustion, and general weakness after illness. The commercial product (sold alongside energy drinks) represents a unique case of a 17th-century medical formula achieving mass-market consumer product status in the 21st century.

unani.source_text: Canon of Medicine, Ibn Sina (1025 CE)
unani.original: السنا: ينقي الصفراء. تُؤخذ مع التمر الهندي.
unani.translation: Senna: purges yellow bile. Taken with tamarind. Ibn Sina's preparation — senna with tamarind to reduce cramping — is still the standard pharmaceutical formulation 1,000 years later.
unani.preparation: Leaves steeped in hot water with tamarind; drunk fasting

modern_research.summary: Sennosides: FDA approved OTC stimulant laxative. Traditional formulation with tamarind (anti-griping) is pharmacologically rational — tamarind acids buffer the irritant effect. WHO Full Monograph Vol 1.
modern_research.significance: Senna is one of the most direct traditional-to-pharmaceutical inheritances — Ibn Sina's 1,000-year-old formulation is still used today.

plants.evidence_authority: FDA OTC approved; WHO Full Monograph Vol 1; in USP.

corpus_links.label: Canon.Book2.Senna
corpus_links.title: Sana (Senna) — the canonical laxative
corpus_links.original: السنا: حار يابس في الدرجة الثانية. ينقي الصفراء والسوداء.
corpus_links.translation: Senna: hot and dry in the second degree. It purges yellow bile and black bile. Ibn Sina documents senna as the primary oral laxative — distinguishing it from more violent purgatives by its moderate degree of action. The preparation: senna leaves steeped in hot water with violet and tamarind to moderate its griping action. This specific preparation — senna + tamarind to reduce cramping — is still the standard pharmaceutical formulation of senna today, 1,000 years later.
corpus_links.preparation: Senna leaves steeped in hot water with tamarind and violet; drunk fasting
corpus_links.condition: Constipation, melancholy (black bile excess), bilious conditions

corpus_links.label: EA.Kosso
corpus_links.title: Kosso (Hagenia) — the tapeworm medicine of Ethiopia
corpus_links.original: [Amharic] kosso — yezar tera, yefit tera — used universally against tapeworm
corpus_links.translation: Kosso (Hagenia abyssinica) — the female flowers used universally across Ethiopia for tapeworm (Taenia species). The preparation: dried female flowers mixed with tej (honey wine) and drunk fasting. Ethiopia has historically had among the highest rates of Taenia tapeworm infection globally, and kosso was the standard treatment across virtually all Ethiopian communities for centuries. European physicians who encountered Ethiopian medicine in the 19th century introduced kosso to Western pharmacy — it appeared in the London Pharmacopoeia (1867) and was used in Europe until anthelmintic drugs replaced it in the 1950s.
corpus_links.preparation: Dried female flowers mixed with tej (honey wine); drunk fasting in large doses
corpus_links.condition: Tapeworm (Taenia saginata and T. solium) — the primary traditional anthelmintic across the Ethiopian highlands

corpus_links.label: EA.Eucalyptus
corpus_links.title: Nech Bahir Zaf — the adopted universal medicine
corpus_links.original: [Amharic] nech bahir zaf — ye mefeseria tera
corpus_links.translation: Nech bahir zaf (Eucalyptus globulus) — introduced from Australia in the 19th century but rapidly adopted across Ethiopia as a universal respiratory medicine. Cobo's documentation of the Australian aboriginal use of eucalyptus (in the archive's Australian corpus) connects here: an Australian plant adopted in Ethiopia within two generations of introduction, both traditions independently identifying the same respiratory application. The cineole content explains the consistent cross-cultural identification of eucalyptus for respiratory conditions.
corpus_links.preparation: Leaves decocted and inhaled as steam; leaves placed in hot water for inhalation; oil applied topically
corpus_links.condition: Respiratory infections, sinusitis, cough, bronchitis, malaria (fumigation)

corpus_links.label: SA.DevilsClaw
corpus_links.title: Devil's Claw — the arthritis medicine of the Kalahari
corpus_links.original: [San and Khoi oral tradition — documented by Zorn et al. and Van Wyk]
corpus_links.translation: Devil's Claw (Harpagophytum procumbens) — secondary storage roots used across the Kalahari for arthritis, back pain, fever, and digestive complaints. The San and Khoi populations of the Kalahari documented devil's claw specifically for joint pain — an application now one of the most extensively clinically validated in all of African plant medicine. European interest began in the 1950s when G.H. Mehnert introduced it to Germany, where it became one of the most prescribed herbal medicines for osteoarthritis. Now EMA well-established use approved for symptomatic relief of joint and back pain.
corpus_links.preparation: Dried secondary tuber decoction; standardised extract 50–100mg harpagoside daily
corpus_links.condition: Osteoarthritis, back pain, fever, digestive complaints — EMA approved

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXIX
On Cassia Fistula

Besides the cassia fistula [caña fistola] that, brought from the East Indies, has been planted and grows abundantly in many parts of these West Indies—being the variety dispensed in apothecaries [boticas]—there is found in certain provinces another wild kind, native to the land, which appears to be of the same lineage as that of India, though distinct in species. The tree that produces this wild cassia fistula is much larger than that of the other variety. The leaf of the one and the other is the same; however, the pods of this wild kind, although they are the same color and shape as those of the Indian cassia fistula, are much longer, thicker, and hollow on the inside, lacking the pulp [pulpa] that the good cassia fistula possesses. corpus_links.title: Inca Policy of Resettlement: The Mitimae System
corpus_links.original:
CAPITULO XXIII

Cómo disponían los Incas las tierras que de nuevo adquirían, plantando en ellos indios extraños, que llamaban mitimaes, y las diferencias que había dellos

Todo el imperio de los Incas, aunque tan extendido y compuesto de tantas y tan diversas naciones, era una sola república, regida por unas mismas leyes, fueros y costumbres, y observantes de una misma religión, ritos y ceremonias
corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXIII

How the Incas Organized Newly Acquired Lands by Settling Them with Foreign Indians Called Mitimaes, and the Distinctions Among Them

CHAPTER VIII
Which continues the same subject

There still remains to be said concerning the customs and vices that the Indians exhibit contrary to the virtue of justice, which this chapter will treat. The caciques [chiefs] and lords of the villages were those who subjugated the people by no other right than that of force and power; and as their acquisition of rule was tyrannical and cruel, so too was their governance. For they did not aim at the welfare and benefit of their vassals, but rather at satisfying their own ambition and greed, reducing the people to so heavy a servitude that there was no difference between it and outright slavery. If the wound becomes infected [foul], chew strailwort [identity uncertain] and yarrow upon it. A wound salve: take yarrow and leechwort [identity uncertain], and boil in butter.

celtic_norse.original: [German folk medicine — Rosskastanie für schwere Beine]
celtic_norse.translation: Horse chestnut — for heavy legs. European folk medicine precisely documents horse chestnut for venous insufficiency — the specifically venous application stands out from most plant medicines.
celtic_norse.preparation: Standardised extract 50mg aescin twice daily

modern_research.summary: Aescin: venotonic and anti-oedema activity — reduces capillary permeability. Cochrane 2012: comparable to compression stockings for venous insufficiency. WHO Full Monograph Vol 2. EMA well-established use.
modern_research.significance: Best-evidenced plant medicine for venous insufficiency — Cochrane: comparable to compression stockings. Traditional European documentation for leg conditions precisely validated by aescin's venotonic mechanism.

plants.evidence_authority: WHO Full Monograph Vol 2; EMA well-established use; Cochrane 2012 comparable to compression stockings.

corpus_links.translation:
CHAPTER XXXVII

On the salmonados [salmon-trout], guavinas, dihachu, vermejuelos [small red fish], barbels, bacallao [cod], corvinas, angel-fish, and cuttlefish

These nine species of fish are found in this South Sea, although they are not as common as others. The bacallao [cod] is smaller than that of Spain, for none is found larger than a third of a vara [approximately 28 cm], and it is rarely caught. The peje-ángelo [angel-fish] has a very tough and rough skin, which carpenters and sculptors use for scraping wood. The cuttlefish here does not have the shell [cuttlebone] that the Spanish one has; it is half a braza [approximately 84 cm] in length.

corpus_links.translation: 1. For a horse's leprosy [scabrous or mange-like skin condition], take harewort, pound it well, then mix with fresh butter, boil thoroughly in butter, apply it to the horse as hot as possible, smear every day, and always keep the salve on. If the leprosy be severe [mickle = great], take urine, heat it with hot stones, wash the horse with the urine while it is hot; when it is dry, smear with the salve, and also apply remedies [leechdoms] internally. Again, take brine [runnings of salt], heat it, wash the horse with that, and when it is dry, smear with fish grease. If a horse be galled [has a sore or abrasion], take stichwort, and goutweed, and maythe [mayweed/chamomile], pound well, add butter, wring the mixture through a cloth, add white salt, shake thoroughly, and treat the gall with it.

ayurveda.translation: Ashwagandha gives strength, is a rasayana, removes fatigue. Premier rasayana plant — for emaciation, debility, weakness in old age. Preparation: root powder in warm milk with ghee and honey at bedtime.
ayurveda.preparation: Root powder in warm milk with ghee and honey; standardised extract 300-600mg
ayurveda.condition: Fatigue, stress, debility, weakness, sexual dysfunction, aging

modern_research.summary: Withanolides: documented cortisol reduction (adaptogen), NF-κB inhibition (anti-inflammatory), neuroprotective. Multiple RCTs: significant cortisol reduction, anxiety relief, strength improvement. Withaferin A: documented anti-cancer activity.
modern_research.significance: Charaka Samhita premier rasayana — 2,000 years of Ayurvedic documentation validated by multiple RCTs showing cortisol reduction comparable to pharmaceutical anxiolytics. Withanolide anti-cancer research among most active areas of current Ayurvedic pharmacology.

plants.evidence_authority: EMA assessment completed; multiple systematic reviews positive; Withaferin A in active cancer research.
plants.priority_reason: 2 traditions · Multiple RCTs for stress and fatigue · Cortisol reduction validated · Withaferin A active cancer research · 2,000 years documented use

corpus_links.title: Ashwagandha Rasayana — the premier rejuvenation plant
corpus_links.original: अश्वगन्धा बलकरी वृष्या रसायनी। श्रमहारिणी।
corpus_links.translation: Ashwagandha gives strength, is aphrodisiac, is a rasayana, and removes fatigue. The Charaka Samhita establishes ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) as the premier rasayana plant — superior to others for building strength, endurance, and sexual vitality. Specifically recommended for emaciation, general debility, weakness in old age, and for those exhausted by physical labor. The preparation: ashwagandha root powder in milk with ghee and honey.
corpus_links.preparation: Root powder in warm milk with ghee and honey; taken at bedtime
corpus_links.condition: Debility, fatigue, emaciation, weakness, sexual dysfunction, aging

corpus_links.label: CS.Chik.8
corpus_links.title: Rajayakshma Chikitsa — tuberculosis and wasting diseases
corpus_links.original: अश्वगन्धा बलादीनां रसायनानि राजयक्ष्मणि। पिप्पली क्षयकासघ्नी।
corpus_links.translation: Ashwagandha and bala and other rasayanas [are used] in tuberculosis/wasting disease. Long pepper destroys wasting cough. Rajayakshma — the 'King of Diseases' — corresponds primarily to tuberculosis and other wasting conditions. The treatment strategy is remarkable: Charaka prescribes nutritive rasayana plants (ashwagandha, bala, shatavari) to rebuild the patient while using antimicrobial plants (long pepper, giloy) to fight the infection. This dual strategy — nutritive support + antimicrobial — anticipates modern TB treatment principles.
corpus_links.preparation: Ashwagandha in milk; Chyavanaprasha (multi-herb amalaki-based preparation)
corpus_links.condition: Tuberculosis, wasting diseases, chronic cough, emaciation

corpus_links.label: CS.Chik.1.1
corpus_links.title: Rasayana — rejuvenation therapy and life extension
corpus_links.original: लभते ह्यायुर्मेधां बलं आरोग्यं सुखं च। रसायनं प्रयोक्तव्यं...
corpus_links.translation: One obtains longevity, memory, strength, freedom from disease, and happiness [through rasayana]. Rasayana therapy should be administered... Rasayana (literally 'path of rasa/essence') is Ayurveda's systematic anti-aging and rejuvenation system — the most sophisticated traditional longevity medicine in any world tradition. The primary rasayana plants include: Ashwagandha, Shatavari, Brahmi, Guduchi, and the Triphala combination. All are now extensively studied for adaptogenic and anti-aging properties.

southern_african.source_text: San and Khoikhoi oral tradition — Van Wyk et al. documentation
southern_african.original: [!Kung San oral documentation — secondary tuber for joint pain]
southern_african.translation: Secondary storage roots used across the Kalahari for arthritis, back pain, fever. The San documentation specifically for joint pain is one of the most precisely validated applications in African plant medicine.
southern_african.preparation: Dried secondary tuber decoction; standardised extract 50–100mg harpagoside daily

modern_research.summary: Harpagoside: COX-2 and iNOS inhibition — validated anti-inflammatory. Multiple systematic reviews and Cochrane-included RCTs positive for back pain and osteoarthritis. WHO Full Monograph Vol 3. EMA well-established use.
modern_research.significance: Best-evidenced plant from African traditional medicine — Cochrane systematic review evidence for back pain comparable to pharmaceutical treatment. Transition from San traditional knowledge to WHO medicine documents the complete traditional-to-clinical pathway.

plants.evidence_authority: WHO Full Monograph Vol 3; EMA well-established use for joint and back pain; Cochrane-included systematic reviews positive.

corpus_links.label: SA.DevilsClaw
corpus_links.title: Devil's Claw — the arthritis medicine of the Kalahari
corpus_links.original: [San and Khoi oral tradition — documented by Zorn et al. and Van Wyk]
corpus_links.translation: Devil's Claw (Harpagophytum procumbens) — secondary storage roots used across the Kalahari for arthritis, back pain, fever, and digestive complaints. The San and Khoi populations of the Kalahari documented devil's claw specifically for joint pain — an application now one of the most extensively clinically validated in all of African plant medicine. European interest began in the 1950s when G.H. Mehnert introduced it to Germany, where it became one of the most prescribed herbal medicines for osteoarthritis. Now EMA well-established use approved for symptomatic relief of joint and back pain.
corpus_links.preparation: Dried secondary tuber decoction; standardised extract 50–100mg harpagoside daily
corpus_links.condition: Osteoarthritis, back pain, fever, digestive complaints — EMA approved

southern_african.source_text: Zulu oral tradition; Kolodziej et al. documentation
southern_african.original: [Zulu — ukuphula: to break through the mucus]
southern_african.translation: Umckaloabo: 'heavy cough with thick phlegm' in Zulu. Used for severe respiratory conditions. Came to European attention in 1897 when Charles Stevens was reportedly cured of tuberculosis. Now standardised as EPs 7630 (Umcka).

modern_research.summary: EPs 7630: the strongest clinical evidence of any plant for acute respiratory infections. Multiple Cochrane-reviewed RCTs consistently positive. Documented antimicrobial against respiratory pathogens, immunomodulatory, and mucosal protective activity.
modern_research.significance: Most clinically validated product from African traditional medicine — multiple Cochrane-reviewed RCTs for acute bronchitis. Complete traditional-to-clinical pathway documented within living memory of Zulu community.

plants.evidence_authority: Multiple Cochrane reviews positive for acute bronchitis; EMA traditional use; EPs 7630 clinically validated.

corpus_links.label: SA.Umckaloabo
corpus_links.title: Umckaloabo (Pelargonium) — the tuberculosis medicine
corpus_links.original: [Zulu oral tradition — documented from 1897 Charles Stevens account]
corpus_links.translation: Umckaloabo (Pelargonium sidoides) — Zulu name meaning 'heavy cough with thick phlegm.' Used by Zulu healers for severe respiratory conditions including tuberculosis. The plant came to European attention in 1897 when an Englishman named Charles Stevens was reportedly cured of tuberculosis in South Africa using umckaloabo, subsequently commercialising it as 'Stevens' Consumption Cure.' Modern clinical research has confirmed significant efficacy for acute bronchitis — the standardised extract EPs 7630 (Umcka) has the strongest clinical evidence base of any plant for acute respiratory infections. Multiple Cochrane reviews positive.
corpus_links.preparation: Root decoction; standardised extract EPs 7630 (commercial Umcka preparation)
corpus_links.condition: Acute bronchitis, respiratory infections, tuberculosis (traditional), sinusitis

east_african.source_text: Ethiopian traditional documentation — Dagne et al. surveys
east_african.translation: Moringa (shiferaw) — 'God's medicine' in Ethiopian practice. Used for malnutrition, wound healing, digestive conditions, and as a galactagogue. WHO recognizes moringa as critical for malnutrition in food-insecure regions.
east_african.preparation: Fresh leaves eaten; dried leaf powder in food; leaf paste for wounds
east_african.condition: Malnutrition, wound healing, digestive conditions, galactagogue

modern_research.summary: Moringa leaves: highest documented nutrient density of most plant foods. Moringin (isothiocyanate): anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer activity. Multiple clinical trials for malnutrition, blood glucose reduction, and galactagogue effect.
modern_research.significance: Three traditions across three continents for malnutrition and wound healing. Nutritional and pharmacological properties inseparable. WHO nutrition recognition. Critical for global malnutrition.

plants.evidence_authority: WHO nutrition recommendations; multiple clinical trials for malnutrition and galactagogue; diabetes blood glucose studies.
plants.priority_reason: 3 traditions across 3 continents · WHO nutrition recognition · Isothiocyanate anti-cancer research · Galactagogue RCT · Critical for global malnutrition

corpus_links.label: EA.Moringa
corpus_links.title: Shiferaw (Moringa) — the miracle tree
corpus_links.original: [Amharic] shiferaw — ye egziabeher tera (God's medicine)
corpus_links.translation: Moringa oleifera (shiferaw) — called 'God's medicine' in Ethiopian traditional practice. Used across East Africa for: malnutrition (leaves contain exceptionally high protein, vitamin C, iron, and calcium), wound healing, digestive conditions, and as a galactagogue (promotes lactation). Ethiopian traditional healers documented the leaves as a complete nutritional medicine — a use that has been validated by modern research showing Moringa leaves have among the highest nutrient density of any plant food. The drum stick tree is now WHO-recognized as critical for addressing malnutrition in food-insecure regions.
corpus_links.preparation: Fresh leaves eaten; dried leaf powder added to food; leaf paste applied to wounds; root bark for digestive conditions
corpus_links.condition: Malnutrition, wound healing, digestive conditions, galactagogue, hypertension
